name: Lee Ufan
bio: A founding member of the Japanese [Mono-ha](/gene/mono-ha) movement, Lee Ufan arranges his installations and sculptures to emphasize the equal relationship between his artwork, the viewer, and the exhibition space. He often juxtaposes natural and industrial materials in site-specific installations; throughout various pieces, steel reeds appear to sprout from a patch of sand, heavy stones perch on cushions, and boulders bookend a towering metal arc. Subdued hues are another signature element of Lee’s work. Throughout his paintings, for example, the artist applies muted colors against light, plain backgrounds. His brushstrokes fade as they end, evoking East Asian calligraphy. Lee has exhibited in New York, London, Seoul, Tokyo, Versailles, and Washington, D.C., among other cities. In 2000, he won the UNESCO Prize at the Shanghai Biennale, and the following year, he was awarded the Praemium Imperiale by the Japan Art Association. His work belongs in prominent collections in Europe, North America, Australia, Asia, and South America, and has sold for seven figures at auction.

name: Qwaya
bio: Under the name of Qwaya that means a contemplation in the night and silence. After he graduated from Sangmyung University with his Fashion and design degree, and then in a short span of time, he has received good responses with unique world of his own while having engaged in various exhibitions of solo shows and curatorial exhibitions. His works serve as an evocation that leads us to a hidden gem of our daily lives with his innermost records and intuitive intense colors. And he has been presenting his artistic outcomes while having collaborative projects with conglomerates and doing numbers of album art works. Qwaya who has been showing a wide variety of spectrum of his activity straddling a borderline between commercial and fine art has been coming to the fore being considered as one of the most emerging artists in the Korean art scene, and those results have been naturally coming down to large attention and popularity by the public.

name: Sori Choi
bio: Choi Sori’s artistic behavior of synesthesia, which transcends traditional genres and media, can be found in the Korean people’s spiritual sense of beauty. Spirituality does not occur when rational reason is in charge of our brains, but when we feel spirits in our body, which bring out the states of Samadhi, intense drive, and trance. Whoever reaches this spiritual state will become mentally elated and physically excited. Since Korea’s Sanggo era, our ancestors have recognized this spiritual state as the only channel to interact with Plotinus’ ‘the One’, Mother Nature, the skies, space, and the universe......Choi Sori feels with his whole body those wavy waves created by the sounds from his beating as they push out the density of air. It’s the pattern from the waves that only he can see through the five senses. Once such sound waves had already left the epicenter and disappeared into distant space, the heart’s core and feelings of resentment (Han) will become purified. As a first step, realizing that emptiness also remains, the artist begins to capture on canvases the traces left behind when the sound waves sweep through. The artist himself feels in his state of resonance, in other words, the Pathos and spiritual states, the feelings Samadhi and intense drive: madness and intoxication, fear, passion and ecstasy, and even the emotions of extreme sorrow... Although these are expressed visually and not through sound, we can experience a sort of hallucination that allows us to hear and feel the same waves that resonate from sounds. This is possible because of the subtleties of our human body called synesthesia. The desire to show the sound he wanted was realized through the beauty of expressing objects and things artistically in three dimensions within a flat surface/canvas, adding another [figurative] annual tree growth ring to his life.

name: Cha Young Seok
bio:
Cha Young-Seok’s serial practice, which cannot be reduced to straightforward object drawing or to its accompanying virtuoso draftsmanship, extends well beyond formalist excellence. While working with a range of subject matter, Cha repeatedly engages in formal experimentation that is closely tied to his own subjectivity. This may explain why his work can initially appear incidental or coincidental, yet upon closer examination reveals a dense accumulation shaped by deliberate intent—each work operating as part of a sequence formed through successive strategic decisions.

Through this meticulous and sustained process of drawing, one is left to consider whether the artist himself is gradually changing, shaped by the very repetition that defines his practice. In this sense, An Elegant Endeavor—the title of his recent exhibition and of each serial work presented, imbued with a sense of unease and strangeness—may ultimately refer not only to the exhibition and its works, but also to the act of drawing itself as Cha’s ongoing, self-reflexive endeavor.

name: Nam June Paik
bio: A major figure of the experimental [Fluxus](/gene/fluxus) movement, Nam June Paik is considered the f​​ather of [video art](/gene/film-slash-video)—his most famous sculptures feature real TV sets. He stacked them in imposing walls, arranged them amid leafy plants in darkened galleries, manipulated them to show distorted imagery, and mounted them into robot shapes. Paik’s practice—which combined music, performance, technology, and film—explored the possibilities of mass media and emerging technologies with impressive foresight. Coining the term “electronic superhighway” in the 1970s, Paik wrote of a near future in which new media technologies would connect populations through global networks; in a sense, he predicted the internet. Paik combined his interests in televisual imagery and wide-scale connectivity in his groundbreaking live performance broadcasts including *Good Morning, Mr. Orwell* (1989) and *Tiger is Alive* (2000). Paik has been the subject of retrospectives at [Tate Modern](/tate), the [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](/partner/san-francisco-museum-of-modern-art-sfmoma), the [Smithsonian American Art Museum](/partner/smithsonian-american-art-museum), the [Museum of Modern Art](/partner/the-museum-of-modern-art), and the Watari Museum of Contemporary Art, among other institutions. His work has sold for seven figures at auction and belongs to prestigious art collections worldwide.

name: Seongbin Gam
bio: His works are associated with the artist’s personal experience of sorrow and grief. The artist records the despair and pain that he suffered from after two tragic deaths of the loved ones. The narrative of sorrow from traumatic event encompasses not only personal experiences but also social circumstances as well. Witnessing others’ distress―death, war, etc.― triggers the artist’s memory and development of visual language.

name: MY Q
bio: My Q was born in Seoul, Korea. He is a multi-disciplinary artist, capable of songwriting, composing, arranging, mixing, cinematography, producing, and stage designing. He has been communicating with the public through music, and now he entered a new path of art creation with the exhibition at 2GIL29 GALLERY in 2021. As a musician who has been working on creating artistic inspiration for more than 20 years, he said, "Music and art fall into the same category of art", and truly devoted himself to painting that allowed him to face his inner side. He intensely built up his art world  through facing himself for more than 13 hours a day, and is indeed solid and attractive. He never went through a formal art course and his various attempts are so diversely colorful that it feels meaningless to place a limit. The artist’s unique painting technique ‘Dub da’ is a process of overlapping layers over and over again inspired from the process when creating music. First create rhythm with drums and bases and create melody with instruments like piano and guitar. The artist builds up diverse texture by painting and splashing colors with palette knives, brushes, paper, and hands. After this process the artist covers the whole canvas with a background color. He created the rhythm by pointing out note by note as a musician, now he spreads visual melodies on the canvas with unique patterns and symbols within the painting. He asks questions about the rapid change in the social environment after COVID, dreaming of a work with a theme that connects us together through containing everyone's concern who’s living in the contemporary era. Saying that it feels like it is not a limited issue in an individual life but a problem that everyone has to overcome together, he explores and expresses something that sparks in ordinary life. His paintings with raw brush marks are closest to pure creation that suggests numbers of struggles and success he encountered as an artist.

name: Hyunsik Kim
bio: Kim Hyun Sik imbues flat enamel planes with depth and texture, working in the realm between painting and sculpture. His body of work includes hyperrealistic images of the backs of women’s heads, [trompe l’oeil](/gene/trompe-loeil) waterfall landscapes, and vibrant, monochrome fields of color that put a modern spin on [traditional Korean](/gene/engaged-with-traditional-korean-art) and East Asian painting. Hyun Sik’s work questions the seen and unseen, suggesting ambiguous narratives. His use of resin draws viewers’ eyes to the surface and encourages them to look deeper and meditate on the image’s many layers and spaces in between, not unlike the Japanese notion of “ma” (*negative space*).

name: KIM DUCK YONG 김덕용
bio: Kim Duck-Yong (b. 1961) was born in Gwangju, Korea, and received his B.F.A. and M.F.A. from the Department of Painting at Seoul National University in Korea. By integrating both traditional and contemporary practices in his work of art, he, on one hand, follows the tradition of oriental paintings by using ancient wood as his canvas, which allows the viewer to sense the warmth of nature through minor details. On the other hand, through highlighting the importance of traditional materials and painting key iconographies that echo with his heritage, Kim primarily explores the contemporary mechanics of Korean society. In other words, Kim’s paintings reveal the change of time with its attribute of intergenerational transience that overarches old and new histories. With works placed in important institutional collections in South Korea such as the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul Museum of Art, Park Soo-Keun Museum, and Gyeonggi Museum of Art, Kim has been recognised as one of the established artists among the Korean art scene.

name: Kwon Hye Jo 권혜조
bio:
Kwon Hye Jo explores the space between observation and perception, transforming fleeting moments of everyday life into expansive painterly experiences. Rather than depicting specific places, her paintings emerge from impressions that linger after the moment has passed—fragments of landscape, shifting light, movement, and memory distilled into colour, rhythm, and gesture.

Working primarily in oil, Kwon constructs richly layered surfaces through intuitive brushwork and a highly refined sensitivity to colour. Her recent practice moves increasingly toward abstraction, where forms dissolve and reassemble, inviting viewers to complete the image through their own perception. Rather than describing a landscape, her paintings evoke the experience of seeing itself.

Kwon has presented six solo exhibitions and participated in more than 150 group exhibitions. Her work has been exhibited internationally at major art fairs including Art Central Hong Kong, Art Taipei, and Tokyo Gendai. Her paintings are held in public and corporate collections, including Hana Bank and Kangdong Sacred Heart Hospital.

Through an increasingly distinctive painterly language, Kwon continues to expand the possibilities of contemporary painting, creating works that resonate across cultural contexts while remaining deeply rooted in the poetics of everyday perception.

name: Kang Yehsine
bio: Kang Yehsine uses imaginative narrative as if it is a storytelling through drawing, sculpture, and painting. She focuses on human emotions that we face in our daily lives and uses a personification of rabbit as herself. By telling a story of her inner mind and experience through her symbolic images, she creates her own world on the canvas, and also on her bookshelf series. In particular, her major bookshelf series show various books and her favorite ones displayed. They show a new ideal of art piece, moving away from the traditional painting style. Her art pieces are recognized not only in Korea, but also internationally such as the Boghossian Foundation and Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. Kang Yehsine is an uprising Korean contemporary artist who is actively works in Hong Kong, Europe and etc.

name: Kyong Lee
bio:
Kyong Lee is a Korean abstract artist whose work reconciles physical and emotional realities through a multi-disciplined exploration of color, material, process and form. She lives and works in Seoul, Korea.

Lee is dedicated to precision in her processes. She meticulously plans her color choices and dedicates a fixed amount of time to the mixing of each color. To create her gradated color paintings, she first layers tape in strips across the surfaces. Each layer of paint is applied over a fixed time span and allowed to rest for another fixed amount of time. This is a process of building up, layering, accumulating. Some of her paintings feature text. For these works, Lee embosses the word she has selected for the piece into the surface first then applies a monochromatic hue that correlates to, and collaborates with, the chosen word. The color occupies the word and fills all of the space around it. For Lee, process is poetic, and essential to the meaning of the work.
In her work, Lee is responding to her emotional experiences within her physical surroundings. Color is her primary visual language. For her, color is not only self-referential. Color also relates to emotional states. It is a way of expressing feeling, of projecting thoughts, and of evoking the natural processes of life. 
Work by Lee Kyong has been exhibited extensively in solo and group exhibitions in Korea and Germany. Recent solo exhibitions include Color as Adjective II in Chonan, South Korea, and Feeling, Language and Color in Seoul.
Work by Lee is in multiple public and institutional collections, including that of the Seoul Museum of Art, the Youngeun Museum of Contemporary Art, and the National Museum of Contemporary Art, Art Bank, Seoul, Korea.

name: Soonik Kwon
bio:
Artist Soon-ik Kwon is growing in the international market by interpreting the unique colors of Korea in a modern way. 
Although it is based on Western materials, the material peculiarity of using sand or graphite with paints is realized with oriental colors and textures, showing a unique sensibility that only Korea can express. The experience of the artist, who also worked as a potter, is continuously revealed in the matiere that appears thickly on the surface of the painting, and in the repeated process of raising this matiere again, the artist delves deeply into herself and discovers the selflessness of the abyss. The continuous arrangement of circles and geometric shapes in the work are reminiscent of op-art represented by Cruise Dies, and also show the possibility of Korean abstraction. Through his repetitive works of painting and rubbing graphite, the purest works of light and color give the audience an opportunity to experience the world of selflessness led by artist Kwon Soon-ik.

name: Minsong Kim
bio: Min-song Kim's work in a dreamlike landscape like a deep night dream is unfamiliar and familiar. The artist captures the scenery of a desert or a jungle filled with exotic and mysterious plants under countless starlights as if pouring, in brilliant colors. The darkness surrounding all directions is not scary or scary, but rather warm. Memories and memories that are weak and faint in bright daylight and settled deep in the mind are surrounded by a faint light when darkness comes. It is these weak but subtly shining memories and memories that support life, and this is the art of the artist.

name: Yun Hee Lee
bio: Yun Hee Lee creates [figurative](/gene/figurative-sculpture) [surrealistic](/gene/contemporary-surrealistic) sculptures in [porcelain](/gene/porcelain). Her [mixed-media](/gene/porcelain) works—ranging from free-standing pieces to [wall-mounted](/gene/wall-sculpture-and-installation) [portraits](/gene/portrait)—have earned her international acclaim: Lee was selected as an emerging artist to watch at the Korean International Ceramic Biennale in 2013; four years later, Artsy named her [one of 20 artists shaping the future of ceramics](/article/artsy-editorial-20-artists-shaping-future-ceramics). Lee draws inspiration from a wide range of recognizable narratives, appropriating the written and visual languages of [traditional Korean folklore](/gene/engaged-with-traditional-korean-art), Dante’s *Divine Comedy*, and [Hieronymus Bosch](/artist/hieronymus-bosch), all of which she reinterprets using traditional Eastern [ceramic techniques](/gene/ceramic). Her works typically feature a recurrent teenaged [female protagonist](/gene/femininity). Often embellished with [glazed patterns](/gene/patterns) and [gold accents](/gene/gold), her sculptures harken to the elegance of traditional porcelain objects but are imbued with an underlying darkness.

name: Se-Yeol Oh
bio: The paintings by Oh Se-yeol consist of everyday objects such as human faces and bodies listed numbers , buttons , flowers , and ties . The aim is to "return to pure childhood”.  So when you first encounter his work , you often misunderstand that it is a child's painting full of innocence . But if you approach the canvas , you can feel a completely different heavy feeling . The " weight " of time is felt in the traces of paint that has been added countless times for any oil at all , using only oil . This is also the reason for the "crack " that naturally occurs to time . It's like the wrinkles on a person's face . His work has no same painting , no pretense . It resembles the memories of our childhood , when we all stayed in the playground all day and left our mark on the floor with branches .

name: Park Seo-Bo
bio: Park Seo-bo’s predominantly [monochrome](/gene/monochrome-painting) experiments with linear abstraction helped define [Dansaekhwa](/gene/dansaekhwa), an essential movement within Korean modernism. Park is perhaps best known for his “Ecriture” series, which exemplifies the artist’s focus on material and process; in order to create precise, cumulative canvases, he penciled marks into still-wet painted surfaces, then layered Korean hanji paper overtop. Park graduated from Seoul’s Hongik University in 1954, when South Korea was still reeling from military conflict with North Korea. He has exhibited widely over the years, in galleries from Seoul and Busan to Tokyo, Los Angeles, New York, and Beijing. His work belongs in the collections of the [Museum of Modern Art](/museum-of-modern-art), the [Art Institute of Chicago](/artic), the Museum of Contemporary Art in Tokyo, and the Seoul Museum of Art, among many other institutions. His precise, [minimalist](/gene/minimalism) practice filters Western notions of abstraction through the lenses of Korean [calligraphy](/gene/east-asian-calligraphy) and Buddhist and Taoist philosophy.

name: Sangyoon Yoon
bio: Yoon Sang-yoon is gaining fame by recording a soled-out at the Hong Kong Art Central in 2019 and winning the grand prize at the 2019 Namdo Cultural Foundation's National Young Painters Contest . He draws abstraction from landscape paintings , embodying dreamy backgrounds and symbolic images of human self . Yoon Sang-yoon , who uses both hands in the canvas , attempts to draw freely with instinct and sense that is not tamed with the left hand , unlike traditional paintings that he works with his right hand . Left-handed drawing , which features faceless characters just like the characters of a dream , gives the his experience and emotions a feeling of being expressed immediately . As for the unidentified ambiguous atmosphere unfolding in drawing , Yoon says it " connects the form that is found by chance when a line is drawn for the first time or something passes by , Invoking the illusion and madness suppressed by consciousness " .

name: Jieun Park (b. 1987)
bio: The artist Jieun Park majors in oriental painting in the university, and now she represents her memories in her travels using both oriental and occidental painting techniques. The reminiscences in her bold strokes are taking us to where we are happy.

name: Taejin Seong
bio: Educated as a printmaker, Taejin Seong channels his experience making woodblock prints into painted wood carvings that blend historic printmaking with contemporary comic-book art. He carves from a single piece of wood, emphasizing the mark of the artist’s hand on its surface. Inspired by the 1970s cartoon robot “Robot Taekwon V”, the central figure in Seong’s works is associated with and responds to a lost childhood and disillusionment with society, while the text carvings in the background are associated with the dissemination of the written word and the origins of printmaking. Together, Seong’s influences draw a millennia-old art into the 21st century and imbue a more contemporary style with historical significance.

name: Lee In Seob
bio:
Lee, In Seob is an artist whose decades-long career is rooted in the natural world. His studio is surrounded by trees and wooded valleys, which serve as the main source of inspiration for his paintings. Exploring the themes of returning and reawakening, Lee’s “From Nature” series suggests natural lifecycles and the coexistence of contrasts.

*Submitted by [Suppoment Gallery](/partner/suppoment-gallery)*

name: Suh Yongsun
bio:
Suh Yongsun, also Yong Sun Suh or Seo Young-Sun (Korean: 서용선; born 1951 in Seoul, South Korea), is a Korean painter and sculptor.
In his art he mainly portrays human existence.
Suh lives and has his main studio in Gyeonggido near Seoul.
Suh Yongsun studied Fine Arts at Seoul National University from 1975 to 1982 and worked as a professor at the College of Fine Arts at this University from 1986 to 2008.
After withdrawing from his long-time professorship, he was elected Korea's Artist of the Year for 2009 and honored with a solo show at the National Museum of Contemporary Art, South Korea.
He was invited to residency programs in Vermont in the United States of America in 1995 and to the Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, both in 2006 and in 2010.
He also worked at the University of Paris in 2003.
In 2001 he was a visiting professor in Hamburg, Germany

name: Huh Dal Jae
bio:
HUH “Jickhun” Dal-Jae inherited the tradition of Korean painting from his grandfather, HUH Baek-Ryun. He began his independent career at the age of eighteen after winning the Korea Art Exhibition in 1970. The world he seeks to reveal through his paintings is not one of finite quantities that can be counted or measured. Instead, he continues the spirit of Oriental painting, which pursues immeasurable value, depth, and expansiveness within a limited space and moment in time.

The ultimate culmination of his practice may be an unpainted, invisible image. The plum blossoms, grapes, and peonies he depicts do not remain as representations of real forms; rather, their physical shapes dissolve, leaving behind their essence and spirit. The cyclical rhythm of Eastern aesthetics—“Jung Jung Dong · Dong Jung Jung” (movement within tranquility, tranquility within movement)—and the countless petals poised to scatter evoke the realm of Muryangsu, an infinite world.

(LEE Gun-Soo, “Hymn of Countless Things,” Plum Exhibition, Eunpyeong History Museum, 2019)

name: Kwon Kisoo
bio: Kwon Kisoo is one of the established Korean contemporary artists. He builds his own world through reinterpreting the traditional ideas into modernism. The artist’s works are recognized not only in Korea but also internationally well known. He also had been nominated to collaborate with GOOGLE for iGoogle Artist Campaign New York in 2008 featured in iGoogle homepage with other key artists. Moreover, he also had been selected as one of the authoritative scholarships foundation in United States called Fulbright Scholar in Residence in 2015. Kwon Kisoo’s art pieces have been collected at the major museums around the world such as at the Long Museum in Shanghai, Asian Art Museum in San Francisco and etc. His works had been exhibited at the 24th Venice Biennale through the special exhibition, Museum of Contemporary Art(MOCA) in Shanghai, Mori Art Museum in Japan and Saatchi Gallery in London.

name: Lee Bae
bio: For much of his career, Korean modernist Lee Bae worked almost exclusively with charcoal. Focusing on this single material, he created monochromatic linear drawings, canvases that featured embedded charcoal shards, and large-scale sculptures derived from carbonized tree trunks. Recently, Lee has embraced resin, ink, and acrylics as expanded avenues of materiality. Texture and gesture remain major aesthetic concerns. Lee received his MFA from the Hongik University Graduate School of Art in Seoul. He has exhibited in New York, Tokyo, Paris, Seoul, Beijing, Los Angeles, and beyond. His work belongs to the collections of the Seoul Museum of Art, the Fondation Colas, the Fondation Carmignac, the [Musée Guimet](/guimet), and the Busan Museum of Art.

name: LEE JUNG EUN 이정은
bio:
LEE Jung-Eun is a Korean artist who works in chaekgado (paintings of scholar’s accoutrements), a genre that flourished during the Joseon Dynasty. Even in an era when paper books and e-books coexist—and when the very presence of books is increasingly questioned—Lee’s paintings of books remain deeply compelling.

She produces traditional Oriental paintings using classical techniques, depicting flowers and everyday objects with quiet precision. Her work is not decorative; rather, it calmly observes and faithfully records the world as it appears. Even the smallest, seemingly insignificant things are rendered as something special through her affectionate gaze.

The painted objects evoke a gentle sense of life, as if they might gather together and softly chatter, each carrying its own story.

name: Ahn Doo Jin
bio:
Mathematical enquiry, art theory and spectacular colour palettes give rise to imagined landscapes and busy installations in Ahn Doo-Jin’s unique practice. As the artist explains, “my work began with questioning what a visual image consists of, developed into creating the notion of imaquark, applying it to a variety of media and opening up its new possibilities.”

Doo-Jin studied a BFA and MFA at Hongik University, Seoul; his artwork draws on diverse influences, from the painting techniques and emotions of Romanticism through to particle physics and the writings of art theorist and philosopher, Arthur C. Danto. After a decade of image research, Doo-Jin created the concept of imaquark, made up of “image” and “quark,” the fundamental constituent of matter. Imaquark is the minimum unit not only of form and material but also meaning, created, patterned and visually expressed through painstaking observation and automatism or unconscious drawing. The result: dramatic, energy-charged creations across a range of media.

Doo-Jin’s work has been shown in Korea, USA and China, and in 2012 was selected for Korean Eye, an extensive survey of contemporary Korean art at the Saatchi Gallery, London. It also features in the Oliver Stone Collection, Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art and the Seoul Museum of Art, among others.

name: Winter Gyeoul Kim
bio: Winter Gyeoul Kim works with abstract painting and drawing to trace sensations and memories that drift beyond the limits of language. Drawing from her experience of moving across diverse cultural and linguistic contexts, she captures fleeting moments through layered strokes, dots, planes, and colors. Rather than serving as tools for representation, these delicately composed visual elements interact to create a resonant emotional space.

name: Yeji Seo
bio:
We spend more than half of our day with other people, and our lives change depending on who the other person is.
In a modern society where there is little time for ourselves, what we feel we need is the relaxation in a comfortable space of our own without any discomfort.
The artist's space in the painting best expresses his identity. The objects in the space clearly show who you are, what you are interested in, what kind of life you are living, and who you are. In addition, familiar objects there give a feeling of stability and tranquility, making it a space to comfort oneself who is tired of the fake life of modern society.
Therefore, 'my own space' is a space where you can focus only on yourself, recover emotionally, and find yourself who has been lost by others.

name: SooYoung Chung
bio:
Chung Sooyoung has participated in a number of group and individual exhibitions internationally and is currently living and active in the UK. Chung’s work is often appreciated as “still life paintings”. However, the artist does not define her work merely to be in genre of still life painting. She intends to
comprehend still life objects and capture the space with active configuration. The displayed space goes beyond simply depicting arranged objects as is. , but comes together in a different sense. The work implies a unique interpretation of the relationship among objects by the artist. Chung Sooyoung majored in paintings in the undergraduate and graduate school at Ewha University then continued her studies at Royal College of Art.

name: SEUNG-YOON CHOI 최승윤
bio: Seung Yoon Choi’s definitive brush touch leaves blue strokes on canvas that move organically, and encounter and overlap themselves to create dynamic images. He expresses the fundamentals of the invisible world with the sensation from color and the movement from the brush strokes. Many of his works are mainly solid blue. It is the color of the essence and ambilaterality for him, which best suits the concept of paradox and balance that he wants to express. It is the primary color of earth when light first encounters the sky and water, and contains both sides of hope and despair, and fervent and cold. With his custom made tools, he dashes off on a canvas laid flat on the floor, and captures both the painterly movement and the moment of abeyance. His vision of the world’s essence is comprised of oxymoron. He often thinks of such unnoticeable things around us, and reads the world of coexistence and balance between the opposites; the universe and the lives, Yin and Yang, beginnings and ends, and so on. His lines and spaces are precisely controlled as if they move, collide, harmonize and ultimately come to life on canvas.

name: YANG Hyun Jun
bio:
Born, February 1980

There is a little girl in my work.

 The girl is having a good time enjoying true freedom.

 I dream of my mother like that.

 Then I draw her.

Reminding myself that my mother, who is my friend and someone who protected the family, was a girl before becoming a mother.

The heartbreaking gratitude for mothers that have not been able to have certain experiences is not just my story, but all mothers around the world.

The direction of my work is always directed to my mother in a series of life connected with the past, present, and future.

The childhood in my work has no affection or memories of my father, so it is filled with longing and adoration for my mother.

You cannot stop the flow of time.

I feel that in the flow of time I started out as a child and it continues to form who I am today.

name: Lee Sejun
bio:
The canvas surface of Lee Sejun (born in 1984) combines abstractions and figurative form, high saturation/brightness, and low saturation/brightness, as well as various surreal objects and landscapes, along with the viewers' unique responses. In other words, he focuses on the diverse phenomena that emerge on the surface of paintings to capture moments where radically different forms and sensations collide. Additionally, he creates "organic paintings" that connect the canvases structurally to form vast scenes. This paradoxically challenges the viewers' simultaneous perception of images, contradicting his impossible desire to depict everything in the world.   Lee Sejun describes the area of accidental brushstrokes, colors, specific objects, and even margins, respectively. This approach goes beyond the traditional painting format that distinguishes the main subjects from the surrounding background and instead fills the entire canvas evenly. It emphasizes the inherent nature of the "flatness" in painting.

Lee Sejun is currently in the Ph.D. program after graduating from Hongik University's Department of Painting.It has had a number of individual exhibitions, including Space Willing N Dealing and HwangGeumHyang in 2023, KSD Gallery in 2020, and Cake Gallery in 2016. He participated in various exhibitions such as Cian Art Museum, Shinhan Gallery, Zaha Museum in 2021, Euljiro OF, Osan Museum of Art in 2020, Danwon Art Museum, Beijing Commune in 2019, Art Space Boan in 2016, Hite Collection, and Seoul Museum of Art. Lee has been selected and exhibited at the Songeun Art Awards in 2023. Participating residences include Goyang Art Creation Space, Nanji Residency, Bukguart Studio, and Yangju Residency, and won the Gasong Art Award and the New York Art Show Grand Prize.

name: Seontae Hwang
bio: Seontae Hwang is known for his lightbox works showcasing serene domestic scenes, created by sandblasted glass and LED lighting. His monochromatic interiors—without the presence of human figures—are contrasted with rich green outdoor landscapes, visible through sun-drenched windows. This juxtaposition invites viewers to contemplate the narratives behind these peaceful views. Educated at Kyunghee University in South Korea and Burg Giebichenstein University of Art and Design Halle in Germany, Hwang has shown his work across South Korea, the U.S., the U.K., and Europe. In 2023, he had a solo show with [Friedrichs Pontone](https://www.artsy.net/partner/pontone-gallery) in New York.

name: MeeYoung Kim
bio:
Meeyoung Kim is an accomplished artist with a diverse academic background in the field of painting. She earned her BFA and MFA degrees in Korean Painting from Ewha Womans University in Seoul, later pursuing Painting at the Royal College of Art in London.

Her academic journey has left a profound imprint on her artistic style, with Asian philosophy, techniques, and colors intricately woven into her work, particularly in her use of oil paints. Meeyoung's artistry has garnered recognition, and her pieces can be found in prestigious collections, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) Art Bank in Gwacheon, Korea, as well as The Work Project Global in Singapore.

When asked about her artistic journey, Meeyoung Kim reflects on her early interest in painting, tracing it back to her time at an art middle school and high school. Her love for drawing and painting naturally led her to art college. Initially drawn to Korean painting, she eventually ventured abroad to London for her graduate studies, where she embraced the challenges of working with oil paints and various materials.

Kim draws inspiration from a wide spectrum of experiences and atmospheres, with no specific subject matter dominating her work. Instead, her paintings are a reflection of the impressions she gathers from her surroundings, whether it's the play of sunlight, enticing aromas, zesty flavors, evocative music, or other sensory stimuli.

In her artistic practice, Meeyoung Kim doesn't just create images; she passionately engages in the act of "painting" itself, using her chosen medium to breathe life into her abstract visions. Her work is a testament to her ongoing exploration of the world through the lens of art, where every stroke of the brush reveals a new facet of her creative journey. Meeyoung's artistic heroes, including Wassily Kandinsky, William de Kooning, Cecily Brown, Alex Katz, and Robert Ryman, continue to inspire her in this remarkable artistic odyssey.

name: Sangmin Lee
bio:
Sang-Min Lee was born in 1966 in Seoul, Korea. He studied in department of Arts Plastiques, Strasbourg Marc Bloch National University, France (MFA) and in department of Objet, Ecole Supérieure des Arts Déoratifs de Strasbourg, France (BFA. MFA). He had  solo exhibition 23 times since 1996 and his works has been exhibited at the National Gyeonggi Museum of Contemporary Art, South Korea and more. He is professor of Chungang University in department of Sculpture, Seoul, Korea and lives and works in Seoul, Korea. He is winner of Contemporain Art Japan, Bourguil, France and The International Snow Sculpture Competition in Quebec, Canada, also he got Eurocreation Prize at the Pepiniere des Artistes, France.
SangMin Lee experiments have involved blurring the boundaries between two dimensional and three dimensional objects using glass as a medium. He defines the “inner side of the universe” as the object of his artistic exploration. One’s interest in the inner side of all things is, after all, a reflection of our concern with universal objects as opposed to specific things. Lee’s reflection on the inner side of the universe is represented through an encounter with the properties of water as the source of everything employing the unique medium of glass. He hopes the image of his glass sculpture overlap with that of water and also intends the action of light as a physical factor enables us to perceive the presence of things.

name: Choi Young Wook
bio:
Choi Young wook graduated from Hongik University, college of fine art in 1991 and graduated from the same university's Graduate School of Art in 2000
The title for Young Wook Choi’s works, which is identical for all of his artworks, is ‘Karma’. The ‘Karma’ series is inspired by the artist’s perspective of viewing the moon jar as an object which possesses a lot of likeliness to our lives and memoirs. The lines on the surface of the porcelain represent the numerous paths we choose in our lives, as well as the various relationships and accounts we encounter, withdraw from, and yet reunite with. The process of adding layers, upon layers of paint to complete his moon jar resembles the way the experiences mentioned above pile up to shape our lives. Furthermore, the perpetual and repetitious method which requires a generous amount of time for the work’s completion suggests that it is an act of self-reflection. As such, Young Wook Choi’s moon jar, which contains multiple messages and significations, stands still yet firmly in its place, allowing us to look back at our own paths. 
Young Wook Choi has had over 30 solo exhibitions including those which took place in Soul Art Space (2016), Gallery A-Cube (Japan, 2013), Art Issue Projects (Taiwan, 2012), Sun Contemporary (2012), Jun Gallery (2011), ArtGate Gallery (New York, 2009), ONO Gallery (Japan, 2006), and Ilwoo Space(2018).

name: Kim Kang Yong
bio: Kim Kang Yong is a leading South Korean contemporary artist known for his distinctive hyperrealistic paintings of bricks, which explore philosophical questions about reality, perception, and representation. Born in Jeong-Eup in 1950, he received both his BFA and MFA from Hongik University in Seoul. Since the 1980s, Kim has developed a unique visual language in which ordinary bricks become powerful metaphors for modern life, influenced in part by the concept of simulacra discussed by philosopher Jean Baudrillard. Using materials such as sand, loess, and kaolin, he creates textured surfaces that combine meticulous realism with tactile experimentation, redefining Hyperrealism through a distinctly Korean perspective. Over a career spanning more than five decades, Kim has gained international recognition, highlighted by major exhibitions including *KIM Kang Yong: Hyper Realistic Bricks* at Sungkok Art Museum in 2023, which traced the evolution of his work from early explorations of alienation to his later monochrome and multi-colored brick compositions.

name: Youngji Lee
bio:
Lee Young-ji's artistry is a harmonious blend of wit and candid expression, making the abstract concept of love approachable and familiar to her audience. Her paintings convey a positive, warm message of love, intertwined with the comfort found in nature-friendly spaces, creating a sense of intimacy and warmth. In her work, Lee symbolically represents self-identity through the image of a tree, a motif that evolves from a sprouting seed to a sturdy, fully-grown tree, mirroring the growth and development of human life.

Her portrayal of trees is not just about their physical presence but also represents the journey of life, from humble beginnings to a state of strength and abundance. The birds that visit these trees in her paintings symbolize the relationships and connections formed throughout life. Through these interactions between the self and the external world, her art sings of love and whispers tales of joy, sorrow, and the range of human emotions. Lee's work invites viewers to reflect on their life's journey and the nature of human connections.

name: Jinu Nam
bio:
Heroes, villains and giant-sized monsters roam the colourful universe created by Jinu Nam, an emerging artist from South Korea whose creations have already appeared in museum shows in Asia and Europe.

Nam graduated with a BFA from Hong-ik University, Seoul, in 2011 and has since completed residencies at Halle 14 in Leipzig, Germany, and the Iksan Creation Center in South Korea. Inspired by cartoons, and drawing on literary influences ranging from Dante Alighieri to Joseph Conrad, Jinu Nam has developed an imaginary world populated by huge, squid-like creatures, intricate patterns and shapes, and an alter ego, the Squid Clown Gentleman. A mirror for modern-day society, this tragicomic universe provides the setting for stories of personal struggle, resistance and forgiveness.

Since his first solo exhibition in 2011, Jinu Nam’s oils and drawings have been exhibited in South Korea and beyond, including at museum venues such as the Iksan Creation Center, the Zaha Museum Seoul and Frappant E.V. in Hamburg, Germany.

name: Stickymonger
bio:
Stickymonger is a New York-based artist whose giant murals transform ordinary spaces into eerie, dreamlike, parallel universes. Looking into the the large eyes of her animation-inspired subjects, the viewer is invited to explore the interplay of darkness and light, as well as the tension between innocence and fear, femininity and anxiety. 
The artist’s early murals were created using hundreds of vinyl stickers, meticulously put together, piece by piece. The method served to create a sense that each image was melting and flowing together, like a river of ink down a gallery’s walls. This dark fluidity at the center of Stickymonger’s work was inspired by her youth in South Korea, where —  growing up in a home next to her family’s gas station — the artist’s imaginative universe was formed while playing in the shadow of oil drums and staring into the reflections of dense black petroleum puddles.
Currently, Stickymonger has expanded her work beyond vinyl to include other mediums such as spray paint and acrylic. As her methods evolve and change, she continues to offer the viewer a portal into a surreal shadow-world of contradictions: as inviting as it is ominous, both delightful and disconcerting.

name: Daewon Yang
bio:
Striking primary colours, formal symbolism and compositional simplicity characterise Dae-Won Yang’s deeply personal reflections on the human condition.

Born in Yangpyeong, South Korea, Yang took a degree in Natural Sciences before going on to complete an MFA at Sejong University in Seoul. His first solo exhibition was held in 1995 and in a career spanning over 20 years, he has developed a unique visual language to explore human nature and our place in the world.

Key to Yang’s practice is the figure he calls Donggeulin (“Round Man”), an avatar that appears in almost all his paintings, actively confronting emotional trauma, inequality or wickedness, searching for identity and meaning. Bold colours, masks, or large black tears are recurring elements, while Chinese characters for abstract concepts such as love, faith or hope also provide inspiration.

Aside from numerous group shows, over a dozen solo exhibitions of Yang’s work have been held across South Korea, as well as in Taiwan and France. He won the Joong Ang Fine Arts Competition (2005), was runner-up in the Songeun Art Festival (2004) and the Kongsan Art Festival (1996), and has completed residency programmes at Taipei Artist’s Village (2002) and Usine Utopik in Normandy, France (2012). Yang’s paintings appear in South Korea’s most significant collections, including the National Museum of Contemporary Art, Gwacheon, and Savina Art Museum, Seoul.

name: Jeong Seongjoon
bio: Jeong Seongjoon, captures the adventures and journey of animals to find their utopia in his works. The transportation for the main characters which are the animals in this case is in color, but everything else is painted in achromatic. He presents questions about whether humans and animals can coexist though contrasting colors, while he puts a desire where the nature and humans can coexist on the canvas. His art pieces were entirely sold out at Beijing art fair and also at his solo exhibition at Shanghai. He becomes a promising artist in China, and his art piece had been recently collected by Bernard Arnault, the chairman and chief executive of LVMH, Louis Vuitton Moet Hennessy.

name: Kim Tschang-Yeul
bio: Internationally acclaimed painter [Kim Tschang-Yeul](/artist/kim-tschang-yeul) devoted half a century to painting luminous water drops in a style that hovers between abstraction and hyperrealism. A founding member of the [Art Informel](/gene/art-informel) movement in his native Korea, Kim enjoyed fast success with his early abstract works, which were included in the 1961 Paris Biennale and the 1965 São Paulo Biennial. In the early ’70s, he began meticulously rendering water drops on canvas, wood, and newsprint, depicting countless beads of condensation in paintings that have sold for well over [$1 million at auction](https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20210526007600315#:~:text=SEOUL%2C%20May%2026%20\(Yonhap\),painter%20\(1929%2D2021\).). While some of his compositions focus on a single droplet that seemingly slides down a monochromatic background, others appear freshly splashed with water. Many incorporate neat lines of Chinese calligraphy, which Kim learned in his childhood. For the artist, who was influenced by Taoist and Zen Buddhist philosophies, this repeated motif offered a means of escape from past tragedy and trauma.

name: Yoon Hyup
bio: Yoon Hyup’s [paintings](/gene/painting) capture the energy and chaos of urban life through kaleidoscopic linework and [pointillist](/gene/pointillism) compositions. Hyup’s minimalist canvases often look like blurred photographs of sprawling city skylines (and occasionally idyllic beachfront views), but are actually composed of precisely rendered abstract acrylic marks, resulting in works that capture both the views and ambient feeling of being in a particular place. Hyun originally worked as a [street artist](/gene/graffiti-and-street-art) and has cited such artists as [Jean-Michel Basquiat](/artist/jean-michel-basquiat/works-for-sale) and [Nam June Paik](/artist/nam-june-paik) as influences, in addition to musicians such as DJ Krush; he also draws inspiration from the free-flowing feeling he gets riding a skateboard. Hyup has exhibited in New York, London, Seoul, Milan, Tokyo, Miami, and Hong Kong and has collaborated with Dior, Tiffany & Co., Nike, [Maison Kitsuné](https://www.instagram.com/maisonkitsune/), and Uniqlo, among others.

name: Chun Kwang Young
bio: Chun Kwang Young is best known for his process-driven “Aggregations”—freestanding sculptures and wall hangings composed of hundreds of tiny polystyrene triangles, which the artist wraps in colored mulberry paper printed in a traditional Korean style. Chun dyes each piece individually with tea and other natural pigments. Once assembled, his works resemble crystal formations or otherworldly, rocky terrains, creating an illusion of depth and coalescence. Suggesting both cohesion and chaos, they’re potent metaphors for chemistry, society, environmental issues, and the human condition. Chun has exhibited widely around the world and enjoyed solo shows in New York, Seoul, Singapore, Tokyo, London, Brussels, Düsseldorf, Milan, and Sydney. His work has sold for six figures at auction and belongs in the collections of the [British Museum](/partner/british-museum), the [Victoria and Albert Museum](/partner/victoria-and-albert-museum-v-and-a), the [Yale University Art Gallery](/partner/yale-university-art-gallery), and the National Gallery of Australia, among others.

name: Changmin Lim
bio: Lim Chang Min was born in Geochang, 1972 in Korea. He studied in Keimyung University in Korea. In 1999, he won the World Studio Foundation Award and was selected as one of three portrait artists by the art magazine, Dialogue. When he was studying at the graduate school of New York University, he was named “best artist” by Peter Campus, who is regarded as a pioneer of video art. He is a professor at Keimyung University. As his work has received international acclaim and he has been steadily exhibiting pieces at international art fairs. He combines unconventional moving and still screens to create his own vibrant and temporal view of reality. His work features ‘a scenery within a scenery,’ each taken at different times and locations, placing a moving image within the window frame of a neat room in a still photograph.

name: Junyoung Kang
bio:
Kang Jun-young (B.1979) was born in Seoul and majored in pottery at Hongik University and the same graduate school. Starting with the 2006 Gyeonggi World Ceramic Biennale Clay Olympics, dozens of exhibitions were presented at leading exhibition spaces in Korea, including Arco Museum and Gyeonggi Museum of Art, and major cities around the world such as Britain and the United States, as well as major Asian regions such as Taiwan, China, Singapore and Hong Kong. In addition, he participated in various international fairs, including Art Central HK Art Central Hong Kong, and received great attention and attention from Asian artists. Currently, his works are housed in the Korean Racing Authority, the National Assembly building, and the Han Hyang-rim Museum of Modern Ceramic Art.

Based on his life and experiences, Kang Jun-young creates works of art that express emotional themes using various media such as ceramics, paintings, and installations. The works actively represent themes such as love, hope, and home in text, and contain intense colors and positive messages. His moon jar works have a different aesthetic from the white porcelain moon jar in traditional Confucian society, and under the influence of hip-hop, graffiti, and pop art, they show modern and cheerful charm through various elements. Through this, the artist conveys messages of positivity, hope, and love, and explores new possibilities in contemporary art.

name: ZikSeong Jeong
bio: Jeong Zik Seong (b. 1976) is a Korean female painter in her 22nd year as an artist and a mother of three children. She has established herself as a painter in Korea with her series of “Semidetached Houses” which she has produced since 2002. She came to be known to the public for her paintings that depicted urban landscapes with her unique abstract brushstrokes, such as “Constructive Abstract/Construction Site Abstract)”, “Blue Collar/Blue Color”, and “The Mechanic” series. She had to move around as often as forty-three times to find a cheap house for rent each time. She rendered this experience in the series of “Semidetached Houses” which interpreted the row house districts of poor hillside villages in Seoul in geometric and abstract shapes. “Construction Site Abstract” series, which emphasized the act of drawing and erasing, is an interpretation of the rapid dismantling and re-building of redevelopment areas in Seoul, which she witnessed while moving around frequently. She rendered the workplace of laborers with her “Blue Collar/Blue Color” series that aimed to create abstractions that reflected the dynamic rhythm of life of the blue-collar class, and “The Mechanic” series that interpreted the ‘workplace’ of the car mechanic with rhythmic brushwork. Pieces of night plum blossoms in “Winter Flower” series depicted people’s wish and hope, symbolized by candlelight rallies. The green monochrome works in “Green Pool” series represented the ravaged soil of Korea following the controversial four-river refurbishment project. With the recent “Contemporary Mother-of-Pearl Paintings” series, Jeong Zik Seong has been exploring the relationship between the change of the four seasons and the changing aspects of natural landscapes and the symbolic expression of art, and making use of the technique of lacquerware inlaid with mother-of-pearl from the perspective of flatness and objecthood of painting.

name: Byen Ungpil
bio:
Byen Ung-pil studied painting for about 10 years in Germany's Muenster Kunst and showed off his self-portrait " Someone " series after returning home in 2006 . 

His works call for a new reflection on human existence by showing the face of a universal human being , not a specific individual . 

It represents individuals that are not free from numerous preconceptions and prejudices with no expression and simple line handling . 

The image of men and women of all ages is different from ordinary self-portraits . 

There may be self-portraits of various variations , but in general , self-portraits , which are the subject of the canvas , are the inner silent cries that the writer himself has built up based on his experience and memories . 
Through this self-portrait , the painter and audience formed a consensus . 
Byun Woong-pil's self-portrait also communicates with the audience through this action . 
The style of erasing rather than filling may be an expression of the obsession as a painter , but these attempts make the audience focus on the inside rather than the exterior of the figure .

name: Inhee Jang
bio:
The visual artist, Inhee Jang was born in Seoul, Korea, in 1979. She received BFA form the School of Art Institute of Chicago and MFA and Ph.D from Hongik University. She had 10 times of solo exhibitions and more than 60 times of group exhibitions include many kinds of international exhibitions and she had collaborated with many different field.
Her art work is about ‘the organic relation between moments and time’ and she has been using various materials and media to show this theme. Her art works cover drawing, painting, 3-D art work, and installation.

name: Seo Gi Hwan 서기환
bio: Artist Seo Gi Hwan uses his paintings as a bridge to empathize with his modern audience, encouraging them to use his artwork as a medium to fantasise desires that they would not ordinarily be able to achieve in their daily lives. These artworks blend reality with fantasy .The artist accentuates the contrast of the figures clothed in formal attire (which are drawn realistically with detailed strokes) with a burst and frolic of floral freedom.  Through this technique their flower person characters are perhaps engaging in their own fantasies through this floral expression. This unique technique is made all the more original as Artist Seo’s human and floral juxtapositions are in fact drawn on silk.

name: Lee Hyosun
bio:
[Sensations Beyond the Curve, Circulating Beings]

I explore the interconnectedness of existence through the relationships between the body, nature, and objects. In an age of hyperconnectivity where the gap between reality and virtuality continues to widen, my work seeks to overcome this sense of isolation by restoring humanity and reimagining the connections between beings. I conduct formal experiments on how the body, nature, and objects are interlinked.

Figures and objects in my work are abstracted into curvilinear and fluid forms, moving away from hyperrealistic representation. These distortions are attempts to visually express postures and connections that are impossible in real life. The curving distortions symbolize the cyclical nature of existence and connection, offering a surreal visual experience. Using soft color gradients and linear brushwork inspired by East Asian painting, I render these forms with subtlety and precision, organically expressing the ties between the body and objects.

The figures depicted are indeterminate beings, lacking fixed identities and containing the potential for continuous transformation and expansion. Often shown without mouths, they explore nonverbal connections beyond spoken language—through bodily contact and sensory experiences.

The subjects in my work are metaphorical elements inspired by myth, personal experiences, and poetry. These motifs layer narratives of past and present, forming stories where time and identity converge. Through this, my work poses fundamental questions about how we exist in the world.

name: Seong Joon Hong
bio:
Seong Joon Hong works on visualizing the foundations and layers of painting on the canvas. The study layers series is part of his research and consideration of the canvas that he is facing on a daily basis. He received his BFA in Painting at the College of Fine Arts, Hongik University, Seoul in 2012.
In 2015 he finished his MFA in Painting at the Graduate School, Hongik University.
He has participated in numerous solo and group shows in Koreas as well as international art fairs.

name: Hanna Kim
bio: Hanna Kim (b. 1981, Busan, South Korea) is a South Korean artist working across painting, sculpture, drawing, and animation. At the center of her practice is a recurring rabbit figure — both an imaginary companion and alter ego — through which Kim renders the textures of everyday life in a whimsical visual language, exploring the quiet but complex realities of human experience. Kim held solo exhibitions at [Gallery Playlist](https://www.artsy.net/partner/gallery-playlist), Busan; [PIBI Gallery](https://www.artsy.net/partner/pibi-gallery), Seoul; Alternative Space Loop, Seoul; Arario Gallery, Beijing; GANA Art Gallery, Busan; Lotte Hotel Gallery, Seoul; Shinsegae Gallery, Busan; and Sewoon Sanga, Seoul, among others.

name: Yeon Hwa Sung
bio:
There is a warmth from the old.
We're supposed to be in the warm atmosphere
I feel at peace.

My work begins here.
Hanji is my peace.
And it contains my most everyday story.

The times have changed rapidly, and the times I grew up have naturally continued the analog and digital era.
It's good now that speed and convenience are taken for granted,
It's slow, but it's also true that I miss the analog era when I was able to be more honest.

Newness was always fresh, but unfamiliar
The cold machine gave convenience, but it was being trapped in another world.
I may have locked myself in the name of the nickname and gradually turned away from me.

When I was young, I scribbled on paper, cut and played, and I meet myself and tell my story. 
My life in it is the story and memory of all of us.
And then, away from us communicating in cold machines
I hope you will be at peace while sharing silent stories together in the warmth.

name: So Youn Lee
bio:
So Youn Lee (b. 1984, Busan, South Korea) explores the relationship between the invariability of self-perception and the fluid self-identity of the post-internet era, starting from ontological uncertainty. Her work reflects on how individuals negotiate internal perception and external reality, exploring human conditions of being that transcend sociocultural boundaries. Growing up during radical changes of Korea and immigration, Lee explores themes of displacement, nostalgia, and emotional fragmentation. Drawing from her generational experience of connecting with virtual characters from games and animations, her visual language captures a longing for places never visited and times never lived. Through imaginative acts, she opens spaces of ontological resistance and new possibilities within the tensions between hope and fear, community and isolation, stability and transformation.

Submitted by the artist

name: Seungtaik Jang
bio: Seung-Taik Jang is a Korean Asian Modern & Contemporary artist who was born in 1959 in Goyang, Korea. He studied in Hongik University, Seoul, Korea and Ecole Nationale Superieure des Arts Decoratifs de Paris, France. His work was featured in several exhibitions at key galleries and museums in Korea. Public collections of his works involve National Museum of Contemporary Art, Seoul Metropolitan Art Museum, Seoul National University and more.

name: Myunggyun You
bio: Myunggyun You, a renowned artist, was born in Busan in 1962. He graduated from the Busan National University and Tama Art University in Japan. He has participated in numerous solo and group exhibitions, including the touring exhibitions at the National Museum of Modern Art in Tokyo and the National Museum of Contemporary Art in Osaka, as well as the Japanese Contemporary Art Exhibition at the Tokyo Metropolitan Art Museum. He has received awards at various competitions, including the Grand Prize at the Tokyo Objet Exhibition and the Grand Prize at the Imadate Contemporary Art Exhibition. After returning to Korea in the late 1996, he almost halted his artistic activities, but he resumed his career in earnest with a solo exhibition in 2007. He participated in exhibitions such as "Off the Wall" at the Clayarch Gimhae Museum in 2010 and "Korean Eye" at Saatchi Gallery in 2012, and he held solo exhibitions at Gallery 604 and Purdue University. In 2013, he moved back to the United States, where he engaged in various fellowships and residencies, including the Cfeva Fellowship and Yadoo Residency. His large installation works exhibited at the Weatherspoon Museum and Socrates Sculpture Park received critical acclaim. His works are collected by many institutions, including Cfeva (Philadelphia, USA), Imadate Culture Center (Japan), Saatchi Gallery (London, UK), RLV (AZ, USA), S.F.A.I (NM, USA), The Macdwell Colony (NF, USA), and AHL Foundation (New York, USA).

name: Won Jae Jo
bio:
Jo Won Jae creates ceramics that explore the intersection of color, texture, and time. Central to his practice is Baeksaek Yuhee (百色遊戱), meaning "a sensory resonance created by color." Using this concept, Jo layers color and texture to express emotional landscapes and the temporality of materials.

He employs a unique technique involving vibration, applying pigment to wheel-thrown clay and inscribing fine dots across the surface using rhythmic vibrations. These points represent emotional tension, transforming fleeting moments into lasting impressions. The bisque firing process solidifies the trace of time, revealing colors and textures that engage sensory perception.

Jo's recent works draw inspiration from ancient pottery. The Elegant Stone Age series revisits prehistoric forms, while the Blue Vessel series visualizes blue as a meditative presence. In Nature’s Perspective, he captures the fleeting moments of the natural world, like dew, within the enduring medium of clay.

Jo holds both BFA and MFA degrees from Korea National University of Arts. His work has been exhibited internationally, including in Korea, Japan, Hong Kong, the UK, Germany, and Taiwan, and is part of notable collections such as the International Academy of Ceramics and the Korea Ceramic Foundation.

name: Park Yunji
bio: Ephemerality is a theme that occupies much of Park Yunji's practice. In her contemplative paintings, shadows of trees and plants are carefully cropped and soaked in muted pinks and placid blues, capturing the fuzzy essence of transient moments. Park applies watercolor and pigment to _jangji_, a thick Korean paper that readily absorbs color, allowing the artist to create layered depth. This effect is apparent in works such as _Red Wind 1_ (2024), where the shadow of a constellation of branches is rendered in a shade of pink so soft and beclouded that it borders on abstraction. Park graduated from Ewha Womans University in Seoul with an MFA in oriental painting. She has exhibited in the South Korean capital at galleries including Gallery Doll, Rund Gallery, and Projectify, among others.

name: Choongmok Yoo
bio:
Yoo Chung-mok was selected as one of the world's 100 emerging glass artists in 2003 by Corning, USA. After being scouted as a senior glass designer at Carlson Glass Works in New York and working for 9 years, he was invited to several solo and group exhibitions in Korea, the US and the UK. , Prague Gallery, Czech Republic, and Global Art Avenue Gallery, USA. Artist Yoo Chung-mok uses glass, a material most similar to real water droplets, on rough textured yellow wood cloth to create her work. The glass water droplets in his works retain unchanging brilliance, but also have the charm of changing the shadows of the water droplets every moment according to the change of light. The artist defines her work as a work of remembering the past and preparing for the present and future.

To the artist, the yellow canvas means the past, and color and glass express the artist's feelings and sensibilities of the present and future. The artist abstractly expresses the harmony of lines, planes, and solids, and vertical and horizontal, which are the basics of all compositions, in his works based on Dancheong and the five colors that represent Korea. In particular, the artist believes that the brilliance of glass plays a role in temporarily forgetting the concept of dimension and has the temporal power of thinking about the past, present, and future at the same time. The artist imagines looking into the past through a transparent glass lens that does not change over time.

name: Dong gu Lee
bio:
The artist fundamentally reflects on how people living in the post-postmodern era are distinctly different from those of past centuries, based on his own personal experiences.
He considers how human thoughts, philosophies, and behavioral patterns have changed in response to major global events—such as the economic crisis just before the turn of the 21st century, the 2008 financial crisis, and the global pandemic that, for many, was the first time they experienced such a reality in their lifetime. He examines how these shifts have shaped contemporary human life and how they differ from those of previous generations.
In this context, the artist engages deeply with both classical literature and the pressing social issues of the present. Taking on the perspective of an observer, he reflects on the thoughts and concerns of people today. Through this process, he channels his inquiries and reflections into his artistic work, expressing his ongoing questions and perspectives as an artist.

name: Byun Sanghwan
bio: Byun Sanghwan is an artist who observes and reinterprets everyday urban objects and phenomena. Approaching cityscapes with the curiosity of an anthropologist, he deconstructs dense environments into micro units, transforming them through poetic metaphors, paradox, and humor. His work invites fresh perspectives on the human world, revealing the layered narratives of contemporary history. Byun’s practice explores the essential conditions of art—such as weight and space in sculpture, surface and pigment in painting, and multiplicity and process in printmaking. Themes of time and the body are central to his work, raising questions that drive new forms of creation.

name: Kwang-Bum Jang
bio:
"We can only feel the past after its dispersal and after its runaway, because we can never touch, suspend or stop the present. Past is actually the onlytime we can outline. Indeed past is the product of accumulation and degradation of time, which is exactly what Jang's artistic creation is about : conceiving layers then destroying them by sanding them to finally show through the runaway of their prints and shapes."

Jang's paintings is composed with two distinct process: the application and the removal of paint.

First, he covers the whole surface of a plain canvas with white paint, then he alternates this application with layers of colored paint. This stage of creation needs 5 to 6 liters of paint and about 2 weeks for a completly dry canvas. This phase represents "materialisation" of time: it passes and gets thicker, gaining material and then comes to a waiting phase.
The artist then proceeds to the removal of the material. By putting round objects of different curves and contours, one by one, behind the canvas, hesands the front side until the layers of colour appear, if not until the white layers.

This way, he creates compositions with intertwined circles, always in different sizes and shapes, delicately related or clearly limited. This techniquerequires a huge attention, gentleness, application and patience.
The result is breathtaking: everything is in movement, everything seems liquid, boiling, running, everything moves swiftly and subtly, even if fixedmaterially on a canvas, on the wall.

Very surprisingly, Jang manages to capture time, and with his finished work, he represents its essence, he manages to create this "impossible" unity between time and visibility.
His creation requires imagination, sensibility and subtlety of the aesthetic and culture of Korea, combined to western culture to create such a unique work of art.

Jang Kwang Bum was born in 1972 in Seoul, he lives and works in Paris France.

name: Kim Young Hun
bio:
Living through the transition between the analog generation and digital generation, Kim Young-Hun is passionate in observing and deciphering the unknown between the 1 and 0 of binary codes. For Kim, such incomprehensibility intrigues him to create disoriented and euphoric paintings: Inspirations such as stripe covered light bulbs, white noise from digital screens, and invisible vibrations from string instruments allow Kim’s works, in his wordings, to “…generate an electronic-like abstract painting language that interferes with some parts of the ambiguous boundaries of our ever-changing digital or reality lives”.

Kim’s works demonstrate a traditional Korean painting technique called Hyukpil (革筆畫), in which the painter mixes various colors and paints with rapid strokes using a leather brush. The multi-colored stripes that seem to flow like ink are made by one continuous brush stroke across the canvas, with the oil colors melting together and permeate into the canvas. One of the distinctive features of Kim’s post-abstract works is the preservation of his raw artistic process: By having just one layer of paint, the trace of his pulsating brush strokes is unedited and simultaneously creates an illusion of a glossy screen.

name: Sundoo Kim
bio: The narrative paintings of Sundoo Kim show a unique viewpoint that combines his studies on traditional paintings of flowering plants and mountain scenery. Unraveling the routine and hardship of life in such way, makes one wonder how the taboos of narrative features in modernist art can be restored. His efforts to combine the tradition of landscape painting, which must be read narrative without narrative, and the aspect of genre painting, which must be read only by narrative, are prominent. The artist calls his works ‘Gil (translated ‘Way’) Painting’. He uses the aesthetics of ‘slow line’ to find the answer to life. To enjoy and to be moved by prosaic things in everyday life is an unusual circumstance but through his works, one can experience such joy of life. Based on his aesthetics of slow line, dream, melody and mind of the slow line is a part of the ‘Way’. The lines tracing the nature of Southern Province are like a calligraphic stroke where the simple and bold lines project a dynamic, yet a delicate scent.

name: WONJE KANG
bio:
Kang Wonje graduated from Daegu university, contemporary Art with master’s degree. And he graduated from painting in Hongik University, painting with bachelor’s, and doctorate degree. The artist has exhibited in Korea, and UK.
Kang Wonje’s ‘Weighty painting’ series is a sculpture made by bonding hundreds of hand-drawn drawings with light brush strokes. This painting-sculpture actually weighs 20-30kg and thus is a heavy painting. Another meaning of “heavy” is “valuable” and “meaningful.” So when one “light” painting is piled up, it becomes another “heavy” picture. This is for the point in which lightness becomes weighty through repetitive acts, or for the moments when meaninglessness is transformed into meaningful.
