name: Doyeon Gwon
bio: Gwon summons fragments of memory into reality and reconstructs them into photographs, intersecting the objects that existed with the world we face now. His major works include 《Twinkle》, 《Nocturama》, 《SF》, 《Bukhansan》, 《Flashbulb Memory》, 《The Art of the Shovel》, and 《Conceptual Dictionary》, and he has participated in numerous exhibitions at the Photofest Biennale, Incheon Art Platform, Seoul Museum of Art, and the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art. He received the Photography Criticism Award in 2011, the 7th KT&G Imagination Center SKOPF Finalist of the Year (2015), and the 10th Ilwoo Photography Award (2019) in the publishing category, and participated in residency programs at the National Museum of Contemporary Art Goyang (2017), Incheon Art Platform (2019), Geumcheon Art Factory (2021), and Nanji Creative Studio (2022). he is the author of Bukhansan (April Snow, 2021) and Flashbulb Memory, (Hatje Cantz, Germany, 2020). His work is in the collections of the Goeun Museum of Photography, the Seoul Museum of Art, and the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art.

name: Jihoon Ha
bio:
Jihoon Ha (born in 1978, Korea) is a rising contemporary artist who has been steadily built a strong artistic career since graduating from the Kunstakademie Münster in Germany. 
He moved frequently during his childhood due to his father's career as a naval officer. The artist’s frequent moves led him to express his impressions abstractly, focusing more on visual, smell, and sound experiences than on specific memories of places or events.
His paintings are a kind of landscape, but also traces of brushwork and paint. A large mass (an island image) occupies the center of the canvas, with the interior filled with colorful paint and brush strokes.
Inside that piece, you'll find the artist's feelings, memories, experiences, and various emotions.

name: Yoo Suntai
bio:
After earning his Ph.D. from Paris 8 University, Yoo Suntai firmly established himself as one of Korea’s leading contemporary artists, with his works featured in prestigious auctions such as Christie’s and Hong Kong sales. His intricate, surrealist paintings have long captivated collectors and art lovers both in Korea and abroad.

Yoo describes his oeuvre as a “forest of objects,” where familiar items from everyday life are reimagined into surreal spaces where time and place converge. Central to his practice is the technique of dépaysement—the displacement of objects from their usual context. By altering their functions or relationships, he instills a sense of unfamiliarity, prompting viewers to question what they see. His work explores dualities—familiar and strange, real and fantastical—and seeks to unify these opposing concepts within a single, cohesive visual language.

Through his meticulous arrangement of objects—each open to interpretation depending on the viewer’s perspective—Yoo creates multi-layered, surreal spaces where different dimensions coexist. By doing so, he invites shifts in perception and sparks imaginative exploration. Yoo, who believes no single word can fully define an object, continues to construct dreamlike, alternate worlds through painting, imbuing each image with multiple meanings and poetic nuance.

name: JaeYeon Yoo
bio: Artist Yoo Jae-yeon's work collects and visualizes fragments that have fallen from the gap between childhood fantasy and reality. The gaps hidden within, for example, the subtle emotions and fragments of ideal and reality, the individual and the society, the past and the present, when they meet, show that this young painter's work is not just enjoyable and energetic, making the work even more curious.

name: Jae Yong Kim
bio: Whether round, square, heart-shaped, or cat-shaped, [Jae Yong Kim](/artist/jae-yong-kim)’s elaborately glazed ceramic donuts deliver the instant appeal of [Pop art](/gene/pop-art). After graduating from the prestigious MFA program at the [Cranbrook Academy of Art](/partner/cranbrook-academy-of-art), Kim began creating to-scale replicas of the sweet fried cake in 2008. Installations that feature walls covered with these colorful [sculptures](/gene/sculpture) have drawn crowds of thousands, and members of royal families in the United Arab Emirates have reportedly purchased entire exhibitions. Each donut is decorated to exist as a one-of-a-kind artwork, first hand-thrown, then hand-painted, often with multiple glazes. Kim embellishes them with eye-catching materials from glitter to Swarovski crystals, with some patterned surfaces referencing other artists, like polka dots as a nod to [Yayoi Kusama](/artist/yayoi-kusama). Touching upon themes like consumption and personal pleasure, Kim has experimented with larger work over the years, creating clay treats the size of inflatable inner tubes.

name: Hwang Gyutae
bio:
HWANG Gyutae’s interest in digital images in the 1980s led to new frontiers, such as digital montage, collage, and compositing. Through an extended cycle of experimentation, he found ‘pixels’ – the base unit of images in the form of dots, in the digital images. Drawn to the infinite possibility and visual potential of these geometric images, he launched his series.

HWANG’s series lacks, or falls short of the basic process of “recording” in photography, and instead harbors “choice” and “magnification.” In other words, his works move away from the traditional process of capturing an object and making it appear on the sensitive film strip and instead focus on discovering a wide variety of pixels in different forms and colors as they appear in the process of choosing and magnifying images and monitors. That already exists for disparate reasons, ultimately visualizing and materializing them through a range of methods. In this process, the products arising from the original image multiply. It does not matter whether these processes are shown in the photographs or not. His total directional work, which he describes as “chosen pixels rather than made products,” must be understood in the larger context of “image” studies rather than seen through the narrow lens of conventional “art” or formal history.

name: Jaehyuk Han
bio:
Through abstract painting, He asks ontological questions about all creation.

By dismantling and recombining the existing ones, he means to restore the infinite possibilities that it had from the beginning, breaking away from the tactic standards of modern society.

Humans and matters have led to an ideal world through interaction until now.

However, we are missing out on so many things in our repetitive lives.

On the face of it, the material has provided convenience through human use.

However, as a reaction to convenience, it brought about the destruction of nature and strict regulations. The controlled system was not enough to satisfy the inner side of life and eventually the vicious cycle as above was formed.

As an artist myself, living in this structure, and also as an individual living in the present frame, He grieves day to day about the social structure that is beyond redemption.

Eventually, art (this work) is a guide that helps modern people who are gradually forgetting the pure inner world of one’s life, accustomed to a controlled life, and stuck in a vicious cycle, to reach the inscape.

The screen showing the artist’s mental anguish and labor lead to a time of meditation and reflection. 

The surface activity of the art piece has no meaning at all.

It simply helps oneself communicate with one’s inner self through the visual sense.
The sensation from unfamiliar forms are re-understood and reconstructed from 0 (nothing), breaking away from the existing data.

By looking inside, the message of what attitude we must take to reconsider our lives and live a better life is the message he intends to convey.

name: Yoo Mi Seon
bio:
Yoo mi seon, born in 1959, is an artist who meticulously captures the flow of life and memory. Her works, crafted through long and intricate processes, exude a serene tranquility. Experiencing her art is akin to delving into a profound essay or savoring a poem, harmoniously blending joy and satisfaction. Over time, her creations reveal a multifaceted beauty, with each delicate touch of gold and silver leaf conveying deep significance. Yoo mi seon invites us to pause, take a breath, and immerse ourselves in the unique world of her art.

Yoo mi seon studied Oriental painting at Hongik University, where she also earned her MFA. She has held 18 solo exhibitions and participated in over 350 group exhibitions both domestically and internationally. Her presence is notable in numerous international art fairs, including KIAF, Art Chicago, Art Expo NY, and Art Central HK. Her works are part of prestigious collections at institutions such as the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, as well as in numerous private collections worldwide.

name: Ran Hwang
bio: Ran Hwang is best known for her large-scale wall installations in which buttons, beads, pins, and threads on wood panels form images of falling blossoms, vases, Buddhas, and birds. Hwang’s installations have also taken on more current themes, exploring the fashion industry and female identities in popular culture. Drawing from Eastern philosophies, Hwang’s method is a meditative ritual in which she first projects an outline onto the wall, then traces its contour and painstakingly fills in the image with her materials, a process that can take up to a month. “The process of building large installations \[is\] time consuming and repetitive,” Hwang has said. “And it requires manual effort, which provides a form of self-meditation.”

name: Lee Kyoungmi
bio: Lee Kyoungmi is one of the cutting-edge artists who is taking a new lead in the contemporary art scene. She studied at one of the high-ranking universities in Korea, ‘Hongik University’ with two majors; engraving print and painting. She has been presenting ‘Street’ series and representing herself with her cat, Nana. She puts her individual experience into art pieces and her unique visual language could be defined as a self-confession; The cat represents herself and she presents various stories such as her childhood memories into the objet. In particular, her art pieces are painted on low-relief wood base or 3 dimensional objects instead of painting on the traditional flat canvas. She has been actively working in America, Germany and etc. and during last year, she received an honorable award from Seokjoo Art Award in Korea.

name: Minjung Kim
bio: [Minjung Kim](/artist/minjung-kim) is renowned for her intricate, abstract [ink paintings](/gene/east-asian-ink-and-wash-painting) executed on delicate mulberry bark paper that she often burns, layers, or twists to create subtle textures. Works from her “[Mountain](/artwork/minjung-kim-mountain-4)” series, which featured in the [2015 Venice Biennale](/partner/56th-venice-biennale), display rows of gently undulating lines that together evoke beautifully lit peaks and valleys. Kim was trained in [traditional calligraphy](/gene/east-asian-calligraphy) and Korean watercolor painting in her youth, which is evident in her refined linework and masterly control of her brush. While her materials are rooted in East Asian artistic traditions, she is informed by Western [abstract expressionism](/gene/abstract-expressionism), which she learned while studying in Milan in the 1990s. She eventually split her time between New York and the south of France, where she continues to create her contemplative [paper works](/gene/work-on-paper).

name: MANE
bio: MANE (b. Seoul, South Korea, 1978) is a Seoul-based painter and sculptor whose work draws on nostalgic pop culture imagery and color palette of the 1980s and 1990s to explore the blurred boundary between memory and fantasy. His paintings and sculptures frequently feature Mariffe, a recurring character and storyteller the artist uses to embody childhood curiosity. MANE has exhibited across Asia, including solo exhibitions at Gallery THEO, Seoul, in 2024 and Whitestone Ginza New Gallery, Tokyo, in 2025. He has participated in group exhibitions internationally, including in Busan, Australia, and Paris.

name: Lee Sujin (b. 1983)
bio:
Lee Sujin delves into the depths of negative emotions, drawing from personal encounters exacerbated by the pandemic. Through her art, she confronts anxiety and fear, weaving them into a tapestry of everyday imagery stripped of their horror context. Lee’s canvases portray a paradoxical world where mundane objects evoke profound unease. Her meticulous yet subdued technique invites viewers to introspect, navigating the nuances of anxiety with each stroke. By juxtaposing tension with tranquility, Lee offers a space for reflection, allowing audiences to confront and empathize with the diverse spectrums of anxiety in their lives. Through her work, she transforms fear into a vessel for introspection and empathy.

name: Beom Jun
bio: Beom Jun, a South Korean abstract artist renowned for his layered depictions of mountains, draws inspiration from his upbringing surrounded by the majestic landscape. Trained at the Kaywon School of Art and Design and Kookmin University, he blends contemporary and traditional Korean mediums to explore creation's essence. Viewing mountains as symbols of cosmic flux, Beom Jun's work intertwines observation and imagination, revealing layers of time and emotion. His art, characterized by serene surfaces and dynamic undercurrents, explores themes of order and chaos, life and death. With a decade of prolific contributions to the art world in South Korea and recent international exhibitions, Beom Jun is poised to make a lasting impact globally.

name: Xooang Choi
bio: Xooang Choi explores the human condition through sculptural works that reflect the complex relationships between the body, identity, and society. He has been creating works that unfold various phenomena arising in the relationship between individuals and society through realistic depictions of the human body. In recent years, shifting to abstract sculptures inspired by internal organs and biological structures, Choi has been focusing on refining his sculptural language and aesthetic sensibility. He also examines the process of actively embracing various intermediate parameters within the artwork, moving away from a subjective position of making sculptural decisions to expand concepts and forms encompassing regions, histories, places, and memories.

name: Young Sam Kim
bio:
Born of an auditory-verbal impairment in Busan, South Korea, Young Sam Kim grew to become exceptionally perceptive to visual stimuli. Kim’s inclination for painstaking observation coupled with his poetic complexion naturally led him to practice the internalization of his highly conceptual motifs. Kim soon developed his own visual language with a depth only few could fully recognize. As Kim refined his intuition for visual literacy, he quickly developed a heightened sense of expression, gravitating toward photography to capture his enlightened, and often-evocative thoughts and emotions.

After receiving his BFA from the School of Visual Arts in 2002, Kim continued to reside and work between New York and South Korea. Traveling to the world’s most celebrated metropoleis, Kim drew heavy inspiration from diaphanous threads of commonalities thought to connect every urbanite on a simple, yet distinctively existential plane despite variations in language, culture, and color. Kim’s oeuvre became a laborious dive into both interconnectedness and mobility – two of photography’s most invincible accomplices. In his first series “A World in the City,” Kim re-contextualized pieces of photography through multidimensional layering and superimposition; he calls this narrative technique a hyper-collage. The digitally collaged images are layered into surreal cityscapes – reminiscent of René Magritte and de Goya’s Magical Realism – that are meant to speak of humans stifled by thick forests of urban landscape and architecture, yearning to fly from the tangible toward a life of transcendence. While his first collection focused on humankind’s longing for truth, Kim’s most recent series “Dark Cities” emphasizes a less optimistic angle.

name: Jin Kyu Park
bio: Park Jinkyu graduated from Korea national university of art in 2011 with bachelor’s degree. The artist has exhibited in Korea and participated art fair in USA. Park JinKyu constructs infinite space through his unique technique. Breathe from top to bottom with gravity with paint and draw a line. After the first line is layered on, he turns the canvas and begins to draw another line that crosses the first line at a right. Considering the process of working on a canvas, virtually all the lines in the work are vertical to the artist. In the solemn moment when his energy and gravity are united to form a vertical line, infinite space begins. The artist asks questions about the world and existence through the repetitive work of stacking vertical and horizontal lines on the canvas, and completes the space painting by finding the harmonious unity of the two relationships.

name: HyunMo Yang
bio:
For Hyunmo Yang, drawing is an observational attempt of self-reflection that leads to a process of balancing through paint. Fragments of daily experiences and emotions manifest as burning lines or dense shadowy spaces—proving the interstices of Yang’s painting and existence.  At a time when many works try to say something, Yang's paintings say nothing. Instead, he explores basic sculptural elements such as dots, lines, planes, and shapes, and the aesthetic experience of such discovery.

Hyun Mo Yang received his B.A. and M.A. in Western Painting from Seoul National University.

name: Seongyeon Jo
bio: Seongyeon Jo closely observes everyday life and objects within her immediate surroundings through photography, exploring the boundaries of still life. She carefully frames often overlooked subjects—old neighborhoods, buildings slated for demolition, discarded furniture, untended plants, and sidewalk blocks—elevating these peripheral elements of daily life into the central motifs of her photographic compositions. Her practice also involves challenging photography’s inherent multiplicity by constructing mise-en-scènes with found objects for shooting, installing photographs alongside the physical items featured within them, and extending the photographic frame through additional artistic interventions. These elements sometimes create optical illusions, appear as bas-relief or brushstrokes, bridging the photographic space with the exhibition environment.

name: Gyul E Kim
bio:
Gyul E. Kim (b. 1990, South Korea) explores art through a process of deciphering signs and symbols that through a retrace of one’s steps, allows for self discovery. Kim reconfigures the boundaries of painting by first composing an image and then producing a canvas shaped to match it. This approach disrupts the traditional rectangular frame and flexibly expands possibilities of interpretation.

Drawing from geometric fragments observed in everyday life and the exaggerated visual language of classic animation, Kim develops a distinctive vocabulary of angular, nonconforming forms. This departs from conventional standards and generates a sense of  visual dynamism and playfulness that is sourced in the artist’s engagement with marginalization and difference. Rather than resolve the dissonance of language and incomprehensibility, her work embraces ambiguity as points of fascination. 

Kim graduated from Sungkyunkwan University with a BFA in Western Painting and completed her master’s degree in Art Therapy at Ewha Womans University. She has broadened her artistic processes through research at the Buk-gu Art Creation Center in Ulsan and the Gunpo Culture and Arts Creation Village Residency. She has held solo exhibitions at ROY Gallery (2024, 2025) and Artforlab (2023), and has actively participated in group exhibitions at the Hangaram Art Museum, Seoul Arts Center (2022), Sangwon Museum of Art (2019), and Kim Ria Gallery (2023). In 2023, she was named among ARTSY’s “Rising Artists of Asia & Its Diaspora” drawing attention from collectors both domestic and abroad. She is currently represented by ROY Gallery.

name: Kwon Neung
bio:
Kwon Neung mentioned that the great history and art will be spread out on our ordinary life. He captures well known figures from the masterpiece on one screen. His motif came from the artist, Charles Baudelaire. As Charles Baudelaire wrote poems on the subject matter of unbeautiful appearance, evil and disgust in everyday life to show not all the art had to focus on the theme of greatness, Kwon Neung also expresses to describe the contemporary life with his own eyes and expressions.

He graduated from one of the top raking universities in Korea, ‘Hongik University’ with the major of painting. His paintings were entirely sold out on the first day at the major art fairs in Hong Kong, Taipei, Miami and etc. He currently lives in Hong Kong and he is actively engaged in overseas at this moment.

name: Min ha Park
bio:
Min ha Park(b. 1984, Korea) observes things that infiltrate into the unknown and cause a reaction at some point and puts them on the screen. This is a reproduction of invisible phenomena, and makes the viewer go through the process of understanding the artist’s sensuous and personal incarnation again in a private sense. The various elements already shared within this process – colors, forms and languages – have ensured the universality of communication thus making dialogue a possibility.  The artist has brought attention to the phenomena that manifest its existence with clarity especially those that reach into the body as stimuli and cause change.

Min Ha Park received her BFA from School of Visual Arts, New York, in 2006 and MFA from Yale University in 2011. She held the solo exhibitions Sun Gone (2019), ONE and J. Gallery, Seoul; Night Swimminig, Skiburn McArther, Los Angeles (2016); No Bones, Platform Place 629, Seoul (2015). Selected group exhibitions featuring her artwork 22nd WHITE NOISE : PIGEON, WHITE NOISE, Seoul (2020); The Camp #1: Timekeepers, Galerie ERD, Seoul (2018); _It's snowing in LA, _AA | LA Gallery, Los Angeles (2018); Clear Confusion, Whistle, Seoul (2017); Unseen Garden, ONE AND J. Gallery, Seoul (2016) and many others.

name: Jaemin Jang
bio: JANG Jaemin’s works begin from experiences of unfamiliar places. Scenes he witnessed, and events that occurred, and various synaesthetic experiences are the materials for his paintings. His brushstrokes are vast and rapid. He uses his bodily motions as much as possible to make each brushstroke. He paints as if wrestling with the tools while withstanding the weight of the brush and viscosity of paint – an attempt to experience the act of painting ardently. JANG’s paintings are re-experiencing a landscape, endured in the past, once more. This is his effort to make the experiences ultimately his own. The brushstroke’s intensity varies depending on the height of emotions and clarity of memories. As movement becomes more extensive and rapid, intuition applies stronger, and unanticipated events irrupt. The memory of the past and the time of the present interact and endlessly evokes new scenes.

name: Zenakim 젠아킴
bio: I am deeply interested in meditation, philosophy, and the human experience. I interpret people's thoughts, actions, and their outcomes through causality and strive to fulfill and refine my inner self through interactions with others. I wish to express the truths that arise from within me through my works and share them with many people.

name: Jeong Bo Young (b. 1973)
bio:
Jeong Boyoung has long been devoted to exploring the relationship between space and light, translating this sustained inquiry onto the canvas. By visually rendering the flow of time and light within a given space, her works evoke scenes that feel simultaneously familiar and subtly estranged. This paradoxical sensation arises from her attempt to suspend time and arrest moving light within the fixed frame of painting.

Her practice begins with prolonged observation of how light shifts over time within a single space. In the early morning, light entering through a window passes over a wooden table placed before it and is cast onto the floor in polygonal forms. As time progresses, these geometric shapes of light climb the vertical wall, gradually narrowing until they vanish shortly after noon. The light that disappears at midday returns in the late afternoon, filtering once again through the window to form a new and distinct configuration.

name: Jimin Chae
bio:
Artist Chae Ji-min sold out his entire work at the Hong Kong Art Basel Solo booth in 2018 . Also , each work is drawing attention on the painters . His work draws between art and everyday life in one screen and leaves the vanishing point in reality and unreality .
The artist notes that his work is " each scene that exists on one screen , but never coexists and is scattered  ".  
By randomly combining the fragments of images discovered at the moment of life , sometimes colliding and unbecoming feelings act as an art device that explores the planarity and spatiality of painting .

name: Jung Kangja
bio: As one of the representative female artists who addressed a turbulent historical ear in Korea, JUNG Kangja had emerged in Korean art circles through the Korean Young Artists Association Exhibition in 1967. In the 1960s and the 70s, when the Korean military government and ideologies were in conflict, JUNG tried to make voices in society through various formative experiments as a member of 'New Exhibition Coterie' and 'The Fourth Group'. Introducing real politics into the context of art by using an artist's body and performance was a challenge to the traditional ideas and a resistance to the social system. However, in 1970, the government started to impose more severe sanctions against all activities using the human body. After her solo exhibition in 1970, JUNG moved to Singapore with her family and spent time away from the Korean art scene for over 10 years. The artist's socially critical mind and subjective spirit in the 1960s were connected to formative experiments in the paintings she was devoted to after her return to Korea in 1981. JUNG's strong willpower became an impetus to allow her to overcome alienation, and a driving force to make her stand in front of the canvas despite the harsh struggle with cancer. JUNG's work over the last 15 years does a poignant job of displaying her interest in something concrete and realistic, something that had expanded into an interest in human beings through abstract, transcendental forms. In short, she wanted to liberate herself through "imaginations that I stretch in my own way in an unlimited, free space that is bound to nothing."

name: Yong R. Kwon
bio: Through his works, Kwon speaks to the intangible beauty of art that can be imagined through the manipulation of light and empty spaces, thus materialized by the colors and shape of his stainless steel. While the light functions as a base ingredient, it also imbues the spirit of his art through giving voice to the forms that are already produced. Through tireless repetition, Kwon's artwork embraces the natural force of light that cannot be controlled by man to produce formative shapes.

name: Jade Kim
bio:
Jade Kim is a visual artist whose paintings and sculptures depict his character MIN, an animated version of his wife, whose personality and characteristics inspire his art. Dreamy eyes, child-like features, and innocent traits characterize MIN, who is often portrayed as a protective and loving character. A peaceful ambience overshadows Kim’s paintings, aiming to find common ground with the viewer. His works also portray the rapid change of the world we live in, and how it sometimes gets out of control.

_Submitted by [Volery Gallery](https://www.artsy.net/partner/volery-gallery)_

name: Gio Yang
bio:
Gio Yang was born in Seoul, South Korea in 1998 and she received a Bachelor Oriental Painting from the Ewha Woman University in South Korea, Seoul in 2023.  She has delivered the meaning of the human condition within the huge keyword of relationship. One person exhibitions of her work have been presented at IlACKJANG, 2022 and EUMC (Ewah Woman University Seoul Hospital) Wellness Art Zone. Her work is presented at Affordable Art Fair, Metropolitan Pavilion, in 2021 and included in the collection of EUMC Wellness art zone. 
She works by creating imaginary stories in her mind and visualizing them on Korean traditional paper called ZangZi. The work has been continued under the title of "Island for One Person." After setting the atmosphere that the artist gives to the island in detail following the story. The materials are freely used in Korean traditional ink and color on the paper according to the imagery. It is explored with varnish, white powder called Hobun, and ink to add depth to the work with a richer texture.

name: Beomsik Won
bio: René Descartes viewed as beautiful the order and coherency of structures designed by a single architect; the purpose of the Archisculpture photo project, however, is to create architectural sculptures by collaging photographs of diverse architectural works from various architects. In this way, the Archisculpture photos are both similar and different to the organic romanticism of old cities built through the works of myriad architects, for they represent the artist’s subjective interpretation and decisions regarding various architects’ numerous designs. If a photograph has a punctum then clearly the architectural works used here will in certain ways be the artist’s punctum and their assemblage will be the Archisculpture photo. These works may also locate and bring together structures with political, economic, or social significance, creating through the work’s studium the illusion of a metropolis. Like collectors who arrange and classify their acquisitions with great care, artists analyze selected city fragments gathered from here and there and with them create their sculptures. What exist now as disparate structures are reborn as beautiful sculptures which retain their diachronic or synchronic histories, or else encompass it all. As the Russian film director Sergei Mikhailovich Eisenstein explained in relation to the montage technique, the collaging employed in this process creates through the collision of disparate elements stories that before remained beneath the surface. In essence, however, it is a photograph of a nonexistent, architectural sculpture.

name: Do Ho Suh
bio: In a practice that spans sculpture, installation, drawing, and film, Do Ho Suh considers notions of home, cultural displacement, and the relationship between architecture and the body. Suh is best known for his large-scale fabric sculptures which recreate his former residences; the artist weaves translucent reconstructions of exteriors, interiors, and appliances. His ghostly, immersive environments and individual artworks bring intimate domestic shapes into the gallery space. Suh studied oriental painting at Seoul National University (where he earned both a BFA and MFA) before receiving a BFA in painting from the Rhode Island School of Design and an MFA in sculpture from Yale University. He has exhibited in New York, Los Angeles, London, Berlin, Seoul, Tokyo, and Paris, and his work belongs in the collections of the [Mori Art Museum](/partner/mori-art-museum), the [Museum of Modern Art](/partner/the-museum-of-modern-art), the [Smithsonian American Art Museum](/partner/smithsonian-american-art-museum), the [Tate](/partner/tate), the [Guggenheim Museum](/partner/guggenheim-museum), and the [Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles](/partner/moca).

name: Kim JiHoon
bio:
Kim Jihoon is a contemporary painter born and based in Jeju, South Korea. His practice draws inspiration from the island's stone walls, vegetation, and natural landscape, translating these elements into a distinctive language of abstraction. Through simplified forms, layered color, and material references to place, his work explores memory, human relationships, and the emotional resonance of landscape.

_Submitted by [Suppoment Gallery](https://www.artsy.net/partner/suppoment-gallery)_

name: Kim Hongbin
bio: Hongbin Kim (b. 1988, Seoul), also known by the artistic name Vanhada, is a South Korean artist whose abstract paintings explore themes of rupture, healing, and nostalgia. He studied painting at Hongik University before moving to New York, where he continues to live and work. Kim’s work is characterized by vibrant color, raw textures, and expressive marks that suggest wounds or openings within the surface, reflecting personal experiences of displacement and transformation. Drawing from both Korean visual sensibilities and contemporary abstraction, his paintings navigate the tension between chaos and regeneration. His work has been exhibited in venues including the Korean Cultural Center Gallery in Tenafly, New Jersey, and Gallery Chang, and continues to engage audiences through its emotionally charged visual language.

name: Hoon Kwak
bio:
Hoon Kwak pursued his education in fine arts in the USA, receiving his MA and
MFA from California State University, Long Beach in 1980 and 1982, respectively. His work was included in the inaugural Korean Pavilion at the Venice Biennale of Art in 1995. The artist currently lives and work in Los Angeles and Seoul.

Kwak’s work represents the profound spiritual world of Buddhism and Eastern philosophy, expressed
through a range of Korean materials. With an indeterminate composition and vigorous brushstrokes, his artworks deeply resonate with audiences. Inspired by the vivid hue of blood, a color the artist deems as the first-ever shade of color in the history of humanity, Kwak’s paintings often feature the deep reddish-brown pigment of iron oxide. To him, the shade of burnt sienna echoes with the primal force of our primitive days, when our ancestors created cave paintings with easily accessible materials such as charcoal, soil, and pigments made with minerals and animal fat. By using ritualistic elements, the artist recreates a connection with this primal materiality.

Kwak also draws inspiration from the ancient earthenware of his hometown; such abstract renditions occur not only in his paintings but also in his installations. As opposed to his paintings, Kwak’s installation works have only been produced during a brief period of time and are low in number. Buddhist thoughts and Oriental philosophy are also at the core of these pieces, eloquently representing his disposition, in that his experimental spirit is infused with an abstract way of expression.

name: Lee Eu
bio: Artist Lee Eu has eliminated all the figurative elements from the canvas in order to concentrate on the substance of materials. Sometimes her works seem like growing moss or like as furrow dug up by wind. However, the most important thing that the artist focuses are thick layers of material ‘Matiere’ by accordance with the flow of time, and conversation that comes from the pleasure of the color. The artist invites us with her high degree of pictoriality along with her sensible experience.

name: JeongHyun Ha
bio: Recognized in the art world for eight individual exhibitions and more than 50 group exhibitions, Jeonghyun Ha is currently a lecturer at Ewha Womans University and Hansung University in Seoul. This artist visualizes her freedom in vivid colour by projecting it into her work.

name: Jong Oh
bio:
Jong Oh

Jong Oh was born in 1981 in Mauritania, North Africa and moved to Korea at age 15. Received his bachelor degree in Fine Arts from Hongik University in Seoul and eventually his master from School of Visual Art in New York, where he now lives and works. 

Korean artist Jong Oh creates minimal sculptures that respond to the given spatial situation. In his compositions, Oh makes use of a limited selection of materials: string, fishing line, Plexiglas, and wooden rods. The works require an increased awareness of delicate oscillations and variations. Jong Oh is thus clearly making a case for an attention to small details, especially in the hectic bustle of everyday life. 

Alternating between sculpture and intervention, intangible image and installation, Oh considers each of his works as a carefully composed visual poem.

In 2016, held a solo exhibition at the University of Connecticut Art Galleries. In 2014-5, he had solo exhibitions at Krinzinger, Austria; Jochen Hempel, Leipzig; and MARSO, Mexico City. He has been in numerous group exhibits worldwide. 

Font: http://www.marcstraus.com/artists/jong-oh/

name: Hansaem Park
bio: All of Park's works are landscapes. The artist has been engrossed in landscapes such as islands and forests, but unexpectedly, landscapes such as islands and forests are merely images that have no meaning. What the artist wants is not a representation of a landscape, but because it is the energy and aura of the space in which it resides. In other words, the invisible aura of the space, the accumulated time, the feeling of oneself when facing the space, and the phenomenon that occurs when the work is brought to a third place are what the artist thinks of interest. Rather than creating a story through the image of an island, the artist wants the viewers to feel the picture in front of his eyes and the time and aura itself contained in the picture.

name: Bang Soyun
bio: Bang Soyun’s art challenges the hierarchy between the digital and physical worlds. As a digital native, she moves fluidly between these spaces, treating experiences in both as equally real. Focusing on moments where reality and virtuality overlap, Bang explores human figures as sensory receptors perceiving the world. Her works span painting, video, and augmented reality (AR). Using 3D modeling software, she visualizes independent narratives and transforms them into various forms. Beyond visual representation, her practice reflects on the creative process, recently examining how her ideas interact with AI image-processing algorithms. This exploration is evident in her latest paintings.

name: Tae Ho Kim
bio: FORMATION AND STRUCTURE Kim Tae-Ho's Art Kim Tae-Ho's art until now can be divided largely into three time periods and methods. First, there is the series on

name: Seungean Cha
bio: 'The weaving of her own time, interpreting and reproducing the trend of art in her own way' will be a representative explanation of the world of artist Seungean Cha. She freely explores the past and present time at her will while building bases on research as seen in her five new works

name: Sukhyung Kang
bio: Sukhyung Kang graduated with his MFA from School of Art in London and studied at the San Francisco Art Institute. He mainly explores the primal act of mark-making, translating abstract imagery, subconscious forms, and autobiographical characters into lines and colours. His layered canvases—built through repeated overpainting, scraping, spontaneity, and rhythmic gesture—embody a sense of disorientation and resistance, revealing a longing for freedom. Drawing on the unrestrained gestures of graffiti and the imaginative visual vocabulary of comics, Kang constructs a personal painterly language populated by ghosts, demons, and other spectral figures. These characters invite intuitive responses and emotional release, bypassing the need for complex interpretation. His work has been widely exhibited, including various galleries and art spaces.

name: Tae-Hyun Lee
bio:
My still life paintings, which capture the various traces and memories of our lives, are not simply a pursuit of beauty but an attempt to draw out my inner thoughts and emotions through them.

It could be the scent of a flower, the essence… or a faint breath, of someone who was once with the object.

Through color and composition, I wanted to metaphorically express the messages… and thoughts of the subjects of the paintings but did not want to attempt to explain them explicitly.

The color blue, which I have been using in my recent work, is also a color that represents me.

This blue, which is cold yet deep and warm, combined with the blue-and-white porcelain adds depth of thought and draws me into another space.

name: Shinduk Kang
bio: Korean artist Shinduk Kang is widely known for her sculptures and on-site transparent fabric installation. Kang’s lenticular works is an interesting interpretation of classical still life paintings. She uses lenticular to capture the visual effect. It’s the lenticular lenses that show the illusion of depth, and the ability to change or move as the image is viewed from different angles. Kang’s distinctive style draws from diverse influences working with different mediums; site-specific installations, sculptures, and prints.

name: Yumi Chung
bio:
Yumi Chung explores the threshold between personal and public space through drawing, painting and installation. She has focused on semitransparent objects to contemplate a boundary between the inside and the outside. Her work comes from observations of the ‘outside’ – our surroundings within contemporary society. These observations provide the basis for her to then examine the sensitive boundary of the outer and the inner space.
Chung's paintings describe imaginary scenes based on her memories of observed surroundings. The virtual space created by the memory can appear either strange or familiar and the space is further elaborated by the combination of the colors on canvas. Different from her paintings, her screen work displays a more spatial approach composed of the space created in between the visible and the invisible.

name: Deokhwan Yoon
bio: Yoon Deokhwan creates a new space by recombining various traces from the beautiful impressions and afterimages of the landscape. Stories exist in this space. It is an ordinary daily life and unfolds with small stories, but those moments come together to create one big story. In the utopia he created, we can dream and realize our ideals.

name: Yun Hyong-keun
bio: A leading figure in Korea’s [Dansaekhwa](/gene/dansaekhwa) painting movement, Yun Hyong-keun was renowned for [large-scale canvases](/gene/large-scale-painting) that often feature meditative bands of umber and ultramarine paint. Yun began to develop his visually stark, technically complex style in the early 1970s; he was particularly inspired by [Mark Rothko](/artist/mark-rothko/works-for-sale)’s [color field paintings](/gene/color-field-painting), which he saw on a 1974 trip to New York. He rose to prominence in [Korea](/gene/korea) and represented his country at the 1995 Venice Biennale. Featuring layers of [paint](/gene/oil-painting) on unprimed linen or mulberry bark paper, Yun’s evocative works have been internationally celebrated following his death in 2007. In 2018, the [National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, ](/partner/national-museum-of-modern-and-contemporary-art-korea)hosted a major retrospective of the artist’s work that traveled to the Palazzo Fortuny in Venice. Yun’s work is included in the museum collections of the [Art Institute of Chicago](/artic), the Chinati Foundation, the Glenstone, [Tate Modern](/tate), and the Tokyo Metropolitan Art Museum.

name: Han Unsung
bio:
In the early 1970s, Han Un-sung studied printmaking at the Tyler School of Art in Philadelphia, where he engaged deeply with experimental approaches to media and acquired a wide range of printmaking techniques that were largely inaccessible in Korea at the time. Greedy Giant (1974), which positions a flattened Coca-Cola can collected from the street across the entire picture plane, marked a pivotal moment in the artist’s evolving understanding of the relationship between image and reality.

From the 1990s onward, Han redirected his attention toward life and nature. Through series such as Fruit Gathering and Flowers, he explored primordial forms and cycles of life, attending to the quiet beauty embedded in the transience and impermanence of existence.

Anchored by a sustained curiosity about new technologies, Han has consistently pursued experimental modes of practice. In 1992, he began working with computer drawing using the software Paint Brush, initiating an engagement with digital media that continues into the present. His iPad drawings, begun in 2021, further extend this trajectory. For Han, the transition from the reproducible medium of printmaking to digital drawing did not constitute a rupture, but rather a natural and continuous evolution of his artistic inquiry.

name: Sane Jung
bio:
Sane was born in Seoul in 1985. 2009, she received B.F.A. Painting & Print Making, Ewha Womans
University, Seoul. 2016, she finished M.F.A. Visual Arts, Korea National University of Art. In her
words, She is an interdisciplinary artist. Her work investigates ideas related to how the meanings
are constructed and deconstructed through exploring paradox, irony, humor, affects, and
encounters in everyday life. She tries to reveal the layers composed in an intricate system and
make them visible in decontextualized conditions. By using a diverse range of media, her practice
spans installation, sculpture, performance, video, photography, and painting.

name: Kapim Lee 이갑임
bio:
Healing Time and Space - Alley

The alley, with its past and present scenery, can be seen as much as the streetlights illuminate it.
It's great to be able to paint the alley, which fills my needs and empties my desires, with my heart on canvas.
As I walked through the alley, the moon and the streetlights followed me, cheering me on, saying, "It's okay, you've tried, you're good.
I miss my mum.
The street lamps in the alley are round and the moon is bright.
My mum, who always smiled and hugged me, is also round.
When I enter that place, the alley, I miss my mum even more. I feel sick.
I find healing and hope in alleys.
For me, an alley is a place where I get energy to live, and for me, work is the act of sharing that energy with you.
-Artist Kapim Lee

name: Choonjae Kim
bio:
The Blank Space in Life

Landscapes in Choonjae Kim's works are dark. However, as Paul Klee said “Art does not reproduce the visible, rather, it makes visible,”  Choonjae Kim wishes to show us what is hidden in the landscape rather than the landscape itself. While the darkness emphasizes the landscape, the distant darkness that seems to engulf the landscape ceases all stories. Such silence cannot be recognized by the senses, contemplative meditation, or introspection. The landscape created by the darkness can only be understood through existential self-consciousness because the landscape is created by essentially intuiting reality rather than transcending it.

Choonjae Kim, who majored in Oriental Painting, says that he still works on oriental paintings. Perhaps, this is why his canvas shows the composition of a traditional oriental painting while the blank space is expressed in darkness, leading to a difference from the oriental painting.

The common characteristic that appeared in the process of him transferring traditional oriental paintings to Western paintings is the background, especially the black blank space. This black background goes beyond the expression of emptiness in the blank spaces of the oriental paintings. Additionally, these black blank spaces are very solid in the sense that all thought processes are precisely concentrated.
The dark background does not just simply emphasize the landscape or try to engulf it. Like the “empty space within myself,” the landscape and darkness are like one single body. Since the cause of pain and despair lies in the uncertainty of existence, “contrary thinking” is necessary to find one’s existence in the process of life. Choonjae Kim shows the true landscape through a reversed perspective which is different from the existing one.

name: Inhye Jeong
bio: Jeong Inhye uses a cactus as a motif to fill the frame with subjective tones of colors and rough brush strokes. The style of her paintings lies on the boundary of realism or expressionism, not too naturalistic yet not entirely synthetic as well. The composition and the color are the most imperative aspect in each piece since it portrays the exterior impressions of the cactus. Especially, Jeong pursue a harmonious frame without any distraction or distortion, and sets her own tones and emotions on the canvas. This is why her works are acknowledged to be more than a simple depiction.

name: Myungmi Lee
bio: Myungmi Lee (b. 1950) broke free from the aesthetic conventions of the Korean art world in the 1970s, where monochrome paintings held sway, and established her own unique art world through her use of primary colors as well as her paintings that encompass figurative and abstract art. In addition to her canvas works, she has completed her own style of painting as a platform for playing, healing and communicating—using flat materials such as cloth and paper. The artist mainly uses such everyday objects as cups, chairs, flowers, flowerpots, animals, and people. However, instead of imbuing each object with meaning, she captures the essence of the form using bright and vivid colors, and opts for simple compositions and flat structures with no regard for perspective or gravity. In her recent works, pieces of canvas are either stitched onto different canvas fabric or presented in the form of a collage, thereby emphasizing the artist’s quintessentially carefree approaches. Furthermore, she actively plays with ‘image-text,’ using direct texts and combining images associated with texts and images that contradict the actual characteristics of objects—as if to question the conventional generation of meaning embedded in language. In other words, she substitutes the way we perceive language and image with everyday play, and by doing so, reveals multiple facets.

name: Joo Lee Kang
bio: JooLee Kang focuses on change of ecological environment, transition of living organism, and evolution, created inevitably, to survive together. She interprets complicated interaction between human and nature in various perspectives, asks for understanding and consideration of our possibility and dignity through drawing and mixed installation. JooLee Kang graduated from Tufts University – School of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston in USA and Duksung Women’s University, and held solo exhibitions at Gallery NAGA in the U.S. (2020, 17, 14), Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art (2018), Gallery Chosun (2018), and Korean Cultural Center in Spain (2018). She also participated in curated exhibitions at Seoul Museum of Art - SeMA Storage (2020), Changwon Sculpture Biennale (2020), Amorepacific H.Q. (2019), Suwon Ipark Museum of Art (2018), Fitchburg Art Museum in the U.S. (2018), and Taipei Fine Arts Museum in Taiwan (2017). Kang has been invited as an Artist-in-Residence at Gyeonggi Creation Center (2018), Cheongju Art Studio (2017), Willapa Bay AiR in the U.S. (2015), and Inside-Out Art Museum in China (2014). She is actively working in both the U.S. and Korea now.

name: Mira Song
bio:
Mira Song is an interdisciplinary artist based in Vancouver, BC and Seoul, South Korea and has exhibited in Seoul, Hong Kong, Toronto and Vancouver. 

She holds a Masters of Applied Arts from Emily Carr University of Art + Design, a Certificate in Garden Design from UBC and a BFA from Korea National University in Seoul, South Korea.
 
Song has been featured in the media and magazine including Vancouver Sun, la Source and Magenta Magazine. Her work is in the private collections in Canada, United State and Korea.

name: Eun-Ha Paek
bio:
Brooklyn-based multimedia artist Eun-Ha Paek’s sculptures give physical form to the artist’s inner narratives and personal history, while exploring broader themes of identity and human experience. Paek’s hybrid approach to ceramics is informed by her background in animation and film. Her attempts to roll increasingly smaller, tighter coils eventually lead her to introduce 3D printing to her practice, enabling detail that would not be possible by hand. The resulting pieces, while finally static, are created through a process that in many ways mimics stop motion animation. Paek’s work, across media, investigates questions of identity through storytelling. Hints of recognizable references and motifs are present in her figures, but this host of characters is the unique product of a visual language developed to give shape to the artist’s internal dialogue.

Born in Seoul, Korea, in 1974, Paek currently lives and works in Brooklyn, NY. She received a BFA in Film/Animation/Video from the Rhode Island School of Design, where she has also been a guest lecturer. Paek’s work has been exhibited throughout the United States and internationally, and she is the recipient of several awards and grants including the Windgate Scholarship and Rudy Autio Grant from the Archie Bray Foundation. Paek’s animated films have screened in the Guggenheim Museum, Sundance Film Festival, and venues around the world. She has been a guest lecturer at the Fashion Institute of Technology, a visiting critic at the Maryland Institute College of Art, and she currently serves on the faculty at Parsons School of Design/The New School.

name: Woolim Lee
bio: Woo Lim Lee who was born in 1972 in Kyoungnam Province in South Korea is a Korean Asian Modern & Contemporary painter. He received both his BFA and MFA from Youngnam University. The figures that appear in the mysterious landscape/portrait paintings of Woo Lim Lee project the artist’s utopian desire for protection and insulation from the consequences of a rapidly expanding and fiercely competitive modern world. People look for beauty in nature, heal their wound through nature, and seek repose and meditation within nature. We dream and have a vision of another world through nature. His work is an evocation of the spirituality of modern people derived from their secret, mystic contact with nature. His work is steeped in a longing for mystic power and incantational imagery.

name: MeME
bio:
Artist MeME, who has worked for the South Korean conglomerate Samsung for 18 years, is a leading pop artist blurring the lines between art and life. Her work, grounded in storytelling that resonates with the public as if it were everyday life, transcends all genres, from flat paintings to digital media.

The name "MeME" is a pseudonym that signifies "Problem Me, Solution Me." Beginning with the 2019 Hangaram Art Museum Design Art Fair, MeME has since held numerous solo and group exhibitions. Combining the comic elements of popular art with diverse visual art techniques, including mixed media, flat and three-dimensional representations, MeME presents a hopeful worldview centered on the subjective lives and happiness of modern people. The materials used in all of MeME's works symbolize human subjectivity, transforming artificial environments to overcome biological limitations and create a world of one's own. The object Pigme reflects the fragility of modern people within the confines of contemporary society. Born as a pig with low self-esteem, Pigme is always wary of his surroundings, possessing elongated ears like a rabbit and a timid, small mouth. The heart-shaped goggles symbolize a lighthouse illuminating a paradise of happiness for Pigme, who dreams of joy and soars with passionate energy. Through Pigme's journey to rediscover his lost self-esteem, the character returns to a state of innocence devoid of self-consciousness and builds a surreal utopia for all modern people chasing their dreams.

In 2023, artist Mimi appeared on KBS TV's "No Money, No Art" and achieved a record-breaking auction price of 21 million won. Furthermore, "Pigme" has become widely known not only to art enthusiasts but also to the general public, and has engaged in various collaborations. Through art collaborations with leading brands such as Samsung Galaxy, Lotte Hotel, KDB Industrial Bank, and Shinhan Card, the brand has established its presence among the public.

name: ByungHo Lee
bio: Byungho Lee (1976- ) received his BFA and MFA in Sculpture from Hongik University, Korea. Interested in sculpture of human figures since the onset of his practice, Lee's work attempts to overcome the solid surface of sculpture that's decided at the final stage of its completion and propose sculpture that's always in state of flux and transition. While Lee's recent works mainly take the form of figurative sculpture, he takes the completed sculpture as an object and reinvents it through a process of repeated decomposition and re-composition rather than merely adopting a method of reproduction. Through this process, Lee's sculptural works take on infinite transformation, lacking a finite concept. Lee has held his solo exhibitions STATUE X STATUE (Shangupgallery, Seoul, 2018), and Anthropometry (Space So, Seoul, 2017), and has participated in numerous group exhibitions including Repetition and Difference: About Time (Busan Museum of Art, Busan, 2019), BODY MATTERS: art as discourse, performativity, representation (Seoul Olympic Museum of Art, Seoul, 2016), Busan Biennale 2010 'Living in Evolution' (Busan Museum of Art, Busan, 2010), and Medicine and Art: Imaging a Future for Life and Love (Mori Art Museum, Tokyo, 2009, etc.

name: Seunghee Lee
bio: Seunghee Lee is a master of ceramic art known for his contemporary interpretation of traditional Korean and Chinese ceramics. He was trained in the Craft Design Department at Cheongju University in Korea, where he studied ceramics, fiber craft, dyeing, and tapestry. He creates much of his work in Jingdezhen, in southeastern China, where he established a studio in 2008 in the historic center of Chinese porcelain production. Since the establishment of his studio, he has won international acclaim for his Porcelain Paintings, the Space of 8mm series, and his Bamboo series.
