name: SHIM Moonseup
bio:
The focus of my work is the dynamic symbolism and circularity of movement. The image that materializes the present progressive time and light is a scenery with time. From visible to invisible, and from audible to inaudible, the numerous lines that are seem to be cut off transcend from something to something else to become transcendental. Not everything that is seen is a true nature of reality. Somethings are invisible within the visible, and there are things that are invisible and yet still remain around us. My paintings correspond to the duality of sculptural thinking and pictorial expressions. After painting the canvas with oil, I start to paint with acrylic. Due to the reaction of oil and acrylic, the screen naturally creates the nuances of the unpainted, hidden, erased and exposed parts. The repetition of physical behavior and the coexistence of time and space sensations forges metaphors that suggest many possibilities. As I continue to paint, new and unexpected world creates. My work has a dual nature of drawing and painting. It is a painting by drawing, and a drawing by painting. The lines from the extremely delicate brush strokes make the paint transparent and the paint invigorates the line. The screen is formed by the balance of the conflicts. The painting runs to an infinite world with no beginning or end. The sea is the origin of beauty. 

2019, Shim Moon-seup

name: LEE SANG SUN
bio:
I don't want my paintings to be confined to any genre. Rather than conveying the act of 'drawing' as a special event or story, the artist's job is to convey the mental and emotional agitation felt at that moment. 220813
Conviction in new work leads to innovation. With constant research and practice, there is always something new to do. I don't want a work to be taxidermized. Diversity is the source of novelty. Always looking for newness through various possible attempts. 220131
Someone said that painting is not about looking on their own, but about looking and feeling. I give a careful look at it.
It could be a tree, a sail of a ship, or a back of a lighthouse.
I give a careful look at what it seems.
Then it may change over and over again. As much as the color keeps changing. The boundary of colors without neutral tint are therefore clearer.220123
I fully Concentrate and fill slowly. Then the colors settle delicately. 220117
I wanted to paint little weird. 211102
Draw a picture just to look into. 210927
Father worried that the waves would be strong when the east wind blew. The east wind blows in my hometown of the East Sea. Saturation and brightness is adjusted from 15 basic colors. The brush strokes finely analyze each color surface and finely adjust it. So it makes a rough but smooth picture. A slightly rough base is used to enhance the texture and allows the paint to permeate naturally and blend in juxtaposition with the base color. 210830
I'm not establishing any principle in my work. There is no such thing as 'no'. Throw away all obsession. But I'll be honest about everything including myself. 210728

name: MoMo Kim
bio: Momo Kim captures contemporary life with a sophisticated and romantic perspective through painting, drawing, i-Pad drawing, and installation. She gathers materials found in everyday life and personal experiences to metaphorically express the culture, lifestyle, and identity of people today. The audience discovers familiar subjects in Momo Kim's works. Vases and flowers, mugs, sticky notes, walking paths, and indoor landscapes are the 'things around us' that have gone unnoticed in our lives. Momo Kim conveys that essential values of life exist within these ordinary, mundane objects and scenes, recording the universal beauty of everyday life that can be remembered far into the future. The artist studied illustration at the School of Visual Arts in New York before receiving her MA in Fine Art from the Academy of Art University in San Francisco. She has exhibited in Seoul, New York, Taiwan, and Hong Kong, among others.

name: Wongi Sul
bio: Wongi Sul is a South Korean visual artist born in 1951. Sul studied in the states and earned his MFA at Pratt Institute, NYC, in 1981. Largely inspired by the art movements of the 1970s, Sul’s work offers a reflection to growing questions regarding postmodern thought. The paintings by him are honest and pure, seeking to reach an existential answer to what it means to be an artist and make 'good art.' Sul’s artwork disrupts stereotypes towards painting and artist intentionality. Rather than situating himself among the myriad of contemporary artists who pursue narrative and linguistic interpretation, Sul’s unique approach to painting holds itself with honesty and purity, focusing on the artist’s rhythmic motion and actionality.

name: Vakki
bio: VAKKI pays attention to the energy generated in the process of creating and moving in orbit of countless humans and objects passing by.  By asking questions about the cycle of existence, creation and annihilation, and interpreting surrounding objects as geometric elements, it has been expressed through VAKKI's unique, delightful visual language.  She is active in a wide range of visual arts, exploring video, interactive media, space, three-dimensional installation, and sound.  Based in Seoul, she has held numerous domestic and international showcases and group exhibitions in Amsterdam, Berlin, Thailand, and New York.  She has also held exhibitions and resident artists at the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, National Asia Culture Center, Nam Jun Paik Art Center, and the National Hangeul Meseum.  In domestic exhibitions, the artiest's imagination has been presented in a pleasant visual language.

name: Meekyoung Shin
bio: Meekyoung Shin, who trained in the classical tradition of European sculpture, is known for her ongoing “Translation” project, which explores the processes of translation and mutation—both literal and figurative—undergone by cultural objects that have been subjected to a change in location. Her “Translation Vases” (2009), for example, are soap facsimiles of Chinese originals created for the European market in the 16th through 20th centuries, painstakingly colored, carved, and painted and displayed on shipping crates. For Shin’s “Kouros” series (2009), she modeled archaic and classical sculptures in soap, preserving their cracks, missing limbs, and other defects.

name: JI EUN PARK
bio: Ji eun Park creates a distinctive and lyrical atmosphere by utilizing lacquer and various natural materials. Lacquer is a natural resin varnish derived from the sap of lacquer trees. Her lacquer paintings exhibit uniqueness compared to traditional lacquer works, conveying a rustic yet elegant feeling rather than excessive ornamentation and providing a sense of warmth. The durability and preservation of lacquer have been proven through the long-term preservation of natural lacquer artifacts. Korea's lacquer culture has a deep history dating back to ancient times and continuing to the present day. Ji eun Park first became interested in lacquer during her major in Oriental painting. As her research on lacquer progressed, she became increasingly captivated by its charm and started using it as her primary material. Working in a traditional manner requires a lot of effort, but the artist adheres to this approach. In addition to lacquer, the artworks harmoniously include various natural materials such as soil, eggshells, mother-of-pearl, and gold leaf.

name: Yunzo Paek
bio:
Looking at Yunzo’s painting means tracing the flow of movements of her hands. Hypnotized, questions arise one after another following her strokes, asking what tools she held, where they landed, and what they engraved. “It was done in flow” The artist notes. “For freedom and fun.” She continues. 
The development of mankind was possible for the leap done by the ultimate tool: the hands. Its function was formed by numerous training nurtured by the coveted knowledge, recording faces and shapes passing through, the words heard, and the thoughts lingering in the mind.
We go on such quests day by day, yet Yunzo steps in to sweep them down like a slide with layers of instincts that speak beyond consciousness. Bold brush strokes and forms penetrate through piles of thoughts, and her figures form a march on the canvas with voices of her precious people and surroundings, along with her memories. Just as our faces changing freely to the circumstances, her objects form a variety of expressions embracing and pushing each other simultaneously. 
The Face series captures parts of this with a gesture of triviality. From comical figures to the maverick with a hat, various appearances are portrayed as a static variable of everyday scenes. These faces bloom in every corner of the space and vitalize with a sense of kitsch, giving a grin to the viewers.
Among them, certain objects whimsically land in the center of the canvas. These figures take audacious steps through the background without looking for the destination, sometimes with hope, sometimes with nebulosity, as if it continues to mark the passing of time.

name: Minjeong Guem
bio: Minjeong Guem was born in Seoul, Korea in 1977. She studied in Hongik University in Sculpture (BFA, MFA) in Seoul, Korea. She is known for media artist. She deconstructs and modifies where she is standing with her imagination and the space that she transform is a video within the screen, and she enjoys thinking and handling this in a material way. In the video, her story is unfolded and another new story is created by structurally deconstructing, transforming and/or reconstructing the space. She participated in several public art projects in Seoul and Busan, and residency programs in Green River project-Korea/Taiwan Exchange Artist Residency in Taiwan, The National Art Studio Goyang in Korea since 2007. The works are owned by various places, including Seoul Museum of Art, Museum of Contemporary Art Busan, Kumho Museum of Art, and National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art.

name: Kim Whanki
bio: A pioneer of [abstraction](/gene/abstract-art) in Korea, [Kim Whanki](/artist/kim-whanki) is revered for his dense dot paintings that appear to radiate outward. Kim is widely considered the godfather of [Dansaekhwa](/gene/dansaekhwa) —Korea’s monochrome painting movement —and his predominantly blue palette has inspired the term “Whanki Blue.” Soothing blue tones fill his most famous work *05-IV-71 \#200 (Universe)* (1971), which was shown at the 1975 São Paulo Bienal and fetched $13.1 million in 2019. While studying in Tokyo in the 1930s, he was exposed to the works of [Henri Matisse](/artist/henri-matisse/) and [Pablo Picasso](/artist/pablo-picasso/). He later lived in New York and met [color field painters](/gene/color-field-painting) like [Mark Rothko](/artist/mark-rothko) and [Barnett Newman](/artist/barnett-newman/). Still, Kim’s paintings are rooted in his native home, nodding to the blues found in Korea’s countryside; he also painted traditional Korean motifs like plum blossoms and moon jars. In 1992, his foundation established the Whanki Museum in Seoul, which holds most of his work.

name: JeeYoung Lee
bio: Working within the confines of her single-room studio, [JeeYoung Lee](/artist/jeeyoung-lee-1/works-for-sale) builds [immersive](/gene/immersive) environments that explore her innermost thoughts. Her dizzying, [surrealistic](/gene/surrealism) installations are often inspired by traditional Korean fables and childhood memories; Lee photographs herself in them before destroying her creations. Early career recognition came in 2011, when Lee was a finalist for the Sovereign Asian Art Prize. She has continued to build on the body of work that she’s titled “Stage of Mind,” creating her own props for elaborate, theatrical spaces. Populated with paperclips, mice, eggs, and other idiosyncratic motifs, they explore themes of joy, anger, anxiety, and the subconscious. Lee does not digitally manipulate her images, which exist as the sole documentation of her laborious handiwork.

name: Mihei Her
bio: Mi-Hei Her is born in Seoul, Korea, 1968. She studied in Pantheon, Paris-Sorbonne University in department of Painting (BFA, MFA, DEA, Ph.D.) and had over 20 solo shows since 2003 in France and Korea. Her very delicate work is known and loved all over the world. Public and private collections of her works are in Seoul, Paris, Amsterdam, Miami, Vienna, Salt Lake City, New York and more.

name: Koo Bohnchang
bio: Bohnchang Koo captures still and fragile moments, attempting to reveal the unseen breath of life. After returning to Korea in 1985, he has been working without boundaries between fine art and commercial photography. With a minimalist approach, Bohnchang Koo photographed a large number of abandoned objects that passed by in time. In the mid-1980s, documentary photography in South Korea still occupied a dominant position in the era. Bohnchang Koo's works convey that photography can select and deconstructs reality according to the needs of artistic demands instead of only expressing meanings by capturing scenes in life. From the beginning of Bohnchang Koo, the following Korean photography artists paid more attention to narrative factors in photography and the cultural relevance in their works.

name: Lee Kun-Yong
bio: Throughout his multidisciplinary, process-based practice, Lee Kun-yong maintains a conceptual commitment to capturing the body’s movement through space. Lee, who is widely considered one of the fathers of Korean performance art, prioritizes concept over finished product throughout his paintings, performances, videos, sculptures, and installations. In his series “The Method of Drawing,” for example, he “performs” the act of gestural drawing in front of an audience. For *Snail’s Gallop* (1979/2017), he turned his body into an instrument, squatting on the floor and making marks as he moved forward. Lee helped establish two collectives in the mid–20th century: the Avant-Garde Group and the Space and Time Group. His work belongs in the collections of the [Seoul Museum of Art](/partner/the-seoul-museum-of-art), the Daegu Art Museum, the Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art, the [Tate](/partner/tate), and the Rachofsky House. In 2020, Lee was featured in [The Artsy Vanguard](/article/artsy-editorial-artsy-vanguard-2020-lee-kun-yong).

name: Soyung Lee
bio: Soyung Lee is an artist based in Seoul and Paris. Lee majored in design at Seoul National University and flew to Paris to study Visual Communication and received MFA in DSAA (Diplôme Supérieur d’Arts Appliqués) at ENSAAMA (École Nationale Supérieure des Arts Appliqués et des Métiers d’Arts Olivier de Serres). She further studied Arts of Image and the Living(Arts de l'image et du vivant) and received Research Master's Degree(Master 2 Recherche) at Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Soyung Lee was selected as the "Illustrator of the Year" at the 2014 Bologna Children's Book Fair(BCBF), and is active not only in picture books and illustrations but also in various mediums such as watercolor, oil painting, and printmaking. She has created numerous picture books, including

name: Lee Heedon
bio:
Lee Heedon combines hanji and paint to create a distinctive, Korean-inspired materiality, focusing on the medium’s autonomous movements and the forms that emerge from it. The semi-solid paint seeps and intertwines across the canvas, producing unpredictable shapes that symbolize yeon (緣)—the various relationships and connections encountered throughout life.

Through the repetitive act of layering paint, the artist expresses an internal flow that begins with the self and expands outward toward the world. The spreading movements of the paint reveal a desire to communicate beyond the material, suggesting a sense of resonance and connection between all beings. In this way, Lee’s work becomes a visual space that embodies the relational nature of human experience.

name: JINPYO JUN
bio:
Jun Jin-pyo graduated from Dankook University College of Arts with a bachelor's and master's degree and completed a doctorate at Hongik University. The artist has seven private exhibitions and he has exhibited Seoul and New York. 
His paintings are comprised of a myriad of lines, and the spaces created by those lines.  They embody an everlasting process that does not have a finished form.  A line is a boundary that separates a space and connects the viewer's gaze to another space. The space created a line is limitless. Objects that have finished forms take only one form, and once they reach that finished form, their completion is recognizable. But in his work, the spaces formed by lines are identified only through the colors filling those spaces, and they continue in perpetuity.

name: Minsoo Kang
bio:
Through my work, I reflect on myself. Each canvas holds a story—sometimes mine, sometimes someone else’s. It may carry my emotions, or those of another.
I blend traditional and contemporary elements in my practice. Inspiration comes from Buddhist philosophy, Buddhist art, Korean folk paintings (minhwa), and ink wash painting. At the same time, I draw from modern sources such as fashion and trends. My work also explores realistic concerns and imaginative questions like “What would I look like in another world?”
My process is entirely planned from start to finish. I avoid randomness and focus on composition and structure. I favor pencil drawing, repeating countless sketches until the final piece emerges. The result is completed with vibrant obangsaek (five traditional Korean colors) and refined techniques.
I mainly depict figures in action, and often aim to express their emotions. However, I deliberately avoid realistic portrayals of faces and expressions. I believe each figure carries a soul, and I want them to serve as storytellers rather than objects of worship. I do not want viewers to interpret the narrative solely through facial expressions. Therefore, I conceal faces or use layered petals as metaphors for emotion.

name: Minhee Kim
bio: Bringing images without narratives, Minhee Kim has experimented with how those paused pictures or endlessly looped frames could be inserted in ‘paintings.’ she attempts to explore the future by looking through the images from the past, so employ the artistic resources from anime or manga and directly apply on the artworks. The paintings have been affected by Japanese cel animation from the 1980s to 1990s, so they are aiming to embody the textures of that period. She could see the future through transparent and dry texture and analogue technique in cel animation rather than digital’s fancy colour scheme and hybridised effects. As like her previous solo show

name: Minyoung Kim
bio: Minyoung Kim explores feelings of both anxiety and regret in dreamlike compositions, channeling personal experiences into her painting practice. Kim’s paintings appear both eerie and lighthearted, featuring recurring motifs of moons, flowers, knives, and anthropomorphic characters. By applying cartoon-like expressions to inanimate objects, Kim transforms scenes from everyday life into sinister moments. There are elements of mystery in Kim’s narratives, conveyed through shadows, muted colors, and an almost blurred finish. Her unsettling paintings echo her own personal cynicism, calling attention to the complexities of modern society. Her process starts with drawings on paper before she begins applying acrylic paint onto unstretched canvases. Kim received a BA in painting and an MFA in printmaking from Sungshin Women’s University. She also holds an MFA in painting from the Slade School of Fine Art. Kim has exhibited her work at [Woaw](https://www.artsy.net/partner/woaw) in Hong Kong and at [Taymour Grahne Projects](https://www.artsy.net/partner/taymour-grahne-projects) in London.

name: Chanoo Park
bio:
Park Chanoo was born in Daegu and grew up in Busan and Seoul. He majored in photography at Seoul Institute of the Arts and began his career assisting photographer Bae Bien-U. He opened his own studio, “Studio ZIP” in 1990, and creates photographs for corporate advertising, magazines including “Home living & Style”, “Luxury”, and “Style H”, and for several architects and designers.
Park travels to natural settings to gather stones, and wanders urban areas, making photographs to support his themes of “Stones”, “Walls”, and “Windows”.

The artist has four private exhibitions experience and he has exhibited in Seoul and Singapore. His works have been acquired by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (Korea) and the Gwangju Museum of Art.

name: Sijong Kim
bio:
Kim Sijong is an artist based in Seoul and London. He studied Media and Public relations at Yonsei University, Seoul, and then received MA for sculpture at Royal College of Art, London. He mainly communicates through photography. By creating composite portrait images or Still Life series that resemble collages of disparate subjects, he has crafted photographic works that appear more like paintings than realistic photographs. Using the camera not as a tool for capturing moments but as a medium for creating new imagery, Kim often seems more like a painter with a camera in his hand, instead of a brush.
Meanwhile, Kim takes a step further by embracing traditional painting materials—brushes and canvases on recent works. Unlike his photographs, which undergo meticulous shooting and editing processes, his paintings naturally and sincerely reflect spontaneous emotions or inner thoughts that arise in his daily life, evoking empathy from viewers. While he works across various media, the overarching theme of his art revolves around identity.
Having experienced various cultures due to frequent relocations from a young age, Kim explores themes such as identity, belonging, and settlement in his work, fostering a sense of connection with the lives of modern individuals.
