name: Byung Jin Kim
bio:
Byung Jin Kim graduated from Suwon University (Major in Sculpture), who joined numerous group exhibitions in galleries and art fairs; also hosted several solo exhibitions in Korea and one in Taiwan. He is an awarded and acclaimed artist in South Korea, which the works are collected by several private collections, such as National Museum of Contemporary Art, Philos Hotel, The Sculpture Park in Gangwon Land and Suwon District Court etc.

His work is composed of countless letters, logos, or shapes that build into another figure. His work are highly elaborate and time consuming. The artwork is first given its initial look through 3D digital imaging or sketches. Based on the sketch, Kim creates the shape using clay, plaster, or FRP plastic. On top of this base shape, he painstakingly molds together these countless shapes or letters in steel to create the exact same shape of the clay. After careful sanding of the molded areas, he layers multiple high quality car paint over an extended period of time while heating at 200 degrees in a kiln. Kim says he finds truthfulness in this labor intensive nature of his work.

name: Yeonsoon Chang
bio: Korean artist, Chang Yeonsoon, known for creating ethereal works of starched indigo, was Artist of the Year at the National Museum of Contemporary Art in Seoul in 2008. She was a finalist for the Loewe prize in 2018. Her work has also been acquired by the Victoria & Albert Museum in London; she is the first South Korean artist in that collection.

name: Jeong Daun
bio: Jeong Daun(b.1987 in Seoul, South Korea) studied Western painting both in undergraduate and graduate programs at Dongduk Women's University in Seoul, South Korea. Although she majored in painting, she uses fabric as a material of artistic expression instead of stereotypical materials of painting to expand the concept into space beyond the stereotype of painting. Pieces of slit fabric stand for Jeong's brushstrokes. Space in her work is filled with fabrics that move beyond the edge of a canvas or are set directly in space. The audience is able to experience a material property's harmony with three-dimensional space molded by the fabric's two-dimensional surface encountering another plane. Jeong has participated in various exhibitions, art fair collaborations with the fashion brand in Korea, Asia and Europe. Her representative artwork is an installation making use of one of the six poles which is 10.8 meters hight supports the museum's roof of the Museum SAN building designed by Ando Tadao. She also has dond a permanent installation at the International Finacial Center in Quanzhou, China in 2022. Her artworks are collected by Hana Financial Group, NongHyup Bank, Vista Walkerhill Seoul, 63 Art Museum, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power, Hyundai  Industrial Development

name: Sa Hara
bio: Sa Hara is a Korean artist born in 1975 who lives and works in Seoul, South Korea. She is graduated with a bachelor’s degree in business administration at Dongguk University. Through Physical Theatre, the artist explores how characters reflect one another, expressing freedom and imagination through bodily performance. With a keen interest in the movement of the human body, observations are transformed into unique works that convey the unrestricted freedom of the mind. Each work contains a narrative, featuring characters and networks of relationships. These relationships are not confined by social or legal structures but instead reflect a worldview of relative freedom. Using the non-verbal language of bodily movement, the characters perform as if on stage, reflecting each other, becoming aspects of one another, and giving rise to thoughts and actions, thus existing through each other and forming the whole. The artist draws inspiration from human movement, real-life stories of relationships, fictional novels, and videos on Instagram and YouTube. Plants, books, music, dance, and various forms of art also provide intellectual stimuli, which are combined with imagination to create the works.

name: Jungjin Lee
bio: Jungjin Lee is internationally revered for breathtaking [black-and-white photographs](/gene/black-and-white-photography) that evoke a deep, meditative state. In her practice, Lee has concentrated on capturing vast, expansive [landscapes](/gene/landscape-photography) from around the globe, from deserts to oceans to mountains. She is interested in eternity and exploring how the landscape might reflect inner emotional states. Working with large-format cameras and printing on handmade mulberry paper, Lee is also known for her technical craftsmanship. Lee began photographing in the 1980s while studying ceramics at Hongik University. In 1991 she graduated from New York University with an MFA in photography. She soon after worked as an assistant to acclaimed photographer [Robert Frank](/artist/robert-frank/works-for-sale). By 1996 her work was regularly exhibited at major institutions, including the [Musée d’Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris](/partner/musee-dart-moderne-de-la-ville-de-paris), the [Whitney Museum of American Art](/partner/whitney-museum-of-american-art-1), and the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](/partner/los-angeles-county-museum-of-art). In 2021, Lee participated in the Bienal de São Paulo.

name: Hari Im
bio:
Im Hari is an artist based in Seoul. The main character in her artwork, "Furry Bread" is created by the artist, as a young mother raising a baby. Furry Bread is a wild being, with an appearance resembling a kitten, that communicates with the exclamation "Paang!"(a pronunciation of the word ‘bread’ in Korean). The abundant fur of the Furry Breads symbolizes the ultimate loveliness. Fur is soft, warm, and it delicately stimulates the sense of touch on skin. Fur represents emotional comfort and intimate communication through gentle touch. Beings covered with fur can bridge the intellectual and emotional gaps between themselves and others, forming a harmonious and complete synchronization without discord.
Im Hari learned from her child, that the true essence of humanity is to be able to love, trust, and accept someone wholeheartedly. The Furry Bread is truly a “communication wizard”, and that was our original form. Im Hari encourages us to reestablish "the sense of fur" - the tenderness - deep within our hearts through the cute creatures. It is the "sense of communication," in other words, love.
Im Hari studied painting at Sejong University. Her solo shows were held in Gallery Ichon, The Necessaries, Gallery DOS, and she had group shows in many other galleries, art museums, and art fairs including the KIAF 2024. She mainly works and exhibits in South Korea, expanding to other regions in Asia and Northern America.

name: Choi Byung Jin
bio:
The Portrait Series has been an ongoing body of work since approximately 2015. The early portraits centered on the artist’s personal and corporeal experiences of obsession, understood as both psychological and physical symptoms rooted in lived experience.

In more recent works, this framework has expanded to address a broader and more persistent emotional condition: anxiety. This shift marks a transition from the articulation of individual experience to the visualization of a more generalized affect, revealing the moment at which personal emotion extends beyond the self and assumes a collective resonance.

Each portrait—identified by an individual serial number—is overlaid with geometric structures that envelop the figure’s face and body. These forms emerge from the artist’s sustained inquiry into the nature of existence and the question of how the self may be constituted, perceived, and objectified.

name: Jinwook Yeom
bio: JinWook Yeom was born in Busan, Korea, 1964. She graduated Pusan National University in department of Painting as major. She now lives and works in Busan, Korea. Her works are collected by National Museum of Contemporary Art in Seoul, Busan Museum of Contemporary Art, Faberge Museum in St. Petersburg and many private collectors. The work of Yeom is characterized by the unique expression of the perception not only the artist but we experience in front of the landscape that would not allow description. Her painting employs an ordinary medium we call oil painting on canvas and the signifiers are an apparent profusion of mountains and trees. Ironically enough, however, she turns away from the shapes of the dense forest mountains and trees create. She represents a spectacle in pure memory. This spectacle avoids perspective and realistic description of the objects.

name: WONKUN JUN
bio:
The young Korean artist Wonkun Jun, who graduated from Düsseldorf Arts Academy in 2004 as a master student of Helmut Federle, describes his pictures as sentiments, as mirrors of his emotions. His partly monochrome color space paintings carry a very personal thumbprint. He does not try to hide the brushstroke, but develops his principle as a painter by way of his brushwork. Through the multi-layered application of thin acryl paint on white-grounded canvasses he develops a color space that exudes a peculiar fascination on the spectators. The surface, which attains a kind of vividness because of the oftentimes coarse structure of the canvas and minute color particles, is given a grid- or line-structure through the brushwork, bestowing an individual rhythm on every picture. 

Jun calls this the representation of emotional moderation. He employs a rinsing technique that creates a color flow from a single stroke of the brush. The colors that are ultimately seen are the result of a long-lasting process of reduction. Starting with shades of black, the artist continuously brightens the picture until, at last, new basic colors are formed which are frequently converted into white. The colors themselves appear as delicate veils on the canvas. Spectators are almost led to believe that they can understand the painterly process and can perceive the various applications of color underneath the surface structure. The result of this process are paintings of poetic beauty and sensual profundity. For Wonkun Jun, an infinitely continued emotional change is reflected by them, a process of moderation leading to a kind of beauty determined by the composition of colors and their repetition.

name: Kappao
bio:
Kappao received another BFA at Brera National Academy in Italy after she studied sociology. She majored in diversely such as painting, photography, craft, sculpture etc. She has been regarded as promising artist as her witted, humorous and colorful objets have been widely celebrated. 
She has held solo exhibitions in numerous galleries and institutions, including The White Gallery in Milan, Galleria Patricia Armociada in Milan, Noblesse Collection in Seoul, and Lotte Gallery in Seoul, among many others. Moreover, as she is the emerging artist, she’s been collaborated with Chason Hotel in Jeju, USM, Living Design Fair in Seoul, APELGAMO ART Campaign and Samsung Galaxy Note.

name: Lee Kiyoung
bio:
Lee Kiyoung, an artist renowned for reinterpreting traditional Korean painting through contemporary visual language, has a process central to their work that involves layering time, action, and thought on Korean paper. This artist accumulates the traces of time and thought through a repetitive process of filling the paper with ink cake, erasing it, and then refilling it.

The final stage of their work is to carve out intricate lines with a sharp knife in a state of utmost concentration and fill these lines with pigment. These deep and intense colored lines, initially hidden within the ink cake-darkened Korean paper, subtly emerge, encouraging closer examination of the artwork. Geometric shapes, like rectangles, transcend the ink cake background, creating a space that appears transcendental yet empty.

Lee Kiyoung's works, derived from deep contemplation on human life, present a unique aesthetic not commonly found in contemporary art. The harmony of ink cake and negative space, the pinnacle of flatness that the surface exudes, and the combination of geometric lines all come together to communicate a unique beauty. Their art, akin to a practice of meditation, offers an aesthetic of emptiness through the endless act of erasure.

• Professor of Korean Painting at Ewha Womans University
• Collections : National Museum of Contemporary Art, Seoul Museum of Art, Korean Embassy in Israel, Korean Embassy in Finland, etc.

name: EVAN 최석현
bio:
Artist EVAN's works always depict moments like a fairy tale. His work makes you feel as if you are in a dream. EVAN has enjoyed telling stories in his various doodles and drawings since he was a child. EVAN inherited the artistic talents of his uncle who worked as a car designer abroad, his mother who is an art director, his father who is a cinematographer, and his grandmother who was a dancer. He was born with a sense of expressing his own unique and vivid colors, his paintings seem to have the power to arouse a richer imagination in the viewer due to his sensual colors.
When EVAN was young, he was inspired and motivated to become a full time artist while he got the opportunity to  collaborate with a famous Chinese artist Yue Minjun for the world's largest solo exhibition in Korea. After his experience at this world class event, he went on to work on the WONDERLAND SERIES which is full of unique and sensual stories.

ONCE UPON A TIME …
Once upon a time… there lived a boy who drew mysterious and fairytale-like moments.
The boy would fall asleep leaning on the moon, dance under the starlight, and play with the sun and shadows.
Sometimes he would overhear the whispers of his friends in the forest about their daily lives and love stories, and he would capture their stories on the canvas and tell them to others.
The fairytale world which the boy drew is filled with mysterious and beautiful moments. He uses magical colors that make the viewers dream happy dreams.
Everyone has their own story. The story can be a dream or a fairytale. It is a mixture of recollections unique to each individual.
These recollections can even be their “love at first sight “
The boy hopes that adults will find a memory that will give them strength, and encouragement for the world ahead. He also hopes that they can forget about all their worries in this busy modern world and have a moment of relaxation while observing his paintings...

name: SEONGMIN AHN 안성민
bio:
Seongmin Ahn

Seongmin Ahn received her B.F.A. and M.F.A. in Asian traditional painting from Seoul National University in Seoul Korea and then received her second M.F.A from Mount Royal, Maryland Institute College of Art. With practical experience and deep understanding of tradition, her work takes Asian traditional painting as starting point and transforms it into something experimental with her own interpretation bridging tradition and contemporary, and East and West.

Ahn held numerous exhibitions, nationally and internationally, including solo shows at Delaware Center for the Contemporary Arts (Wilmington, DE), Queens College Art Center (Flushing, NY), Wong Center, and Stony Brook University (Long Island). She also participated in and contributed to big projects such as, Power and Pleasure of Possessions in Korean Painted Screens (Wang Center, Stony Brook University), Garden (National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea), and Hanji Project: Hanji Metamorphoses (curated by Yu-Yeon Kim, numerous location in Chelsea). 

Ahn is a two times grant recipient of the Pollock Krasner Foundation Grant and the first prize winner from the AHL Foundation, Visual Art Competition. Her exhibition has been also reviewed on Washington Post (Washington D.C.), the Philadelphia Inquirer, NY Arts Magazine, Baltimore Sun (Baltimore), Plain Dealer (Cleveland) and other press outlets. 

Ahn has taught numerous art classes and workshops at cultural institutes in New York area, including but not limited to, Art Students League, School of Visual Art, Queens Museum, Metropolitan Museum, Asia Society, Stony Brook University, Fashion Institute and Technology, Korea Society, and Korean Cultural Service.

name: Minki Kang
bio:
Kang Minki is creating a new genre, "steel paintings" with the theme of "the sculpture+paintings". It is a technique to express the three-dimensional effect of modeling and the matière of the painting by placing a stainless steel object on a stainless steel plate like a canvas. The artist conveys ‘relationships’ and ‘internal changes’ through his works. In the recent series "Ma Monde", he three-dimensionally expresses the brush touch of various colors that contrast with a flat background which means society. He says that he wants to live an independent life with his own color in the world like the title of the “Ma Monde”, not a life being led in the frame of society. His works, which have strong design elements such as concise expression and sensuous color, suit everywhere in modern spaces, especially satisfying the sensibilities of the younger generation.


CV
The artist obtained a master's degree in Sculpture from Sungshin University. He held six solo exhibitions at Mansion9, Jeongsu Art Center, etc., and participated in numerous group exhibitions and art fairs. He received the "Emerging Artist Award" at 2021 BIAF New Wave., and also won numerous awards in the Grand Art Exhibition of Korea, the Invitational Exhibition of Modern Korea Sculpture, etc. He is loved through various activities like artist collaboration of single album covers with Sound Kim and Home zone.

name: Park Sang Mi
bio:
Park Sangmi’s work is grounded in contemplations on nature, while adopting a mode of discourse that addresses nature as it exists within spaces shaped by the contemporary era. Based on situations and emotions rooted in individual histories, she intervenes in scenes from everyday life, developing planar works in which plants serve as metaphors.
At the center of her work are achromatic plants. These ink-rendered plants are situated within spaces composed of diverse colors. On the pictorial plane, Park orchestrates scenes of coexistence in which three elements—monochromatic plants, spatial structures, and color—are brought into harmonious balance. This sense of “coexistence” conveyed in her work, revealed through nature and space, as well as through atmosphere and emotion, extends warm greetings and quiet consolation, prompting reflection on a path toward harmony. The calm and comforting palette and composition, where plants imbued with the deep resonance of ink coexist with gentle colors, offer a subtle sense of solace and repose.

name: Seok Ho Kim
bio:
Sometimes the person I meet feels a little unfamiliar. It seems like this person is perhaps a collection of other people's memories. They exist narrowly as an identity of a person or the role of the person, and broadly as an identity in a social network where actual senses are not present. I feel that these various beings are constantly colliding with the multiple, simultaneous identity, so I draw the portrait of the state of self-conflict caused by the multiple internal identities. 

  I find a model that matches the image I thought of, photograph him/her, scan it and obtain the image. I visually relocate the person's space, color, and collage and then transfer them to a canvas. My work is formatively elaborate but unlike the hyper-realism, which renders a completed image on to the canvas, I proceed my work by borrowing the method of collage, synthesis and realistic methods. This work tells us about the other side of the story and the multiple identities that are spoken having its base on reality. 

  The distorted portrait series talks about the restricted reality trapped inside the screen, the present state of which self-realization conflicts with reality, and the sense uncertainty felt by modern people. It may be inevitable that modern people living today have complex thoughts and chaotic identities, because humans adjust to the given environment. Just as we do, however, we hope that it will serve as an opportunity to take a closer look at ourselves.

name: Gwon Osang
bio:
GWON Osang is a sculptor who has constantly questioned the identity of the sculpture and tried to converge new experimental media into the new form structure. His varied approach for exploring the existence of sculptures is composed of five series, Deodorant Type, The Sculpture, The Flat, New Structure, and Relief. The "deodorant type" was shaped in ‘ISO-pink(hardened Styrofoam)’ to break the notion that sculpture must be heavy, and the outer edges were covered with hundreds of photographs directly taken or collected for supporting light sculptures and expanded the sculpture while presenting new materials. 

"The Sculpture" is a series that unravels the meaning of traditional sculptures that try to realize the ideal of the time in the closest proximity to reality. Considering the definition of sculpture by using bronze, a traditional material of sculpture, to bring the high-value consumers, the ideal of the 21st century such as Lamborghini and Bugatti, close to the actual shape but makes the surface treatment which has not been refined, unlike the traditional method. "New Structure" is a series of works that have been expanded to three dimensions by adding Alexander Calder's Stabile concept to the "Plat" series. The series, which mainly occupies space with aluminum structures, adds to the characteristics of existing image acquisition and placement, and artist who travels between 2D and 3D, the question of "the relationship between sculpture and space". The latest series, "Relief," is a new method of traditional carving, by building the two-dimensional plane in three dimensions, after realizing the exclusive image collection and arrangement on a flat, original version.

name: Kim Eull
bio: Kim Eull (b. 1954), is centered on drawing transmitted via a variety of mediums including objects, paintings and installations, in an attempt to give form to contours of his deepest thoughts and ideas. For the artist, drawing is not just an art form, but also the accompanying emotions of life that are later transferred to the drawing.

name: Yang, Jung Soo 양정수
bio:
The emotions that we humans experience throughout our lives are incredibly diverse.
When I observe myself, various energies constantly vibrate within me, and there are moments when accepting pain feels beautiful. My work is a journey towards mental liberation and freedom, driven mainly by things that are not visible; my intuition, as well as the curiosity and affection for myself and the world. Moreover, I believe a civilization that can be understood and empathized with the heart is one that we must strive for, our destiny. The earth, the universe, culture, us. We are interconnected.
Through my work, I want to share a series of ongoing processes of progress together.
We will continue to evolve, savor and move forward, and I want to keep the doors of fantasy wide open until the end of my world.

name: Hyegyun Kim
bio:
Kim Hye-Gyun articulates the multifaceted scenes of everyday life—familiar yet often overlooked—through sculptural objects arranged on shelves. Her works consistently feature rounded, endearing human figures alongside various everyday objects. These figures evoke the form of a roly-poly toy or resemble Matryoshka dolls, in which one figure is nested within another.
In her practice, the doll functions as a central motif symbolizing both the origin of existence and the relational nature of being. Although the self may appear singular, it is shaped by the multiple roles one inhabits within the intertwined structures of family and society. Individuals exist within an ongoing lineage—linking oneself to one’s mother, and her mother before her—and thus cannot be understood as isolated entities. The sculptural form of layered dolls contained within a larger figure represents the self as constituted through these continuous and inseparable relationships.
Through her work, She seeks to convey narratives born of perpetual encounters and relationships, and of lives lived collectively within shared experiences.

name: Jiyeon Song
bio:
Song Ji-Yeon's artistry is deeply rooted in self-observation and urban life. Her paintings capture the essence of daily city existence through a unique blend of familiarity and mystery. Seeing Seoul's cityscape as a living, breathing entity, Ji-Yeon's work offers serene yet complex reflections of urban life. She employs a detached, contemplative viewpoint, inviting viewers to share in her perspective of the city, transforming mundane settings into serene, lyrically complex spaces.

 Her approach to painting involves a thoughtful process of adding and removing layers, a method that embodies introspection and reflection. This technique narrates stories of time and existence, revealing the depth and nuances of urban life. In Ji-Yeon's hands, the urban landscape becomes a natural habitat, not a series of challenges but a setting for a life fully embraced. Her work offers fresh perspectives on contemporary realities, making the ordinary cityscape a subject of intriguing exploration.

 After graduating from Hongik-University, Song Ji-Yeon has made a significant mark in the art world, participating in over 50 Art Fairs across Seoul, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Busan, and holding more than 10 solo exhibitions in cities like Seoul and Paris. Her unique vision captures the essence of city life, offering viewers a portal into scenes that are both deeply personal and universally relatable.

name: Hyojin Park
bio:
Hyojin Park was born in Andong, Korea in 1974. She studied in Ewha Woman's University in Sculpture (BAF, MFA) in Seoul, and got a Master's degree at Goldsmith college, University of London, UK. She examines human desires and expresses her utopia by utilizing the phenomenon of coincidence and inevitability through the method of flowing resin.
She was invited to a special exhibition at the Saatchi Gallery in London in 2019, where she collaborated with Roland Mouret and received great attention. She presents works that want to break down the boundaries between sculptures and paintings through various colors.

name: Jukhee Kwon
bio: By manually shredding pages of abandoned and unused books with great precision and patience, Jukhee Kwon creates waterfall-like hanging sculptures. Kwon is fascinated by the transformation of ordinary objects into non-ordinary ones: the closed book opens expanding itself from a reading material into a new object taking on a new existence, both physical and metaphorical. Through a process of de-construction and creation, the artist strips the book back to its very primary material, lending the sculptural forms an arborescent quality.Not every book captures Kwon’s attention however. “Abandoned”, vintage or simply worn books that have a story, in the sense of previous ownership, in addition to the tale written inside are the treasures Jukhee looks for. As much as her creativity modifies the physical appearance of an old book, it also alters its story and its meaning. The closed book opens: the words, finally free, spring out invading the space; the sentences are broken, but new sentences and new meanings are created. The words do not follow any grammatical logic nor there is even a need for one. The full meaning of the book is lost and the shredded paper looks like a disembowelled mess but a new object is born, inspiring a profound sense of wonder.

name: Park Youngsook
bio: PARK Youngsook (1941-2025) studied originally History at the Sookmyung Women's University where she also completed her graduate studies in Photography and Design. She began to exhibit photography works in 1966 and her then extraordinary female awareness was visualized in a certain exhibition, in 1975. It was her solo exhibition organized by ‘Women’s Association’ to commemorate ‘International Women’s Year’, established by the United Nations. PARK exhibited various photographs subjectifying social issues including women’s reality today under the theme of

name: Jae Hyun Lee
bio:
Jae Hyun Lee expresses “cynical realism” through figuration and abstraction, translating inner states. 

His artistic practice and process are inspired by his childhood memories spent in a small and pretty moon village. People with colourfully coloured faces, animals, and objects interpreted in a paranoid and straightforward manner, coexist and express themselves as the artist and someone else. He emphasises texture and layers, while the painting frame, completed by welded and painted on metal, is also a part of his artworks.

name: DuRi Baek
bio:
Duri Baek’s paintings focus on the interaction of light and shadow as a way to reflect on everyday dualities. Using mostly green and yellow acrylic, she depicts natural scenes, trees, rocks, and roots, where light filters through and suggests shifts in time, mood, and attention. Her work often explores contrasts such as concealment and exposure, chance and intention, and how these forces shape perception.

Born in 1984 in Seoul, Baek studied visual communication design at Hongik University. She has held solo exhibitions including Cheon-yi at CDA Gallery (2023) and Light Collector at Gallery MARCHH (2022), and participated in group shows in Seoul, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Tokyo. Her work has also been shown at art fairs like Art Busan and THE PREVIEW SEONGSU. In addition to painting, Baek has published illustrated books related to her visual practice.

name: Kyumin Hwang
bio: Kyumin Hwang (b. 1992) was born in Daejeon, South Korea, and focuses on the instinctive five senses that can be felt in screens, spaces, and objects that encourage erotic imagination. By recording and re-sensing the body through the process of visualization and tactilization, Hwang attempts to explore the body that has been sensed against the body that resists it, and the body that is being encroached upon to be sensed. His selected exhibitions are the solo exhibition 'Adultery Mural (2023, Dongyanjang, Daejeon)', the group exhibitions 'Flowers (2023, THEO, Seoul)', 'Don't look at me with those eyes: Bizarre things (2023, THEO, Seoul)', and 'Loose Connection (2018, former Namdo Office Area, Daejeon)', and he participated in the publication of ‘Pong: The Stranger's Eye’ and the ‘Pong: Locality Workshop’ and other projects.

name: seung youn Lee
bio:
Seung youn Lee studied design in Korea and Narrative Environment in the UK, and her work is inspired by folk tales, local beliefs, and mythology.
Before the pandemic, she used carpet as a material to depict mythological imaginings of various civilizations that she experienced while traveling around the world.
She has exhibited her iron drawings and contemporary mythology at ZK/U in Berlin, Asia Culture Center, Changwon International Sculpture Biennale, and Seoul Museum of Art.
Based on drawing, she works with various mediums such as steel, acrylic, light panels, fabric, and video, and her recent works include a series of light panels and a large-scale balloon and kite installation that depict stories about our future after the pandemic in the sky.
As an avid traveler, the artist finds unique iconography in unfamiliar countries and creates her own images based on them, bringing mysterious and unfamiliar stories to her work.

name: Kim Hwan
bio:
With bold strokes and vibrant colors, Kim Hwan's artwork exudes a captivating energy that draws people in. He strives to convey his pure state of mind through his work, without adding personal experiences or any conscious intentions.

Kim Hwan's approach to painting can be described by two key philosophies: '무념무상' (freedom from all ideas and thoughts) and '성성적적' (clear mind, and serenity, or the luminous transparency of the void and serenity). These philosophical concepts are reflected in his artwork, allowing for free interpretation and evoking various emotions depending on the viewer's circumstances, thoughts, and experiences. This approach leaves a lasting impression on viewers, ensuring that his artwork remains unforgettable over time.

Moreover, the artist utilizes a combination of acrylic and oil paints, employing a unique method to mature the oil colors before use. This process results in a rich and nuanced palette, allowing for the creation of intricate and vibrant hues in his paintings.

name: Wook-kyung Choi
bio: Wook-kyung Choi was born in 1940 in Seoul, Korea and passed away at the age of 45. After graduating from the College of Fine Arts at Seoul National University in 1963, Choi moved to the United States where she lived and worked for nearly fifteen of her twenty-year career as a professional artist. In the United States, she studied at the Cranbrook Academy of Art and received her MA in Fine Arts from the Brooklyn Museum School of Art. Choi taught as an Assistant Professor of Painting at Franklyn Pierce College from 1968 to 1971. In 1978 she returned to Korea and taught at Yeungnam University as an Associate Professor of Painting and later as a Professor at Duksung Women’s University while she continued to engage in her artistic practice. The Korean art scene during the 1960s and 70s, the time period when the artist actively worked both in the States and Korea, was dominated by two movements; the first was the so-called Korean Avant-garde, a loosely-affiliated movement that was primarily focused on performance and installation-oriented art practices and the second was Dansaekhwa. With strong influence from Abstract Expressionism and Pop Art, which were trending in the United States at the time, Wook-kyung Choi made a lasting contribution, challenging orthodoxy within Korea and establishing the importance of individual practice independent from mainstream ideas of the Korean local art scene. Throughout her oeuvre, Choi worked on a wide range of works, including abstract paintings, ink drawings and collages as well as figure drawings.

name: artnom
bio:
ARTNOM studied Korean painting in college and worked at a character design company for a few years. ARTNOM’s work began by finding the connection between Korean painting and character. The folk painting that ARTNOM used as motive is a drawing that contains the hope of commoners during the Chosun dynasty. During that time, folk paintings were practical artworks that had a clear usage in people’s lives. They would attach them on
the front gate on New Years, give them as gifts, or have weddings in front of folding screens that have folk paintings drawn on it. They depict the lives and philosophy of people during that time most accurately because they were intimately involved in the lives of the commoners. Also, artists who drew folk paintings did not leave any marks on their drawings. Because of that, they were able to not confine themselves in a specific form and use their imagination.

name: Lee Sang Yong
bio:
I was born and raised in a small village on the hills. Running around and exploring nature was the one  thing I enjoyed to do, the other was drawing and painting objects that I could easily find around me to assemble together.  To this day I often use flowers, birds, fish, and other animals based on my memories in my childhood as subjects. Besides Nature I also like assemble and dismantle old fashioned and aged objects in order to make an interesting new form, which gives off a different impression from the original ones. 
In all of my works my childhood memories still has a very influential impact on my works. 
Still, if I had to say something about what I wish for my future artwork. I would have to say that I wish  for it to have a stronger connection with people's emotions, and their daily lives. - Artist note

name: Jeong Yeon Kim
bio: Artist Jeongyeon Kim debuted in 2023 with the group exhibition at Bincan Studio in Seoul, South Korea. After successfully completing her first solo exhibition at at Artlogic Space Gallery in Seoul, she has participated in numerous solo and group exhibitions and art fairs. Jeongyeon Kim continues to actively pursue her work as an artist to this day.

name: Shin Seung-Hun
bio: Shin Seung-Hun is a South-Korean artist born in 1979 who lives & works in Jeju Island, Korea. He is considered by critics as the new Korean Takashi Murakami. The pure world of the artist depicts and dreams of a beautiful world from the perspective of a woman named Chunja of Jeju Island. The character Chun-ja' is the mother's name. We are having a great time together with Jeju Island as we dream of beautiful nature that represents the wild plants and the creatures. Based on the beautiful nature of Jeju and the story of a girl named 'Chunja', we expressed our work in a way that gives happiness and rest to us who have exhausted modern civilization and fierce selfishness.

name: Sangsun Bae
bio: Sangsun Bae is a Korean Artist living and working in Kyoto, Japan. A graduate of Musashino Art University, Tokyo, Sangsun studied for her Doctoral Thesis at Kyoto city University of the Arts, during which time she won a scholarship to study in London at the Royal College of Art. Twice selected for the prestigious VOCA art prize in Tokyo, Sangsun has shown internationally Europe and throughout Asia and is currently represented by Lee & Bae in Korea.  She is now based in Kyoto. The art of Sangsun Bae consists of semi-abstractive forms associated with ‘cords’, ‘braids’ and ‘balls of string’ drawn with serene yet dynamic lines or given ceramic form. Her repeated motif of intertwining ‘cords’ and ‘threads’ hints not only at the feminine decorative handicrafts of ‘Maedup’ (the traditional Korean art of knot making), but also a kind of biological vitality of form and line, as if one is witnessing to the fluid growth of blood vessels, nerves, hair, or perhaps vegetation. Though known for her abstract and introspective style. The work of Sangsun Bae is an ongoing exploration of the types of connections that exist between individuals, connections capable of holding relationships, communities and whole societies together, but which are equally susceptible of becoming self-entangled, frayed or of unravelling entirely. In a recent research project Bae chose to investigate the complex historical and emotional ties between Japanese citizens born in wartime, occupied, South Korea, many now in their 80’s and 90’s. By carefully avoiding an overtly political approach, she focuses instead on the deeper nature of human identity and belonging.

name: Don Sunpil
bio:
DON Sunpil is an artist who presents our conversational methodologies in the form of pieces. In order for readymade objects to exist in contemporary society, there must be an intersection of numerous thought structures. DON believes that this process is akin to the use of our language and signs. In this context, DON carves out his artwork based on the notion that mechanically mass-produced objects, irrespective of the form, are like our conversations in that they are instantiated pieces of our own reality.

DON received his BA as a print major from Hong-Ik University, and then his MA as a plastic art major from Seoul University of Science and Technology. He held a solo exhibition at Audiovisual Pavilion in 2016, participated in London's Coronet International Festival in 2017, and held another solo exhibition at Taste house in 2018.

name: Ha Chong-hyun
bio: Ha Chong-hyun’s muted, [process-oriented](/gene/process-oriented) paintings made him a leading figure of [Dansaekhwa](/gene/dansaekhwa), South Korea’s [monochrome painting](/gene/monochrome-painting) movement. He began experimenting with [oil](/gene/oil-painting) on burlap in 1974, and this style of [painting](/gene/painting) has become his trademark. Ha gained international prominence during a [resurgent interest in Dansaekhwa](/article/artsy-editorial-amid-renewed-interest-in-korean-dansaekhwa-art-ha-chong-hyun-continues-to-experiment) in the 2010s. His inclusion in the 2015 Venice Biennale preceded a sale at Christie’s, where one painting exceeded its high estimate with a winning bid of $145,171. The [Museum of Modern Art](/artist/museum-of-modern-art-new-york/works-for-sale)’s acquisition of one of his canvases followed. Ha’s signature technique, *bae-ap-bub*, involves pushing paint through the loose weave of [burlap](/gene/use-of-fabric) to create distinct textures. Through this process he emphasizes the [materiality](/gene/focus-on-materials) of the painting surface, transforming it to dynamic effect. Ha has also recently [exposed his surfaces to smoke](/gene/altered-and-substituted-canvases), which subtly affects his colors and signals another chapter in his decades-long experimentation.

name: Hae Jin Jeong
bio: 2016 Completed a Ph.D. course in Fine Arts at Dongguk University, Korea 2005 MFA in the Dept. of Traditional True Colored Painting, Hansung University, Korea 2001 BFA in the Dept. of Fine Arts(Oriental Painting), Hansung University, Korea

name: Hobong Kim
bio: Kim, Hobong was born in Korea and graduated from Hong ik University, Seoul. After graduating Graduate school from the same university, he worked in Seoul and won several awards in major art competitions. When he came to New York, he was attracted to video art at New York University Graduate School (Studio Art), and he had worked on videos and exhibitions for many years in New York after graduation N.Y.U.. He then moved to New Jersey and continued to work on the painting work, having several solo and many selected group exhibitions. He also participated KIAF in Korea, LA Art fair, Affordable Art fair in USA.

name: Ahhi Choi
bio:
Ahhi Choi was born in Hyogo Prefecture Japan in 1983. The curvilinear
movement in the work of Ahhi Choi is both buoyant and ecstatic, expressing
the innate sense of adventure the artist possesses. He was recognized
after exhibition in New York in 2014 and has since exhibited internationally
including in the United States, France, Italy, Korea, Singapore and Hong
Kong.
Ahhi Choi’s work can be perceived as reflection of his subconscious mind.
After his study in Los Angeles he traveled through the Western United States.
During that trip, Choi explored the expansive network of National Parks, from
Death Valley to the Grand Canyon to Yellowstone. It was during this stateside
excursion that the artist developed an intimate bond with the grandeur and
majesty of nature. Upon his return to his home city of Kobe, a malaise set
in over Choi, it was the cramped and overcrowded lifestyle of urban Japan,
which was causing him to feel nostalgic. Taking the flashes of inspiration that
the artist experienced in day-to-day life he began to take ink to paper forming
an abstract diary of his adventures. Letting his hand move organically
across the page, Choi would interpret the silhouettes, pictures, words and
letters from the well of his memory into energetic lines that are ubiquitous in
throughout his work.
In addition to painting, the artist has also extensively engaged in other artistic
creations, including the design of shoes, fabrics, wine labels, cell phone
cases and CD covers.

name: Haneyl Choi
bio: Haneyl Choi explores sculpture’s formative potential as a narrative framework, yielding symbolic configurations of individuals, archetypes and sites of encounter that engage multiple visual perspectives and elicit indeterminate interpretations. The ambiguity that pervades Choi’s oeuvre informs his ongoing inquiry into sculpture’s expressive potential as both signifier and signified, and bespeaks his critical stance toward identity politics, consumer culture, normative social structures and postmodern discourse in contemporary art. These works eschew traditional logics of appearance in favor of radical visions that render alternative modes of perception and project unorthodox attitudes toward contemporary civil concerns. Through this idiosyncratic and irreverent sculptural practice, Choi implicates notions of subjectivity, superficiality and substance as contradictory elements in the expanded sculptural field.

name: Doowon Lee
bio: Doowon Lee (b. 1982, South Korea) is a self-taught Korean artist working in mixed media. His works on wool, hemp, cotton, and paper combine Korean ink with natural fibers sourced during his travels — including wool from Pakistan, hemp from Nepal, and khadi cotton from India. His cosmology treats nature, animals, and humans as continuous rather than distinct, manifesting as whimsical, narrative-rich compositions. In 2023, he presented a solo exhibition at the Saatchi Gallery, London, and in 2024 was selected as a representative artist for the Busan Biennale. He is represented by ACA Galleries, New York

name: Joeun Kim Aatchim
bio:
Joeun Kim Aatchim (b. South Korea, 1989) is a painter and multimedia artist based in New York City. In search of transparency in vision and voice, Aatchim draws audiovisual essays. Her recent research focuses on the poetic translation of her stereo blindness –a lifelong condition rendering her unable to perceive depth– and the psychology of womanhood. The source materials for her images are almost exclusively generated from her observations and memories: what she sees and recalls and the fusion of the two. That, combined with her eye misalignment, makes the distortion of the figures and spaces almost inevitable. Her technique references Korean traditions of painting on silk. Bones and skin, fish, milk, honey, e!s, and insects are some of the materials that Aatchim has used as a work surface. She has also experimented with various sizing methods from different cultures to control the transparency, viscosity, luster, and sheen of binders with which she mixes the mineral and earth pigment.
Her works seem to waver with staggered outlines and overlapping transparencies, suggesting the elusive nature of memory and perception. Aatchim’s translucent surfaces glimmer with hand-mixed mineral pigments, enhancing the imagery’s ghostliness.

name: Sangik Seo
bio: The work of Seo Sang-ik , who is famous for his reinterpretation , is a modern-day authentic painting . He reinterprets conditions and situations that sometimes feel different or the same , showing reality of the picture , from personal history to the appearance of the overall system of society . His own storytelling talent shone as he combined everyday life with imagination within the canvas . It is not easy to find one's own color , but after several attempts , Seo Sang-ik perfectly understood the principle of color and created his own style of painting with only a few colors . With acrylic paint as the base and oil painting on it , the overall color and density of the space are further enhanced in the work . " I want to get rid of the stereotype that painting should be like this and work freely , " says his world of works are boundless .

name: Wonwoo Lee
bio: Wonwoo Lee reinterprets fragments from everyday lives through his unique sense of humor and wit, thus interrupting everyday routine and revitalizing mundane subject matters. The imagination that giants cast away anxiety, symbols of luck (clovers, stars, rainbows), trivial conversations, and objects of distorted shapes and meanings work as self-defensive jokes and a sign of warning towards the banal world. Lee is a versatile artist who works across a variety of genres including performance, sculpture, paintings, photography, video, and text. He is a member of ‘…Joketta Project’ and 'MLH,' a multi-genre group. He has been actively exhibiting works at various museums including Seoul Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), Art Sonje Center (Seoul, Korea), Amore Pacific Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), and Songzhuang Art Gallery (Beijing, China), and has gained significant attention from both local and international curators, critics, collectors, and related art professionals.

name: Kim Dukki
bio:
Kim Dukki acquired his BFA in Oriental Paintings from Seoul National University, which is the
number one university in Korea. His artworks mainly utilizing western media tacitly reveal his
root in oriental paintings. Depicted with his unique, splendid color palettes, His story of family
contains debris of routinely happiness remaining unfaded even through the season shifts. Home
is the place representing happiness and containing trivial memories of happiness from our daily
lives for the artist, Kim Dukki. He brings back the subject of 'family' to his canvas to reawaken
the meaning of family to his viewers. In 2011, the artist had been selected from various press
reporters. Also, his art pieces had been collaborated with Leeum Samsung Museum of Art, and
collected by National Museum of Modern and Contemporary art, Seoul Museum of Art, and etc.
He is not only a well-recognized in Korea, but also internationally acknowledged artist.

name: YuJin Ju
bio: Everyone has their first memories. We all start life with a record of the date and time of birth in this era we live in, but rather than such a physical form, I believe "first memory" could be more dominant to mark the beginning of life.  When I think of my first, many traces of the old past jumble up, roaring their own stories in the pile of others. Among those, I follow the clearest, which leads me to the scene of a 4-year-old me riding a swing in the playground. Full of the yellow light of the setting sun cast over the playground when other kids went back home for dinner. As the swinging stopped, I started questioning why I rolled my feet, why I had to go home, what kind of trouble I'd get into if I didn't go back... These endless questions all came down to one, which was about "The moment soon to be over and the moment soon to begin again." These philosophical questions were too big for a four-year-old that it claimed the loudest voice of all the past moments who argue to be the first.  The very first memory - the very first question - was very challenging. I felt like I could never come down the swing since I couldn't answer the question. But it was also the beginning. The enormous question had huge doors, and as I walked into it, there were countless moments of varying worlds. That made me dream. Nevertheless, the act of repeatedly rolling my feet increasingly turned into worthless labor. I turned to the side, and there was the Sisyphus struggling to roll a stone like I'd seen him in the book. The great artist Camus once said that we have to imagine Sisyphus smiling at times while he forever carries the stone. It was not easy to see his face, though. We were constantly moving in our own directions.  So I thought I should keep a record of this. To let him listen to the voices I heard among many others, not to let them fade into the unknown realm but to reconnect them to the present even if we don't see each other.

name: Yoon Suk One
bio:
Yoon Suk One (b. 1983) lives and works in Seoul, South Korea. He studied Contemporary Art and Community Design at Konkuk University, Seoul. He has been credited with expanding the scope of contemporary Korean painting, 
Yoon’s works condense into certain sentiments. Using historically and geographically diverse statuary as imagery, the artist focuses how the passage of time is marked on these monuments, e.g., by erosion, weathering, natural disaster, and war. The artist creates scenic images that incorporate his own psychological reactions as he views the statues in a landscape. 
Yoon creatively transforms original landscapes by enhancing or subtracting the texture of the original scenery. This practice can be seen as a psychologically doubling process of recording both existing absences as well as absences which are still to come—that is, what is about to fade away. Ceaselessly retracing the irreversible passage of time, Yoon’s works exhibit a deeply emotional process. As the works progress, the images once used as a subject matter undergo a steady transformation, eventually becoming estranged from their original meaning. Moreover, they create an unprecedented screen of imagery and texture. 
Yoon was  selected for the  37th Joongang Fine Arts Prize. He is an artist in residence at Cheongju Art Studio, Cheongju, and Gyeonggi Creation Centre, Ansan. In Seoul, he has exhibited at Gallery Baton, the Seoul Citizens Hall, Culture Station Seoul 284, the Seoul Arts Centre-Hangaram Design Museum, and in Gwangju, at the Gwangju Biennale Pavillion.

name: Sooyeon Hong
bio:
Life is on a continuum Objects settled in the SooYeon Hong’s works do not possess a distinctive form. Therefore, the monochrome side that fills the whole frame catches our eyes first. About the time we are immersed in the solitude emitted from the monochrome side, the delicate tremble that shakes the tranquility is captured. Although that something which cannot be labeled seems like a crystallized image because it does not have a form, it shows its afterimage at the very next minute. The contour of the image is not fixed but slides into the mysterious moment between segments. However, the working method of Soo-Yeon Hong is the opposite. Rather, it progresses with thorough calculation and intention. The calculated slope of the canvass, the transparency created by having a certain amount of paint float on top of another layer and the next, and the timelines acquired through this. Through these elements, a layer is a form yet something that exists as the afterimage of the next form. This sort of structure can be recognized as another form. However, as these layers become accumulated, the whole screen is recognized as the fluid image that slowly evolves. Even when trying to define it by segmenting it into a minimum unit, it evolves towards yet another point.
Reiteration and overlap, exposure and concealment, that is, the meaning is achieved by ‘layers’, not by ‘a layer.’

– Excerpt from critic by Dae-Beom Lee, Art critic

name: Song E Yoon
bio:
Song E Yoon (Born in Busan, 1983~ )

(www.songeyoon.com)


Song E Yoon is a New York-based Korean artist. She was born in Busan, South Korea, in 1983. 

She started her first solo exhibition 'nighttime climbing' in Topohus, Seoul in 2008. She shows off her unique lighting installation and media art with black lights which never happened visual effect as mysterious and quiet in that exhibition. Starting with this exhibition she invited solo shows, art fairs, and project shows in many galleries and museums. In 2011, she move to New York City and she has a solo exhibition 'essence' in Newyork minded gallery,2014. Recently, she presented at ARTNYC.  You can find her works on online platforms such as Artsy, Artnet, and ART NYC's official webpage.(artnycnewyork.com)

Experience
 She developed into a very intensive artist with various experiences like this process. She has expressed her creativity through many solo and group exhibitions, such as big city Seoul, Busan, Daejun in Korea and NewYork, Miami in U.S.A. Jakarta in Indonesia. In 2011, the National Museum of Modern art association (ARKO museum, Gwangju Museum, and Busan Museum of modern art) introduced her as a representative young artist of Korea. That is a very glorious opportunity in her art history. She shows up installing the title of 'The university's credit rating' in a dark space with sounds. That is considered one of the best installation work in her art history. 
Moreover, she has participated in the international art fair at Ritz-Carlton Hotel SAFA /Seoul and AFAH Mandarin Oriental Hotel / Hong Kong.  And she has had various exhibitions in the U.S.A from 2013 to the present including solo shows in NewYork minded gallery in 2014, and 2018.

name: Chung Sang Hwa
bio: Chung Sang-Hwa is a central figure of Dansaekhwa (also known as Tansaekhwa), a central artistic development in postwar Korea that offered a fundamentally different approach to modernist abstraction. Though the term translates literally to “monochrome painting,” Dansaekhwa is rather characterized by its labor-intensive processes, repetitive gestures, and reductionist aesthetics. Rooted in the Korean informel style of the late 1950s to mid-’60s, Dansaekhwa emerged in Korean institutions and galleries in the 1970s and has been attributed to the work of a loose constellation of artists that also includes Park Seo-Bo, Lee Ufan, and Yun Hyong-Keun. Over his nearly six-decades-long career, Chung has developed a singular, meditative process of repetitively applying and removing paint from his canvases, resulting in multilayered, tactile monochromatic surfaces.

name: Hong Kyoung Tack
bio: Born in Seoul in 1968, Hong Kyoung Tack holds B.F.A in Painting from Kyoungwon University. Hong has vigorously attracted public attention since 2000 showing various series that include

name: Barn Miryung
bio:
Barn Miryung
‘Encounter – Longing for a Cosmos’

Artist Barn Miryung studied at Hongik University and the University of Tokyo and is a well-established mid-career artist who has been actively exhibiting both in Korea and internationally.

Her work is surreal in that it expresses encounters between reality and a transcendent, otherworldly realm.

As if spaces filled with light have been transferred directly onto the canvas, her paintings are saturated with extremely delicate particles of luminous brightness. These light-constructed surfaces emerge through dozens of brushwork layers that demand long periods of time and immense patience, allowing inner colors to slowly accumulate and rise. The resulting surface, from which traces of the artist’s hand seem erased, evokes the texture of a fresco mural and reveals the sedimented traces of time.

The encounters with the other shore—the ideal world we dream of—are profoundly quiet, peaceful, and beautiful. Through these beautiful meetings, we continue to dream of a “new world,” renewing the way we live each day.

name: Suki Seokyeong Kang
bio:
Suki Seokyeong Kang (b. 1977, Seoul, Korea) is a multidisciplinary artist focused on painting, performance, installation and video. Interested in creating a visual language of balance and harmony, Kang situates her work in the space between the abstract and the representational, as well as the organic and the geometric, in order to create a visual representation of the human condition. Kang also draws heavily upon archaic verse, particularly poems and ideographs, in order that “the work is carefully structured with a concern for how each individual can move forward with history, worries, and anxieties that are situated in the vertical time of their existence. The work is metaphorical—as an artist, I am working through the dilemma of existing in a society where history and the present coexist.” 

With an interest in the wisdom offered by history, the artist studies her own cultural tradition—including aesthetics, philosophies and ideologies—in order to look through the timeline between tradition and the contemporary in diverse ways. 

Kang now lives and works in Seoul, and recently participated in the 2019 Venice Biennale and Art Basel Unlimited, was awarded Art Basel’s Baloise Art Prize in 2018, and the 13th SongEun Art Award in 2013. Select solo exhibitions include her 2018 show Jeong 井 at the Tina Kim Gallery in New York, and Black Mat Oriole at the ICA in Philadelphia. Also noteworthy is her participation at the 2018 Shanghai and Liverpool Biennials. Her work is held in the collections of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, the Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, the Seoul Museum of Art, Korea, as well as that of the National Art Bank, Seoul.


_Submitted by [Tina Kim Gallery](https://www.artsy.net/partner/tina-kim-gallery)_

name: Kim Myoungjin
bio:
“Edgewalker_A Space Odyssey”
2023 KIAF Highlight Artist

The works of Kim Myoungjin can be described as a form of Pop Surrealism, where popular culture and narrative intersect. Through a rich combination of drawing, painting, graffiti, and spray techniques, he creates vibrant, energetic worlds that unfold like literary adventures, inviting viewers into imaginative stories filled with life and movement.

Kim Myoungjin was selected as a 2023 KIAF Highlight Artist, a program dedicated to showcasing outstanding emerging artists who are shaping the future of contemporary art. He has consistently attracted strong interest from collectors at major international art fairs and has achieved notable success abroad. During Miami Art Week in December 2016, he was selected by the renowned art platform Artsy as one of the “50 Artists to Watch.” He was also recognized as an Outstanding Artist in the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism’s KIAF competitions in both 2016 and 2017, affirming the artistic merit of his work.

His artworks are included in the collection of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea through its Art Bank program, and he has actively expanded his creative practice through collaborations with the fashion brand ADLV (Acmé De La Vie).

At the heart of his artistic universe is “Edgewalker,” an adventurer who walks the boundaries of worlds and is always the first to encounter the new and unknown. “A Space Odyssey” is among the most vibrant and dynamic series in his oeuvre. The lively landscapes that unfold within these colorful spaces represent a bright journey shared by both the artist and the viewer—a cheerful narrative and a personal odyssey through the vast universe of life itself.

A natural dreamer, Kim transforms the ordinary moments of everyday life into experiences charged with awakened sensitivity and wonder. Through his work, he guides us into exhilarating realms of imagination, where reality and fantasy seamlessly converge.

name: Jung Jungyeob
bio:
Jung Jungyeob is an influential artist at the forefront of the Korean feminist art movement. Her diverse body of work, which includes painting, installation, and performance, is deeply informed by feminist and ecological perspectives. The 'Red Bean Series,' her signature collection, is acclaimed for its focus on the unseen labor of women and for capturing the vitality of the earth within each tiny seed.

Jung's artistry extends beyond the canvas to embody a broader narrative, one that draws from the mundane—red beans, beans, and spring greens—to comment on labor and life. Her work is a continuous exploration of coexistence, weaving together the threads of daily existence with the collective narrative of all living beings.

• 2022 Lee Joong Seop Art Awards
• 2020 Gender Equality and Culture Awards 
• 2019 Goam Leeungno Art Awards
• More than 20 solo exhibitions and many group exhibitions

name: Jung, Jae-chul 정재철
bio:
Jaechul Jung's art practice started out from realistic reproduction, but it has gone through the collapse of the reliance on reproduction, and is now facing a complete end of it. His work from 2008 to early 2009 were preoccupied with the theme of 'survival of the fittest'. The economic order of the post-IMF financial restructuring and the globalization that engulfed the world in the universal capitalism led the artist to first-handedly experience the winner-take-all paradigm of the society. However, the artist through the dice on the boxing stage, and spread the 'survival of the fittest' world on the canvas. 
From 2012, Jaechul Jung started to pursue people in extreme difficulty in the reality. From 2012 to 2013, his work is largely divided into two themes. One is the voice of the public figures like celebrities, politicians, and social activists. These are voices that are given a place in the world. The other is the voice of the people who is not heard. These people struggle every day because they are not heard. The former theme involves African-American human rights activist like Malcolm X or Martin Luther King and politicians of various popularity/notoriety, and the latter theme involves victims of the nuclear disaster in Chernobyl, the underprivileged children of the slums in the Middle East, the albino children in Africa, and orphans of the Korean War.
He chose to dismantle the rules and disintegrate the form into smallest units in order to become more frank and to leave as much room for interpretation as possible. The dispersed forms that completely fills the canvas are paints that were left after a sweep of strong colors in fierce competition with one another. These chaotic loose constellations form an unstable arrangement that can be dispersed out at any moment in the overwhelming colors that fights for its space. Hence, in the crumbles of the vibrant lines that are at war, in the world of overwhelming collapse, the faces get to keep their fleeting voices.

name: Jimin Im
bio: One key theme that penetrates artist work is memory. The artist has been expressing the image of her inner memory through painting based on photography, but a change has occurred in her recent work. Consciousness, which has remained in the memories of the past, goes into memories inside me more and more, but does not stay in the memories, but brings them into the present. In previous works, thoughts were drawn on the screen with images filtered and organized. But now, the unfiltered images are being drawn on the canvas. A variety of hand movements, threads, confetti, fruit, etc. appear on the screen, and pieces of irrelevant pictures are gathered to create a single screen. She will continue to open this consciousness world without another filter paper. Through painting, one can only see the story on the surface, and some can read my monologue and hidden princes.

name: Chae Hyun Oh
bio: Sculptor Chae hyun Oh, specializing in granite, has been dedicated to stone sculpture for 40 years. His experience in Gyeongju greatly influenced his sculptural experience, believing that granite with its solid and unchanging properties is the optimal material to express Korean strength and emotions. By sculpting the figure of Buddha in stone, he reinterprets Korean culture and values in a modern context. Through works like 'Happy Tiger,' he symbolizes our nation with the tiger. All of his tiger sculptures have smiles, resembling the Buddha's smile, conveying warmth and hope. Chae hyun Oh describes his work as extracting a form from nature's creations with minimal craftsmanship in stone. The high intensity of granite work is an absolute battle against time and involves significant labor. Despite this, Chae hyun Oh persists in stone carving because he believes that among all the traces of artificial elements in nature, stone remains the longest. Carving might be difficult, but once engraved, it lasts forever. Chae hyun Oh has built his artistic life over the past 40 years through stone carving and will continue to contribute to the development of art through sculpture.

name: Sung Suh
bio:
Sung Suh is a New York–based conceptual and socially engaged artist, creative leader, and founder of Frozenism, a conceptual art framework that explores the intersections of time, memory, archives, nature, and society. Developed from his 2010 thesis project Frozen at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago (SAIC), Frozenism is grounded in the philosophy of “Time Frozen, Art Alive.” Through processes of freezing, preservation, and transformation, it examines how memories are preserved, erased, and reconstructed across personal and collective histories.

Working across photography, installation, sculpture, film, sound, performance, and visual communication, Sung transforms ice into a temporary archive of human experience, revealing the fragile relationship between permanence and change. His recent work expands Frozenism into contemporary issues including climate change, environmental vulnerability, social memory, and urban transformation.

Sung’s work has been exhibited internationally in New York, Chicago, Boston, Seoul, Germany, Belgium, and Hong Kong, including a featured presentation at Art Central Hong Kong. Through Frozenism, he presents a socially engaged artistic vision that keeps memory alive through art while encouraging critical reflection on contemporary society and environmental change.

name: Koo Jeong A
bio: Koo Jeong A(b.1967), who lives and works across the globe, has gained the attention of the international art world through her distinctive artistic practice of examining the fragile and ephemeral nature of objects and everyday lives to highlight their poetic mundaneness. Koo works across a diverse range of media—from poetries, fictions, installations, paintings, moving images, audio works, and architectural projects—and her delicate and detailed works question the boundaries between the fact and fiction and the actuality and imaginary. Koo held solo exhibitions at Kunsthalle Düsseldorf (Düsseldorf, Germany), Dia Art Foundation, Dia: Beacon (Beacon, USA), and Centre Pompidou (Paris, France) and gained her international stature. She participated in various group shows including Venice Biennale, Liverpool Biennale, Gwangju Biennale, The Jewish Museum (New York, USA), The Guggenheim Museum (New York, USA), the Fondation Louis Vuitton (Paris, France), and Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (Seoul, Korea). Koo was a finalist for the Hugo Boss Prize in 2002, won the Hermes Korea Prize for contemporary art in 2005, and was named as ‘2016 artist of the Year’ by the Korean Cultural Centre UK.

name: Jihee Kim (b. 1983)
bio: In an abstracted exploration of her private identity, Jihee Kim paints, draws, and collages illustrative images of her body with an obscured face. In her earlier work, Kim painted and drew brightly colored, almost symbolist self-portraits of her nude body wearing a zebra or horse mask. The masks render her anonymous and draw attention to her animalistic sexual impulses. More recently, Kim created a variant of these works, focusing on the flowing hair of faceless women. She also placed collaged images of fashion models from magazines atop the pages of library books. Akin to marginalia doodles, the subconscious quality of Kim’s work allows for insight into her private desires and sense of self.

name: Shim Bongmin
bio:
Artist Sim Bongmin is a widely recognized and popular artist who was selected as a ZOON-IN emerging artist at the Korea Galleries Art Fair in 2023 and received the “Star Artist Award” from KB Financial Group in 2025.

Rendered in a lyrical realist style, his works feel as though a single scene from childhood memories—filled with brilliant spring flowers, fresh breezes, on a summer night when the blue sky was filled with shining stars, lush greenery, and at times a world blanketed in pure white snow—has been gently paused in time.
These images, both beautiful and innocent, offer a sense of freshness while quietly cleansing and soothing the viewer’s mind.

name: Minju Kang
bio:
Minju Kang is a painter currently studying at Kunstakademie Düsseldorf (Prof. Thomas Scheibitz).
She received the 2022 Baker Tilly Artist Grant.

name: Daehun Kwon
bio: DaeHun Kwon was born in Seoul, Korea in 1972, studied in Seoul National University in Sculpture(BFA, MA). He moved to London in 2002 and studied in The Slade School of Fine Art, UCL, London, UK. He won the Jack Goldhill Award for Sculpture at the Royal Academy Summer Exhibition. He now lives and works in Seoul and London. Kwon works with sculpture, installation and performance. His work is imbued with a distinctive sense of time as marking material objects including people in such a way that they become signs of their part in the configuration of moment (the artist refers to the Korean expression ‘Chalna’ which he translates as ‘the very moment when a thing or a phenomenon is developing’). In his painted sculptural objects Kwon depicts highly specific but fleeting interrelations—between individuals performing often seemingly insignificant actions, physical things/objects realised with an acute feeling for their uniqueness and the registration of light. These objects achieve a phenomenological deep realism that is spiritual in the sense of an observed transfiguration of some secular, mundane subject matters. The method of realism the artist adopts is associated both with the careful observation of physicality as a species of truth to materiality and a willingness to place the physical within an appropriately fragile continuum sensitive to a kind of perceptual impressionism. This as a kind of limit case for the real. Kwon has institutional shows include USB: Urban Nomadism, Hangaram Art Museum, Seoul Arts Centre, Seoul, 2009, Your Mind’s Eye: Digital Spectrum, Seoul Museum of Art, Seoul (2008).
