name: Lee Gil Rae
bio:
Inspired by Nature, Korean artist Lee Gil-Rae often crafts sculptures from steel and copper wires that mimic a surreal, leafless forests that one can meander into. Despite the man-made nature of his well-crafted spiralling branches, they still remain organic in aesthetic, drawing the viewer to admire the sculpture's intricate exteriors that imitate the curves of aged tree bark. With rapid deforestation, Lee Gil-Rae's trees exist within a liminal space of organic and man-made, reflecting the constructed simulation of nature which is apparent in cities.

Lee Gil-Rae has participated in several exhibitions in Korea, America and Japan and features in numerous permanent collections. A true homage to Nature, his enormous forests of copper capture the rapidly depleting forests for eternity.

name: Hyong Nam Ahn
bio:
yong Nam Ahn, a Korean artist born in 1955, is known for his sculptures that combine lights, sounds, and movements. Inspired by Kinetic Art from the 1960’s, Ahn earned his MFA from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1980. He has created public sculptures for esteemed institutions and corporations, including McDonald Corporation in Kirkland, WA, The Mayor’s Advisory Committee on Art & Culture in Baltimore, MD, McCormick Place Donnelly Hall World Convention Center in Chicago, IL, and HMHC Hackensack Meridian Health Medical Center in Hackensack, NJ.

Ahn is fascinated by the ever-changing nature of the environment and strives to visually express this dynamic. He uses mixed media and controlling devices to vividly convey his inner thoughts. Through his art, he also explores the impact of technology on human relationships and the natural world. Despite the constant changes in the world, Ahn believes that the essence of human relationships and the universe remain unchanged.

In his recent works, Ahn draws inspiration from natural occurrences such as moonlight and migrating birds. He often incorporates sound and light to address formal aesthetic challenges, exploring how they can serve as both the subject matter and the foundation of contemporary art.

name: Woo Kuk Won
bio: Woo Kukwon is a promising artist who was selected as one of the 20 artists for the 32nd JoongAng Fine Arts Prize which is one of the important awards in Korea. He held numerous solo exhibitions since 2009 and recently his art piece has been collected at 'Culture Convenience Club company' which is a Japanese company that operates Tsutaya, nationwide bookstore in Japan.  Furthermore, his paintings had been collected at various museums in Korea such as 'National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art', 'Seoul National University Museum of Art' and etc.

name: YOO JUNG HYUN
bio:
Yoo Junghyun’s works focus on tensions created from physical characteristics of brush strokes such as the speed, movements, and pressures. The form of nature in her drawings is presented as a fairly natural appearance rather than a clear event. The artist’s technique of painting is based on changes rather than plans and this resembles the characteristic of nature quite well. As she is naturally immersed in abstract things, shapes of plants appear in her works.

This is because she focuses on accidently discovered forms and shapes during the process of creating her pieces instead of working on a specific subject, forms of nature are generated at the boundary between figurative and non-figurative worlds. She continuously repeats a series of steps such as brushing on the canvas at high speed, generating bubbles unintentionally in this process, wiping or removing brush strokes that she has created, and covering shapes that habe been already painted. Through this process, the artist actively converges her own formative choices and brings inevitable forms onto her canvas.

name: Nam Kyung Min
bio:
Nam Kyung Min reflects on her life as an artist, describing the intense focus, solitude, and emotional ups and downs of her daily practice in her atelier. She finds deep fulfillment in the immersive act of painting, likening it to the spiritual engagement described in Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina. Though not every day is productive, she turns to nature and classic literature for clarity and healing, reminding herself that true creative joy comes from inner peace and sincere love for her work.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Nam explored the lives of iconic women like Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, and Princess Diana. Through painting their private rooms, she highlighted the contrast between their glamorous public images and the quiet, often lonely realities of their personal lives. These works emphasize shared human desires for peace, love, and introspection, revealing how even cultural icons long for the same emotional comfort and freedom as ordinary people.

Nam’s “Artist’s Atelier” series captures the creative spaces of both herself and historic painters such as Vermeer, Monet, and Velázquez. Her studio becomes a metaphor for the inner world of the artist, filled with meaningful objects like butterflies, candles, and mirrors that symbolize the soul, time, and self-reflection. Through her symbolic language and reverence for artistic tradition, Nam invites viewers to interpret her work personally and find their own connections within the visual narratives she creates.

name: Yoo Geun-Taek
bio:
Yoo Geun-Taek is a significant figure in contemporary Korean painting. Since the 1990s, he has been
exploring the redefinition of visual narratives derived from observation and the influence of the Dansaekhwa art movement that swept the Korean painting field of the 70s and 80s. Geun-Taek’s work is energetic, hypnotic, sensual and meditative.

His practice interweaves the traditional techniques and materials of Korean painting—hanji (a traditional Korean paper crafted from the inner bark of the mulberry tree), natural inks, and oyster shell powder. Over years of refinement, Yoo has developed a deeply tactile and visceral visual language, characterized by dense, assertive gestures and the rhythmic repetition of forms. His process involves layering ink and oyster shell powder in a labor-intensive accumulation, creating richly textured surfaces that evoke both material depth and temporal resonance. These distinctive paintings are imbued with what Yoo describes as "a new space of accumulated time," a poetic reimagining of Korea’s contemporary history, while also gesturing towards the evolving future of Korean painting.

name: Lee Mijung
bio: Lee Mijung transforms her art pieces into touchable objects by creating a sculptural sense on a canvas. She focuses on expanding the meaning of each image and creating a flexible scene which can be interpreted in various situations in a physical space. After graduating from one of the high-ranking universities in Korea, ‘Hongik university’, she participated in major solo exhibitions at OCI Museum, Gallery KunstDoc, Art Delight and etc. She also had chosen as residency with the Kuandu Museum of Fine Arts in Taipei and selected as OCI young creatives. Moreover, her art pieces have been collected at ‘Kuandu Museum of Fine Arts’ in Taipei, ‘National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art’ in Korea, OCI Museum of Art in Korea and etc.

name: Um Tai Jung
bio: UM Tai-Jung is one of the Korean abstract sculpture's first-generation pioneers. Since his fascination with the materiality of steel during his undergraduate studies at Seoul National University in the early 1960s, Um has devoted himself to metal sculpture and investigated materials and resources throughout his career that continues to the present. In 1967, he caught the art world's attention as his emblematic steel sculpture A Scream won the Prime Minister's Prize in the 16th National Art Exhibition, and in the seventies, he presented copper sculptures that revealed a remarkable contrast between the material's internal and external sides in terms of color and texture. In the 1980-the 90s, Um's abstract copper sculptures with a prominent vertical structure referred to Eastern philosophy concerning the ideas of the celestial and worldly, as exemplified by his Heaven, Earth, and Human, and the 90s' Bronze-Object-Age series reflected the shapes of Korean traditional wood furniture and pillars. From the 2000s on, Um has been putting more emphasis on form-based works made of aluminum boards and steel frames that illustrate coexistence and reconciliation of mutually exclusive elements-such as Yin and Yang, and time and space-through the formal language of the vertical and horizontal, sculptural qualities of lines and planes, and aharmonious palette of silver and black.

name: Sukyoung Kang
bio: Suk Young Kang was born in Seoul in 1949. He majored in pottery at Hongik University and Graduate School, and studied pottery at École Nationale Supérieure d’Arts et Métiers. After returning to Korea, he served as a dean of Ewha Women's University's College of Formative Arts and a director of the Pottery Institute for 30 years, working hard to study and foster younger students. Ironically, from ‘Slip Casting Technique’, which was considered to lower the value of the work because of its main use in industrial works that were easy to reproduce, he implemented his own production method that maximizes aesthetic intuition. Rather like removing the fancy technique and extracting the source point that reaches infinite formability, his work converges to white, the purest achromatic color. The ‘culture of texture’, which should be dealt with mainly in pottery in particular, the cultural characteristics expressed in texture in other words, the Korean aesthetics is fully captured in his work. His work, deeply melted in ‘Korean white beauty’, has already been recognized internationally for its formativeness. Since 2003 his work has been permanently owned and displayed at the International Pottery Olympic Park in Athens, Greece, and is also owned by leading domestic institutions such as the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) and major overseas museums such as the Royal Albert Museum and the Brooklyn Museum.

name: Won Seoung Won
bio: Hundreds of photographed images taken by the artist herself transform into a fantastical image through her elaborate working with the computer. The imaginary space with a story renders the contemporary individual's life of yesterday, today, and tomorrow, and extends to the community life where that individual belongs to. In her work composed of the artist’s distinctive views based on a realistic logic and the unfamiliarity by delicate imagination, the profound and heavy subject of humans is revealed as a wit and visual amusement, as well as evoking an analog feeling. Her work from an existing incident, in reality, delivers subtle emotions. And the image containing a story begins to infinitely expand onward like a three-dimensional picture book that keeps unfolding new time and space page after page.

name: Chan-Hyo Bae
bio: Gender, culture, isolation, prejudice, and stereotypes are explored in the work of Korean photographer Chan-Hyo Bae (born 1975, Busan, South Korea). Since graduating from the Slade School of Fine Art in 2007, Chan-Hyo Bae has expressed in his work the feelings of cultural and emotional estrangement he experienced when he first came to study in England. Several series with the title Existing in Costume (2007-16) saw him posing in a variety of female historical western costumes, integrating himself into a history and society from which he felt excluded. Researched in meticulous detail, he created elaborate scenes of himself as a noblewoman from Elizabethan to Regency periods.

name: Jay, Choi
bio:
It is difficult to perceive with our eyes where the wind originates and where it flows. However, you can finally feel the flow when you look at the fluttering hair and fluttering blades of grass. J. Choi captures the wind through the image of a swaying field. The wind implied by the passing brushstrokes represents an uncontrollable external environment and the resulting trials.
Enduring hardships is ultimately a single task. So, in the screen captured by artist J. Choi, there is only one house. This captures the image of a human being who has no choice but to always be alone at critical moments in life. The shape of the house, firmly rooted alone amidst the blowing wind, seems to melt into the landscape, but exists as a solid entity and acts as a kind of refuge and sanctuary.
Taking the shape of a landscape but simultaneously depicting the inner shape, the artist goes back and forth between reality and virtuality, which inevitably conveys an ambivalent sensibility that combines figuration and abstraction in his work. This tendency hints at the current artist, and the work leads the audience to a unique boundary area where his inner world and the external world meet.

name: NAM SANG WOON
bio:
Nam Sang Woon is an artist who has garnered attention for his unique visual expression, which is rarely seen in contemporary art. His renowned "BLUE MOON" series, while utilizing traditional oil painting techniques, breaks conventional methods by constructing colors and textures in a multi-layered fashion. This creates visual depth and complexity, resulting in striking blue hues and intricate textures that are almost unbelievable as mere paintings. This remarkable series stands out for its intense chromatic tones and delicate texture representation.

Nam has been highly regarded as one of the most skilled artists since his twenties and is even more renowned among fellow artists. His students, who are also actively working in the art field, further highlight his influence. Nam is considered one of the most promising artists in his early fifties within the K-ART scene and is expected to be a leading figure in the future of South Korea's art world.

Nam holds a Ph.D. from Hongik University. He won the Grand Prize at the Seoul Museum of Art Creative Artists Association Contest in 2000 and the Grand Prize at the Gyeongnam Culture and Art Center Gaecheon Art Contest in 2001. Currently, he is an invited professor teaching Western painting at several national and private universities.

name: Leehaiminsun
bio: Leehaiminsun(1977-, Seoul) had been interested in things that are marginalized from within the everyday, ambiguous scenes, elusive existences, or objects which, although they are mutually related, are alienated from landscapes. Such inquiries had been steadily in progress since the artist’s earlier works. In the early 2000, the artist sought the possibility of mechanical organisms amidst reorganizing the occupation of space and the arrangements of objects from paradoxical structures of life through various mediums such as drawing, objects, installations, films, etc(‘A Solo Exhibition of an Unfamous Artist’, ‘Becoming Blood Becoming Skin’). Then, in the mid 2000, the artist deconstructed spaces formalized in blueprints and payed attention to the peripheral structures, thereby subverting familiar spaces, reorganizing the dormant organic energy and showing them.(‘The Rental Space Modified Bodies’) Afterwards, since the latter half of 2000, the artist, up to today, continues to work with painting, drawing and installation, gradually putting painting at the center.(‘The Half Dead Things’, ‘Water and Rice’) In this way, the artist shows, through her works, dealing with the organic structures of the world where artificial things and natural things, organic matters and inorganic matters are mixed together, and they can neither be separated by humans, animals nor machines. This spans in between the subject and the object, the outside and the inside, landscape and object; the relationship between them is closer to co-existence and advocacy, rather than conflict or hostility. For example, there is a scene where bodies of a certain structure are placed, leaning against each other, like lumber supports added onto a tree. Like such, the artist, through her works, had constantly been embracing and adjusting the mutual bodies and landscapes which is supported by delicate beings.

name: Koh Sang Woo
bio: Koh Sang Woo has a taste for controversy. His images may look beautiful, but the stories beneath needle away at the unspoken do’s and don’ts that tie us up in social and cultural obligations. His last exhibition in his hometown of Seoul, South Korea, was almost pulled at the last moment due to a call from KBS, the Korean equivalent of the BBC. It featured one of their presenters, with her husband, in a state of undress and, more importantly, without their permission. Another show picturing a mixed race couple was simply avoided and mothballed, to avoid offending ‘cultural sensibilities’. And yet it’s hard for us in the West to believe by just looking at the work. Koh’s art is part painting, part performance, documented in photography. Carefully choosing his subjects for their personal stories, he paints directly onto their bodies as he works, and then reverses the colours in the final exposure to give his photos an unmistakeable electric vibrancy. In one way, he is an artist that paints photographs, and sees the world in reverse. But this reversal is also a social statement, a means of subverting the way society can push people away from their ideals, and make them compromise and change to accommodate social pressures. In True Stories, all his photographs probe the kind of subtle conventions that restrain and limit their subjects – be it corporate control, racial prejudice, or the pressure to “be the best” as in his Portrait of a Girl / Portrait of a Woman” series. The works thus become a kind of release and defiance, beautifully rendered. And it’s his Eastern form of kicking against the system that makes Koh’s work so interesting. Not in the obvious punk aggressive way, what the West is used do, but a more discreet and suave manner of counter-culture, balancing Korean values of discipline and respect with the need to make a point.

name: Choi Suk Un
bio:
Choi Suk Un (b. 1960) graduated from the Department of Painting at Pusan National University and received his M.F.A. from the Graduate School of Fine Arts at Hongik University. Drawing on ordinary moments from everyday life, he transforms the familiar into artistic subjects, creating compositions marked by formal tension and a distinctive emotional sensibility. In recent years, he has focused on the motif of the figure, constructing still and contemplative scenes that seem to preserve the essential nature of contemporary life.
Choi has held more than 45 solo exhibitions, including those at Gallery Now (Seoul, 2025), Garam Gallery (Seoul, 2023), the National Library of Korea (Seoul, 2011), and Kumho Museum of Art (Seoul, 1993). His work has also been featured in numerous group exhibitions at institutions and galleries such as Jeonnam Museum of Art (Gwangyang, 2021), Busan Museum of Art (Busan, 2021), the Yeosu International Art Festival (Yeosu), and Jeju Museum of Art (Jeju, 2017).
He has participated in residency programs at Fangxian Art District Creative Studio (Hubei, China, 2024), Friday Island of Haengchon Cultural Foundation (Haenam, Korea, 2021), Imado Studio of Haengchon Cultural Foundation (Haenam, Korea, 2019), Gwangju Museum of Art Beijing Studio (Beijing, China, 2011), Jeju Museum of Contemporary Art Creative Studio (Jeju, Korea, 2010), and Gana Art Busan Creative Studio (Busan, Korea, 2008).
His works are held in the collections of Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art, Gyeongnam Art Museum, Gwangju Museum of Art, Daejeon Museum of Art, Busan Museum of Art, Jeonnam Museum of Art, Kumho Museum of Art, Jeju Museum of Contemporary Art, Chungkang College of Cultural Industries, Haengchon Cultural Foundation, Geoje City, Kyobo Book Centre, and other public and private collections in Korea and abroad.

name: Eunhyea Choi
bio: Eunhyea Choi graduated a BA in Painting and Print Making, an MA in Painting and also completed a Ph.D in Painting at Ewha Womans University, Seoul. Eunhyea Choi renders experiential space and time into two-dimensional paintings through the lens of a ‘continuous multilayered space’. Memory is the main subject of her works, expressed in the spaces created by the interaction of light and shadow with various materials, and the communion that transpires over this duration. Choi’s work begins with the collection of light. The artist transforms the shape of light into photographs, drawings and texts, and superimposes the images to create new spatial structures that capture its organic movements. Spaces formed by lines and planes are filled with the movement of light presented as blurred colours in the paintings pulsating with warmth.

name: Seoul Kim
bio: Seoul Kim (formerly known as Sohee Kim) was born in 1983 in Daegu, Korea. She received her BFA from Hong-ik University in Seoul, and her MFA and PHD from Tama Art University in Tokyo. She studied printmaking and most often creates color etchings with hand-coloring. Kim is known for her humorous portrayals of people, objects, and spaces in exaggerated city life scenarios. Her work often deals with people becoming objects and vice versa. She uses laughter to critique and explore the human experience, especially compartmentalization and isolation in her COVID-19 series.

name: Bosun PARK  박보선
bio:
Park Bosun is an artist who continues to explore the themes of inner emptiness and anonymity in the human experience. She adopts visual strategies such as Photoshop’s transparency grid and pixelation to reveal the invisible textures of emotion. While her early works expressed feelings of alienation and existential loss, her recent paintings quietly capture the subtle tremors of emotion and connection within scenes of everyday life. 
The figures in her works appear with erased identities, offering space for viewers to project their own experiences and emotions. Her practice reflects the loneliness and unease of contemporary life, while gently embracing its inherent complexity. Park discovers emotional landscapes within the fragments of daily life and renders them with a refined, sensitive gaze.

name: Eunsil Lee
bio:
2014  M.F.A in Oriental painting, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
2006  B.F.A in Oriental Painting, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea

name: GBDAY
bio:
Artist GBDAY’s interest in art grew when he first encountered skateboarding culture and fashion during his adolescence. The artist later began to work on graphics and paintings during his studies in graphic design at university. His artistic stage name, "GBDAY," stands for "Good Day & Bad Day," which contains the artist's desire to illustrate different experiences and emotions of his daily life. His stage name and its meaning profoundly influenced the world of his work and its creation. 

The artist gains inspiration from human relationships, emotions, and social phenomena he captures daily. His work mainly deals with themes around love, separation, emptiness, and death. The artist links these themes with the skeleton motif, influenced by tattoos, skateboarding culture, and hip-hop and band music he listened to. The Skeleton motif symbolizes an equal and pure being that everyone, regardless of gender or race, can sympathize with and illustrates the world beyond reality and death. Moreover, Cherry denotes the uncertainty of life, desire, and fruition, and Butterfly portrays life after a newborn death. 

GBDAY uses drawing as a subject that best reveals himself. His works mainly focus on graffiti and pen drawings, although he continuously experiments with various styles and media to develop a unique work. He currently uses graphite and acrylic paints for most of his works, aiming to expand his ways of expression. Furthermore, the artist frequently presents parody-based works where he adds a twist to an existing painting or work that may be familiar to the audience. The artist claims he enjoys creating parody-based works because he wishes his audience to approach art more easily and have some fun interacting with his work. 

"Life Goes On" is a message that signifies not only GBDAY's art but also his life philosophy. The artist intends to deliver joy and happiness to the audience through his work, conveying the bliss of our life journey.

name: Hur Kyung Ae
bio: Hur Kyung-Ae was born in Gwangju, South Korea, and currently lives and works in France. In France, she gained a wider scope of artistic creation. She experimented with various media, but eventually, her preference for painting prevailed. She returned to it with newfound inspiration: by scratching the pictorial surface of one of her canvases with a sharp blade, she discovered a new vision and sense of well-being. This process, which she describes as “awakening”, is both meditative and aggressive, and draws a lot of attention to her work today. She is linked to the younger generation of the ‘Dansaekhwa’ movement and is earning increasing international acclaim.

name: Bang Jeong-A
bio:
http://bjart.net

  Bang Jeong-A (b.1968) has held a sustained interest in the realities of South Korean society since the 1990s. She began carving out a place for herself in the art scene thanks to her work delineating the everyday lives of ordinary individuals, especially those of Korean women. Her point of view has since broadened in spectrum to encompass various social and environmental topics. Since 2020, Bang has been giving expression to socio-political issues through large-scale pieces and is currently considered one of the leading artists active in the fields of Asian feminist and environmental work. She has participated in solo and group exhibitions at various locations including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (MMCA), Busan Museum of Art, Gwangju Biennale, Asia Culture Center, Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, and Arario Gallery Beijing. Her works are held in collections at the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, MMCA, Busan Museum of Art, Seoul Museum of Art, Daejeon Museum of Art, Gyeongnam Art Museum, and National Maritime Museum of Korea.

name: Shine.L (Si In Yang)
bio: Path of Light, Shine Lord Artist Shine.L (real name: Yang Si In) majored in textile design at Hanyang University and traveled through Canada, the United States, and Europe capturing creative inspiration within an artistic framework through "artworks and poetry." The primary meaning of Shine Lord: Shine Road is ‘Creator of Light’ but the phrase also carries the nuance of “Path of Light”through its linguistic tone. Shine Lord follows the intersection where painting, literature, and the philosophy of truth in the Bible converge, leading to a path where human intellect and the inspiration of nature flow into the artist’s creative process. The wisdom that guides the artist’s autonomous life runs through this current. Drinking from the wellspring of inspiration drawn from unconscious memory and the truth of enlightenment, the artist seeks to convey a message that transcends the language of painting. Artist Shine.L's

name: SANG-KWON LEE 이상권
bio:
Lee disassembles familiar features of the subjects and reconstructs them using several colors, brush  strokes and complex veining directions. The complexity of constantlychanging the size and direction of  light and color seems to be a formative feature of Sangkwon Lee’s landscape. Initially, the audience who encounter the image that is mixed with diverse angle and point of view, won’t be able to focus on the picture due to the illusion of shaking. For this reason, the forest, path and rock will appear in a flat view. 
Painting of Landscape usually desires depth. Specifically, this profundity is thought and expressed not only by the outside but also by the inner scenery. Unlike the precedence landscape work, this is rearranged based on the artist's individual experiences and directed towards a special impression and meaning. 
In the works, audiences find the typical scenery of the metropolitan area where urbanization is processed in a short period. The scene is an irregular mixture of the urban and rural areas, as well as mixed-pot of tradition and modern. Simultaneously, the order and culture of tradition is roughly dismantled, and a new order and culture is introduced violently. Over time, when the order and culture of a new species intertwined with the past and the present appear, we could recognize the object of the new landscape painting. Overall, Lee’s landscape calmly reproduces this change in Paju. Following these steps, Sangkwon Lee endures the weight of time and depth.

- Noam Kim, Director of Chong Keun Dang Arts award

name: Anicka Yi
bio: With unconventional materials such as soap, potato chips, expired powdered milk, snail slime, and tempura-fried flowers, Anicka Yi makes tactile and fragrant sculptures, paintings, and installations that are simultaneously seductive and grotesque, imaginative and rooted in science. The artist often draws on biochemistry, anthropology, and philosophy, exploring themes such artificial intelligence, sexism, migration, and climate change. Fragrance is often at the heart of Yi’s work—a way of subverting the dominant male gaze within the art world. For You Can Call Me F (2015), she worked with a pungent paint derived from bacterial samples culled from 100 Asian American female friends and colleagues. In *Auras, Orgasms, and Nervous Peaches* (2011), fragrant olive oils leak from the walls of a tiled room. Yi won the Hugo Boss Prize in 2016 and was awarded the Tate Turbine Hall Hyundai Commission in 2020. She has exhibited at the [Museum of Modern Art](/partner/the-museum-of-modern-art), the [Guggenheim Museum](/partner/guggenheim-museum), the [Fondation Louis Vuitton](/partner/fondation-louis-vuitton), [Kunsthalle Basel](/partner/kunsthalle-basel), and the Cleveland Museum of Art, and participated in the Venice Biennale, the Whitney Biennial, the Lyon Biennale, and the Gwangju Biennale.

name: Jun Young Kang
bio: By using various media such as painting, pottery, and drawing, artist Junyoung Kang works on breaking down the boundaries of media and introducing new possibilities of pottery in contemporary art. For the artist, the theme “Romantic Love” becomes the motive of the work. The images and texts appearing in his work are trajectories of all time based on his life experience and are autobiographical sensibilities derived from thorough thinking and personal experiences. The artist expresses this emotion as “love” in a nutshell.

name: Min Joo KIM
bio:
Minjoo Kim is an oriental painting artist who thinks and understands the world through images rather than words. Her works combine the formativeness of modern painting and characteristics of the traditional landscape painting to create an ideal space for thoughts and ideas that escape from reality and the material excesses of the modern society.
The forms of nature fill her works with detailed and repetitive expressions, and this makes the audience fully immersed in the process of deep thoughts. While meticulously painted leaves require a great deal of efforts, the result of her patience is fully reflected on the canvas. Minjoo Kim’s thoughtful landscape, which reinterprets traditional landscape paintings from her own perspective, provides visual stimulation to the audience through restrained imagination. The word “Sayu (thinking and understanding the world),” which appears in the title of her work quite often, plays a role in expanding the audience’s sympathy toward hers works.

name: Mackerel Safranski
bio:
Mackerel Safranski (b.1984) has long been interested in the perception of her body, a perspective shaped by her personal experience with a long-term eating disorder. She draws from literature, news, and daily observations to construct the stories and images of the figures in her paintings. Ambiguous objects and fragmented scenes often appear in her work, creating a mysterious, uncanny atmosphere—as if something is on the verge of happening. The narratives within her work, which subtly hint at themes of migration, labor, violence, desire, relationships, and isolation, reflect her interest in exploring the “external body” as something we perceive and respond to within social structures. Recently, Safranski has expanded her practice to include video and installation, focusing on how narratives shift across different media.

In 2008, Safranski was selected for the exhibition Young Korean Artists, an annual exhibition organized by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, to showcase promising young artists. She has held solo exhibitions at A-Lounge, Seoul (2021); Soma Drawing Center, Seoul (2017); and participated in group exhibitions such as Hexed, Bexed & Sexed, West Den Haag, The Hague (2023); Walkie Talkie Shaking, Art Space Boan, Seoul (2022); One Escape at a Time, the 11th Seoul Mediacity Biennale, Seoul (2021); VIA Animation Festival, Viborg Museum, Viborg (2019); Matters of Women, Seoul National University Museum of Art, Seoul (2018); and An Artist’s Attitude toward Labor, Incheon Art Platform, Incheon (2016).

name: Yaerim Ryu
bio: Combining wordy titles with pictures made of elaborated backgrounds and settings, Yaerim RYU’s (b. 1994) practice investigates the definition of and the divide between painting and illustration through collages of narratives. Yaerim Ryu had solo exhibitions at Show and Tell, Seoul, and Shift, Seoul. She has participated in group exhibitions at Gallery Func, Shanghai, Doosan Gallery, Seoul, BGA maru, Seoul, and Bergstaffel, Stuttgart. In 2022, she was part of “Now & Next” by Frieze and Chanel Korea and the “Review Project” of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Korea. In 2023, she has an exhibition at Gallery Kiche in Seoul.

name: Manna Lee
bio: Artist Lee Manna explores the depths of unfamiliar experiences and inner psychology found within everyday landscapes, channeling these through his distinct use of color and technique. Over time, he meticulously builds up the density of his works through repetition. Lee describes his approach by invoking Camus: "Camus speaks of the 'strangeness' that emerges when one encounters the external world as 'itself,' rather than through convention. This notion closely aligns with what I term 'unfamiliarity.'" This idea extends to what he calls 'accidental encounters,' where the mundane spaces we encounter daily suddenly present themselves with a captivating unfamiliarity. These serene yet profound landscapes offer a moment to meet another side of oneself. Lee Manna persistently captures these fleeting instances in his art, ensuring they are expressed with persistence and depth.

name: Dongyoung Kim
bio:
The practice of Kim Dongyoung explores the profound dialogue between the visible and the invisible. By weaving together line, color, and space, Kim captures the intangible relationships that bind self to other and humanity to nature. Merging Eastern concepts of emptiness with Western abstract materiality, her work transcends the visual to become a meditative field for perceiving life.
Having completed her B.F.A. and M.F.A. at the University of Kentucky, Kim earned a Ph.D. in Fine Arts from Hongik University. Her work is represented in major international collections, such as the Seoul National University Museum of Art, the Sabae Contemporary Art Center (Japan), and the Enrique Norten Collection.

name: PARK KI ILL
bio:
Park Ki-Il reconstructs fragments of memory shaped by his personal experiences onto the canvas. His work often begins with recollections such as witnessing the neighborhood where he once ran and played with friends transformed into a barren landscape by redevelopment, or imagining the comic books he longed for as a child piled up in some forgotten warehouse.

One of the distinctive technical characteristics of Park Ki-Il’s practice is his use of the airbrush. Rendered with extreme realism and meticulous detail, yet without visible brushstrokes, his paintings can closely resemble printed images. Because airbrushing applies paint in exceptionally thin layers compared to traditional brushwork, the physical thickness of the paint is almost imperceptible.

name: Kim Byung Joo
bio: Kim Byung-Joo expresses a new dimension of space through a series of laser-cut steel reliefs in the form of a grid. Kim Byung-Joo’s grid structure "Ambiguous Wall", in which the boundary between inside and outside becomes ambiguous depending on the viewing angle, simultaneously creates and dissolves the boundary between inside and outside. The artist, who graduated from the Faculty of Sculpture at Hongik University, UAL Chelsea University of Arts in London, England, with a Master in Fine Arts and a PhD in Sculpture from Hongik University, continues to be active in the national and international art world by not only participating in Art Miami 2021 and 2022, but also having a solo exhibition in Montreal, Canada in 2022. Large reliefs are collected and exhibited at major art institutions such as the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art Art Bank, the Seoul Museum of Art and the Pohang Museum of Art, as well as Terminal 2 of Incheon International Airport.

name: N5bra
bio: Seoul based artist N5BRA(South Korea, b. 1995) is a street artist, beginning with illustration he expanded his scope of activities to painting. N5BRA’s world of work began with nude drawings that contain personal emotions and experiences that were traced during his military service. The physical scale of his works grew enormously as he shifted his medium to wall painting and graffiti whilst directing his works to themes of contradictions and ills of society. The artist drew on paper, canvas, and walls the problematic scenes as an enlightening testament to what he directly witnessed, sensed, and then captured onto his art using ink, spray paint, masking tape, markers, and acrylic paint. The fickle nature of his work, which gave unconstrained freedom on materials, subjects, or settings stemmed from his early past when he painted on the streets and studied painting at Hongik University. His first solo exhibition

name: Jina Jung
bio:
Jina Jung (b.1990) creates paintings and new media art that alter the invisible properties of changing water, wind and other elements in nature. She captures images of nature  and transforms these images into quixotic landscapes.  For Jung, her artistic process culminates in reassembling the “visible and penetrable landscapes” formed in virtual space into paintings on canvas. Through the process of transforming and capturing landscapes of reality into an unfamiliar images, she provides an opportunity to questions and examines the logic of subverted nature.

Jung studied Oriental Painting at Ewha Womans University and received her BFA and MFA from this institution. She went on to graduate from the Interactive Telecommunications Program (ITP) at Tisch School of the Arts, New York University, where she continued to experiment with technology-based art. In 2019, she held residencies at Pause Kreativ in Germany and Untitled Space in China and has held numerous solo exhibitions including at ROY GALLERY (2022, 2025), Hidden M Gallery (2024), and Prompt Project (2023). She has participated in numerous group exhibitions at major domestic and international institutions and platforms, including Moran Museum of Art (2012), Sejong Center for the Arts (2016), Hangaram Museum of Art (2021), Seoul Auction Gangnam Center (2021), Gallery Park (2021), and Shanghai 1-Art Gallery (2020).

name: JungOuk Hong
bio: Hong Jung-wook raises fundamental questions about the stylized square frame and why it should always be hung on the wall. He continues experiments on shapes that can harmonize and breathe within the entire space. If the traditional concept of painting means an independent space separated from the actual space as a 'trompe-l'oeil' that reproduces the three-dimensional space, Hong Jung-wook can directly intervene in the actual space as a substantial three-dimensional form by modifying the meaning while using canvas and frame. The canvas frame, which only existed as a support for the painting, changed into figures such as triangles, pentagones, octagones and circles in his works to show its formability. This brings us a new awareness of looking at only a wide part of the canvas.

name: Hwang Seungwoo
bio:
BRIEF OVERVIEW – SCULPTURAL PRACTICE

My work consists of forms which depict the flow of time, capturing traces of destruction and transformation.  It is a means of recognising who I am and where I am.
Actually I am made aware of my existence during the process of working, through making each cut very carefully, keeping a certain depth and distance between each of the cuts.  The primary aim of the cutting is not to reproduce the appearance of books or paper; its value is equally in the actual process of working towards realising a concept.
Every piece of art is based on each artist’s identity. This identity provides artistic originality and for this reason, each artist constantly seeks to find the source of artistic originality.  
In summary, my art is based on “flexibility”.  This comes from my heritage, the culture of Korea.
In spite of the development in technology and Great influence of Western culture on Eastern culture, I, as a man who has been grown up and living in Oriental culture that has different way in understanding the relationship of Nature and Human.
What is the way of Oriental thinking and Living?
It seems to be there are many different way of understanding of Nature in which, as a whole, Taoism has been eminently taking an important role along with Buddhism and Confucianism within the context of traditionalism. 
The Eastern religious and philosophical views as such on nature derives me asking a new question on the subject ; How do we manifest ourself in this world in order to establish and find a place to co-exist in art and life, living and understanding.

name: Sukwon Park
bio:
Sukwon Park(b. 1942), a visionary of modern Korean abstract artist, is known for his work that gives a strong impression and fresh shock by breaking away from conventional sculpture and painting. In particular, Schorched Earth, the winner of the 1968 National Exhibition, is considered to be Sukwon Park's early masterpiece, which was a sensational sculpture at that time. His understanding and expressing various materials and nature has a lot of influence on Korean art world.
After exploring abstract expression in the early 1960s and minimalism in the 1970s, the artist synthesized the previous works in the 1980s and established an independent world of works. The change in the subject from ‘Scorched Earth’ to ‘Mutation-Relation’ through ‘Accumulation’ implies elements of 'segmentation' and 'conjugation'. Mutation-Relation means stacking, which means cutting or dismantling various materials and then stacking them again. The artist's work of structurally re-accumulating cut objects can be seen as the influence of minimalism, but it also contains a naturalistic interpretation that exposes the texture as it is, unlike artificial and upright minimalism. His work is differentiated from the minimalism of other artificial concepts in that he considers the deformation of matter that occurs in the making process, or even the traces of material left behind, to be the essence of the work.
‘Scorched Earth’ means ‘a state of being devastated and ruined by fire,’ which means ‘blacken soil.’ It is a representative work of modern sculpture that was born with the theme of chaos and tragedy in Korean society after the war. The blighted spaces like the scorched earth, and the traces of tension in which the intense energy of the moment escaped sharply from the original space, express the anger and shock of the time that the artist experienced.natural state. The artist's work not

name: Sunghong Min
bio:
민성홍은 추계예술대학교, 샌프란시스코 아트 인스티튜트 대학원에서 회화를 전공했다. 첫 개인전 《The Island: Garden》(디에고 리베라 갤러리, 2002)을 시작으로 뉴욕, 로스엔젤레스, 브뤼쉘, 서울에서 개인전을 선보였고, 산책자의 시선(경기도미술관, 2016), DNA (대구미술관, 2016), 창원조각비엔날레(2016), 광주비엔날레(2018), 서울미디어시티비엔날레(2018) 국내외 다수의 기획전에 참여해오고 있다. 

작가는 버려진 사물과 공간 설치 작업을 통해 외부의 자극과 변화로 인해 갈등하고 고민하는 현대인의 처지, 갈등을 해결해나가는 과정, 다양한 관계성을 이야기한다. 최근에는 사람들이 버린 가구나 생활 집기, 옷걸이 등에 바퀴를 달고, 그것들을 무대 위로 이동시켜 움직임을 주는 방식으로 작업해오고 있다. 연출된 무대 공간과 각 사물들의 변형과 재조합을 통해서 작가와 대상, 재료와 시각적 결과물 등 작게는 미술, 넓게는 사회 속에 존재하는 다양한 관계를 보여준다. 작가는 이처럼 재료를 활용하거나, 행위 하는 제작과정을 전면에 드러내는 프로젝트를 진행한다.

name: Ho Sangun
bio:
Ho Sangun blends the familiar with the unfamiliar, capturing everyday scenes using paper and colored pencils. Through his ongoing project “Ho Sangun’s Reproduction Office,” since 2012, he listens to others’ stories while conveying his observations through drawing. Originally focused on humor and empathy in Korean culture, his recent work in Germany explores cultural clashes and unfamiliar aspects in ordinary scenes, reflecting his life as a cultural outsider. Ho approaches everyday life with optimism and curiosity, documenting the seemingly trivial yet profound elements that contribute to our existence with reverence and awe.

_Submitted by [oaoa](https://www.artsy.net/partner/oaoa)_

name: Aedam Kim Donghyung
bio: Aedam Kim Donghyung was born in Busan in 1992. He pursued a major in Oriental Painting and earned his Bachelor of Fine Arts (BFA) from Dankook University in 2018, followed by a Master of Fine Arts (MFA) from Hongik University in 2020. Having been influenced by his father, who worked in construction from his early days, architectural elements are prominent in Kim’s works. Among these, the most representative is the texture resembling the surfaces of building walls. This texture reflects Kim's contemplation of the relationship between nature and artificiality, inspired by his observations of cracked, rusty, or peeling surfaces on buildings. Through this, he came to visually perceive the coexistence of nature and artificiality. In order to incorporate this observation into his work in a fundamental way, he focuses on the materials used in the base layer of his creations. Kim starts by applying construction materials in multiple thin layers onto the canvas to create a unique rough texture. Once this is dry, he attaches traditional Korean paper, called hanji, to the surface. For Kim, construction materials represent artificiality, while Korean paper signifies nature. He conveys the coexistence of these elements by combining these materials in his art. Furthermore, Kim’s works predominantly feature the color white. This reflects a paradox he encountered when he painted over his existing artworks with white gesso, in an attempt to start afresh during a period of creative stagnation. He realized that in order to achieve the goal of erasing or “emptying” past works, one must paradoxically complete “filling” the canvas with white. Through this experience, Kim came to define white as a color that simultaneously embodies emptying and filling. In a similar vein, his work accentuates all ambivalent relationships, such as those between nature and artificiality, and emptying and filling.

name: Ham Sup
bio:
Sup Ham (b.1942) has worked with hanji, traditional handmade Korean paper, as his primary medium for over 30 years. Using an- tique manuscripts, Ham transforms the original appearance and nature of his material through a process of dying, soaking, tearing and kneading the pieces of paper before superimposing them in layers onto the canvas. The dried surfaces subsequently undergo a variety of techniques to create the desired tactile effects - pound- ing, stamping, rolling and cutting - similarly echoing the process of hanji production. Through his palette of traditional Korean colors made from natural dyes, Ham’s work of contemporary abstraction reveal an East-West stylistic synthesis marked by a traditional Korean aesthetic.

The painting-like character of Ham’s hanji compositions stems from his Western artistic training and education. Born and raised in the Gangwon provincial capital, Chuncheon, a rural area known for its natural beauty, Ham has participated in numerous exhibitions at internationally renowned venues, including the Hyundai Art Gallery (Seoul), the National Museum of Contemporary Art (Seoul), and the Museum für Asiatische Kunst (Berlin).

name: Suh Seung Won
bio: Suh Seung-Won received his BFA and MFA in Painting at Hongik University, where he served as a professor for 33 years. One of the inaugural members of the Origin Group (1963), Korean Contemporary Printmakers Association (1967), and the A.G. (1969), Suh was invited to participate the 1975 exhibition Five Korean Artists, Five Kinds of White at the Tokyo Gallery and played a significant role in the advent and evolution of Korean avant-garde movement. He has held numerous exhibitions at prominent art institutions in Korea and abroad including National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (Gwacheon, Korea), Seoul Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), Sungkok Art Museum (Seoul, Korea), Brooklyn Museum (New York, USA), Galerie Perrotin (Paris, France), Tokyo Central Museum of Art (Tokyo, Japan), Fukuoka Asian Art Museum (Fukuoka, Japan), Hokkaido Museum of Modern Art (Sapporo, Japan). Suh participated in international art events such as Sao Paulo Biennale, Biennale des Jeunes Paris, Gwnagju Biennale, Busan Biennale. He was awarded the 5th Grand-Prix Korean Art Exhibition Grand Prize (hosted by Hankook Ilbo), the Korean Art Critics Association Best Artist Prize, and Oh Ji- ho Grand Prize (hosted by Gwangju City Hall). His works are included in the permanent collections of the Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (Gwacheon, Korea), Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), The British Museum (London, UK), Guggenheim Abu Dhabi (Abu Dhabi, UAE), Mie Prefectural Museum of Art (Tsu, Japan), Shimonoseki City Art Museum (Shimonoseki, Japan).

name: Jeenee Lee
bio: Jeenee Lee was born in Busan in 1969. She majored in Oil Painting at Pusan ​​National University and the same graduate school. She moved back and forth between Busan and Seoul, participating in numerous solo and group exhibitions and currently living and working in Busan. Jeenee Lee make us meet the unexpected 'thing' at one moment, a fantasy that makes something appear. It leads us to something which is not individual, something which is not showing up on the canvas, and a time zone which doesn't belong to now. The cushions on the sofa are not reproduced objects. They make time go away with the exclusion of any stories, and anything there. Her materials or figures try to show 'something', which is aroused or created by the moment of discontinuity. We note her because of the temporary experience, the deviation of time and place, getting over the present. Traces or moments of activity are revealed on Jeenee Lee's sofa or couch. However, on top of that, a certain existence is lost, and at the same time, it captures the precious part of life as a real medium.

name: Ha Taeim
bio:
Experience the vibrant works of Ha TaeIm, the renowned South Korean artist taking the world by storm. With a captivating blend of bold colors and stunning compositions, TaeIm has solidified her position as a true visionary in modern art.

But her art is more than just visually striking. It carries a powerful message of female empowerment, celebrating the strength and beauty of women. Through her captivating pieces, TaeIm invites each viewer to be inspired, express themselves, and pursue their passions.

Prepare to be captivated by TaeIm’s unique vision and embark on a journey of self-discovery. Her thought-provoking art offers a window into her world, while encouraging viewers to explore their own inner selves in new and meaningful ways. Get ready to be inspired, unleash your creativity, and find your own path to empowerment through the artistry of Ha TaeIm.

name: Sang Hwan
bio:
Sanghwan (b. 1991) is an artist whose multidisciplinary practice encompasses sculpture, ceramics, painting, and installation, exploring personal experience and the traces of existence. Through the transformation of emotions and memories gathered from everyday life into visual forms, the artist investigates themes of disappearance, substitution, and the instability of being.
In major series such as Santo and Lumps and Things in Contact, Sanghwan employs black, lump-like sculptural forms as symbolic embodiments of fragmented emotions and states of existence. These forms accumulate, lean against one another, or disperse across space, revealing conditions of relationship, balance, and tension. Through this visual language, the artist examines the fragile dynamics of being that emerge between the individual and society.
Sanghwan’s work can be understood as a process of sculptural inscription—one that begins with ordinary experience and expands into fundamental inquiries concerning life, memory, and existence.

name: Kwon Daehun
bio: Born and raised in Republic of Korea, Kwon Daehun graduated Seoul National University with both bachelor’s and master’s degrees. Within a few years, he has enrolled in Slade School of Fine Art to graduate with MFA degree. Since then, Kwon has been actively involved in numerous exhibitions in UK, France, and Republic of Korea, receiving acknowledgement of excellency of his sculpture practice. In 2005, he had earned the Bursary award from RBS (Royal British Society of Sculptors). In 2011, he had been awarded The Jack Goldhill Award from The Royal Academy of Arts Summer Exhibition 2011. Kwon’s practice consists in sculpture, installation and performance. His work is imbued with a distinctive sense of time as marking material objects including people in such a way that they become signs of their part in the configuration of moment (the artist refers to the Korean expression ‘Chalna’ which he translates as ‘the very moment when a thing or a phenomenon is developing’). Kwon currently live and work in Seoul, Republic of Korea as an artist and a professor of Seoul National University, Republic of Korea.

name: Choi Byungso
bio:
CHOI Byungso (b.1943) employs a unique methodology of transforming substance materiality through the erasure of newspaper content by repetitive and executive mark-making with ballpoint pen and pencil, a process he has continued for over forty years. Choi holds a very special position in Korea’s contemporary art world, for the intellectuality and engagement found within his works fall in line with the monochrome paintings that dominated the Korean art scene in the ‘70s. His participation in major Korean monochrome art exhibitions, including A Facet of Contemporary Korean Art (Tokyo Central Art Museum, 1977), École de Seoul (National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Gwacheon 1976-79) and Korea’s Modern Paintings (National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Gwacheon, 2012), brought him to be designated as a member of the monochrome movement, but that is only a fragmentary categorization.

Earlier works, such as an arrangement of iron pins on the floor with one hanging from the ceiling; decaying mackerel within the exhibition space; reading photographs as text, and more, lay their roots in the Korean experimental art movement. Alongside Park Hyun-gi and Lee Kang-so, Choi was a featured artist in 1974’s Experimental Korean Art Exhibition; he also led Daegu Contemporary Art Fair for 5 years and belonged to the 35/128 Group, a powerhouse of Korea’s avant-garde movement. In his work Untitled (Bird) (1975) (previously exhibited at ARARIO GALLERY Cheonan), Choi examines the relationship between image and language by listing six words, ‘sky, cloud, wind, birds, flying, meeting,’ besides a National Geographic photo of two birds; this, too, fits well into the context of Korean experimental art.

name: Hannaz
bio:
"I have an idea that some men are born out of their due place. Accident has cast them amid certain surroundings, but they always have a nostalgia for a home they know not."
THE MOON AND SIXPENCE
 
"They were not born where they were supposed to be but elsewhere."
 
This quote from William Somerset Maugham's novel "The Moon and Sixpence" has lingered in the artist's life. For half a decade, Hannaz traveled along the warm sun on the beaches of Europe, yearning for the unknown homeland she could possibly build in every place she visited. However, she soon found herself wanting to leave to yet another location, like a rubber ball bouncing never knowing where to go. 
 
During those days in Europe, she once thought about coming back to her country by the 60s. That plan came forward 20 years quite unexpectedly due to Covid-19, making her nestle in Jeju, Korea. It has been more than a year she has visited every corner of the island, trying to build her place in the scenes she grew up watching on TV and photos on the calendars.
 
Nevertheless, she found herself bouncing off again, for she realized those exposures only gave her another illusion about Jeju. She became a stranger in the familiar, having to build her unique perspective on the island. This exhibition presents this year-long journey of Hannaz, showing various landscapes of Jeju Island with herself mirrored to the rubber ball.

Hannaz has been educated at Istituto Europeo di Design Milano, Italy, in Photography, and at Ewha Woman's University for Oriental painting, Korea.

name: Lee Myoung Ho
bio: Combining a respect for nature with a highly conceptual investigation into image making, Myoung Ho Lee has been photographing the trees of his native Korea since 2006, isolating them from their surroundings through the imposition of a white canvas backdrop. Lee works slowly, observing each tree for four seasons before photographing it. Through digital retouching, he removes evidence of the canvas’s support structure, so that it appears to float unaided behind the tree that it frames. At once deadpan and playful, the resulting photographs highlight the beauty and physicality of the trees, while also flattening them, causing them to appear as unreal, two-dimensional images inserted into the landscape. Through this interplay between nature and artifice, Lee collapses the traditions of portraiture and landscape painting and photography, examining the nature of representation and its effect on nature itself.

name: EunHa Jung 정은하
bio:
I explore the meanings of time, existence, and connection through cities and bridges unfolding in different time zones and light, as well as through old towns and river landscapes.
A bridge is not merely a physical structure spanning space; it is a symbol that connects human existence and destiny. The moment of crossing the bridge becomes a passage linking past and future, inner self and the outside world—a crossroads where all our lives meet.
The landscapes bathed in the colorful hues of sunset, evening, and morning light seem unchanging, yet they lie within the ceaseless flow of time. These moments touched by light evoke the fleeting beauty and impermanence of existence, while carrying within them hope, resolve, and emotional resonance.
A city is a space where human desires and memories intersect, generating both pain and healing. Especially at the boundary where darkness and light coexist, it poses questions about life’s fundamental irony, contradictions, and reconciliation. The old city and warm sunlight linger briefly within the vast current called ‘time,’ symbolizing inner peace, self-discovery, and the fundamental solidarity of human existence.
In my paintings, light becomes a mysterious junction that transcends disconnected time and space to unite us as one. I hope the interplay of light, color, and place in my work will transform ordinary moments into something extraordinary.

name: Eunmi Kim
bio: In my art work, I optionally made landscape for the audience to approach from near and far. So the 「Zoom in zoom out」 series is created in a way a smart phone is used in our everyday lives. In other words, using a touch screen is a familiar life style for all of us with multiple purposes including travel and taking pictures. There is temporality in this art work but no priorities exist unlike everyday life or literature that has flow of time. Moreover, the colored side, pattern, and the shape of the building are not just placed in a row but in a way  these are approaching some kind of climax. The circulation of time seems to be cut off by placing a comparatively large colored side among the buildings densely arranged and one can recall a sense of rhythm from the repetitive action of increasing and decreasing the size of the screen.

name: Sangmyun Lee 이상면
bio:
Since 1995, he has been active as the guitarist and singer-songwriter of the Korean punk band Crying Nut. Alongside his music career, he works as a recording engineer and producer. In 2026, the band marks its 31st anniversary. He is currently pursuing a Master’s degree in Painting at the Graduate School of Fine Arts, Hongik University.

In his visual practice, he constructs imaginary mental landscapes and explores the beings that inhabit them. These entities need not exist in reality—much like the aliens, goblins, or extinct creatures continually reimagined through cinema and literature. Though unseen, they persist vividly within collective memory and imagination.

Within these fictional yet familiar environments, provisional communities emerge between humans and invented beings. The tensions and dilemmas of our world inevitably surface there, where characters and humans confront them together, seeking alternative resolutions.

Speculations on future technologies, portals to other worlds, and evolving emotional states expand into layered narratives. Through the continual weaving and transformation of unfamiliar

name: Ju Young Kim
bio:
Ju Young Kim (*1991, Seoul, KR) explores transitional states and transit zones in her sculptures and installations by combining industrial transportation modules from airplanes and cars into symbolically encoded works. She blends these with stained glass, cast metal, ceramics and plastic, thus bringing together high-tech objects with hand crafts techniques. The works are characterized by surreal elements that have been extracted from their original context and open up a new perspective on the phenomena of the globalized world. In her conceptual explorations, she examines the relativity of space and time from the perspective of a transcontinental traveler. She combines her own experiences and feelings with objects and reflects on the extent to which belonging, origin and borders shape and form identity. Landscape motifs and traditional symbolism meet industrial products and transportation systems to paint a picture of an accelerated society in which different cultural and temporal components collide.

Ju Young Kim studied at the Academy of Fine Arts Munich as a Meisterschülerin of Olaf Nicolai and was awarded the 2024 Debutant Grant for her diploma project AEROPLASTICS. Her works have recently been exhibited in group exhibitions at Printgallery in Tokyo, Kunsthalle Recklinghausen and Lothringer Halle 13 in Munich. Kim will open a solo exhibition at the Kunsthalle Mannheim in the summer of 2025 and participate in the Singapore Biennale this fall.

name: Jian Yoo
bio:
Jian Yoo (South Korean, b. 1982) explores how invisible flows of time and emotion take form as structures through light, material, and space. Emotion is understood as the most delicate trace of existence and the most private record of time. 

Accumulated time, shifting emotions, and traces of experience continuously circulate—gathering, dispersing, and moving. These flows are not depicted but take form as structures that can be perceived through the senses.

Formed through the accumulation of countless mother-of-pearl fragments, the surface holds both stillness and movement. As light and perception shift, the work operates as a field where time condenses and expands.

Mother-of-pearl is a language that records light and reveals change. Carefully inscribed through this language of light, the surface exists as the structure in which invisible flows become visible.

name: sanghoon ahn
bio:
AHN Sanghoon majored in Painting at Jung-Ang University, received his Akademiebrief and was a Meisterschueler at Kunstakademie Muenster. The artist constantly raises meaningless questions what painting is to him and experiments the nature of painting expanding into space. 
He held solo exhibitions at GALLERY CHOSUN(2018,Seoul), Incheon Art Platform (2018, Incheon), Kreis Museum(2016, Osterburg, Germany). He participated in various group shows including exhibitions at Oil Tank Culture Park, Soorim Cultural Foundation, Gyeonggi Creation Center, Plan B Project Space, Incheon Art Platform, Tempelhof Museum, Kunsthalle Muenster in Germany and many more. He has participated in several artist residency programs including Kunsthof Dahrenstedt, Incheon Art Platform, Gyeonggi Creation Center and will be working as an artist in MMCA Residency Goyang in 2020.

name: Seo Jiin
bio: Seo Jiin is a Korean contemporary artist whose practice situates painting within expanded material and spatial conditions. Rooted in abstraction, her work examines how memory, time, and bodily sensation accumulate on surfaces, approaching painting as a durational and process-based medium rather than a purely optical one.Her paintings are constructed through repetitive gestures and stratified layers of pigment, producing tactile surfaces that evoke geological formations, atmospheric light, and temporal sedimentation. Circular and modular formats play a central role in her practice, allowing individual paintings to function both as autonomous works and as components of larger spatial configurations.In recent years, Seo has expanded her practice to include ceramics, treating clay as a painterly material and embracing the unpredictability of firing as part of the work’s formation. She received a BFA in Painting and Sculpture from Chung-Ang University, Seoul, and has presented solo exhibitions in Seoul, as well as group exhibitions in Korea and Tokyo.

name: Felix
bio:
When enthusiasts and aficionados ask “how” to classify art, Felix answers: “why?”
 
Pursuing a distinctively integrated means of conveying his message, Felix forwards the cause of the Pop Art generation, led by artists such as Murakami Takeshi and Andy Warhol, by emphasizing the concept that art may draw inspiration from any source.
 
His artist’s oeuvre encompasses characteristics of various art styles and periods, including Pop Art, Cubism, and Deconstructivism. In his works, one can readily see the influences of  predecessors such as Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque. Yet by unmistakably placing his works in the genre of Pop Art, through his choices of subjects, Felix continues to blur the lines between high art and low art. He similarly, and simultaneously, fractures the boundary between modern art and contemporary art.
 
Felix’s flagrant use of pop culture imbues his works with the peculiar taste of Kitsch art, a pop art quality devoid of matiere technique, to which he applies the distinctively Cubist expression of rearranging the fragments of a subject. His unique approach entails not merely a variation on the classical styles, but a fusion and continuance.
 
The majority of Felix’s works testify that a person, or subject, is composed of much more than the single image on the surface. The fragmented figures are infused with a myriad of emotions such as passion, resentment, compassion, frustration, pleasure, and fear. This multifaceted approach allows for the simultaneous coexistence of different emotions, something that is usually very difficult to perceive.Felix’s deconstruction of his subjects is a reminder and encouragement to look beyond the confines of constructed identity, and the prejudices that inherently come with classifications.

name: Yoon Dong-Chun
bio: Yoon Dong-Chun (b. 1957 in Hwaseong, Korea) graduated from the College of Fine Arts at Seoul National University and received his Master’s degree from the Cranbrook Academy of Art in the United States. Yoon grounds his practice in society and everyday life, using sharp satire to confront the absurdities of contemporary reality across various genres. Since 1988, he has held numerous solo exhibitions and participated in over 300 group exhibitions, working across painting, installation, printmaking, photography, and drawing. In 1992, he was awarded the Gold Prize at the 4th International Asian European Art Biennale. His works are included in the collections of major art institutions in Korea and abroad, notably the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, and the British Museum.

name: Han Young Wook
bio: Han Young Wook creates portraits of anonymous figures by scratching aluminum panels with needles and painting oil paint on top of the scratched surface. The particular medium allows the artist to intricately carve aluminum panel and create a hyper-realistic texture of fine wrinkles, hair, and eyes filled with life that cannot be reached with canvas and paint. Han strides to bring the subject into life by making thin and thick scratches on the aluminum with different kinds of tools and painting into the crevices for depth. When the light hits the crevices, the aluminum reflects light that delivers a remarkable experience to the viewers, creating an illusion that the painting is three-dimensional or almost like a sculpture. The glistening surface of the aluminum panel, especially on the eyes of the subject, creates a dramatic mood that instantly pulls the viewer into the painting. Just like the quote “eyes are the window to the soul”, Han’s painting allows the viewers to imagine the life story and emotion of the people carved on the panel.

name: Young Jae
bio:
Young Jae is a South Korean painter who reconstructs fragments of personal memory into warm, fairytale-like narratives. His work begins at "Odo," a remote seaside village where his grandmother was born—a place reachable only by navigating steep cliffs and dense forests. For the artist, Odo is more than a geographical location; it is a repository of memories, echoing his grandmother’s gentle touch and the silent, unconditional acceptance he experienced in his youth.

In his compositions, Young Jae introduces two symbolic figures to weave these memories together: the 'Cat' and the 'Whale.' The cat serves as the narrator and observer, moving through different layers of time to guide the story. In contrast, the whale embodies longing and compassion—a majestic presence that, while rarely seen in reality, constantly resurfaces in the ocean of his mind.

Technically, Young Jae’s practice is rooted in traditional Oriental painting, characterized by a meticulous process of layering soft graphite on Hanji (traditional Korean paper). By repeatedly applying graphite, he creates a dense, velvety monotone surface that absorbs and reflects light with a subtle shimmer. This labor-intensive accumulation of graphite mirrors the slow build-up of human memory, lending a physical weight to his ethereal subjects. Through this unique fusion of material depth and poetic storytelling, Young Jae invites viewers into a universal space of consolation and spiritual reunion.

name: Hijo Nam
bio: Hijo Nam's artwork is an orchestra comprised of many instrumental sounds-each material having its own unique echo contributing to the whole creation. The scraps she works with were used long ago; there is still evidence of their incredible age. These scraps could have once been a part of a garage ceiling or even a doorway. The possibilities are endless. Nam's role is to understand the historical imprints left on these pieces and to modernize them into sculptures from her own perspective. She had gone as far as to completely break apart her ceramic sculptures, and then fuse the broken pieces with all the other materials, to create a symphony of sound, like a conductor that unifies an orchestra.

name: Namjoo Kim
bio:
Born in Seoul in 1968, Namjoo Kim is a visual artist based in the U.S. After earning a Bachelor and Master of Visual Arts in Seoul in 1992, She completed another Master’s degree at the School of Visual Arts in New York in 1994.

Namjoo has exhibited work nationally and internationally, exploring themes of identity, culture, and perception. Currently, She is focused on a series of mirror paintings that reflect the layered experiences of Korean American identity. Namjoo creates vibrant images that spark conversation and reflection, encouraging us to engage with our own inner worlds.

name: In Kyung Kwon
bio: Kwon In-kyung, who mainly captures landscapes through painting techniques, has been using acrylic paint along with traditional mook, and has shown her unique expression technique of collating pieces of old books. The canvas is filled with unrealistic scenes, including which are close to the artist’s daily lives such as houses, rocky mountains, rivers, and apartment. The landscape without perspective and reality is surrounded by distorted and mixed scenery, and the river stream or mountains encircled like a castle, reveals a lump of space. The artist calls the exposed space "Heart-Land." This space, which can be interpreted as the center, or the middle, or heart, symbolizes the ultimate peace and refuge for escape from an uneasy reality. Just as the fragment of an ancient book, which is based on time, is read as a movement toward the source of life, the artist expresses the inherent agony of human beings pursuing Utopia.

name: Jeah hyuck
bio:
Jeah Hyuck is a South Korean artist, based in London and Seoul. He started his artistic journey at the University of the Arts London, completing a foundation degree in 2017. Then further completing a first-class honours degree from Goldsmiths, University of London, in 2020. 

Hyuck navigates the complexities of being part of the British diaspora. His art is deeply influenced by his personal journey of living in an unfamiliar society. Hyuck delves into the narrative of identity, exploring his own endeavours to assimilate and the internal conflict of erasing aspects of his cultural identity to mimic the behaviours of the locals. This duality of existence – between his South Korean heritage and his adaptation to British culture – is a central theme in his art, offering a unique perspective on the universal quest for belonging and self-discovery.

In his compelling series of 'brain sketches,' Jeah Hyuck offers a raw glimpse into his suppressed inner thoughts, bursting forth onto the canvas (Jang ji) with an intensity that captivates and challenges. This technique, known as automatism, sees Hyuck tapping into the depths of his unconscious mind, allowing a spontaneous and unfiltered flow of artistic expression. His method echoes the legendary American artist Jackson Pollock, known for his revolutionary drip paintings, which were born from the spontaneous acts of hand movements. Similarly, Hyuck utilises instant words, visually written in a stream of consciousness style, to convey his inner dialogue.

name: Kim Dong Yoo
bio: Kim Dong Yoo plays with perception in meticulously composed paintings that are never quite what they seem. He principally focuses on two celebrated series: “Double Images,” featuring large-scale canvases encompassing multiple images that are revealed as viewers shift position; and “Face,” iconic portraits of celebrities throughout history, composed of hundreds of tiny, individual portraits of other famous figures, rendered entirely by hand. These works merge his interests in the history of painting, world history—especially WWII and the postwar period—and celebrity culture. “I have a preference for celebrities as the main subject of my art,” he explains. “I have loved movies and gossip about the actors since my childhood.” In his works, Kim goes deeper than gossip, making the familiar extraordinary and challenging us to see the world through an alternative lens.
