name: Youmee Lee
bio: YouMee Lee was born in Seoul, Korea in 1969, studied in Ewha Womans University in Sculpture(BFA, MA) in Seoul, Korea and School of the Art Institute of Chicago in Chicago, US. She is known for Korean Paper Sculpture. She participated in residency program in Lee JungSeop Art Museum(Jeju, Korea), CITE' INTERNATIONALE DES ARTS(Paris, France), Gana Art Jangheung Atelier(Kyonggi-do, Korea) since 2002. She has many solo and group shows, including art fairs, both at home and overseas. In Lee's  works which treated existence in terms of cosmological point of view like Buddha preaches meaning of emptiness which came up with a thought that what does matter is not secular reality of human being like everyday life, agony, relations and so on. One thing she would not put down so far is the realization of its essence, not various expressions of forms themselves, which could not be reached out, and which thoughtful human being tries to pursue ceaselessly. Therefore a important thing is a perspective for characters to hold. They do not look to a specified direction in the works. They do not bow and turn away the world nor shut down the mind. Rather they contemplate the world as if meditating with the eyes half-closed and raising the head. The characters in works became an ascetic on the way to getting enlightened through long patience and asceticism. As the meditative part of the characters is solely represented in the works this time, their structure from the secular to the holy is more expanded than before. They are the forms of human being but they are not specified ones and show abstractness of the artist’s elaboration to try to pursue the essence.

name: Lee Lee Nam
bio:
Timeless beauty and cutting edge technology come together in the exquisite video creations by Lee Lee Nam, one of Korea’s most prominent new media artists.

Lee Nam first trained as a sculptor, graduating from Chosun University in 1995. The moving image soon became the artist’s chosen media, however, enabling him to overcome what he viewed as the limitations of sculpture and connect more directly with viewers; Lee Nam finally specialised in New Media at Yonsei University, completing a PhD in 2007.

From his early stop motion creations and experiments in animation, Lee Nam developed digital reinterpretations of classical masterpieces, moving versions of landmark pieces such as Jan Vermeer’s Girl with a Pearl Earring and Leonardo Da Vinci’s Mona Lisa, along with traditional Asian artworks. Static images give way to a poetry of subtly changing landscapes. “Perhaps I have in me the teachings of Taoism that sees the return to the original purity and simplicity,” says Lee Nam, who views his works as opportunities for quiet and calm in a hectic world.

Lee Nam’s work has featured in group exhibitions across the globe, including at the Venice Biennale, The Saatchi Gallery, London, and the National Museum of India. Lee Nam has hosted individual shows in Korea, USA and Australia, among others, and his creations feature in the permanent collections of Korea’s most prestigious museums including The National Museum of Contemporary Art, Seoul Museum of Art and Savina Museum.

name: Cody Choi
bio: Cody Choi, who has been consistently active as a visual artist and cultural theorist since the 1980s, explores the cultural identity and relationship of authority within contemporary society. Choi touches upon topics of cultural maldigestion, third-culture created by the clash of different cultures, the beauty of such hybridism, and simultaneously occurring new social phenomena—all of which Choi experienced as a foreigner in the US. Choi gained his stature as a world-renowned artist after participating in a solo exhibition at Deitch Projects (New York, USA) and an inaugural group exhibition at the Musée d’Art Contemporain de Marseille (Marseille, France) in the mid-1990s. From 2015 to 2017 he had a retrospective traveling show at Kunsthalle Düsseldorf (Düsseldorf, Germany), Musée d’Art Contemporain de Marseille (Marseille, France), Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz (Chemnitz, Germany) organized by art-historian John C. Welchman. Choi was a representing artist at the Korean Pavilion for the 2017 Venice Biennale. His publication includes Topography of 20th Century Culture (2006) and Topography of Contemporary Culture (2010), which are critiques about contemporary society and culture.

name: Jaeeun Jeon
bio:
Jaeun Jeon is an artist based in Korea whose work explores the notion of place beyond the visible, drawing from personal memory and sensory experience. 
Her practice unfolds through painting and mixed media, where layered surfaces and textile elements function as a means of connecting past and present. Rooted in autobiographical narratives, her work weaves together spatial structures and emotional landscapes, gently inviting viewers to reconsider everyday places from a contemplative perspective. 
She received her M.F.A. in Painting from Sookmyung Women’s University, has teaching experience at the university level, and has participated in approximately 50 group exhibitions.

name: Kim Chang Young
bio: Kim Chang Young’s painting hyper-realistically reproduces image of desert onto the canvas. From afar, the painting seems almost like a photograph for the way it is painted in much detail. However, when observing up close, the viewers can tell that the canvas is covered with real sand and the light and shadowed parts are painted with oil. This creates an illusion and confusion to viewers making it difficult to them to distinguish which part of the painting has real sand or paint. The painting evokes the optical illusion in which even the actual sand looks like paint. What Kim intends to do is to make a new approach to our perception of reality, which, after all, is comprised by both the direct sense of reality and complexity of illusion.

name: Keun-Tai Kim
bio: Kim Keun-Tai (b. 1953) was born in Seoul, Korea and he graduated from Chung-Ang University in Seoul. Kim had his first solo exhibition in 1988, and he has since had works exhibited both at home and overseas: Germany, Japan, Vietnam, Hong Kong and the US. While he is often associated with the Dansaekhwa (單色畫) movement, through deep philosophical and aesthetic research he has always sought to go beyond the conceptual limits. At a time when his contemporaries were primarily preoccupied with making figuration known as hyper-realism, the young artists’ attempt to reverse the older generation’s abstract art: Kim showed more of an affinity towards Dansaekhwa (單色畫). Kim’s work has been presented in galleries and museums including Korea’s Chosun Ilbo Art Museum, Germany’s Galerie Konrad Munter and Hong Kong’s Whitestone Gallery. His works are collected by Sungkok Art Museum, PyeongChang Organizing Committee for the 2018 Olympic & Paralympic Games and KEB Hana Bank.

name: Eunjoo Song
bio:
-Sky Literacy: Adding a Touch of Cedar Wood Painting-
“Sky Literacy” refers to a process of aesthetically understanding and expressing the sky with the whole body, a process of using the unique imagery of the sky to reach a point of Sky Aesthetics, or a process of renewing feelings for Mother Nature, or the sky that we gaze into every day and finding new hope by receiving a sense of comfort. Sky Literacy may also indicate a record of one’s everyday life and express an understanding of the sky with an aesthetic interpretation for a piling of such records.

name: Sangdeok Ra
bio:
Ra Sang-deok is a contemporary Korean artist who draws inspiration from elemental forces such as fire, charcoal, and heat to create powerful visual imagery. His work reinterprets the movement of flames and the traces they leave behind through a unique sculptural language, conveying layers of time and emotion embedded within the canvas. The vivid red energy that contrasts against dark backgrounds, along with ash-like textures, reflects his artistic exploration of nature’s transformations and the cycle of life.

Ra’s work goes beyond simple depiction of forms, revealing both the primal power of nature and the inner energy of the human spirit, resulting in an intense sense of immersion. Through numerous exhibitions and art fairs across Korea, he continues to present an evolving body of work, establishing a distinctive visual world within the Korean contemporary art scene.

name: Young-il Ahn
bio:
Young-Il Ahn was a Korean-American painter born in Gaeseong (now in North Korea), celebrated for his luminous abstractions inspired by the natural world. A child prodigy, he won numerous art prizes and studied at Seoul National University before immigrating to Los Angeles in 1966, where the light and seascape of California profoundly influenced his work.

A transformative moment in 1983—when Ahn became lost in ocean fog while fishing—sparked the genesis of his iconic Water series. The revelation of sunlight shimmering across the waves became a spiritual and aesthetic breakthrough, anchoring his lifelong exploration of perception, repetition, and radiance.

In 2017–18, Ahn became the first Korean-American artist to receive a solo exhibition at LACMA, with additional solo shows at the Long Beach Museum of Art in 2014 and 2017. Upon his passing in 2020, ArtNews honored him as a “trailblazing painter of radiant abstractions.”

name: Jeehye Song
bio:
Jeehye Song (b. 1991 in Seoul, lives and works in Düsseldorf) completed her studies at the Düsseldorf Art Academy in 2021 as a master student of Prof. Andreas Schulze. She has received numerous awards and grants in Germany and internationally. Her solo and group exhibitions span galleries and institutions across Germany, Denmark, Finland, Italy, South Korea, and the United States. In 2025, the artist was awarded the Art Prize Junger Westen and in 2024 she was shortlisted for the Paula Modersohn-Becker Art Prize. Her works are in the collections of Kunsthalle Recklinghausen, Germany; PARK SEOBO Foundation, South Korea; Sparkasse Gera, Germany; Artothek Köln, Germany and Nielsen Collection, Denmark.
 
Song’s painting combines formal precision with conceptual depth and raises
essential questions about the role of the artist and the significance of painting today. Merging surrealist elements with a sensitive approach to composition, the artist creates visual spaces shifting between reality and imagination. Her works often reflect their own process of creation, highlighting doubt, decision-making, and revision. The surreal functions as a space for thought in which visible and invisible, personal and collective, merge.

name: Soyoung Seo
bio: Soyoung Seo is an artist who converts figurative components into abstract images. She recently worked in several fields, including graphics, painting, design, and illustration. She develops her work in the form of collages, pursuing the unique atmosphere formed by the collision of unrelated places and objects, and is fascinated by humans’ raw and unrefined emotions. Since she describes her work as a series of daydreams and investigations, she allows the audience to join the beautiful and unstable realm of dreams and unconsciousness that we lose as we grow older, providing a vibrant world of inner sensations.

name: CHUNG, Hyun
bio: Materials chosen by Chung Hyun are usually from discarded waste that no longer has a purpose. Through sleepers, charcoal, asphalt concrete, and mixed stones - materials in which have been thrown away in contemporary society – the true side of human being is revealed. Chung Hyun does not alter the material much, but he tends to correspond and try not to lose any of the material’s particular characteristics, rather concentrates on bringing out power carried within out onto the surface.

name: Lee Jaesam
bio: Lee Jaesam paints scenes of reflections of the moonlight on the trees, forest, and waterfall. Charcoal is made by burning wood, and charcoal only used in basic drawing like sketch rather than used in actual paintings due to its lack of accuracy. However, Lee Jaesam is the one who uses the charcoal as the medium on his canvas. He says the charcoal does not only contain black color since it exists as a black space. While acrylic or oil paintings show the color by reflecting lights, the charcoal makes the black space by absorbing light like a black hole. What the artist observes is not the object itself but the inner image in between the objects which give formation to silence, and the eroded landscape in the 'unexplored' present in the midst of the dark spaces within the depth of the forest.

name: Nam Jeeyeon
bio:
Nam Jeeyeon creates wire drawings that position human figures at the boundary between drawing and sculpture, using wire as if it were a line. The lines formed through the repetitive process of twisting and connecting wire are not merely contours, but reveal the grain of existence accumulated over time, through action, and in human relationships. Her figures are presented as states closer to traces or afterimages than solid mass, and the emptied faces evoke a universal human condition beyond specific individual identity.

The artist focuses on the idea that human beings are formed through interactions with spaces, objects, and memory. Emotional traces and residual memories are translated into linear structures that occupy both surface and space simultaneously. Notably, the shadows cast by the wire-constructed forms become another drawing, expanding the boundaries of the work. As light shifts, the figures create a subtle visual impression of trembling, emphasizing ephemerality over material solidity.

Nam’s practice resonates with the concept of expanded drawing and process-based art. While adopting sculptural structures, her work is fundamentally a spatial drawing a condensation of time and bodily gesture. Nam Jeeyeon received both her BFA and MFA in Metal Crafts from Sookmyung Women’s University.

name: Kim Kiseok
bio:
Kim Kiseok explores the contemporary human condition by portraying isolated figures within personal spaces symbolized by simple geometric forms. Since the early stages of his career, he has utilized labor-intensive techniques such as building up thick layers of impasto and employing dynamic splattering to create rich, tactile surfaces.
During his formative years, Kim focused extensively on the human figure and anatomy. However, this period was less an anatomical study and more a profound exploration of how to convey deep-seated emotions through the physical form. Building on this foundational research, the artist has since cultivated a unique worldview, revealing it through a distinct expressionistic style that balances raw energy with controlled composition.
Beyond his major series, Kim’s portraits and small-scale paintings offer an intimate look at the evolution of his artistic narrative and expressive shifts. These works reflect his ongoing search for a delicate balance between "painterly qualities" and "narrative depth."
Kim Kiseok’s path to art is as unique as his style; he transitioned into the world of fine arts after studying mechanical engineering at both the undergraduate and graduate levels, holding his first solo exhibition in 2010. His works have been consistently acquired by collectors from his early career to the present and are held in prestigious institutional collections, including the Art Bank of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA), Korea.

name: Moonassi
bio: Moonassi was born in Seoul in 1980 and studied Oriental Painting at Hongik University. He began his artistic career in 2010 and is primarily based in Seoul while occasionally working abroad. His name, derived from the Buddhist term Mu-a (無我), reflects his intention to move beyond self-centered thinking. Working exclusively in black and white, he combines ink and acrylic on hanji (Korean paper) to create minimal yet expressive compositions. His work explores human relationships and the shifting nature of emotions, often depicting figures in introspective, ambiguous spaces.

name: Jazoo Yang
bio:
https://www.jazooyang.com/
https://www.instagram.com/jazooyang_art/

Jazoo Yang is an artist based in Berlin, enjoying a prolific career spanning Korea and Europe. Yang has attracted attention with her experimental works that traverse the boundaries of various genres, including painting, installation, live painting, public art projects, and street art. The central themes of her work reflect on experiences almost all contemporaries face at least once in their lives—loneliness, alienation, emptiness, futility, and a sense of gradual dehumanization of our times. Yang sometimes employs intense and rough imagery to convey the devastation experienced by those marginalized from society's mainstream—highlighting the ensuing loneliness and bitterness. Paradoxically, she emphasizes the positive value of genuine communication through her practice.
Her work is emotive and sensuous, showcasing a direct interaction between the materials used and the act of creation. Yang's unique spontaneity and speed are evident in the various spaces she works on, including canvases and walls. While her visual artworks already exhibit a strong dynamic quality, her intensity and artistic prowess become even more pronounced during live painting sessions, where the act of painting itself is the art. This is also seen in her performances, where she collaborates extensively with artists from other disciplines. It is this drive that motivates her to continuously push beyond the confines of genres.
Ultimately, Yang aspires to rekindle the sense of community disconnected by the widespread epidemic of isolation. She aims to strike a balance between universal ideals and realism, drawing from a broad spectrum of emotions elicited by art, life, aesthetics, and reality.

name: Sim Raejung
bio:
SIM Raejung takes man's most base internal confessions of inherent loneliness and anxiety, extreme compulsions and obsessions, and expels them through antipodal black and white drawings full of heavy, murky energy; only to be followed by tens of hundreds more drawings compulsively overlapped and compiled into animations. Broadly, they seem to find their start in a detailed narrative construct eaten away by the artist's personal anxieties, but the narratives of a soul eaten away, fragmented piece by piece and dispersing without bind, without pause-ironically, they come to a conclusion in fumbling attempts at, or perhaps a yearning for, communication. 

SIM Raejung was born in 1983 and received her BFA and MFA from the Department of Fine Arts at Seoul National University of Technology. Sim has held solo exhibitions at ARARIO Museum and Space Hue (2016), and has participated in a number of group exhibitions, including "60sec ART", Savina Museum of Contemporary Art, 2016, Seoul; "ARTSPECTRUM", Leeum, Samsung Art Museum, 2014, Seoul; "Young Korean Artists 2013", National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, 2013, Seoul; "Doing", Kumho Museum of Art, 2012, Seoul; "TOMORROW_OPEN ARCHIVE", SOMA Museum of Art, 2010, Seoul; among others. She was selected for the first edition of the SOMA Drawing Center Archive in 2006, and has participated in such residencies as Tokyo Wonder Site, Japan, 2013; MMCA Residency Goyang, National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, 2013; SeMA NANJI Artist Residency, Seoul Museum of Art, 2015; and now, in 2018, is a resident artist at the atelier of Cité Internationale des Arts, Paris, backed by Samsung Foundation of Culture.

name: Hyeseung Lee
bio:
Hyeseung Lee intricately weaves the ordinary and profound into her artworks, drawing scenes like staircases leading to the unknown or expansive landscapes. Her quick strokes capture familiar yet ambiguous images, inviting viewers to project their narratives onto her canvas. Rooted in Eastern perspectives, Lee emphasizes the harmony between humans and nature, portraying mountains as the source of life’s essence. Her work transcends mere depiction, evoking emotional responses that resonate deeply with viewers, prompting introspection and contemplation. Through her work, Lee illuminates the interconnectedness of all beings, from the minutest entities to the grandeur of nature, urging us to embrace quiet moments and embark on inner journeys of self-discovery.

name: Hansaem Kim
bio:
Hansaem Kim holds a BFA in Fine Art from Hongik University and MFA in Fine Art from Seoul National University of Science and Technology.

Kim creates works that exist at the intersection of analog and digital, reality and imagination, life and death, luxury and kitsch. His art draws inspiration not only from the digital culture of his time but also from various subcultures such as comics, games, novels, classic films, and merchandise. He often intentionally combines two or more genres or formats, using the paradoxical energy generated from these clashes as a key element of his work. For instance, Kim produces images in the form of 2D interfaces and RPG video games within digital environments, blending them with physical materials like wood, resin, and gold leaf to extend them into real time and space. His method of active remixing and grafting creates an imaginative space where existing narratives of reality can be twisted and reimagined.

name: Minkyung Jo
bio:
MinKyung Jo (b.1996) is a Korean visual artist and printmaker.
Although she majored in Western painting, she became captivated by Buddhist art and printmaking techniques, leading her to forge a new path in the genre of “Buddhist printmaking.”

Her practice centers on the modernization of Buddhist art, reinterpreting traditional Buddhist paintings (bulhwa), which have long existed solely as objects of worship and devotion. By exploring their potential as contemporary artistic motifs, She creates a new visual language within Buddhist art—one that had not previously been seen.

name: Bek Hyunjin
bio: Bek Hyunjin(b.1972) has been actively performing across diverse fields as a painter, installation artist, performance artist, musician, actor, director, and graphic designer. His painting, which he intuitively carries out immersed in the process without any plans or purpose, shows Bek’s construction ability as a versatile artist. As for Bek, the surface of canvases is the ground where gesture, motion, poetical and musical rhythm merge. Bek has held numerous exhibitions at major art institutions such as the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (Seoul, Korea), Plateau Samsung Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), Art Sonje Center (Seoul, Korea), Shanghai Minsheng Art Museum (Shanghai, China), and Kunsthalle Wien (Vienna, Austria). In 2017, he was chosen as the nominee/sponsored artist for the ‘Korea Artist Prize 2017’ of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea. As a singer-songwriter, Bek works actively as a member of the Uhuhboo Project, the first-generation indie band, and a project band Bahngbek. A maverick actor who steadily practices his omnidirectional artistic activities, Bek appeared in movies The Day He Arrives, Gyeongju, and Keys to the Heart.

name: MANWOOK
bio: MANWOOK paints a conceptual painting about the symbiosis between humans and non-human species. Humans, animals, plants, and objects are placed in one scene, and humans are expressed without gender, and the main color of the painting is fluorescent. For her, fluorescent color is an undecided color that attracts attention, but it is difficult to see as she gets closer and can be seen properly from a distance. Looking at the world from the perspective of the other, expressing the coexistence she thinks in fluorescence, and this fluorescence color eventually thinks it is the artist herself. The artist intends to expand the area by utilizing not only the painting area but also media and installation methods in her exhibition.

name: Soonok Kwun 권순옥
bio:
The Ego Bird(ego, 離苦) is a constant companion in my work.
It is the little child within me.
Worn down by the demands of home and work, I wandered from place to place, seeking healing for the invisible wounds I had accumulated.
Over the past decade, that wounded inner child found solace and strength through painting.
Now, adorned with delicate flowers on its once-tattered feathers, it lifts its head proudly and opens its beak wide to sing of happiness.
Together, we revisit emotions felt during travels near and far, playing freely across the canvas.
My process is intuitive—I move objects as I please, using a variety of tools and materials.
Water, clouds, boats, trees, flowers, and the Ego Bird form the core of my themes.
The landscapes I depict are drawn from memory, yet they stray far from reality.
I simply enjoy the imprinted images and motifs that linger in my mind.
Composition and perspective are of little concern. I place each element where I want it to be.

내 작품에 늘 함께하는 이고(ego, 離苦)새
이고새는 내 안의 작은 아이다.
집안일과 직장일로 부대끼며 알게 모르게 쌓인 상처를 치유하려고 이곳저곳을 기웃거렸다.
지난 십 여 년 상처 받은 내 안의 작은 아이는 그림을 통해 치유되었고 튼튼해졌다.
망가진 깃털을 예쁜 꽃으로 장식하고 고개를 당당히 들고 크게 입 벌려 행복을 노래한다.
국내외 여행 중에 느낀 감정을 함께 추억하며 화면 속에서 노닌다.
내 작업은 여러 가지 도구와 재료로 기분 내키는 대로 사물을 옮겨 놓는다.
물, 구름, 배, 나무, 꽃, 그리고 이고새가 주제이다.
풍경 이미지를 기억 속에서 찾지만, 사실과는 거리가 멀다.
기억 속에 각인된 이미지와 소재들이 그 안에서 즐길 뿐이다.
구도도, 원근도 괘념치 않는다. 두고 싶은 자리에 그들을 배치한다.

name: Seo Hyun Sohn
bio: Seo hyun Sohn is an artist who draws “psychological landscapes.” Her works are the result from the meditative process of planting seedlings of emotions and accumulating time, like cultivating a virtual garden outside of reality. While her series of works, which crosse the boundaries between pixels and paintings, looks like a background of a game, it is actually an inner landscape permeated with comfort, avoidance, and desires. Nature, which grows in the city and exists only as an object of contemplation, now comes back to life as a fantasy reconstructed in her memory. The artist’s landscapes are familiar yet unfamiliar and evoke the audience emotions beyond everyday life.

name: Jae Youl Jeoung
bio:
Jae Youl Jeoung writes poetry in space. Consistently exploring themes of “memory” and “relationships,” he substitutes language with visual elements—objects, texts, or photographic images—using them as poetic language arranged within three-dimensional spaces to visualize poetry. Just as poetic language conveys meanings beyond the surface of words, the personal significances behind the chosen objects and moments in his work are imbued with metaphorical forms. Jeoung selects objects or scenes that vividly express this open attitude of possibility, based on personal experiences and sensibilities, and reconsiders their conventional uses, states, or roles. Space serves as a crucial foundational element in his work.

name: Sun Me
bio: SunMe’s practice is often described as “sweet and harsh”: her works seduce the eye with brilliant color, yet reveal themselves—at close range—as painstakingly constructed objects. What first appears to be a lush flower painting is, in fact, a relief image built from multiple cut “fragments” of a single bloom. She sketches a flower on hardboard, divides its tones and colors into layered parts, hand-cuts each piece with a knife, and repeatedly paints the fragments before stacking them with adhesive, step by step, until depth and shadow bring the flower into full presence. This labor-intensive process produces a surface that is not merely painted but assembled, where edges and cast shadows become an essential part of the image. She has held thirteen solo exhibitions, including Time in Bloom, Sagunja of Shadow, and La Sacre du Printemps, and has been invited to major art fairs such as Korea, Miami, Singapore and Hong Kong. Her work has also been featured in numerous group exhibitions at museums and institutions in Korea. Her works are held in major corporate and private collections, including Lotte Department Store, SeAH Holdings, IBK Bank, ELLE Golf, and Stayrak Hotel, among others.

name: Jihyung Nam
bio: Nam ji hyung has continued to create works to maximize the human-nature interactions. He uses all living creatures on Earth as subjects of his works, but in the early days, his main subjects were fish and butterflies. in the

name: Choi Youngbin
bio: Choi Youngbin explores the tension between her ego as an observer and the world through paintings. She says that the act of painting is made between the gaze at herself and the state of the senses permeating nature. The work of pushing lumps of paint, structuring the spreading colors, and leaving traces of herself in repeating patterns is a process of moving between the disappearance and resistance of the subject. Her paintings are records of the will to unite with nature while ultimately staying on the border. She confines the tension of the senses in artificial gestures and order, and in the end, only the eyes of the observer remain. Choi Youngbin's paintings exist not as finished images, but as an act of pushing herself.

name: Heekyoung Jeon
bio: Jeon Heekyoung earned her BFA and MFA in Painting from Hongik University. With 20 solo exhibitions since her debut in 2006 and over 150 group exhibitions worldwide, she has developed a robust and distinct language. In 2013, she was awarded the ‘Artist of Tomorrow Grand Prize’ by the Gyeomjae Jeongseon Art Museum. She has exhibited and participated in residencies at renowned institutions such as the Bundanon Art Museum in Australia, the Guandu Museum of Fine Art, and the Taitung Art Museum in Taiwan, as well as recently at Art Lab Sanyang in Korea. Numerous art institutions and public agencies have added her works to their collection, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art and the Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art. Jeon abstractly expresses a world in painting where deconstructed forms and rhythmic colors intertwine with organic elements such as light, wind, and climate. For her, painting serves not only as a complete work in itself but also as a means to acquire narrative within the structure of a series of painting installations experienced in physical space.

name: MOOA 무아
bio:
MOOA (Hyeyoung Oh) is an illustrator, Fine art painter lives and works in Busan, Korea. 
She worked as an artist and Swimwear creative director in New York and her artwork has been shown in London, New York, Miami, Milan and Seoul.
She uses abstract line figures based on the absolute quality of drawing skills ; sensuous but punctual. her paintings are explicitly sexual, eye catching and creative. Their strong and vibrant colors give unexpected funs and suprises.
She believes that performar as an artist would be the highest moves to make the world a better place.

name: Joy
bio:
Joy Kim has been interested in a variety of art fields since he was young. Ever since he encountered street art, he went to art highschool, however soon disappointed in their curriculum limiting the individual creativity. After graduation, inspired by his trip to Europe, he studied film in college in the US. His career as an artist began through social media, majorly based in NYC. Having exhibitions with David Zwiner and Sotheby’s, the artist is actively communicating through his art and getting spotlights as an emerging artist.

The artist does not simply view art as a tool for expression or a kind of language. He utilizes art as a medium to convey liveliness. The artist describes this as an "implementation of the spirit of the contemporary time” by saying that every moment in human life is meaningful. Recording these moments, the artist naturally communicates with people as a process. Through his work, the artist wants to remind us of the joy of relaxation to our sick minds overwhelmed with social issues we are experiencing in contemporary.

name: Tae KIM
bio: Tae Kim ( B. 1986) lives and works in Seoul, Korea. In 2010, Kim received her Bachelor’s of Fine Arts degree in Oriental Painting from the Seoul National University where she later studied for her Master’s degree in the same discipline graduating in 2013. In addition, in 2016 Tae Kim graduated with a Masters degree in painting from the Slade School of Fine Art, UK. In 2022 Tae Kim received her Doctor of Fine Arts in Oriental Painting at the Seoul National University. In her work, Kim explores online human connection as a deeper relationship than that of the flesh to flesh.  Her art is inspired by the imaginations of players met in online battle games and their short mythic episodes. In this way, the resulting artworks investigate emotional experiences as well as mixed culture and history.

name: KIM Byoungho
bio: KIM Byoungho inserts circuitry into metallic sculptures, presenting unique oeuvre of sound sculptures that create electronic sound. His works are described by tubes that stretch out from a certain focal point, with a steady electronic sound. The forms in which long narrow tubes stretch out in one or in many directions from a bulky center point juxtaposes with the swift sense of movement and the metallic coldness of his works. The metallic works are processed precisely according to the regulations of the parts and blue print the artist has designed, following the production method of mass production system, and reflecting the social structure of conventions, customs and standards. Here, the artist inputs calm electronic sound, and the sound flows in a slow simple manner that doesn't interfere with the sculptural element of the work freely traverses between material and non-material, and visual and aural, allowing the viewer to experience a force that overpowers the space.

name: Jung Kwangmin
bio:
Jung Kwangmin’s intricate, light-responsive surfaces evoke the spiritual discipline of ancient rites. Known for his signature "Glass Mandala" technique, Jung sprinkles fine glass powder onto glass plates to create layered, meditative compositions that are fused in a kiln without the use of adhesives. This repetitive, labor-intensive process is inspired by the Tibetan Sand Mandala, yet Jung seeks to fix the fleeting image, embodying the human desire to capture longing and memory. From the narrative explorations of The Little Prince to abstract inquiries into the Forms of Sound, his work transforms the fragility of glass into a medium for existential reflection.

Jung earned his Master’s in Glass Design from Kookmin University, where he also served as an adjunct professor. His artistic practice has been widely recognized in international competitions, including the Toyama International Glass Exhibition in Japan and the Cheongju Craft Biennale. Jung has exhibited at prestigious venues such as Somerset House in London for the Collect Art Fair. His works continue to explore the tension between the material and the spiritual, establishing a unique presence in contemporary glass art.

name: Lee Dongwook
bio:
LEE Dongwook's works are the most realistically grounded with everyday reality. His choice of medium or method of expression is drastically private and lean toward his personal life and taste, but his work often contains serious observations of the individual in modern society's struggle to get through a daily routine or act as a critique or accusation of reality. His cynical and distanced gaze is filtered through humor and wit, but the content is always serious, and even grave at times. Through human figures, residues, traces that are meticulously positioned amongst humanoids made of Sculpey, trophies, rock collections, and other items, LEE offers a calm portrait of the eternal return - alienation, balance, division, and isolation as they arise from the indivisible relationship between humanity and its society.

LEE Dongwook participated in a solo exhibition at the Arario museum Dongmun Hotel II(Jeju, Korea) in 2017, Corner Space (Seoul, Korea) in 2014, Charlottenlund Gallery ( Stockholm, Sweden) in 2013 and Arario Gallery Seoul (Seoul, Korea) and Doosan Gallery (New York, US) in 2012, and Brain Factory Gallery (Seoul, Korea) in 2004. He also participated in "Pillars" (Arario Gallery, Seoul, and Korea) and "Really?"(Arario Museum in Space, Seoul, Korea) in 2014, "Korean Eye"(Art Design Museum, NY, US) in 2011, "Made in Popland"(MMCA, Gwacheon, Korea) in 2010, Bulgar Collection (Berlin, Germany), "Korean Eye" (Saatchi Gallery, London, UK), "peppermint candy" (National Art Museum, Buenos Aries, Argentina) in 2008. In 2011, he joined the Doosan Gallery as a New York Residence artist. His works are part of many significant collections such as the Burger Collection (Germany), the Rubel Collection (USA), the National Museum of Contemporary Art (Korea), and the Arario Museum (Korea).

name: Wanki Min
bio: Wanki Min takes photographs of stars in ways to identify solutions for how he could combine astrological factors within photography. He aims to combine multiple microscopic aspects of small, busy, everyday lives that surround him to initiate a project with an idea that he may be capable of presenting a unique perspective of the world. Min combines photographs of cities, people, and landscapes taken around the world with photographs of the stars taken with a camera attached to a telescope as well as straight photography itself. He then pushed some of these photographs further by applying alternative processes to explore the light.

name: Kim Chong Hak
bio: Born in North Korea in 1937, Kim Chong Hak is an eminent figure in contemporary Korean art. Widely known as the “Painter of Seorak”, Kim evokes Mount Seorak—the third-highest mountain in Korea, situated in the east of the country— on his canvases with motifs from nature, such as flowers, insects, and weeds.

name: Bongsang Yoo
bio: The world Bongsang Yoo creates that ethereal, suspended somewhere between hope and despair, never imposes meaning on the viewer. Instead, it invites quiet contemplation. Whatever one encounters within these works is entirely left to the viewer, reflecting the artist’s deeply introspective approach. There is a certain melancholy in this distance, in the way Yoo refuses to dictate meaning that even though the sheer physical labor and meticulous process behind his pieces would seem to warrant a declaration, a message. But Yoo remains silent, choosing instead to pursue quiet innovation. He creates dreamlike landscapes using an unexpected medium: nails. His process begins with a panel so heavy it cannot be lifted by hand, it must be hoisted into place by machine. Onto this massive surface, he uses an air tacker to insert 15mm headless pin nails, each driven only halfway in, leaving 7mm protruding. What results is a world of light shaped by the shadow of reality, seven millimeters of darkness, created by something as tangible and industrial as a nail.

name: Woo Min Jung
bio:
Minjung Woo is an artist who graduated from Seoul National University in 2010 with degrees in Painting and Industrial Design. In 2017, she pursued her studies in Painting at the university's graduate school. She specializes in clay work, creating panels that serve as boundaries with the world, where she carves and colors them to convey stories about the boundaries between reality and ideals, transience, eternity, and the struggles of existence.

Her early works, like "The Great Escape" (2015), explored walls and murals as symbols of the boundary between reality and ideals. She experimented with mural techniques applied to architectural panels, delving into both physical space and the metaphysical.

Her major works include the "Beheaded" series (2016), inspired by headless Buddha statues in Gyeongju, which represent the fluctuating boundary between the moment and eternity. "Nevertheless" (2017) reflects on the persistence of willpower despite dissonance between reality and ideals. "Sing for Eric" (2018) extends the narrative to a universal human story about transience and eternity, using deformed panels to capture the ephemeral nature of crashing waves.

In "Surmising" (2019-2020), she explores the moon's surface, symbolizing change, stasis, and repetition. "I TRIED" (2019-2020) features figures in a series of movements, illustrating change and movement.

The "BER" series (2021) continues the theme of consecutive movements, depicting daily acts, attempts, and efforts of people. It incorporates icons like fire, bees, and stars in its storytelling.

Finally, "Eggs, Rocks, and Shards" (2022) and "OIC" (2022) series modify frames from "Sing for Eric." "OIC" visualizes Morse code for 'O', 'I', 'C,' representing long and short sounds.

name: Yun Kyung Jeong
bio: Yun-Kyung Jeong describes the marks she makes on unprimed canvas and silk as being “like controlled exhalations filling a space.” The Korean painter, whose works play with perspective and exploit empty space to create complex, vaguely architectural environments, finds inspiration in Gothic architecture and biological processes. Raised in Korea but educated largely in the United Kingdom, Jeong now splits her time between the two countries and has been credited with finding a delicate balance between Eastern and Western artistic traditions. Jeong renders her delicate ecosystems in muted tones, sometimes using digital engineering tools such as axonometric projection to create immersive, three-dimensional worlds of overlapping planes. These hybridized landscapes—influenced as much by naturally occurring patterns as by manmade objects—are often inspired by humankind’s fascination with idealized utopias.

name: Suh Se-ok
bio:
Suh Se-ok (1929–2020)

Suh Se-ok was a pioneer of abstract ink painting in Korea and a master who led the modernization of traditional Korean art. As a founder of the "Mungnimhoe" (Ink Forest Society) in the 1960s, he broke away from conventions to establish a new visual language. His signature "People" series simplifies human forms into essential dots and lines, capturing the dynamic energy of crowds through rhythmic, dance-like brushstrokes. Praised for perfectly blending Eastern spirituality with modern abstraction through the mastery of ink tones and negative space, his works are held in prestigious collections, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (MMCA), Leeum Museum of Art, and the British Museum.

name: Jo Gyuhun
bio:
Jo Gyuhun was born in Incheon, Korea, in 1982 and graduated from Hanseo University, majoring in animation. Jo is based in Incheon and his works have been showcased at prestigious Korean art fairs such as the Busan International Art Fair and Seoul Art Show. He began to paint these “Children Hiding Their Faces” as he was inspired by a significant scene of a film that he has fortuitously come across, in which a girl in a white shirt is crying with her hands covering her face. This scene left a strong impression on him and later encouraged him to paint with children as his subject.
As he explained his concept, he mentions that he can feel these different feelings and expressions of children hidden behind their hands, and he also hopes the audiences can enjoy the moment when they are imagining the facial expressions behind these hands.

name: Cheong Hyeong Yeol
bio:
Cheong Hyeong-Yeol's art perfectly embodies the cultural richness of South Korea. Growing up, he was immersed in the traditions, folklore, and the natural beauty of his homeland. His early years were marked by a deep connection with the legacy of Korean art, including its profound tradition of ink painting and calligraphy. His artistic foundation shows the deeply philosophical influences of a culture that emphasizes harmony with nature and self-cultivation. 
 One of Cheong Hyeong-Yeol's defining characteristics as an artist is his remarkable ability to merge tradition with innovation. His work beautifully encapsulates the spirit of Korea’s artistic heritage, especially in the realm of ink painting, while at the same time infusing it with a fresh and modern perspective. At the heart of his art is the captivating dance of ink on paper. His brushwork, both bold and delicate, weaves intricate patterns and expressive strokes that draw the viewer into the very essence of the subject. His compositions often feature harmonious juxtapositions of light and dark, inviting the observer to contemplate the interplay between positive and negative space. 
 Cheong’s themes are deeply rooted in nature. He immerses himself in the landscapers of his home country, basking in its richness. He then further explores the impressions as he begins relating his experiences ink onto paper, telling the tale of his homeland. His compositions feature intricate patterns, delicate textures, and precise lines, inviting viewers to explore the layers of symbolism and storytelling within each piece.
 As an artist, Cheong is not only preserving Korean cultural heritage but also contributing to its evolution. His work serves as a bridge between the past and the future, connecting generations and fostering an appreciation for the artistic traditions of Korea.

name: Shin Sun Mi
bio:
Shin Sun Mi, who has held various exhibitions at art fairs in Hong Kong and contemporary art galleries in China and Korea, is known for her unconventional combinations of Eastern painting techniques and modern themes. Shin is actively engaged with publishing books nationally and internationally such as Bolognese, Italy. Themes of her work are ranged widely with personal and cultural motives. Including one of her recent artwork themed on the K-pop song “Gangnam Style” of three women dancing using dance moves from the song’s music video while each wearing the traditional attire of China, Korea, and Japan. Shin reinterprets the motif of the woman wearing “Hanbok”, Korean traditional clothing by applying diverse themes such as “Hallyu”, Korean cultural wave with a uniquely witty approach which can be characterized as Korean style Pop Art.
 
Having spent most of her childhood bedridden due to illness, Shin often features “Ant Sprites” in her paintings. Imaginary ant sprites, with whom this young girl believed came out from hiding to play, are just as important to her paintings as her main subjects. They add an intensely personal touch. All of her work including the women in some of her work, who pique the viewer’s imagination by boldly rebelling against the traditional image of the Korean woman, were created by the artist’s exquisitely detailed brushwork, resulting in the life-like quality that characterizes Shin’s depictions of people. She is now continuously involved in publishing books of her story telling work, and participating various collaborative exhibitions and art fairs in Hong Kong and Korea.

name: Minjoo Kim
bio: Minjoo Kim, who majored in oriental painting, uses traditional materials such as Jangji(Korean Paper), Chinese ink and powder pigments. She is making most of powder pigments that afford warm and soft tone colors compared to vivid oil painting. Although the materials are from the past, the subject matter of Kim's work encounters the present. The theme of 'Thought' and 'Stroll' frequently appear in her works: 'Forest of Thoughts', 'Stroll', 'Scenery of Mind'. She creates ideascape rather than depicting the real landscape as in traditional oriental painting. Contemporary culture puts us in a situation to think, work and react constantly thanks to developed technologies. The space in her canvas reveals still moments that allow viewers to stay away from reality and stroll around.

name: Haegue Yang
bio: Known for using utilitarian household items, from space heaters to extension cords, and placing them out of context, Haegue Yang’s works reflect the transitory nature of the artist’s own experience of living and working in multiple locations. Her works in video explore displacement and alienation in both geographical and personal terms through a combination of fiction and documentary. Yang’s visual, sound, and olfactory installations reveal the intersections of public and private. To this end, she often includes complex formations of ordinary Venetian blinds, which provide porous boundaries for viewers to navigate around. The installation *Non-Indépliables* (2006 –2011) features drying racks clothed in layers of colorful yarn or adorned with hanging lightbulbs, wires, and assorted pieces of fabric.

name: Nam Tchun-Mo
bio:
Born in 1961 in Yungyang, South Korea. Nam Tchun Mo lives and works in Daegu, South Korea & Cologne, Germany. He holds an MFA from the School of Fine Art at Keimyung University, Daegu, South Korea.

Through the repetition of simple lines and a mixture of natural oriental colors, Nam Tchun Mo creates works beyond the boundaries of sculpture and painting. Dynamic and rhythmic lines built on the surface of the canvas create harmony between light and shadow areas. His paintings are sculptural pieces where the lines are infinite space.

Color and light are the key ingredients of Nam Tchun Mo’s art. He is constantly playing on them, exploiting the most varied resources of the chromatic spectrum: orange, yellow, blue, while not neglecting the subtle modulations of black and white.

Nam Tchun Mo is an artist representing the new generation of the Korean monochrome movement, Dansaekhwa.

Recently, he won 1st prize from the Hachonghyn Foundation as a great master of the Dansaekhwa movement.

name: Yunmi Kim 김윤미
bio:
Yunmi Kim’s Mother-of-Pearl Lacquer–A Harmony of Nature and Tradition
Yunmi Kim delicately captures the essence of nature through the traditional Korean craft of mother-of-pearl lacquer. The iridescent glow of nacre reflects the shifting seasons and landscapes with subtle precision, offering a distinctive aesthetic where tradition and modernity gracefully converge.

The artworks are created using traditional Korean techniques.
The process begins with preparing a wooden frame, which is carefully covered with hemp cloth to add both durability and a natural texture. On top of this, multiple layers of natural lacquer—extracted from the lacquer tree—are applied. Each layer is finely polished to enhance depth and resilience.
Finally, delicate fragments of mother-of-pearl are meticulously placed onto the surface, allowing light to be captured and life to be infused into the work.
This process embodies the strength of natural materials and the refined beauty of traditional craftsmanship. Through lacquer, a painterly expression unfolds—bridging nature and art in a quiet, meditative rhythm.

name: Jae Ko
bio: Jae Ko transforms rolled paper and colored ink into swirling [curvilinear forms](/gene/curvilinear-forms) which usually reflect [bulbous](/gene/bulbous) shapes. Sprawling across gallery walls, these works sometimes spill onto the floor to create her [immersive](/gene/immersive) installations and captivating [wall and floor sculptures](/gene/wall-sculpture-and-installation). Her notable installation *[Flow](/artwork/jae-ko-flow-1)* (2018) shows layers of the artist’s signature rolled paper at a monumental scale. Ko’s earlier works involved placing paper along the edge of the ocean where the tide meets the sand, allowing it to be washed over and submerged by water; she would then sculpt the altered material into new shapes. Ko has had solo exhibitions at prestigious institutions including the [Contemporary Arts Museum Houston](/partner/contemporary-arts-museum-houston) and the Taubman Museum of Art; she has also participated in group shows internationally.

name: Hyun-Sook Song
bio:
Hyun-Sook Song was born in 1952 and grew up in a mountain village in Korea. In 1972 she travelled to West Germany and soon after that she began to draw and to paint. In doing so she often gave voice to her nostalgic memories of her beloved motherland. Over several decades she created paintings with only a handful of motifs or themes: clay pots, silk ribbons draped around posts, or woven textiles hung on a thread.

Song developed both a very distinctive style and a technique that blends elements from the West and the East. She chose to use tempera, a type of paint made by mixing pigments with egg yolk. This technique was widely used in Western painting in the Middle Ages, notably because of the paint’s opaque character. Song, by contrast, uses tempera in a way that is almost transparent: the brushstrokes are economical but accurate. Each brushstroke represents a single movement and there is no room for doubt.

Her artistic outlook has been heavily influenced by Eastern philosophy and calligraphy but also by her love of nature, the body and her materials. She sees painting as a performative happening. She places the stretched canvas on the floor of her studio and balances above the painting on a simple wooden plank that is placed above it. In doing so she is in a state of utter concentration and meditation. The intensity of the painting enables her to work for only a few hours per day. This does not prevent her from going to the studio every day to maintain her dexterity.

Although her formal language may be limited, the variations appear endless. The works can be approached from both an abstract-meditative perspective and a figurative-symbolic viewpoint. The ‘wooden poles’ refer to a simple form of shelter, while the fabrics often suggest the age-old tradition of ramie weaving in the region of her birth. The paint that thins out as the line progresses symbolizes the finiteness of life and the dying out of hope.

name: Jungwon Phee
bio: The ‘Untitled: Black Path’ series of the artist's works consist of a black background, symbolic figures, deep and shallow cracks and bends, and numerous layers. Its goal is to achieve the most fundamental, primitive, and pure abstraction possible, with an emphasis on abstract expressionism and minimalism. The black background of the work represents his personal meaning and the direct visual act that closes the audience’s eyes at the same time. The artist uses the method of watching the abstract work, as if the audience were imagining themselves, watching the work, which, of course, also applies to the watching of his work as well.

name: Jo Eunsi
bio:
Jo Eunsi (b. 1999) is a Seoul-based painter whose work explores the logic of resemblance and visual structures of inference. Working primarily in oil on canvas and panel, she creates compositions that combine natural elements—such as mountains, waves, and stones—with geometric signs and abstract symbols. Jo’s paintings suggest that resemblance is not just a matter of appearance, but a conceptual relationship formed through structures, patterns, and spatial logic. Through layered surfaces, visual metaphors, and playful arrangements, she invites viewers to construct their own meanings by tracing visual clues and intuitive systems. Her practice also expands into installation, incorporating sculptural elements like plywood and volcanic stones to suggest physical forces, hidden systems, and cyclical relationships.

Jo holds both a BFA and MFA in Painting from Ewha Womans University. She was selected as a semifinalist for the 2025 KIAF HIGHLIGHTS program, and she will present a forthcoming solo exhibition at FIM, Seoul in 2026. She has presented her work in solo and group exhibitions across Seoul.

name: Yujin Huh
bio: Artist Yujin Huh (b.1978) is a female painter who majored in western painting at Hongik University and the graduate school, established herself as a painting artist among Korean painters. Her realistic portrayal with traditional oil paints, which is based on ‘extreme realism’ that is close to photography, has been loved by the public for more than 20 years. The paintings she recreates have a distinct aesthetic that no one can imitate, and the reason is because she is faithful to the essence of painting in the complex and diverse history of contemporary art. Artist Yujin Huh says that ‘the moment she draws’ is the reason she exists, and it also makes her alive. Armed with her relentless, flexible brush strokes and tense breathing, no one can imitate the way she paints. Consist of privately hidden artistic enthusiasm and visible desire that are free and beautiful. Colorful paintings of transparent and smooth surfaced processed objects, with precarious properties that are easily broken, represent our human sociology.

name: Daeyong Byun
bio: Daeyong Byun was born in Busan, South Korea in 1972 and studied sculpture in Busan National University with a Master’s and doctorate from Busan National University as well. He held a number of individual and group exhibitions at galleries and participated in many art fairs. His works are also on display in other public spaces, both indoors and outdoors. Public collections of his works involve Eden Valley Ski Resort, Heungkuk Life Insurance, Amore Pacific Museum of Art, Samsung Airport Railroad Station, Pohang Museum of Art, Pohang, National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, MBC Broadcasting Station and more.

name: Lee Koz
bio:
Lee Koz (b.1997) explores the accumulation of memories through the unconscious and the act of recording them, delving into the imaginative narratives that emerge as personal records are transformed into images. Her J-D series began as a dream journal documenting recurring dreams, rooted in the dissonance she experiences when specific memories underlying a dream diverge from how scenes unfold within it. To make sense of this, Lee writes down her dreams and then incorporates fragments into her paintings, where memories, scenes, and records take shape on the canvas. Each element holds a unique position and emphasis, sometimes exaggerated, reduced, or altered. In this way, her canvases become spaces where dreams and memories overlap, giving rise to new narratives.

Her Training Journal Drawing series, on the other hand, consists of drawings and paintings inspired by detailed training logs she kept—through writing and video—while participating on a recreational baseball team. For Lee, the act of recording serves as both a response to inner uncertainty and a driving force behind her creative work.

Lee Koz earned a B.F.A. in Painting from Ewha Womans University, where she is currently pursuing her M.F.A. Her solo exhibitions include Apple or Bird, A-Lounge Contemporary, Seoul (2025); Repetitive Description of Techne, A.P.23, Seoul (2023); and In This Air-Raid Shelter, Space Poolmoojil, Seoul (2021). She has also shown work in group exhibitions such as Holding onto the Round Hollow, Gallery Ebb&Flow, Seoul (2023); Explode-Revive-Record, Annpaack, Seoul (2023); and How to Detect Ambiguous Signals, A.P.23, Seoul (2023).

name: Sujin Shin
bio: Sujin Shin is an artist known for her interactive print installation and painterly printmaking works alluding to repetition and intersubjectivity. Korean, Shin was born in Seoul in 1972 and has lived and worked in Seoul. She achieved a PhD in Fine Arts from Seoul National University, Korea and a MFA in printmaking from the University of Wisconsin-Madison. She had 13 times of her solo exhibitions in Seoul (Korea), Tokyo (Japan), and Several Cities in U.S. She has also curated exhibitions including Crossing Gene: American and Korean Printmaking Exchange Exhibition. She received the First Place of the Show from Frameless 99: National Juried Exhibition of Works on Paper and several kinds of fund from Korean government. Her works are collected by Nora Eccles Harrison Museum of Art (Utah), Madison Art Center (Wisconsin), Seoul National University Museum of Art (Korea), the Art Bank at the National Museum of Contemporary Art in Korea, (Korea) and others.

name: Sungpil Chae
bio: Sungpil Chae graduated with a BFA and MFA in Oriental Painting from Seoul National University and later completed an MFA in Plastic Arts at Université Rennes 2 in France. He is a contemporary artist known for his evocative earth- and water-based paintings that explore the elemental forces of nature. Deeply rooted in Eastern philosophy, his work captures the primordial harmony of the universe through organic processes using soil, ink, water, and natural pigments. Often referred to as the "Artist of Earth," he collects soil from different regions to use as both material and motif, creating immersive landscapes that resonate with memory and origin. His works have been widely exhibited across Asia, Europe, and the U.S., and are held in major public collections including the National Museum of Contemporary Art (Korea), Seoul Museum of Art, and Hôtel de Ville de Paris.

name: Chae Jungwan
bio:
Chae Jungwan is a painter who visualizes the social discontent and anxiety experienced by individuals within contemporary society. His work seeks to transform personal frustration into shared awareness, encouraging reflection on structural social issues rather than isolated individual problems.

Recurring figures with shaved heads and suits appear throughout his paintings. By minimizing individual traits, these characters function as universal stand-ins for members of society, emphasizing that the issues he addresses transcend class, gender, and generation.

While his work carries a critical and often somber tone, it is grounded in a belief that confronting uncomfortable realities is essential to social change. Chae approaches discontent not as pessimism, but as a necessary condition for imagining a more conscious and equitable society.

Chae Jungwan graduated from Kaywon University of Art & amp; Design (BFA, Animation). Since his debut solo exhibition in 2016, he has held 12 solo exhibitions and participated in numerous group exhibitions and international art fairs. He is the recipient of the Gallery WE Young Artist Contest Award (2025) and the Silver Prize at the Ulsan International Art Fair Emerging Artist Competition (2024).

name: Kim Byungjong
bio:
Kim Byungjong is widely recognized as one of Korea’s leading contemporary artists, known for translating Eastern philosophy into a distinctly Korean visual language. 
His work embodies a deeply meditative spirit, rooted in traditional thought yet expressed with a modern sensibility.

His signature series, The Song of Life, is a visual exploration grounded in Eastern reverence for life. Through motifs such as flowers, children, birds, fish, and pine trees, Kim evokes the primordial imagery reminiscent of Goguryeo murals and the free-spirited composition of Korean folk paintings (minhwa). These elements, rendered in vibrant colors, come together in a lyrical longing for an ideal world.
Over the course of his career, Kim has held more than fifty solo exhibitions in Korea, France, and beyond. 

In the spring of 2014, he held a major solo exhibition at the Jeonbuk Provincial Art Museum, followed by a highly acclaimed show at the Today Art Museum in Beijing in 2015. 

The Kim Byung-jong Art Museum stood in his hometown of Namwon, and his works are housed in prestigious institutions around the world, including the British Museum in London, The Contemporary and Modern Art Museum of Korea.

His invitational exhibition, “Hwahong, Pungjuk”, will be held at the Guangzhou Museum of Art from June 15 to July 14, 2026.

name: SAMBYPEN
bio:
Born in 1992, SAMBYPEN spent his early years in Europe and the US. He went to Parsons School of Design in New York but decided to drop out. The artist started to create parodies of commercial images, noticing the similarities between the propagandistic images of a socialist country and the billboards in Times Square, New York. SAMBYPEN began to build his career as an artist in 2015 by creating a work that parodies Bibendum, the Michelin mascot. After his first solo exhibition, the artist has held numerous exhibitions and developed into one of the most promising contemporary pop artists since his debut. 

In his vital spirit of parody, the artist combines and reinterprets specific brands or culturally iconic objects. His early works were driven by personal emotions and experiences, while his recent works explore more of the societal issues that surround us. The artist humorously reproduces iconic paintings and movie posters by rearranging them and adding context. 

SAMBYPEN is known for its unique approach to working backward in technological development within modern society. He creates digital graphic designs on his computer before transferring them onto wood, which he then cuts with a machine. After painting the wood by hand, he finally implements it onto his canvas. This painting technique combines a standardized square canvas with a free-curved wooden object creating a three-dimensional effect. The artist's desire to blend technology and hand-painted colors shines through the technique, which seamlessly fuses modern innovation with classic methods.

According to the artist, the purpose of art in society is to offer a distinctive experience to all individuals rather than just a privileged few. The artist believes that this experience should help people break away from the confines of reality and view the world from a new perspective through his artistic vision.

name: Yerin
bio:
Neo-pop artist Yerin has worked professionally as a fashion designer, graphic designer, and creative director for the past ten years. Yerin developed an original textile pattern based on the rotunda staircase of The Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art. She envisioned herself as a fine artist while working with renowned photographer Mario Testino for PearlLam Gallery in Hong Kong as the chief designer for a cosmetic brand. 

During her second solo exhibition, Hide and Seek, BeauBeau will be the emotional interpreter of everyone, while at the same time tuning into the artist's inner truth. It is by resorting to painting as a self-remedy that the Neo-pop artist is able to endure inherent ambivalence and avoid being biased.

With a strong focus on paintings, Yerin hopes to reach as many people as possible through collaborations and various media while maintaining a Neo-pop style accessible to all.

name: Yunsung Lee
bio:
Yunsung Lee (b.1985, South Korea)  constructs a distinctive painterly language by hybridizing the visual grammar of manga and anime of Japanese popular culture rooted in  his youth with Western sculptural traditions and  Greco-Roman mythology (Laocoön, Danaë, Venus, among others).

By actively incorporating the expressive grammar of Japanese comics as compositional elements in his paintings, Lee intersects subculture and mainstream art-history. Manga “panels” are translated into diagonally cut canvases or figures fragmented through optical illusion, while empty speech bubbles function as abstract devices that suggest new narrative potential. Central to his practice are figures modeled after the sculptural form of the “Torso”—bodies with missing limbs—which emerge as recurring formal motifs. These fragmented figures, combined with vivid color, decorative patterning, and dense compositional layering, generate scenes both visually charged and layered.

Overlaying disparate characteristics of classical and modern, Eastern and Western, and tactile brushworks of oil painting and flatness of animation, Lee pulls images and values of Western art’s vast history into the present and explores new perspectives of sensorial perception and contemplation.  

Lee studied Western Painting at Chung-Ang University and expanded his international practice through the Doosan Residency programs in Seoul (2014) and New York (2016). He has held eleven solo exhibitions, including at Doosan Gallery Seoul (2015), Doosan Gallery New York (2016,) Museum Wave (2024), and YK Presents (2020, 2024), and has participated in over thirty group exhibitions in Korea and abroad, including at Space K Daegu (2017), Schema Museum of Art (2023), Space Hohwa (2023), Ananti Culture Club (2023), and Tuesday to Friday, Barcelona (2023). His works are held in institutional collections including Doosan Art Center and Space K. A solo exhibition at ROY Gallery is scheduled for 2026.

name: Jibin Im
bio:
View works.
SHARE
Im Jibin is known for his trademark 'Bear' motif, a toy-like, schematic figure which can be reproduced in a multitude of colors and surface finishes, as if it were a commercial, branded product. There are a variety of iterations at various scales: some are simply heads, some whole and some free-standing. Most are designed to hang on a wall and are carefully arranged in regimented groups reminiscent of the enticing displays of the retail world.

The artist often speaks of consumer capitalism and its promotion of 'insatiable appetite'. His practice evokes related ideas of production, promotion and acquisition. The seductive nature of his sculptures and the arrangements of his exhibitions and installations conjure up scenarios of material desire. Satisfaction appears to be guaranteed until the next version of the bear is released - a sensation which is familiar to all in the hyper-commercialized, developed world. This artist makes clear that the art market is, apart from its cultural concerns, very much a market, subject to all the familiar wants and perceived needs of its participants.

name: Sang Hwan
bio: Sang Hwan's work begins with his cat,'Santo'. The artist shows the relationship between companion animals and companions about what people are missing in a materialistic society. The dogs and cats in the work are not just cute and adorable. While the appearance of the wild remains, the time spent with the owner shows a solid coexistence between them.

name: Kulim Kim
bio: Born in 1936 in Sangju, Korea, Kim Kulim holds a significant status in Korean contemporary art history as the founder of Korean experimental art. Retaining a rebellious attitude towards existing values and customs, Kim has produced a wide scope of experimental works ranging from paintings, prints, sculptures, installations and performances to land art, video art and mail art. He has also been involved in experimental plays, films, music and dance. In 1969, he released 'Relics of Mass Media', considered Korea's first mail art and also produced 'The Meaning of 1/24 Second', a seminal work in the history of Korean experimental film. Kim was a founding member of AG(Korean Avant-Garde Association), through which he led avant-garde artistic practices that emphasized concept and process. In the 1970s, he founded The Fourth Group, an avant-garde art group consisting of young artists and intellectuals in various fields, pursuing intermedia art combining art, play, film, fashion and music. Later in the decade, he set off to Japan to begin experimentation with print and video art, and in the 1980s, he traveled to the United States to seek new ways of artistic practice. Kim's major exhibitions and performances include 'Korean Historical Conceptual 1970-80s: Jack-of-All-Trades' (Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art, 2011), 'Like You Know It All' (Solo retrospective, Seoul Museum of Art, 2013), 'A Bigger Splash: Painting after Performance' (Tate Modern,2012), 'From Death to Birth' (Performance,Asia Culture Center, 2015), and 'The Song Within the Heart, The Resonance Within Poetry' (Experimental music recital, London, 2019). His works are owned by more than 30 museums including Tate Modern, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, and Tate Library Special Collections.

name: Jiyeon Lee 이지연
bio:
I explore light and time by holding the warmest moments of my life within the essence of water. Rather than pursuing a fixed image, my work records the slow accumulation of light and time through layered surfaces.

Through repetitive processes—carving resin, applying color, and building up layers—light permeates and refracts within the material, becoming time itself. These layers function as both physical structures and vessels of memory.

Inspired by childhood memories of rivers, seas, and shimmering light, I translate afterimages of these moments into forms that hold—such as moon jars and vessels.

Using gold leaf and resin, I transform ephemeral materials into enduring depths of light. My work invites viewers to encounter their own memories within these shifting reflections of time.

name: Sojeong Lee (b. 1993)
bio:
The life we live, see, and experience around us is, according to Sigmund Freud, only the tip of the iceberg of consciousness. Our feelings, motives, and decisions are, in fact, influenced by the unconscious mind as the primary source of human behavior. Impossible to reach purposely and protected by various defense mechanisms (such as repression or denial), this part of the iceberg is revealed only in tongue slips and through dreams. And for Sojeong Lee (Cheongju, 1993), documenting these flashes of unconsciousness became a pivotal aspect of her artistic practice.

Art is often used as a means to convey emotions and ideas beyond what's possible with common verbal communication. It is also a way to help deal with certain aspects of life and understand one's position within a greater whole. So, for South Korean artist living and working in Düsseldorf, this particularity formulated the first concepts that her artistic practice revolved around. And according to renowned theories of dream function - the thoughts, images, and sensations occurring in a person's mind during sleep might have a similar purpose. Whether enabling to process trauma, providing simulative training in dealing with threats, or helping and promoting the learning process, they reveal things that are impossible to notice awake or through conscious observation. And this particular realization prompted Lee to modify her overall practice and the entire oeuvre into a visual diary of the subconscious. Documenting her own dreams and nightmares, most of them scary and involving running away or flying on a paper plane for dear life (and always succeeding), she went way beyond forming a language to speak of her emotional states, the solitude, alienation, or strangeness.

 Strongly influenced by omnipresent manga aesthetics while growing up, it was the idea of making comics that sparked her initial interest in creative expression.

name: Hyangro Yoon
bio: Yoon Hyangro (b.1986) received her BFA in painting from Hongik University and MFA in Fine Arts from Korea National University of Arts. She recently finished her residency at DOOSAN Gallery New York, followed by a solo exhibition, Liquid Rescale in 2017. Previously, she participated in exhibitions at leading institutions including Seoul Museum of Art (2018, Seoul), Atelier Hermes (2017, Seoul), Digital Art Center of Taipei (2016, Taipei), Arko Art Center (2015, Seoul), Ilmin Museum of Art (2015, Seoul), and National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (2015, Seoul). Yoon will participate in 2018 Gwangju Biennale.

name: Kim Inbai
bio: KIM Inbai's works center on the idea of the range. The artist sets up a range of possibilities in the point of compromise he finds between interesting concepts and their feasibility of manifestation. KIM continuously strives to surpass these limitations, which is reflected in the exhibited works that are completed through the harmony of movement, rhythm, and time. KIM first divides the human body into different parts, including the head, torso, and limbs. Each of the parts delicately portrays the physical muscle structure of the body like a reek sculpture. Although the heads are missing eyes, nose, and mouth, and the torsos are limbless, the details of the muscles clearly identify the posture of the body. Dynamic sense of movement can be read on the tight muscular limbs and the group of still male torsos that express movement with changes in color.

name: Insane Park
bio:
Insane PARK has been an artist who has explored the correlation between the visual- and perceptual- culture, based on interest in media and images. By analyzing and dismantling the conventional images in recognition that is repeatedly exposed through the media, the artist attempts to express the essence and limitations of the human being who perceived through the eyes. From the initial cable-painting of a portrait to neon-work which explores the relationship between text and images, presents the moments and facts that we have been ignored by finding small clues of daily life and reconstructing with an editor-like attitude.

Each randomly collected image, particularly on a particular subject, focuses on stimulating the perception of the image, not our sense of image association, from portraits to pornography. For example, a face that appears to contain the essence of a person, and even a portrait, is divided into several units through the duty of a light coat, which is a duty to impart our eyes, which are diversified and cognitive, which we want to understand, cools our eyes and stimulates the relationship between similar images and thoughts. In addition, the artist distorts a ubiquitous and predictable image at random. Based on such oversupplied images, the work is questionable in the media format and is post-production to re-use existing art rather than completely new. Like DJs, He remixes and programs existing references as an editor rather than a creator.

name: Yikyung Kim
bio:
Yikyung Kim (b.1935) is one of Korea’s most well respected ceramic artists, and a pioneer in the ceramic arts. Her works bring Korea’s ceramic heritage into the modern world, favouring a coexistence of aesthetic beauty and general practicality.

Kim’s ceramics are influenced by Joseon baekja (white porcelain), which are prized for their simplicity and naturalness. They are made using the ancient throwing technique, which offers flexibility and efficiency, allowing Kim to produce works that lack artificial traits and remain true to the material. Kim employs faceting to reveal the different characters of the clay: softness and sharpness, warmth and coolness, time and rhythm.

Kim studied at Seoul National University and the College of Ceramics at Alfred University in New York State. While in New York she had opportunity to meet Bernard Leach, and was profoundly influenced by his teaching. She is professor emerita at Kookmin University, Seoul.

Her work is included in the numerous public collections, including National Gallery of Contemporary Arts, South Korea; British Museum, UK; National Museums of Scotland, UK; Victoria and Albert Museum, UK; Smithsonian Institution, USA; Philadelphia Museum of Art, USA.
