bio: Taeyoon Kim (b. 1982, Korea) studied Live Action at the California Institute of Arts in Los Angeles before earning a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Film and Video from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Kim had solo exhibitions at Blinded Coincidence, ONE AND J. Gallery, Seoul, Korea (2016); Taeyoon Kim – Solo Exhibition, MAAP Gallery, Queensland, Australia (2016); Erratic Routines, ONE AND J. Gallery, Seoul, Korea (2014). Selected group exhibitions include Scaffolds of Meaning, Mine Project, Hong Kong (2019); No Live, Cosmo 40, Incheon, Korea (2019); Gone Fishing, Whistle, Seoul, Korea (2018); The Camp #1: Timekeepers, Galerie ERD, Seoul, Korea (2018); Log Into the Balance, Hidden M Gallery, Seoul, Korea (2016); OgoGago, City Gallery Wellington, Wellington, New Zealand (2014); Sporadic Sway – Part 2, ONE AND J. Gallery, Seoul, Korea (2014); We are Just Bits, ONE AND J. Gallery, Seoul, Korea (2013); Particle Universe, MCM Storefront Gallery, Hong Kong (2011); AV is not TV, Gallery Busker, Chicago, USA · Rodan, Chicago, USA (2006).

name: Lee Woojun
bio: Leewoojun is a Seoul and Incheon based photographic and sound artist. He explores landscapes, urban environments, and the relationships humans form within them through long-term observation and documentation and continues to develop exhibitions and projects mainly focused on photography and sound. More information and portfolio can be found on his website: https://www.leewoojun.org

name: Han Sungpil
bio: Han Sungpil practices art mainly by means of photography, video, and installations, covering subjects such as environmental issues, originality & imagine, history, and the relation between the real and the represented. He also enjoys understanding diverse cultures and exploring nature further interpreting our everyday world. Sungpil’s sensibility in his work often includes a sense of humor, while including sublime elements of beauty. His works have been exhibited and collected at notable museums and biennials around the world, including U.S.A, France, Germany, England, Spain, Italy, Belgium, Russia, Slovakia, Lithuania, U.A.E, Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Cuba, Argentina, Mongolia, Japan, China and Korea.

name: Jin Woo Lee
bio: Jin-woo Lee's work comes from a process of putting charcoals on Korean paper and repeatedly covering them with Korean papers. Lee chooses Korean paper, Hanji, as his main material of his works, hoping to reflect his identity as a Korean artist. He places charcoal powder on top of Hanji and scrapes the surface with an iron brush to create an irregular three-dimensional surface. Jin-woo Lee relieves his thoughts and mind through the repetitive process of pasting layers of Korean papers. Through such endless, aimless repetition, he dreams of disappearing. The world in which he emptied out and filled himself through such hard work is a world of spirituality. The thick layer of Lee’s work gives you a meditative impression that reminds you of life and death and such majestic atmosphere with its unique aura is the characteristic of Lee’s work.

name: Choi Yeong Geol
bio:
Choi Yeong-Geol is trained in Oriental painting and is recognized for his realistic depictions of nature, achieved through meticulous observation and a profound sense of empathy. While his works are grounded in traditional techniques, they clearly diverge from conventional modes of classical landscape painting. In this way, his practice embodies a balance between tradition and modernity, as well as between academic rigor and a romantic sensibility.

Choi approaches nature with a sense of reverence and sublimity that borders on the spiritual. Through careful surveying of each scene, he seeks to reconstruct nature with objective precision, deliberately restraining personal emotion and subjective expression. This disciplined attitude reflects key aspects of mystical romanticism, while simultaneously resonating with the ideas of the British painter John Constable—particularly his belief in “realizing pure perception from natural phenomena.”

In Choi’s work, the majesty of nature is not limited to grand or monumental landscapes. It is equally present in modest subjects, such as a small waterfall. By applying the visual language of traditional landscape painting to contemporary contexts, his work offers a gentle reminder of values easily overlooked in modern life: the possibility of spiritual purification through harmony with nature.

name: Park Taehong
bio:
Park Taehong is an artist who explores the accumulated strata of the human inner world within silence through an honest painterly language.

Park Taehong has consistently explored the psychological landscape of the human interior and the inherent tension of existence. Born in Seoul, his practice focuses on visualizing emotions that elude verbal articulation—the profound inner states that accumulate within silence.
Silence is the central tenet of Park’s work. Rather than an empty void, it represents a temporal layer where emotions and memories are most densely concentrated. By rendering these "strata of silence," the artist reveals, through his distinct painterly language, the discomfort and raw authenticity that arise when individuals confront their true selves.
His palette is restrained yet marked by potent contrasts. Specific colors and forms symbolically evoke suppressed emotions, condensed energy, or an introspective gaze. Rather than providing an explanation of emotion, these elements invite viewers to experience and project their own sensibilities onto the canvas.
Park Taehong’s works are held in prestigious collections, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA), Korea, various municipal art museums, and the JoongAng Ilbo. He has established a significant international presence, participating in major art fairs such as KIAF (Seoul), Art Central Hong Kong, and international fairs in Singapore, Miami, and New York.
Awarded the Honorable Mention Prize at the 13th Asian Biennale, Park has solidified his position as a prominent figure in contemporary Asian painting. His work is critically recognized for its refusal to aestheticize emotion, offering instead an unembellished and honest reflection of the human condition as revealed through the depth of silence.

name: Hyunkyoung Shin
bio: Hyunkyoung Shin was born in Gimpo, Korea, and graduated from the Department of Painting at Seoul National University in 1983. Since 2021, she has been working at her studio in Gonjiam, Korea, cultivating an ecological space while creating her art. She has held 15 solo exhibitions, including <'Space of Difference'_Space Mom Art Museum), <'Breath'_Gallery Art Side Beijing Space / Galerie Helhof_Frankfurt), and has participated in numerous group exhibitions.

name: Eemyun Kang
bio: Eemyun Kang is known for her fluid, lush paintings of nature and the process of morphology. Her works occupy the space between the conscious and unconscious, reality and myth, and abstraction and figuration. This state of perpetual metamorphosis parallels Kang’s own experiences. Born in Korea but educated in England, Kang reflects her cultural displacement in the hybridity of her art. She imagines her works as narratives and is inspired by mythology, folklore, and mycology, yet her paintings defy linear storytelling, instead imagining time as circular.

name: KwangHo Shin
bio: Inspired by the exuberantly painted compositions of the [Action Painters](/gene/action-painting) group of [Abstract Expressionists](/gene/abstract-expressionism), KwangHo Shin works with oil paint and charcoal on canvas to produce portraits that merge inner states with outer appearances. Often working at a grand scale, he creates sketchy, vigorously executed images of human figures, heads, and faces using a multicolored patchwork of brushstrokes. In some compositions, his brushstrokes obscure his figures, whose contours can just be made out amid the pigment. In others, faces and forms are more clearly articulated. The conglomerations of marks make such forms appear almost sculptural. By replacing flesh and features with thick strokes of pigment, Shin reflects the tumult of thoughts and emotions that lay concealed below our surfaces and that fundamentally shape our identities.

name: Hyena Kim
bio: For Hyena Kim, paintings serve as a diary of sorts, in her exhibition Days we see how scenes from her everyday life are recorded in her painterly style. The paintings seek to render life beautifully, not just the moments one would normally consider to be beautiful like flowers or clouds, but trifling things as well such as pots and eggs. The interest of these works lies in the expression of beauty one can find in the interaction of these seemingly mundane objects. Even in everyday routines where there is nothing new or exciting, everything touched by the artist’s gaze is transformed into a special beauty. Hyena’s representational style is one that is gestural and superimposed with shapes and colors that are indicative of the ethereal lens with which she views the world. In an art world saturated with strong narratives and avante-garde theories, the freshness of Hyena’s straightforward artistic approach is uniquely charming

name: Isaac OZ
bio:
"Isaac Oz" is an artist group consisting of originator Lee Seung Hwan, developers Kim Yoo Jung and Kim Ji Myung, and performers Kim Hyo Jung and Jeon So Hee. 

In popular music, producers, composers, and singers achieve top-tier results through a highly specialized division of labor and chemical synergy. A film director is not a monarch who monopolizes the identity of a single work but rather an alchemist who draws out the best chemical combination. In these fields, the chemical synergy of division of labor is naturally accepted. However, in all areas of art, it is only in fine arts (contemporary art) where the solipsistic thinking of the capital ‘I’ still prevails. The capital ‘I’ refers to oneself (‘I’) and also represents the first letter of ‘identity.’ It is also the ‘I’ of the id, one of the three components of Freud’s personality theory.

Isaac Oz is a project that seeks to overcome the ‘I’ through close division of labor. Isaac Oz rejects the myth of art by killing the identity of ‘I’ and the id of ‘I.’ It introduces the artist’s name as a brand within the title of "artist" to ally with the system while resisting the capitalistic structure. We do not live as a subject or self, nor with self-consciousness. We can only live inter-subjectively. Inter-subjectivity means living in a relational way, constantly being influenced by others, the other, the world, and the universe, and returning that influence.

name: Nam Kwan
bio: Born in Kyungbuk, South Korea in 1911, he studied in the Tokyo University of the Arts in the 30s. Fascinated by the artists such as Soulages, Manessier, Poliakoff and Picasso, he decided to leave for Paris in 1954 where he enrolled into l’Académie de la Grande Chaumière. Starting from 1958, he took part in Salon de Mai. Ever since the 50s, he was influenced by lyrical abstraction and became one of the pioneers of Korean abstract art while remained faithful to his cultural and artistic roots. His dreamy and timeless universe, at the boundary between the East and the West, is composed of symbols, hierarchy and writings.

name: Kim Seungjoo
bio: Kim Seungjoo subjectively distorts the meaning of the ruler whose function is to demonstrate the absolute standard constructed by the society. Through the distortion of the ruler, the artist hopes to offer the opportunity to contemplate a human’s consciousness and to perceive the circumstances around the individuals. The significant characteristic of her works is that each number from 0 to 9 on the ruler are not placed as order, and they rather turn out to be an independent object. Thus, the generic role of a ruler, which is to ‘measure’, is destructed, and the irregular numbers are also implying that the definition of numbers is faded.

name: Taewon Ahn
bio: TAEWON AHN (b.1993) explores the saturation of reality in images, transforming distorted digital creations into tangible artworks on canvases and sculptures. The artist's pet cat 'Hiro' symbolizes this process, translating the artist's subjective narrative into an objective sensation. His works for Frieze Seoul 2023 included a newly created painting and several of his sculptures from his series ‘Hiro’ where he contorts images of his pet cat to comment on the nature and lifespan of images in the digital sphere. Recent exhibitions include his solo show at Plan X Gallery in Milan, 2023, and group shows at WWNN, 2023, Museum of Contemporary Art Busan, 2022, and The Hole, NYC, 2022.

name: CCREATT
bio:
Born in 1994, Seung-gyun, known as CCREATT, studied industrial design at university. During and after completing his studies, the artist developed a keen interest in 3D modeling. He used his creativity and imagination to transform virtual objects into digital art, videos, and figures.

CCREATT’s works portray the search for self-identity, lost in a fast-changing world dominated by commercialism. The artist creates 3D models of influential figures, such as artists or celebrities, by capturing their distinct features and characteristics. These figures are then transformed into memes with added symbolism within the digital space.

The characters' emotionless facial expressions enhance the implicit meanings and emotions of each figure. Additionally, the small props and items placed beside each character not only symbolize them but are also closely linked to modern society.

The artist portrays how commercialization is deeply ingrained in our society. Through his art, he reveals what may be concealed or overlooked and encourages viewers to reflect on their own relationship with these issues. While his primary focus is on creating 3D figures and reproducing famous paintings, the artist is always exploring new styles and mediums, constantly expanding the boundaries of his art.

name: Dain Yoon
bio:
Korean born Dain Yoon does not identify as a “makeup artist.” She is a classically trained, fine artist who happens to use herself as her canvas. And in that process she experiments with other mediums as well, such as: oil painting, performance, sculpture, video, large-scale land art, etc.

Dain Yoon goes by the name @designdain on Instagram, where she exhibits her beautiful body and face illusion paintings. Although her art looks Photoshopped, it is actually 100% authentic, painted by herself on herself in mirror image. Any painting can take anywhere from 3 hours up to 12 hours. Her perfect illusions of eyes, lips and faces have many gazing, feeling dizzy or even freaked out.

Miss Yoon attended the most prestigious arts schools in South Korea: Yewon Arts Secondary, Seoul Arts High School and Korean National University of Arts, where she graduated both at the top of her class. Great painting skills however, are only half of her magical equation.

Yoon’s sharp observation and fascination with the complexity of human beings is what elevates her art to a higher level: “The real face reveals itself underneath the hand that hid it, expressing how the first impression of a person does not tell the whole story.”

With ‘Illusion art,’ Yoon has explored multi-faceted ways to eloquently express a person’s diversity, as well as the portrayal of sensations arising from the impressions of her artistic upbringing. When it comes to her inspirations, Dain takes on a humble point of view: “Anything, even in very ordinary life, could be great inspirations… As long as one takes on a unique perspective.”

name: Lee Jeonglok
bio: Lee Jeonglok explores the diversity and spirit of the Korean landscape and national identity with nonspecific, dream-like photographs that reveal the invisible yet essential elements of a scene. Created using long-exposure photography and both natural and artificial light, the “Tree of Life” series features seemingly bioluminescent trees, which appear to illuminate the hidden vitality of the natural world. The “Decoding Scape” series positions the phonetic letters of the Korean Hangul alphabet as hieroglyphs; they are meant to be contemplated and unraveled to uncover the meaning of nature and the Korean spirit. By melding the natural with the artificial, and the organic with the geometric, Lee visualizes the powerful yet imperceptible forces around us.

name: Myunggeun Ko
bio: Myung Keun Koh is a Korean Asian Modern & Contemporary artist who was born in 1964 in Seoul. He graduated from Dept. of Sculpture, Seoul National University with B.F.A degree and from Pratt Institute in New York with M.F.A degree. Their work was featured in several exhibitions at key galleries and museums, Koh has held solo exhibitions and participated in group exhibitions domestically and internationally. In his other works, Koh also draws inspiration from archaic architecture, representation of the human body and identities.

name: Sangbin Im
bio: Sangbin IM has garnered global recognition for his photographs that display his distinctive picturesque sensitivity. IM’s representative works are People and Artificiality series, which are composite photographs created by merging photos of different cityscapes and historical sites taken from different angles at different times into an exotic landscape photograph with automatic digital tools. Through his scenes of re-contextualized time and space, IM questions the fleeting moments of the phenomenal world and combines the “non-action” and “action,” showing his novel approach to the real world. IM earned a B.F.A. in the department of Western Painting from Seoul National University, an M.F.A. in the department of Painting and Printmaking at Yale University, and then completed his doctorate in Art and Art Education at Teacher's College, Columbia University. He held exhibitions at Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (Seoul, Korea), Seoul Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), Gyeonggj Museum of Art (Ansan, Korea), Osaka Museum of Modern Art (Osaka, Japan) and also participated in various art projects including the Seoul Mediacity Biennale. IM currently teaches at the College of Fine Art of Sungshin Women's University.

name: Heejo Kim
bio:
Heejo Kim's dreamy figurative paintings feel like fragments of a memory, each lived though curvy, clay-like forms huddled together in moments of domesticity and candor. Kim's vibrant color sensibility draws our attention into these quietly meaningful moments, while light serves to illuminate, confront, and sometimes hide portions of narrative, an expression which reveals much about the artist’s experience as a young woman in Seoul and her desire to find comfort and identity in space. 

“Tenderness, to quote Roland Barthes, is an ‘infinite and an insatiable metonymy’ for love. The figures’ gentle gestures in my paintings are a metonym for their ineffable silent desire to be loved by others. The figures move their hands and bodies delicately as if everything around them were fragile and could break easily if touched…they keep a careful distance from each other. This distance expresses waiting for affection from others rather than trying to seize it right away. This is how they protect their hearts, but it is also a way of giving love as an active practice. Even if their love sometimes takes a long time to be noticed, it is always there.” 

 -Heejo Kim, from “Alone with you"

Heejo Kim (b. 1995, Seoul, Korea) received her MFA in 2023 from the LeRoy E. Hoffberger School of Painting at Maryland Institute College of Art. She is currently based in Baltimore, MD.

name: Kwon Young-Woo
bio: Kwon Young-woo graduated from Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea with a BFA in Oriental Painting in 1950, and an MFA in Oriental Painting in 1957. His first solo exhibition, held at Shinsegae Gallery, Seoul in 1966, drew broad attention from colleagues of the Korean and Japanese avant-garde but also sent ripples through Western art circles. Kwon employed layers of hanji Korean mulberry paper, which he glued on a flat plane leaving visible traces of actions such as puncturing, pressing, scratching, and tearing the material. In performing this technique Kwon relies on his fingers as the main tools of production highlighting the structure of the support. By the time of his first visit to Paris in 1975, Kwon’s process had become very refined. Sheets of varying thicknesses were pushed and pulled into mountain-like forms, the application of more delicate surface layers often resulting in a gauzy veil that covered the entire artwork in a luminescent haze. In 1978, sponsored by the French government, he moved to Paris. There he began experimenting with puncturing the surface of the canvas with a sharp tool. Additionally, the re-introduction of colored inks, which had been central to his training in Oriental Painting, allowed Kwon to further investigate the compositional and haptic potentialities of medium and support. The interplay of various layers of different paper lets the ink spread unevenly across its torn edges, forming patterns that stress the technical and material variations in the work. In 1989 Kwon returned to Korea and settled in Yongin, Gyeonggido, where he established a studio and continued to expand his practice, exhibiting new works until his death in 2013.

name: Wang Seongjeong

name: Kim Hee Kyung
bio:
"The beauty of nature is nothing less than the light of life. Kim Hee Kyung expresses the light of life emitted by nature by means of abstract language." Korean artist Kim Hee Kyung specialises in works that are inspired by nature. Using Hanji, a traditional Korean paper made of mulberry tree pulp, she sculpts multi-dimesional sculptures that are reminiscent of blooming flowers. Hanji is Kim's material of choice as it is able to breathe, much like trees, and accommodate colouring, providing both painterly inspiration and symbolic meaning. 

At present, she is the Dean of the College of Art in Suwon University. Her works are in the collection of leading companies, galleries, and institutions.

name: Heemin Chung
bio: Heemin CHUNG(b.1987) pays attention to the characteristics of the images produced in the digital environment and culture, and the way of experiencing them. She strives to explore the meaning of painting and how it relates with the unfamiliar sensations in the new circumstance. CHUNG received her BFA in painting from Hongik University and MFA from Korea National University of Arts. She held her first solo exhibition at Project Space Sarubia Dabang in 2016 and her works in group exhibitions have been presented at venues including National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, Visual Audio Pavilion, Kumho Museum of Art, HITE Collection, Korean Cultural Center in Hong Kong, Archive Bomm, Post Territory Ujeongguk and more. She is one of the current artists-in-residence at Incheon Art Platform 2019.

name: Dongi Lee
bio:
With a deep interest in images that are easily consumed and distributed in pop culture, Dongi Lee has brought to the fore his artistic language that reflects the stereotypes of modern society. 

In 1993, Lee created his first character “Atomaus”, a figure mixed from two iconic characters: Walt Disney’s Mickey Mouse and Osamu Tezuka’s Atom. Portrayed in numerous situations that hint at social symbols and contexts, “Atomaus” has played a pivotal role in Lee’s works that not only speaks about pop culture but also about reality. 

Creating a densely layered surface where a wide variety of visual and philosophical elements, including animations, advertisements, classic & modern paintings, and abstract art, are merged into one canvas, Lee addresses the realities and interactions we face. The various elements are lined up and overlapped, illustrating the complicated and disparate relationships between objects and phenomena.

name: Jinny Suh
bio:
The works revolve around themes of chickens, birds, and nature. Particularly, Suh's creations aim to convey traditional values to modern audiences, consistently portraying serene and elegant freedom. By anthropomorphizing vibrant Korean colors, chickens, birds, and butterflies, the artist wishes for human life to be richer and happier. Using Hanji (traditional Korean paper) as the main material, Suh strives to bring warmth and comfort to the stark, schematic living spaces of contemporary individuals.
Their efforts to showcase the warmth and cozy imagery of Korea, as well as seeking universality through Korean elements, have led to numerous purchases by Western collectors. Suh graduated from Ewha Womans University with a major in sculpture and was awarded an honorary doctorate from IAU University in the United States.

서은진(Jinny Suh)
작품들이 닭과 새와 자연을 소재로 하고 있다. 
특히 전통적인 가치를 현대인들에게 전달하려는 서작가의 작품들은 항상 여유롭고 우아한 자유로움을 그려내고 있다. 화려한 한국의 색과 닭 그리고 새, 나비 의인화를 통해 인간의 삶이 보다 풍족하고 행복하길 기원하며, 주요 소재인 한지를 통해 삭막하고 도식화된 현대인의 주거공간에 인간적인 따스함과 편안함을 제공하려 애쓴다. 따뜻하고 포근한 한국의 이미지와 정서를 보여주려는 시도와 한국적인 것을 통해 세계적인 것을 찾으려는 시도는 서구의 많은 컬렉터들의 작품 구매로 이어지고 있다. 
서 작가는 이화여대 조소과를 졸업하고 미국 IAU대학에서 명예 박사학위를 수여했다

name: Hye Ryun Jung
bio: Hye Ryun Jung was born in Busan, Korea in 1977. She finished her undergraduate graduate courses majoring in sculpture at the Busan National University. Currently, she has completed her doctoral program. She gained public attention as she was awarded the Artists of Tomorrow Award by Sungkok Art Museum in Seoul, Korea, in 2004. Jung was selected as an up-and-coming artist by the Songam Arts & Cultural Foundation and has won the Bongsaeng Young Culture Award, Ha Jung-woong Young Artist Award, a grant from SeMA (Seoul Museum of Art) for New Artists, and the 2012 Young Sculptor Prize of the Kim Chong Yung Museum. The artist has held solo exhibitions at domestic and international museums and galleries such as Kuandu Museum of Arts in Taiwan, The Busan Museum of Art, Sungkok Art Museum, OCI Museum of Art, and SOMA(Seoul Olympic Museum of Art).

name: Kim Seung Young
bio:
"I used to look for a departure point of my thought in an ancient place like Pompeii. While in an empty, crumbled place, I used to feel so many sounds and resonances amassed during that time." ー An interview with the artist

Kim Seung Young's art takes the form of time couched in a language from nature. Past scenes and things in the stra tum of time Kim has faced display forms of their secretly kept origin. Hidden trifles on earth are revealed to him and narrate the story of nature laden with the whispers of eternal time. Like an archeologist, Kim interprets traces and sounds engraved in his everyday life and explores 'an other world' transcending the phenomenal world. He tries to capture the world unseen and unheard and present it in reality in his own distinctive way, but it is in no way easy to reveal this explicitly. This is because that is the space time a myriad of forms and echoes are heaped up in as an elemental world that is within us but of which we are unconscious. In the world brimming over with unknown contradictions, Kim goes on to his own lonely journey even in the repetition of despair and enlightenment. And in the middle of this journey, he creates another world full poetic resonances by tirelessly drawing out fundamental things hidden behind the reality.

name: Eunphil Cho
bio:
After majoring in sculpture in the Department of Fine Arts at Pusan National
University, Cho, Eun Phil earned her master's degree (MFA) from the Slade School
of Fine Art at University College London, followed by a doctorate in fine arts at
Pusan National University. Since her first solo exhibition in 2002, she has held
23 further solo shows to date, at venues including the Project Space Sarubia,
Noblesse Collection, Kimsechoong Museum, and others. She has participated in
exhibitions at national and public museums such as the Busan Museum of Art,
Gyeongnam Art Museum, and the Seoul Olympic Museum of Art, as well as a
number of international exhibitions, including Gangwon Triennale and Geumgang
Nature Art Biennale. Cho has produced a great variety of works using blue as her
primary sculptural element, and has won multiple awards, including Grand Prize
at Busan Biennale Sea Art Festival, Gold Prize at the Invitational Exhibition of
Modern Korean Sculpture by Chuncheon Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation, and a
Bongseng Youth Culture Award.

name: Min Byung-hun
bio: Min Byung-hun’s [black-and-white photographs](/gene/black-and-white-photography) are recognized for their gauzy, painterly quality. Influenced by Eastern and Western painting traditions, his gelatin silver prints depict such phenomena as fog, snow, and rushing water. Min hand-develops his images in the darkroom, often keeping his tonal values in a narrow, hazy range described as velvety. Even when working with [nudes](/gene/nude), his subjects appear semi-abstracted. His quadriptych *TR037; TR038; TR039 & TR040*, from the “Trees and Flowers” series (2008), [sold](/artist/min-byung-hun/auction-results) for $38,702 at auction in 2008. Born in Seoul, Min studied music and engineering before pursuing photography in the early 1980s at artist Soon-Tae Hong’s studio. Exhibited internationally at galleries and museums, his work is collected by institutions such as the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](/partner/los-angeles-county-museum-of-art); the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston; and the [National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea](/partner/national-museum-of-modern-and-contemporary-art-korea).

name: Yoo Youngkuk
bio: Yoo Youngkuk, a pioneer of abstract art in Korea, was born in 1916 in Uljin. Yoo’s works are characterized by their striking colors and geometric shapes, depicting harmonized landscapes where natural elements are translated into bold, abstract forms. Yoo’s career took flight in the 1930s when he moved to Japan and began studying art, honing his skills in painting and sculpting. Returning to Korea in 1943, Yoo actively sought to foster the modern art movement, which he championed through leadership roles in avant-garde groups like New Realism, the Modern Art Association, and Contemporary Artists Exhibition. Throughout his career, his art remained an ode to nature, with mountains being his signature motif. A major retrospective mounted at the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul to mark the centennial of his birth helped solidify Yoo’s legacy.

name: Chun Kyungja
bio:
Chun Kyung-ja (1924–2015) is one of the most celebrated and commercially significant figures in modern Korean art history. Known as the "Magician of Color," Chun broke away from the male-dominated traditions of East Asian ink wash painting to pioneer a vivid, surrealistic style of "Chae-saek-hwa" (Korean color painting). Her work is instantly recognizable for its bold use of primary colors, layered mineral pigments, and hauntingly expressive portraits.

Born in Goheung, South Korea, Chun studied at the Tokyo Women’s School of Art in Japan. While her early training was in traditional techniques, she quickly developed a unique visual language characterized by the heavy application of crushed rock pigments (seok-chae) on hanji paper, creating a texture that is both matte and luminous.

Chun's oeuvre is deeply autobiographical, often exploring themes of solitude, narcissism, and feminine resilience. Her signature motif—women with hollow, staring eyes crowned with flowers or snakes—serves as a projection of the artist’s own psyche. Her 1952 breakthrough work, Mode of Life (featuring snakes tangled together), famously marked her liberation from personal tragedy and cemented her status in the art world.

Throughout the 1960s and 80s, Chun traveled extensively across Africa, Latin America, and Europe. These travels infused her work with exotic landscapes and vibrant, tropical hues, distinct from the muted palettes typical of her Korean contemporaries.

Key Achievements & Collections:

Legacy: Chun donated a vast collection of her works to the Seoul Museum of Art (SeMA), which houses a permanent exhibition dedicated to her legacy.

Collections: Her works are held in major institutions including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA), Korea.

Market: Chun Kyung-ja holds a "Blue Chip" status in the Asian art market, with her large-scale portraits of women commanding record-breaking prices at major auction houses like Seoul Auction and K Auction.

name: Sea Hyun Lee
bio: Sea Hyun Lee is known for his series “[Between Red](/artwork/sea-hyun-lee-between-red-016dec01)” (2006–present). These [oil paintings](/gene/oil-painting) take inspiration from his time in the Korean military surveying the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), an area that serves as a physical buffer between North and South Korea. Lee left Korea in 2003 to study at the Chelsea College of Arts where he received his master’s degree. Drawing from memory, he creates detailed landscape paintings of the symbolically loaded region; these are rendered in crimson tones that simultaneously reference the infrared glasses the artist used on his night watch duty and serve as markers of the complicated and painful legacy of his native country. Lee’s canvases are not overtly political, but they pointedly combine elements of both North and South Korean terrain, fusing the two halves of the divided Korean Peninsula in a gesture that registers as both nostalgic and utopian.

name: Ingee Chung
bio: Ingee Chung is a graphic designer based in Seoul, Republic of Korea. He is interested in a printing process that prints continuous tones with discrete halftone. Enlarges the image to find halftone patterns or discrete bitmap gray-scale to recreate the image. As a result of his practice, the simple elements of design, such as point, line and plane are exchanging its roles and spinning on surfaces with the illusion and distortion.

name: Yang Woon Chul
bio:
Yang Woon Chul is a South Korean contemporary artist whose practice originates from a fundamental ontological inquiry: "Who, what, and how can something exist?" Central to his work is the belief that existence is never a solitary state but is continuously formed through the "encounter of two or more." Whether exploring the relationship between canvas and pigment or the observer and the observed, Yang visualizes the world as a dynamic structure of interconnectedness. 

In his early series, the canvas and color operate as a single organic body. His characteristic blue planes shift in hue upon meeting the surface, suggesting that identity is not fixed but fluid within its environment. Accentuating these fields are yellow lines that function as "breathing holes"—conduits for light and air that transform the flat surface into a circulating, living space. 

Yang’s recent investigations introduce confronting semicircles and layered white dots, probing the duality of perspective. By juxtaposing oil and acrylic, or singular forms that appear different depending on distance, he highlights the coexistence of identity and diversity. From the orange glows of a sunset to the deep azure of the sky, Yang’s work captures existence not as a static entity, but as a shifting phenomenon defined by distance, condition, and the profound act of facing one another.

name: Nina Park
bio:
Nina Park obtained a bachelor’s degree in illustration at Kingston University in the UK. As an illustrator and painter, she took part in numerous exhibitions as well as collaborations with the local government, financial industry, fashion corporations, and other organizations.

She focused on painting than illustration in 2022 and she has depicted unique composition of her own universe with colour and humour.

From the beginning, Her artwork attracted the interest of the 272 gallery in London because of the London pop style in her painting. Finally, her artwork gets spotlighted by many art collectors after the 272 gallery pre-ordered all of her paintings. Now her artwork has started to get lots of attention.

She made an exclusive contract with Gallery Aile but also collaborated with popular overseas galleries, which are Mozuku Gallery in Taiwan, Maison Ozmen in France, Waluso Gallery in the UK and Pops Gallery in Spain.

She is releasing her new artworks through Gallery Aile and she is going to have group exhibitions and solo exhibitions in Seoul and overseas from August 2022 to June 2023.

name: Miseon Jeon 전미선
bio:
KOI 

The painting was done using a knife adding thick layers of contrasting colors, creating the illusion of dynamic motion and great depth. This technique is used to create a simple and contrasting, yet powerful impression.
From afar the paintings appear defined and exact. However, when viewed up close, the contrasting colors and textures quickly come into focus expressing dynamic movement.
This aspect of my painting fills me with great joy and enthusiasm. I incorporate my inner happiness and gratitude into every work that comes from my hands. Every work I do has positive energy and happiness.
Because of the special significance of the Koi fish in Asian culture, I devote all of my artistic energy to making them as dynamic, rhythmic, and vivid as possible. I hope this will bring joy, energy, and inspiration to everyone who has the pleasure of seeing it.

name: Seo Hyun Kim
bio: Seo Hyun Kim is a South Korean painter whose work explores material process and compositional form. Kim works by layering, cutting, and reassembling materials to construct complex visual structures. Her gestural paintings often suggest ambiguous exchanges between figures, conveying emotion without explicit narrative. Kim’s practice bridges traditional painting techniques with contemporary approaches to abstraction, emphasizing tactility and tension.

name: Kim Sunggun
bio:
The Stroke: A trajectory created by numerous traces

A dynamic stroke that fills the canvas. From afar, it appears as a single stroke, but up close, it was made up of countless traces. 
He had filled the canvas meticulously with pen lines, expressing the unveiling of existence through the distance, space, and gaps of relationships. This practice has served as a foundation, leading to the creation of a single big stroke formed by numerous lines. To capture the significant moments of the creation, he has changed materials and techniques.
The beauty of life is composed of accumulated small moments. From the moment of birth, carrying the destiny that must continue to walk, we live these moments that come together to form life.
To express this imagery, he layered paint on the canvas dozens of times to create a sense of thickness and meticulously carved intricate lines with sculpting tools to add a dynamic quality to the strokes. He wanted to show both distant and close perspectives by portraying the strokes as trajectories formed by numerous traces.
The contrasting concepts of building up and carving away, big strokes and small engravings of lines, and compositional use of empty space and densely filled strokes, are perhaps reflections of the essence of life, which is the contradictions, conflicts, and integration of both encountered throughout life.
In the process of creating artwork, he encountered the idea that the essence of life is not determined by beauty or ugliness, success or failure, but rather by the persistent act of living itself. Every moment of living is a stroke, and the shape, direction, dynamism, and momentum of the strokes are formed by every single day we live.
He built up and carved away to create artwork while embracing this humble truth of life. With each step, steadily and proudly creating his own stylish strokes, the artist cheers for himself and for everyone on their own journeys.

name: Jun Kun Choi
bio:
Choi Junkun graduated from Hongik University, college of fine art in 1991 and graduated from the same university's Graduate School of Art in 2001. The artist has exhibited in Seoul, Tokyo, and Beijing.
Choi Junkun’s work consists of black stones painted on canvas with black ink. He applies the ink in layers, piling up the repeated strokes of a small brush to compose the stones. The painting is comprised of solid black stones and a dense white background. The white background is meant to simultaneously portray the sea, the color white, and the sky. It is everything and nothing, and black stones run across it like a bridge. Additionally, the stone landscape tends to extend onto the next painting.
Choi's paintings allow for the simultaneous existence and non-existence of objects within the painting. In this contradiction, the stones are not only stones, but the color black. The background is neither the sky nor the sea, but the color white. As the black is shaped into a stone, the white is shaped into the background. His painting is set between these two achromatic colors. In fact, these works are surprisingly clear and simple compared to his past paintings. This simplicity presents the power of the passage of time.

name: 윤시현 SiHyun Yoon
bio:
SiHyun-Yoon
18 solo exhibitions,
14 art fairs, 105 team events, and 9 awards.
The fugue of life
My work is a life-praise.
Particles, the smallest unit of life, gather to form and continue life through the evolution of
creation and extinction, emptiness and filling.
The question of "Where did I come from?" went to the starting point of life and there was a
star at that starting point.
Stars are the starting and ending points of life and are mysterious spaces with numerous
stories.
Stars that encompass matter and spirit are objects of worship and admiration and an
imaginary world.
When I was young, the fairy tale, which was said to be a star when I died, was an object of
imagination, and I felt it was a session to the essence.
Deferred extinction and generation repeat the difference and continue the phenomenon of
life.
Human existence is a moment in space and time, and it is smaller than a dot, but it
constantly sings the song of life.
