name: YiYi Jeong-Eun
bio: YiYi Jeong-Eun’s works represent things that live freely. The artist draws nature she has experienced with bold and cool brush strokes including birds flying in the sky, heat shimmer in spring, willows with their branches drooping in the cool breeze. The beginning of these works commenced when she was fascinated by how an abandoned mining town recovered with the relentless healing power of nature. She enhanced materiality to express the liveliness of nature, and this has led to her unique style of paintings with a three-dimensional aspect. In this exhibition, she added a new method of peeling off a layer of accumulated paint to better express the wildness. Nature is a medium and energy, offering her vivid sense of being alive. The artist captures nature on canvas, crossing the boundary between abstraction and figuration, and the condensed energy of nature penetrates the canvas and is transmitted to the audience.

name: Oh Younghwa
bio: Oh Younghwa, who is actively working in Beijing, studied at the Department of Fine Arts at ‘Saint-Petersburg state university’ in Russia and graduated with honors from ‘Chosun University’, Furthermore, she completed achieving the master’s course of Arts at ‘China Central Academy of Fine Art’. Her paintings continue to be based on her own cat with her unique refined sense. Since she is interested in stray cats which are on the border between the city and the nature, she looks at the possibility of coexistence between people, nature and the relationship for the future. She participated as a resident artist at Beijing Residency, Gwangju Museum of Art. Furthermore, she was invited by a leading Chinese gallery to participate in various exhibitions.

name: GWAXNG
bio: Through both figurative and abstract interpretations, Seonggwang Yun (b.1999) invites us to confront out instincts and primal emotions. The air spray and physical brushstrokes of the monsters in his works aggrandize their expressions and visualize the tension between the suppression and release of emotions. For Yun, the monsters embody the suppression of emotions and function as a medium to project the viewer's memories and emotions. Going beyond language, the artist focuses on non-verbal communication such as facial expressions and gestures. The clothes worn by the monsters actively reflect the artist's taste as demonstrated by the various hats. These devices conceal their faces while reinforcing their presence—condensing mechanisms of modern culture.

name: Eunjung Lee
bio:
'We' are not living alone in many things that exist. People who interact with each other are made up of 71 percent water and 18 percent carbon, 4 percent nitrogen, 2 percent calcium, 1 percent potassium, and a spoonful of rare elements. It is not that one person is born special, but sometimes he or she has something special and ordinary.
The artist reminded her of waves in this way like this. The waves are swept away. But even in that, one molecule, several properties, move vigorously in its own direction. A sea that is not special, the nature of water is the same as ours. As the waves hit the rocks, countless droplets of water cut through the air in the sky, but they go back into the waves. As if nothing had happened. A moment's specialness draws attention, but it goes back into the crowd of cheers. Using scattered and combined structure and images, the artist talks about the form and relationship of society.

name: Cha Jong Rye
bio: Cha Jong-Rye’s wooden sculptures (typically wall- or table-mounted) form lyrical patterns that express notions of creation, infinity, and eternity. Her method of working with wood is unique in that she layers hundreds of delicate pieces and sands them down by hand to create three-dimensional canvases with richly textured, [impasto](/gene/impasto)-like surfaces. Accentuated by the interplay of light and shadow across their surfaces, her sculptures stand out for their fluidity, appearing from a distance like rumpled bed sheets or rolling sand dunes. Other sculptures feature smooth knobs of various sizes that allude to fantastical lunar landscapes. Recently, she has also developed a penchant for covering surfaces with graceful cones with finely fluted sides. According to the artist, the cone “is the first form to break through the flat surface and, at the same time, the last form that arrives at the sky.”

name: Kwon Dae Sup
bio:
Dae-sup Kwon has devoted almost 30 years of his life to the creation of the Moon Jar and is considered its latter-day master. The complexity of creating these extraordinary works; the long firing time, high kiln heat and meeting Kwon’s exacting standards, all conspire to make his Moon Jars exceptionally difficult to produce. Typically, he is left with no more than 4 to 6 works a year.

Kwon received his BFA from the Hongik University, Seoul, South Korea in 1979. His has been exhibited widely and is included in many collections.

name: Sujin Park
bio: Sujin Park (SONGINPARK) has consistently explored emotion, the relationship between self and others, and the gaze formed within structures of repression and control, while continuing to engage with the idea of beauty. She works across both analog and digital media without limitation. At times, she renders ineffable emotional states through abstraction; at others, she transforms tangible and figurative elements—such as hair—into abstract patterns. Her current practice operates as a means of expressing emotion and subjective beauty.

name: Jeayeon Hong
bio:
Jeayeon Hong (b. 1947) is the artist whose works are on minimal art and action painting. From mid 1980s, the Vast Nature has been started to take as the major theme of his art works. From late 1990s to present, after experiencing an enlightenment during the course of work, he produces works based on the aesthetics of small decisions of everyday life which flows towards "emptiness" and "nothing", and he is committed in carrying the topic to his works.
Jeayeon Hong took key positions in Korean art market and played as an active influencer to artists. The positions are the Vice- President of Korean Fine Arts Association, President of Koeran Contemporary Printmakers Association, etc. He is also the professor of Kyunggi University of Fine Arts and devoted his whole life in growing young artists.
Held more than 45 solo and 800 group exhibitions in domestic and overseas. He is an active painter as his journey continues with fully scheduled exhibitions throughout 2022 and year 2023.
His works are collected by top museums such as British Museum of Art, Seoul Museum of Art, AMAC Museum of Art in France, Kwandu Museum of Fine Art in Taiwan and a lot others.

name: Jiwon Kim
bio: Jiwon Kim has been exploring the nature of painting by focusing on the aesthetic act of ‘drawing and painting’ for the past 30 years. Delving into the subject, Kim depicts subliminal images that are generated when normalcy and symbolism intersect. Mendrami series (2002-) is his representative series amongst his diverse painting series including Canvas Fly (2014-), Landscape (2002-), and Take Off (2002-).  His Mendrami series can be regarded as a still life of a commonly found flower, a symbol of human desires and dignity, and the artist’s meditation diary that reflects his introspection of himself. Kim has held solo exhibitions at Daegu Art Museum (Daegu, Korea), Kumho Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), HITE Collection (Seoul, Korea), Art Space Pool (Seoul, Korea), and participated in various group exhibitions including Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, Seoul Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), ARKO Museum (Seoul, Korea), Yanhuang Art Museum (Beijing, China), and National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts (Taichung, Taiwan). His works are in the public collections of Museum of Modern and Contemporary Arts, Korea, Leeum Samsung Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), and Sonje art Center (Seoul, Korea). Kim is currently a professor at the School of Visual Arts of the Korea National University of Arts.

name: Kyungah Ham
bio:
Kyungah Ham’s sculptures, videos and embroidered works delve into the realm of the socio-political – questioning the labor, politics, nationhood, social identity and freedom of information in her native Korea. She explores her nation’s history as a provocateur, subtly building layers of meaning with each step in her process to kindle an enduring political discourse. Her embroidered works embody an approach initiated by Ham in 2008. Here, she collects information available in South Korea – ranging from images of Western abstract paintings to South Korean slang – and, through an intermediary, sends them as a blueprint to be embroidered in North Korea. Through the works, she extends the offer of authorship to the embroiderers, as they must occasionally alter the works due to censorship. On the surface, the works are luminous and poetic, but the real material lies in the process of information and communication within. 

Kyungah Ham (b. 1966, Seoul) received her BFA from the Seoul National University and MFA from the School of Visual Arts in New York. She has participated in exhibitions in South Korea and internationally, including at the Kunstmuseum Bonn; Kunsthalle Düsseldorf; Charlottenborg Exhibition Hall, Copenhagen, Denmark; and the Museum Moderner Kunst Stiftung Ludwig Wien, Vienna, Austria. Her work can be found in numerous public collections, among them, Victoria & Albert Museum; Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art, Seoul; MMCA, Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea; and the Seoul Museum of Art.

name: Lee Jung Woong (b. 1963)
bio: Korean artist Lee Jung Woong is best known for his meticulous [trompe-l’oeil](/gene/trompe-loeil) oil paintings on Korean rice paper that depict traditional Chinese brushes saturated with ebony ink. The [hyperrealistic](/gene/hyperrealism), reflexive works both celebrate and question the incessant influence of traditional Chinese painting on contemporary Asian art. Lee’s perfectly rendered brushes, shadows, and splatters—reproduced at a larger-than-life scale on massive canvases—imbue his work with a humorous, pop art-inspired quality that connects ancient techniques to contemporary perspectives.

name: Mawz
bio:
Artist MAWZ has been drawn to Disney animation films and cartoons since childhood. While studying Fine Arts at Chung-ang University, the artist created a character to represent himself and painted the world through its eyes. 

The artist's work explores surrealism and symbolism, conveying messages of reality's absurdity, personal concerns, social situations, and aspirations. His work conveys social, cultural, and personal concerns through the use of symbolic imagery, featuring poetic symbolism and animated expressions. The symbols used include envelopes, ribbons, and eagles, and their meanings can be interpreted in different ways based on the viewer's perspective. His recent work revolves around exploring the absurdity of reality and social issues. He continuously experiments with new materials and conducts thorough research on the subject's background or history to add more depth to his work. 

The artist’s defining characteristic is his use of Matière, which is conveyed through simple and implicit expressions with cheerful colors and thick brushstrokes of paint. Before starting any artwork, the artist meticulously documents the content or stories he intends to convey. He draws inspiration and motivation from his imagination, surroundings, and personal experiences to depict his unique perspective in his work. His recent work emphasizes background and three-dimensional elements over characters and icons from his earlier pieces, adding depth and highlighting the message. His animated style and expressions capture deep concerns across diverse subjects and allow for varied interpretations among viewers.

The artist collaborated with various brands, including McDonald's, Volkswagen, Cass, and SM Entertainment, to communicate with the public. MAWZ uses the process of creating art as a means to illustrate his personal exploration of the future unknown. He seeks to share his journey with the audience to spread positive energy and convey optimistic promises of life.

name: Lee Jinju
bio:
LEE Jinju's work begins from questions thrown repeatedly in life. The negative events and emotions of the past, which were not even wanted, endlessly appear and disappear within everyday life.

LEE continuously asks herself what becomes the device which arouses memories from within the uncomfortable 'ventilation' one does not wish to face, what are the common structures of memories and in what way do memories, which survived without having been forgotten, manufacture. She wonders why people with Alzheimer's do not only lose memories of the past but cannot live the present and cannot imagine the future and where the boundaries are between memories, dreams, and conscience. What are the afterimages of images, made by her perception from the cognitive force of memory surpassing time and space, like? What becomes visible during the process of inner quest starting from these questions is recorded as her work.

From the superfluous cut to a well-made frame, following their softly soundless stories, cuddling the insignificant and petty motifs of every day, she discovers the unconscious sensuous layer that is hidden inside. At that moment, Lee becomes a melancholic adventurer and every day is reborn into things of the extraordinary.

name: 08AM
bio:
The characteristic of the work is that it highlights the three-dimensional effect of form in flat painting and creates a unique atmosphere. It proves the reason and existence of existence through creative activities and contains social messages of the times.

After the 2012 Miami International Exchange Exhibition, he was invited by the Mississippi State University (MSU) to develop his work through international activities such as exhibitions at Art Gallery and Lacuna in Chicago.

He won the Cut & Paste 2013 (WCO) competition held in Seoul in 2013 and became interested in characterization.
After experiencing street art and art markets in New York in 2017, based on a new understanding of pop culture, I tried borrowed art fused with existing expression methods, and so far, the energy has been developed in various forms.

name: Kwak Seungyong
bio:
Kwak Seungyong explores new possibilities for creation through the encounter of traditional art materials, namely nudity and hanbok.
He delicately reveals the respective temporal gaps and psychological changes through the process of repeatedly drawing the same image. Using a delicate airbrush technique, the past and the present slowly blend together, and the story of the old times is revealed elegantly and gently in the slow wait.
The past is constantly summoned and reinterpreted through the present, and new meaning is acquired within it. The women in these familiar classical masterpieces offer a quiet beauty that is both new and imbued with the depth of time. Through these works, Kwak Seung-yong calmly and deeply unfolds the story of life in which the past and the present are connected.

name: Park Eunyoung
bio:
Park Eunyoung refers to herself as a painter who records and collects colors. The artist’s attitude toward her works is clearly revealed in the titles of her works. Her working style is quite interesting. The artist repeats the process of transforming emotions and sensibilities that appear in certain experiences into colors through contemplation and accumulating them one by one. When the completed color screen appears at the end, the work is finalized by naming it with a verb which is connected to the color through the interaction with the work.
One of the biggest charms of Park Eunyoung's world of work is connectivity. Her work is powerful enough to be enjoyed alone, but her works’ values shine even more once you understand the flow between her works and between her exhibitions. The audience is stimulated countlessly and exercises imagination during this process. At the end of this process, the audience’s experience is evoked and expanded into another world.
Park Eunyoung explores the formative language between symbols (words) and materials in the form of work where unconsciousness and consciousness coexist. Just as several words come together to form a sentence, each work is given a meaning and narrative between her works, forming a single structure as an abstract painting and providing indicators that allow the audience to view from various perspectives.

name: Haengeun Ha
bio:
Ha Haengeun is constantly on the move. Her artwork on canvas whether small or big size shows
strong acrylic colors. She is creating a world which is familiar and foreign at the same time. Rooting 
in the East but full of quotations and symbols of equally East and West. 
Reflecting while drawing – drawing while reflecting, she is crossing the borderlines thriving the 
present, the past and the future. The face of her central character is like a multilayered mirror
aggregating diverse aspects: the sphere of being born merges into the sphere of life resulting in 
the only knowledge we have: We are bound to die. She calls her alter ego the old child, the border 
rider or NaNa, which has a complex meaning going far beyond the translation of ‘I’, touching the 
universal spirit of I, me and you.
Highly skilled in Eastern and Western painting techniques. Graduate of Hongik University Seoul, 
South Korea. Since many years her work is presented in South Korea, HongKong and Taiwan, 
Austria, Germany and France. Worldwide collectors. (text by aks)

name: Myonghi Kang
bio:
Born in 1947 in Daegu, South Korea and settled down in France in 1972, Myonghi selects painting objects from the nature and presents a world that is captured by her unique sensibility, in abstract strokes of strong personal character.

Apart from her museum exhibitions and poem parties, in which she works with poets to pair poetry and painting, Myonghi conducts a quiet life and focuses on the pursuit of her ideal art of painting. Nevertheless, she has gained recognition and respect from prestigious experts in academic circles, including philosopher Philippe Lacoue Labarthe and poet Alain Jouffroy. Mr. Dominique de Villepin, the former Prime Minister of France, is also a poet and an art critic with a wide knowledge in abstract form of art. He has given full of praise of Myonghi as an artist, and describes her as "a gem known only to insiders".

name: Jeehui Hong
bio: Agnes Jeehui Hong (B.1986) born in Seoul, studied graphic design at Kaywon University of Art & Design and worked as a commercial designer. However, she entered the path of fine art with a desire to capture her inner self and has been recognized as a prominent artist collaborating interesting projects with global brands. She tries to infuse the journey of exploring femininity that seems vulnerable but strong inside into the work. It is a process of creating an organic relationship with the outside world by listening closely to the artist’s personal story as a single woman, thus she chooses a material that can reinforce the connection beyond physicality. The glass bottle, the artist’s main object for the past few years, is easily affected by the external environment but never loses its natural shine and transparency even if it is shattered. The material property of glass, which does not lose its core despite a fragile exterior, is the essence of the femininity that she sees. Rather than pursuing genre completeness, it is an expression of the will to capture the inner psychic landscape, and an effort to approach the essence of the story through active removal. As the audience resonates with the artist’s mind, one discovers their own story. In the exhibition

name: Koo Hyunmo
bio: Koo Hyunmo blurs the boundaries of two seemingly dichotomous notions such as reality and fiction, principle and phenomenon through his distinct poetic lyricism and spatial approach to ordinary materials that include paper, branches, and stones. Koo’s installation works are open to interpretation according to the viewer’s standpoint and the object’s location. His works infiltrate the gap between time and space and revert our previous understanding of them. Koo has been workings in different cities including Berlin, Leipzig, and Dresden. In 2009, Koo received the Art Award from MPI-CBG, the birthplace of Nobel laureates as well as an institution devoted to encouraging interdisciplinary research in the fields of basic science, humanities, and arts. Koo’s works are included in the collection of Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden (Dresden, Germany).

name: Choi Jeong Hwa
bio: Choi Jeong Hwa creates art from the most humble of materials, finding inspiration in soda bottles, shopping bags, and colorful plastic dishes from the 99-cent store. Inspired by the harmony and chaos of the urban environment, the artist, architect, and designer undermines the hierarchy of the museum by installing his pieces on the outside of buildings. He has created a 10-story installation made from 1,000 discarded doors, and decorated Seoul’s Olympic Stadium with garlands made from 2 million pieces of trash—transforming the building’s surface into a glittering jewel. In other pieces he explores ideas of artificiality and permanence through the use of plastic food and flowers. He declines to categorize his work, leaving the audience to define his pieces on a personal level. As his motto states: “My art is your heart.”

name: Youngkyun Lim
bio: Lim Young Kyun was born in Daegu, Korea. After completing his B.F.A at Chung-Ang University, M.F.A at New York University and studied in International Center of Photography (I.C.P), New York. Starting with the Grand Priz in 1973 at Photo Contest for High School Students granted by Korea Photography Association he has been awarded Top 10 Photographers nominated by curator Mary Forest who had worked at Smithonian Institute in Washington D.C, in 1985 and granted Fulbright Award  in 2000 and etc, and he also had the invitational exhibition at British Musuem in 2007. He worked as a reporter of Joong-ang Daily Newspapers in New York (1983-1988) and contributed his writings and photo works to daily newspapers and magazines in Korea as well. He used to teach in New York University and Chung-Ang University. His works have been collected by Museum of Modern Art (New York), International Center of Photography (New York), Kodak Photography Museum, Landesmuseum fur Kunst und Kulturgeschichte Oldenberg (Germany), National Museum of Contemporary Art, Kwacheon, and other major museums in the world. His publications are Destiny (Munster stadt Museum), Daily Life Landscapes (Youlhwadang), Portrait of Artist (Ahn Graphics Publishing Co.), Young Kyun Lim Art Vivant, (Sikong sa Publishing Co.), and etc.

name: Kim Junki
bio:
Kim Junki is a contemporary Korean artist whose work explores perception, existence, and the relationship between self and other through the material conditions of mirrors and light. He employs mirrors not as simple reflective surfaces, but as structural devices that dismantle fixed viewpoints and transform perception into an ongoing, dynamic process. By scratching the reverse side of mirrors and allowing LED light to pass through, Kim’s distinctive “light painting” technique produces layered images where visible materiality and invisible sensation intersect, revealing the conditions through which the self and the other are perceived within fluid and shifting relationships.
Kim received his MFA in Oriental Painting from Hongik University. He has held 13 solo exhibitions in cities including Seoul and Sejong, and has participated in numerous institutional and curated exhibitions, including contemporary art exhibitions at the Cheongju Museum of Art. His awards include the Danwon Art Grand Prize at the 26th Danwon Art Festival and an Excellence Award at the 6th Gwangju Hwaru. His works are held in major public collections, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (Art Bank), Seoul Museum of Art, Jeonbuk Provincial Art Museum, Cheongju Museum of Art, Kim Hong-do Art Museum, and Art Museum Ryeo.

name: Dongyoon Kang 강동윤
bio:
Mother-of-pearl paintings are my language and small gesture of breathing with the energy of Mother Nature.

I put my love, gratitude, and happiness into it.

Mother-of-pearl paintings convey the healing energy of Mother Nature's gift to us, not only for its outward beauty, which is expressed through the encounter between Mother Nature, created with God's love, and the brilliant, vibrant light of mother-of-pearl, but also for its “clearing and calming properties” and its symbolism of birth, rebirth, rebirth, auspiciousness, abundance and fertility, which can contribute to the calming of the mind and heart.

The mother-of-pearl painting, which is conveyed through love energy and healing energy, is a new creation and is colored with another light of life in Mother Nature by adding my little sincerity to the shell containing sea energy, which is Mother Nature that accepts and embraces everything in low and low places

How happy would you be if you could charge up a little bit of Mother Nature's healing energy through this painting, which will always accompany you on your path to a rich and happy life, dispelling turbulence and stabilizing your mind?

name: Hoh Woo Jung
bio: Hoh Woo Jung represents his own pure abstraction by consistently exploring infinite possibilities and moderate variations found in the most fundamental combination of lines and faces. He collects images of various objects that emerge with interest in events and thoughts in modern society and expresses the meaning and the hidden side of them in the form of paintings.

name: Kim hyunjin
bio: Hyunjin Kim depicts the intangible world and non-existent objects from her imagination on the canvas. In her paintings, she uses minimal brushstrokes to give the objects great depth, and as a painter, she is building her own artistic world by focusing on the act of painting and the moment itself. She has participated in group exhibitions at Art Space 3, Seoul (2022); WESS, Seoul (2022); Perigee Gallery, Seoul (2022); Tiger Strike Asteroid, Los Angeles (2023); and solo exhibitions at Gallery 175, Seoul (2022), M3ta, Seoul (2023) and sangheeut, Seoul (2024).

name: Jieun Choi
bio:
Born in 1992, Jieun Choi majored Korean painting at Dongguk University and continued her studies at the National University of Arts in Karlsruhe. Currently, she is pursuing her artistic career in Germany. At the heart of her artistic expression is the creation of abstract images, skillfully capturing the transient and ephemeral qualities of the moment.

Choi seamlessly integrates the soft curves of her subjects with abstract backgrounds, crafting a unique visual narrative that places her characters within a distinctive and captivating realm. Through this, she delves into the intricate and nuanced aspects inherent in the linguistic and subtle nature of the human body. The artist pursues mysterious, intuitive, and sensorial expressions, skillfully capturing the inner narratives and psychological realms of her characters through the intricacies of their gaze and tension.

The artist's creative process navigates the delicate balance between abstraction and concreteness, cycling through phases of creation and destruction. She sculpts her narratives with unexpected forms and situations, elevating the tension and mystery of the characters through moments of anticipation and unwavering pursuit.

Choi endeavors to immerse viewers in an experience of intuition and empathy by infusing her characters' gestures and gazes with profound meaning. In doing so, she cherishes the exploration of boundaries between the unconscious and conscious realms, forging innovative narrative structures. Through this distinctive approach, Choi actively seeks profound engagement with the audience, persistently delving into the dynamic exchange of meaning and emotions within the realm of art.

name: Park Jong Kyu
bio:
We are not able to know about the universe, no matter how much we try. Neither natural science nor life philosophy can give the clue. Everything is nothing but the world of frame. Nevertheless, there must be a definite perspective approaching the universe. From a broader view, this can be fractals or bubbles. Looking at it smaller, it can end up being “nothingness” beyond molecules or particles. Park Jong-kyu deeply concerned on the movement of perspectives of the self and the process, and this made him pay attention to the features of computers. The essence of a computer work consists in the fact that it is not the product created by the self. It is a computing structure based on a binary system created by 0 and 1. This simple arrangement is more rapid and precise than human calculation does. When the computing capacity outpaces humans, humans transform into nothing but a tool of the computer. Long time ago, Park Jong-kyu predicted the possible fall of human existence as a means to save and operate computers. Out of the arrangement of 0 and 1 with the orderliness that is even beautiful, this becomes a phenomenon. The computer provides us with a beautiful screen, harmonious sounds, mathematical answers and accurate prediction results. However, not all calculations and programs based on 0 and 1 can be perfect. The more the computer carries out calculation, the higher the entropy will be. With increased entropy, the computer will be tired making a noise. However, if we enlarge this uncomfortable phenomenon called “noise,” this manifests an orderly aspect as well. The noise is rearranged as digital virtuality, in other words, pixel images, and the computer printer transform the pixel images into the substance called “contact papers.” Beyond defense of innocence and its destruction 
_Jinmyeong Lee, Former Chief Curator of Daegu Art Museum

name: Lee Dongi
bio: Dongi Lee (b. 1967) takes special interest in images that are easily consumed and widely circulated in popular culture. In 1993, he created Atomaus, a new character inspired by Mickey Mouse and the Astro Boy from the Japanese cartoon. Portrayed in various situations implying social signs and contexts, Atomaus has since established itself as a major icon of contemporary art. Lee employs various elements ranging from cartoons, advertisements, and internet to classical paintings, and abstract art and shows the way they form complex layers in society. Since 2010, he has focused on exploring diverse cultural phenomena and facets of modern society through his ‘Eclecticism’ series. This series takes the form of layered paintings, whereby countless visual images from multimedia and digital media are overlapped and juxtaposed with everyday scenes. The complex combinations of words from the web and images reveal elements of sub-culture. The numerous images contained in his works do not deliver specific narratives or meanings. Lee presents a new aspect of the consumer culture society, and realizes a visual bricolage.

name: Moon Mean
bio: Using homemade materials, Moon Mean creates works that reconstruct large and small events that happen to him and his surroundings. He prepares solid and light atypical blanks by layering macerated Hanji and paints on them with turbid pigments he calls metallic tempera. Like the moon hanging over a smudged horizon, the silhouette of the ceiling in his room at night with unknown time, the ripples in the river as someone else would have seen, scenes with no name or owner are slowly transformed by the artist’s hand into uneven images. For him, reality is an opaque mass of too many superimpositions to grasp clearly. Fragments of images stored in his phone or glimpsed on social media overlap and intermingle in a foggy field of faded light, transforming them into abstractions. Flowing on the edges of painting and sometimes borrowing from sculpture and installation, Moon’s work questions the gap between reality and fiction, truth and misunderstanding, memory and fact.

name: Bohie Kim
bio: Kim Bohie, a prominent figurative painter, has continued to explore bringing modernity to Korean painting through her exquisite visual languages that she has developed while researching the traditional styles of Korean and Western paintings. Kim Bohie delicately expresses beauty and purity of nature closely observed in daily life such as plants, gardens, seas, and surrounding sceneries. Embracing the composition and perspective of Western painting, she continues to work on an organic combination of each element in her work by accepting Eastern approaches that emphasize vividness and harmony.

name: Dongwan Kook
bio:
Dongwan Kook(b.1979) works on the unconsciousness and the way reaching it with drawing, painting, sculpture, and books. The dream archive work, which has been continuing since 2007, melts the relationship between herself and dreams into the characteristics of books and sculptures by comparing the arbitrary relationship between language and memory. The drawing
‘Hoigwang-Banjo’ using ‘free association’ is a tool to discover herself in the present, and the artist 
develops the painting series that enlarges the drawing several hundred times by observing in detail the unconscious. Shifting the disciplined gaze to the social phenomena that pierce her life, the dreamer pays attention to the artistic connection between the individual and the society.

name: Byun Kyung-Sup
bio: Byun Kyung-Sup is a Korean artist born in 1957 who lives and works in Gwangju, Korea. She studied painting at the College of Fine Arts, Hongik University in Seoul where she graduated with a bachelor's degree in 1980. Shortly after she moved to Arlington, Texas with her husband where she dedicated her time rearing her children. Although from a wealthy family, she never considered their help a fallback and chose to build her life independently. During this period, she took up a job as a seamstress, which was one of many occupational identities she embodied to support her family. This is when she discovered the beauty and pain of an honest, albeit painstaking, labor. It wasn't until 20 years later that she returned to Korea to study Fine Arts in the Graduate School of Chonnam University in Gwangju, Korea and held her paintbrush again. Ever since, her day-to-day work has been focused on painting infinite dots, which reflects her experience as a seamstress and her love of stiches. She now resides in Gwangju, Korea with her husband, a retired professor. She translates the concept of sewing into her work. Each tiny dot in her paintings resembles a stitch that requires a precise, purposeful brushstroke. Just like you can't simply glue one garment to another, and each piece of clothing a result of a meaningful compilation of stitches, her work seeks to connect the seemingly insignificant dots to create a dimension for self-reflection and to remind myself that what may seem like a small dot can be part of a much larger, beautiful picture.

name: Kwangik Song
bio:
Artist Kwangik Song uses paper to create artworks. Applying or scattering paint on paper is  nothing but the departure point of his work.
In Song’s art such a property of things derives from naturalness and historicity. Hanji, or  Korean paper made from the inner bark of paper mulberry trees, contains the time in which  life is engendered through wind under the sun and the breath of the land. He does not cut  the paper precisely. He applies paint to the back of a piece in order to revive the serenity  and plainness of hanji. He does not fill empty spaces with colors, even though there are some sections that have been less saturated with colors due to how the paper’s fibers are  entangled. He simply feels about for spots where art stays according to hanji’s intrinsic grains.
To Song, materials are more than objects. The artist mentions that his consciousness  becomes one with his body and he begins to occupy himself with his work once its direction  and plan have been determined. When he is amid such acts, his existence is revealed not  only through his own life but also through the world surrounding him. His narratives are  formed and imbued in his scenes one by one. They pertain to spaces and times in which his  work encounters his body. 
His scene suspended from thread-like time vibrates in the gaps between pieces of hanji. The  depth stemming from the height of the erected hanji pieces arouses a variety of resonances.  They become lines or planes depending on the visual angle or space where they are erected.

name: Dongwook Suh
bio: Dongwook Suh (b. 1974, Korea) received his B.F.A of fine arts in Hongik University in Korea and DNSAP of École Nationale Supérieure d'arts de Paris-Cergy in France. He held solo exhibitions The Taste of Painting, ONE AND J. Gallery (2020); The Showroom: Summer-Beach-Dazzling II, Space Willing N Dealing, 2020; Atmosphere, Noblesse Collection (2019); Atmosphere, ONE AND J. Gallery, Korea (2017); Night Ride, Gallery SoSo, Korea (2015); Art of Painting, ONE AND J. Gallery, Korea (2013); Day for Night, ONE AND J. Gallery, Korea (2011) and others.  Selected group exhibitions featuring his artwork Flashback,  ONE AND J. Gallery, Korea (2019); Dialogue, Sueno339, Korea (2018); Edge of the Night, OCI Museum of Art, Korea (2016); The Shadow of the Future: 7 Video Artists from Korea, National Museum of Contemporary Art - MNAC, Romania (2013); Move on Aisa, Alternative Space LOOP, Korea (2012); The Cinematic-Montage, Seoul Museum of Art, Korea (2009).

name: Kim Nam Pyo
bio:
Nampyo Kim is a Korean contemporary artist with a background in Western Art. Through techniques of Western painting and the world view of traditional Korean painting, the artist represents the shapes and figures inherent in human unconsciousness with his unique style of art.
Regarded one of the most important figures amongst Korean contemporary artists, Nampyo Kim’s works are highly sought after. His works are a part of important private and public collections including Seoul Museum of Art, and Art Bank, a subsidiary of National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea.

name: Youjin Yi
bio: In her multifaceted artistic language, Youjin Yi unites objective references and abstract, painterly structures. Her works depict landscape spaces occupied by persons, animals, objects or hybrids. Seemingly dematerialized they fuse with their environment, emerge or take shape.

name: Lee HeeJung
bio: Lee HeeJung’s paintings begin with the accumulation of dots, lines, and planes—an intuitive process through which a forest gradually takes form. Receiving the countless hues and energies of nature as they are, the artist captures the forest as a singular, living current. In

name: Po Kim
bio: Po Kim's career was characterized by an ever-evolving style, and an eagerness to seek out new areas of inspiration for more than six decades. Born in 1917 in South Korea, Kim came to United States on a fellowship at University of Illinois in 1955 and eventually moved to New York City two years later. From Abstract Expressionism, to realistic still lifes, and to Figurative Expressionism; each decade saw a drastic change in Kim’s work. His works from the 1980s onward included the largest of his oeuvre, as if he were accumulating artistic styles by orchestrating the elements of his previous work. Rich in narrative, these canvases contain personal themes and mysterious alternative realities filled with animals, humans, and nature. In 2005, Po Kim and his wife Sylvia Wald established the Gallery that bears their names, the Sylvia Wald and Po Kim Gallery, in New York City. When Kim passed in 2014, he left behind a strong legacy in his paintings and the innumerable artists he inspired.

name: Dongwook Kim
bio: Seoul-based S. Korean artist Dongwook Kim explores reflection of the ever-changing present in the flow of time. The familiar things he encounters daily are transformed into universality and abstraction, inviting viewers to explore the emotional landscape of his works. Dongwook Kim's gestural expressions convey the raw and fundamental emotions of everyday life, flowing naturally in a state of immersive expression with each brushstroke. Through this organic process, he creates a rich experience that allows viewers to delve deep into the moment through the layers of time he portrays. Dongwook Kim debuted in Tokyo, Japan, with a group exhibition at 8th Gallery, followed by solo shows at Print Bakery, Objectless, Gallery Clip, Corner Gallery, and many more.

name: Kim Hyun-chul
bio:
Kim Hyun-chul (b. 1959) graduated from the Department of Painting at Seoul National University(SNU) and completed his graduate studies in traditional East Asian painting at SNU. Since his graduate school years, he has served as a research fellow at the Kansong Art Museum.

In the early stages of his artistic journey, Kim trained by copying masterpieces from ancient China and Joseon Dynasty and by sketching directly from nature. He has continued the legacy of traditional Korean painting through works such as true-view landscape paintings inspired by the style of Gyeomjae Jeong Seon, as well as portraits and flower-and-bird paintings. At the same time, he has embraced modern materials and techniques in his practice, embodying the philosophy of “honoring the old to create anew” (法古創新).

Kim has established a distinctive style marked by blue-toned surfaces, aesthetic simplification and use of negative space, and the striking contrast between azure landscapes and white mist. These elements have earned him recognition as a leading figure in contemporary Korean painting.

He has held solo exhibitions at Gyeomjae Jeong Seon Art Museum, Hanbyukwon Art Museum, Gallery Ichon, Artreon Gallery, Gong Art Space, and Gallery Hanok, and has participated in numerous group exhibitions at art museums, galleries, and institutions.

name: Shinyoung Park
bio:
Shinyoung Park holds BFA and MFA in Painting from Seoul National University, and MA in Print from Royal College of Art. 

Park translates the cultural and social characteristics of various environments encountered into a subjective visual language. Geographical movement is the driving force of life that continues her to meet new places and people, and she steadily captures the different worlds she observes through various media such as prints, drawings, and installations. In addition, the limitations of synchronic and diachronic senses experienced in contemporary life let her take a fresh look at the myriad events that occur beyond her own space and time. The fragments of images collected through various media are subjected to formative editing many times in her hands. The unique smudged, scratched, and scarred surfaces of her works lead the viewer from the real landscape to the dimension of the unreal, where they become symbols with secret stories.

name: Eun Chun
bio: In the 19th century, photography was extensively applied to a wide variety of fields and often pursued blindly. It shows a great yearning toward a new visual world where one sees everything. In the history of photography, evolved through science, pseudo-science, positivism and religious cult, there appear “dreamers” who wanted to see the invisible. The unique tools of each “seer”, the astronomical instruments of astronomers, everyday objects of Foley artists, the tactile language of the visually impaired, and the visual language of the hearing-impaired are the extended sensory organs for them to see the invisible. The sensory organ can be compared to a window to the world because we come to understand the world as we see it, listen to it and touch it. The figures I have dealt with in my work ceaselessly invest themselves in communicating with the world outside the window and do not suspend their yearning for seeing a world on the other side. What I saw in them was the faces of dreamers. --Artist's note

name: Gyeore Lee
bio:
Gyeore Lee has been creating a painterly space through canvas and experimenting with various possibilities within it. The term 'possibility' in his works may refer to a space where practical problems have been or can be resolved, or a space without psychological limitations or obstacles. The artist's continued exploration of these themes is closely related to his personal characteristics. Lee has always faced challenges in immediately and accurately perceiving subjects due to a congenital visual impairment. He especially mentions experiencing many uncomfortable situations in human relationships due to his visual difficulty. 
The efforts to overcome the limitations of vision or to embrace it as part of his daily life would have naturally prompted a keen awareness of inconvenient, challenging, or contradictory situations in the world for Lee. And this would have led to encourage him to consider possibilities of improving, navigating through, or interpreting the situations differently.
Gyeore Lee studied painting and received BFA(Summa Cum Laude) and MA at Seoul National University, South Korea. He participated in the Leipzig International Art Programme and the International Summer Residency Aschersleben, Germany, mainly exhibiting in both countries.

name: Kim Chun Hwan
Young Do Jeong
bio: Young Do Jeong has been depicting the collision between the inner mind and the external world in his paintings, based on images he acquired while growing up in two different cultures of the East and West. His paintings are metaphorical and descriptive, exploring human being’s innermost feelings of loss, pain, and misunderstanding through psychoanalytic interpretation. Jeong's paintings, created with a variety of mediums including acrylic paint, oil paint, ink, spray, color pencils, graphite, transcend the boundary between abstract and representational art, creating a sense of tension within the canvases surface. Jeong received his B.F.A. in painting at Rhode Island School of Design and an M.F.A. in painting and drawing at Tyler School of Art at Temple University. His bold paintings have captured the eyes of collectors and art-related professionals.

name: Jaeseok Lee
bio: Lee Jaeseok has been exploring the subject of similarities between human bodies and objects for several years based on his own experiences in the military service. It is important to contemplate the significance and implication of signs in Lee’s works for understanding his outlook. Signs appeared even in his prior works could be seen as ‘the second name’ schematically given by the artist to several means such as machines, goods or even temporarily confined people under strict order to achieve an ideal goal the peculiar group sought.

name: Jeong Ju Jeong
bio:
Jeongju Jeong, a sculptor and media installation artist, explores the interplay between light and space. He studied sculpture at Hongik University and earned his Meisterschüler title in Germany in 2002. He obtained a Ph.D. in Art from Kookmin University in 2015 and has been a professor at Sungshin Women's University since 2012.

Jeongju Jeong's interest in light began during his time in Germany, where he experimented with light entering through windows and its relationship with space. He created works like "Light shape" (1998), "schauhaus" (1999), and "Dormitory" (2000), using cameras and videos to explore the dynamics of seeing and being seen.

Back in Korea, he expanded his work to encompass urban spaces, including "Dukidong Rodeo Street" (2005) and "Zenda Plaza" (2005). His pieces often reflect on the history and memories associated with specific architectural spaces.

Jeong's video works, such as "Lobby" (2010) and "27 Rooms" (2017), continue to delve into the psychological aspects of light, gaze, and space. He also explores abstract spaces through 3D animation videos like "Passage" (2016) and "Light in Room" (2018).

In his sculpture works, including the "Facade" series, Jeong abstracts the formative relationships between spaces and light. Recently, he has been focused on materializing light itself in series like "Curved Lights" (2021~) and "Metaphysical Star" (2021~).

For Jeongju Jeong, light is both an abstract concept and an entity that transcends the social system and interior spaces, making it a central theme in his artistic exploration.

name: Park Hyung-jin
bio: Park Hyung-jin was born in Seoul, Korea in 1968. Park has been working on the concept of "Everything is connected" since 1994, exploring the content of Korean shamanism. The artist often works by going into the mountains, feeling the colors of natural life, breathing in the clean air, and experiencing the cycle of nature. The human-created framework of society is also considered to be part of the cycle of nature, which is also part of the cycle of the universe, and has been continuing his work. The work is expressed through my body as a signal from space.

name: Sangwon Shin
bio:
an unsteady shape

pile up one after another
Place the ink on top, dry it, and grate it repeatedly. The canvas cloth containing the ink leaves a mark, seeps in, and leaves another mark. There is no physical change, but stains are repeated and multiple layers of virtual space are created. Impersonate emotions faithfully. Wipe off the screen as the expression of emotions becomes more or less decorative at some point. I finally got a step closer to the emotion I knew after wiping out the previous repetition. However, I felt unsatisfied for a while, so I picked up the brush again and created a space on the screen.

In the meantime, all the work will be stopped in the unstable form.
Unstable shaping creates a sense of heterogeneity that makes me look really unstable, but the more I look at it, the more I feel that peace and inconvenience are stimulating me. I have learned that emotions are born more than works that I thought were perfect, and that there is a charm that makes me look back again, and now I believe that there is a place where emotions dwell in unstable shapes.

name: Sungmi Lee
bio:
www.sungmileestudio.net

Sungmi Lee uses variable, ethereal materials to create works that manifest her personal experiences and thoughts across various media, including drawing, sculpture, and installation. Rather than conventional materials typically used in fine arts, Lee employs fragile and hard-to-control substances such as broken glass shards, smoke, and soot. Her work derives meaning from objects whose utility has lapsed, extracting universal significance from abstract forms.
For Lee, the creation process is as crucial as the final piece itself. The repetitive, labor-intensive process she engages in is time-consuming and akin to a form of asceticism, possessing therapeutic significance. She views the art-making process as a meditative, spiritual practice.
Lee was born in Seoul, Korea, in 1977 and moved to the U.S. during her teenage years. She earned a master’s degree in sculpture from the Maryland Institute College of Art. Before participating in a group exhibition at MoMA P.S.1 in New York, the artist held a solo exhibition at C. Grimaldis Gallery in Baltimore, Maryland. In 2009, she was featured in Younger than Jesus: Artist Directory by the New Museum, New York, and has since taken part in numerous significant invitational and group exhibitions. Lee has represented Korea’s young artists, showcasing her work at the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in Washington D.C., the Korean Cultural Center in New York, and the Art in Embassies shows organized by US Ambassadors to the Republic of Korea, Kathleen Stephens and Sung Kim. Having previously been based in New York, Lee returned to Korea in 2011. Since then, she has continued her artistic career, participating in many solo and group exhibitions at prestigious venues such as Gana Art Center in Pyeongchang-dong, Gana Art Hannam, Doosan Gallery New York, Kim Chong Yung Museum, National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (MMCA), Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art, and Nam-Seoul Museum  of Art.

name: Shin Jehyun
bio:
www.shinjehyun.com

  Born in Seoul in 1982, Shin Jehyun gained an education in the theory and practice of modern and contemporary art at the Sungkyunkwan University School of Art, where he would go on to pursue his master’s degree and Ph.D.
  Using extended research, Shin pursues the smallest uncertainties that arise from deeply personal experiences and lays out the information which he collects through such processes in the form of diverse media, including paintings, sound art, performances, video art, publications, and installations. For instance, he has engaged in work on the problem of gentrification in art spaces, the history of South Korean plantations, and the inequitable system behind art museums, revealing the ironies and paradoxical hidden aspects which emerge between socio-political issues and individual experiences.

name: Sylbee Kim
bio:
http://sylbeekim.net/
  
  Sylbee Kim (*1981, Seoul) is a South Korean video artist based in Berlin since 2005. Kim’s video installations experiment with digital and physical making processes to imagine sociopolitical grounds for less destructive ways of living and dying. Kim’s display structures and handling of audio-visual languages propose pluralistic perception of our reality.  
  Kim held solo exhibitions at Mélange Cologne, Nevan Contempo Prague, and Insa Art Space Seoul among others. She participated in group exhibitions at Gwangju Biennale, MMCA Seoul, SeMA Biennale Mediacity Seoul, Kunstverein Göttingen, and Neuer Berliner Kunstverein. Kim was resident artist at Gasworks, London and is the first Asian board member of bbk berlin––The Professional Association of Visual Artists Berlin.

name: Ahn Sung Kyu
bio: Ahn Sung Kyu is a Korean artist born in 1966 who lives and works in Suwon, South Korea. Sung-Kyu is an artist who has intensively focused on painterly space and visual structure through his work. From the “Monument” series he focused on 10 years ago to today’s “Border” series, Ahn’s works reveal vividly realistic forms. However, the emphasis was rather on the experiments and questions about the visual structure in the space of painting, and on reflections on the visual frame. In the “Border” series also, featured in this exhibition, Ahn Sung-Gyu composes the picture-plane not with the standard composition of 5:3, but with a proportion of 9:1 between the sky and structures on the ground, drawing viewers’ eyes toward the border dividing the two areas, and creating extreme tension. Furthermore, he produces a rather unfamiliar picture-plane, quite different from ordinary landscape paintings, by reaching towards the limits of tension with hyper-realistic dense description. But such tension and visual focus are soon restored to a wide pictorial space that eases visual the tension, and then enables us to get closer to the significance of the borders of visual tension. Here, the space created by the artist can be read as a point of self-awareness about the borders of perception looking at the present era, and a frame through which to see the world. As seen in his delicate depiction of buildings, while minutely observing the limits of the smallest parts, Ahn Sung-Gyu sometimes reveals the boundary of perspective approaching exactness and extremity paradoxically through an extreme contrast between the architectural structures and the opposing areas, and in other times he manipulates and uncovers the limits of the observer through breaking away from natural hues and achieving visual alterations in certain frames of the window-like canvases. Such limitations are on one hand, a perception of the limits of the artist himself, but on the other hand, a statement about the essenti

name: Byul Kim
bio:
Byul Kim shows an unfamiliar landscape in which cacti and frogs coexist and get entangled.
The artist, who spent her childhood in anxiety, confusion, frustration and pain, was positively inspired by a frog that shrank and then jumped further and higher.
Through the figure of a frog coexisting with the sharp thorns of a cactus, he revealed his desire to jump over barriers, obstacles, and threatening grips to take a proper place in the world. The artist graduated from the Department of Painting at the College of Art and Design at Konkuk University and the Department of Painting at the Graduate School of Hongik University. She has participated in 6 solo exhibitions, group exhibitions and art fairs

name: Hongmin Lee
bio:
Bulging muscles, strident colour and graphic, visceral metamorphoses characterise Hongmin Lee’s acrylics, oils and digital artworks. His subjects transform into monsters; powerful, grotesque beings that speak of themes such as despair, determination and coming of age. As the artist himself explains “I believe the human body is an assembly of will and I try to express it with a bunch of twisted muscles.”

Lee studied animation at the Korea National University of Arts, and cites artists including Akira Toriyama and Katsuhiro Otomo as influences. After graduating, he set up the arts collective Goo For Brothers, along with Seungchul Oh and Jaejung Beck. With a shared love of kaiju and experimental imagery, the three have been working together since the early 2010s in illustration, fine art, graffiti, comics and animation.

In parallel, Lee has continued to develop his individual fine arts career focussed primarily on painting. He completed a residency in Bangkok, Thailand, in 2014 and has participated in various groups shows in South Korea, including at the Seoul Museum of Art. His first solo presentation took place in 2015.

name: Lee Na
bio:
Lee Na (b.1986) is a South Korean artist who has a BFA in Fine Art from Kyungwon (Gachon) University, Seongnam, Korea and an MA in Art&Space from Kingston University, London, UK. She has exhibited in numerous group and solo shows in South Korea and her works are in the public art collections of SeongNam Cube Museum, the Seoul Metropolitan Government and the  GyeongGi Cultural Foundation.

Lee Na’s works mostly develop through painting, drawing, collage but also sculpture and video out of childhood pictures. She creates ambiguous landscapes with a combination of photographs and memories with human and animal figures.  These figures create a story spontaneously composed from landscapes experienced by Lee Na both in South Korea and elsewhere. Consequently, her works deal with notion of a meeting between the familiar (proximity) and the unfamiliar (unknown). Through this constant ambivalence, her works aim to stimulate the imagination.

name: Chung Chang-Sup
bio: A prominent figure in the [Dansaekhwa](/gene/dansaekhwa) movement of the early 1970s, Chung Chang-Sup sought to honor the [natural world](/gene/nature) in his [minimalist](/gene/minimalism) paintings, based on his Taoist belief that art must find balance with nature to create harmony. Part of the generation of [Korean](/gene/korea) artists active after the country’s liberation from Japan in 1945, Chung infused his work with [traditional mediums and techniques](/gene/engaged-with-traditional-korean-art). Over his career, he frequently employed *tak*, a paper made from the inner bark of the mulberry tree, a species native to Korea, to create large “unpainted paintings,” in which he molded the tak by soaking it in water. Chung has exhibited widely, including at the 2015 Venice Biennale and a 2010 retrospective at the [National Museum of Contemporary Art](/partner/national-museum-of-modern-and-contemporary-art-korea) in Gwacheon. His works are included in the [Museum of Modern Art](/partner/the-museum-of-modern-art)’s collection.

name: Anyong Jung
bio:
I worked with image of ‘smoke’ which is the phenomenon that can’t be grasped though it’s visible. This work requires visible approach and research as well. In last five years, I’ve carried out various experiments to produce and install sculpture with new images. Recently, overlapping pictures led me to expand its domain and it aims to establish creative and matchless color.
  
 My works is exhibition to express personal expression and suggests new direction of modern art. The phenomenon of smoke it’s visible but we can’t touch it is sculptured and installed to show the evolving art form and create new genre at the same time.
  
 The image of smoke begins from thin, fine line it seems blur but it’s made of various images with blurred line or white line or thick and solid lines etc. One of my works is made with flat plate and it’s to express the image of smoke in digital technique. And it utilizes Ink wash painting skill that express image with brush and ink stick. (Ink wash painting skill: 1. Express the image with brush and ink stick. 2. Express the overlapped colors through three ink technique.) Overlap the image of smoke and produce new format through expression with the lines in order to inherit the traditional art technique and display progressive and complex art form at the same time.

name: Mongjoo Son
bio: Mongjoo Son is born in 1978, Busan, Korea. She studied in Pusan National University in South Korea and Chelsea college of Art and Design in London, UK. She has 11 solo exhibitions, including ‘Young island swing’ sculpture project, Busan, Korea and several group shows, including 'Dialogue in Art', LEE & BAE, Busan, Korea. She also paricipated in 2018 Gwangju Biennale(Gwangju, Korea), 2015 Chungju international Craft Biennale(Chungju, Korea) and 2008 Busan Biennale(Busan ,Korea)

name: Gimhongsok
bio: Gimhongsok says he is used to “experiencing the world secondhand”: reading Korean translations of English texts or watching Korean interpretations of western television shows. He takes the imperfections and pitfalls of such translations as the starting point for his sculptures, installations, videos, and performances. Most works begin with a piece of text. Stripping that word of its given meaning, he begins to associate it with various objects, building an accumulation of text and objects that eventually suggests a fictive narrative or reality. In [*Material*](/artwork/gimhongsok-material) (2012), the artist plays with a non-textual translation: he translates the form of a balloon into resin. Stacked in a column, the resulting objects resemble buoyant objects; one expects them to topple or weightlessly float away. However, their weight grounds them, disrupting viewers' expectations and creating a fissure between one's expectations of form and the reality of material.

name: Su Kim
bio: Artist Su Kim is a Busan-born installation artist who has been constantly interested in the essential and changing process of the nature of objects and the relationship between objects. The artist expands the process of changing things as they interact with other objects or due to such exchanges to fundamental questions about wounds, despair, and healing in relation to others. The artist seriously and cheerfully solves the structural problems that arise in the relationship and that prevail in daily life. In the process, the artist goes beyond the simple nihilism of the relationship, and nevertheless reveals the possibility of healing that individuals have received in the relationship. To release, Objects selected as works receive new values. What makes the artist's work unique is that it gives us new values to familiar objects, but also reveals its original function, blurring the boundaries between art and daily life, and inducing questions.

name: Park Chan-kyong
bio: Park Chan-kyong (b. 1965) is an artist and a filmmaker based in Seoul. His subjects have extended from the Cold War to traditional Korean religious culture, from “media -oriented memory” to “history reconstruction.” He was also as an artistic director of Media City Seoul 2014 (International Media Art Biennale). He has produced media based works such as Sets (2000), Power Passage (2004), Flying (2005), Sindoan (2008), Radiance (2010), Anyang Paradise City (2011), Night Fishing (2011, co-directed with Park Chan-wook) and Manshin (2013). His works have been exhibited in international venues, such as Iniva, London, Taipei Biennale, Anyang Public Art Project, Gwangju Biennale in Korea, De Appel Arts Centre in Amsterdam, Red Cat Gallery in Los Angeles, Kunstverein in Frankfurt and many others. He has won various prizes including Hermès Korea Misulsang (2004), Golden Bear Prize for short films of the Berlin International Film Festival (2011) and Best Korean Film of the Jeonju International Film Festival (2011). Park’s work has been a part of several renowned institutions’ collection, including Kadist, Paris & San Francisco; Seoul Museum of Art and Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nantes.

name: Jung Eun Hye
bio:
The character in the drama ‘Our Blues,’ who played the role of Yeong-ok’s (played by Han Ji-Min) twin sister Young-hee became a hot topic of conversation with her intense presence, reflecting the tendency of the actor Jung Eun Hye. She is an active painter who has painted caricatures, moved into Jamsil Creative Studio of the Seoul Cultural Foundation, and painted portraits since 2016 at the Moonho-ri River Market in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province, and has painted more than 4,000 faces so far.

Jung Eun Hye has Down syndrome, developmental disabilities, mental symptoms, and social disabilities in public interactions. When the support for education facilities for the disabled disappeared as adults, social disconnection and regression came, overlapping mental diseases, schizophrenia, and tic appeared, and eventually, hallucinations also occurred. That is when she started painting.

Painting was the only medium that allowed her to start communicating with others. Her symptoms of schizophrenia have disappeared since she started painting. At the River Market, held in June 2022 in Moonho-ri, Yangpyeong, she made people smile by complimenting their natural beauty to those who asked her to paint their faces pretty. She was slowly adapting to society and starting to have genuine conversations with others.

After the drama's success, the non-mainstream and minority characteristics of the "difference" in the art field have been converted into their strength. Society’s reaction to her work also significantly changed in a good way, touching many people's hearts with her work.

name: Jeimin Kim
bio:
In Kim Jeimin’s paintings, grass is not presented as a site of dramatic events typical of genre literature or cinema. Instead, it appears in humble and unassuming forms—grasses that rarely register in memory, yet have continuously occupied the margins of our everyday environment. These small presences are scattered across the corners of streets, quietly asserting their existence within the spaces shaped by human activity.
The grasses grow in close adherence to surrounding structures, following the contours of surfaces stained by dust and grime rather than resisting them. Their unpredictable flexibility, coupled with their small scale and persistent freshness, lends them an air of innocence. It is precisely their apparent insignificance that allows them to embody the traces of arduous daily life within their roots, while their leaves seem to carry the visages of ordinary individuals.
The artist’s presence is implicitly inscribed in these images. The shadow cast over the grass suggests the artist’s own body, bent in observation, mirroring the posture of grass pressed down by footsteps and flattened by passing winds. Within the artist’s gaze, the grass transforms into a subtle self-portrait: rendered in light green tones that energetically fill even the smallest spaces, and in tenacious roots that fracture and penetrate brick and stone. Unaware of this projection, the grass remains simply grass—an unassuming subject through which the artist reflects upon resilience, humility, and the quiet persistence of everyday life.

name: Lim Hong
bio:
As a pop artist and a doctoral researcher specializing in Clinical Counseling Psychology at CHA University’s School of Medicine, my creative practice functions at the intersection of contemporary visual culture and the complexities of the human psyche.

By synthesizing the vibrant, accessible lexicon of Pop Art with a rigorous clinical understanding of psychological narratives, I explore the ways in which collective emotions and individual internal states are manifested through popular imagery. My work transcends mere aesthetic representation, serving as a therapeutic inquiry that invites viewers to deconstruct the psychological layers embedded within the modern social landscape. Through this interdisciplinary approach, I aim to bridge the gap between artistic expression and the profound insights of mental health science.

name: Jonghae Jeong
bio:
Jonghae Jeong's(b. 1948) works coexist with a subtle balance of strong expressiveness and realism. He finds the basic formations of oriental painting in calligraphy and seal engraving, extracting the possibilities as paintings, and attracting the sense of touch. Calligraphy and seal engraving are areas that show the highest level of formability that can be produced in a plane. The work process of the artist starts from selecting a specific object as a material, draw it with several strokes on a cloth or newspaper, and then cut it with scissors and attach at flat surface as a collage. He cuts differently from the original so that it reflects the unique cut sharpness that can be seen when using scissors. Rather than being drawn, it feels like a stone was scratched with a knife. The work finishes by attaching this cut-out cloth to the paper again. The lines are painted in ink and acrylic. Ligaments have only been replaced by cloth and knives with scissors. It is his intention to gauge how the essence of visual art, which develops in the thin space of images and letters, shapes and abstract symbols, planes and bumps, is interpreted in modern art/modern oriental painting today. This also has a meaning beyond the limitations of flat painting. The dancing and rhythmic lines are the artist's sensitive emotional tremor, vibration of the nerves of the body and breaths.
The artist graduated from Seoul National University, which is the most prestigious school in Korea and awarded from top National contest and selected as top artists for 3 times from National Exhibition, which is held every year. Served as a jury of Korea Grand Art Contest. Held 10 times of solo and more than 150 times of group exhibitions in Korea and overseas. Exhibited the most prestigious and honorable venues such as Sejong Cultural Center, Seoul Museum of Art, National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Hoam Gallery, which is run by Samsung Group, and lot others.

name: Lee Na Jin(이나진)
bio:
Great Gratitude ! You have raised me, oh wind and flowers !
                    
If you look at the artwork, the shiny crown and necklace of the animal will attract your eyes. These represent the painter’s memories when she spent her childhood in Cambridge, England. The crown and necklace which Queen Elizabeth wore contain agony about the process of becoming an adult and what a mature adult would look like, which is expressed by the characteristic of various tones of gold color. 

The reason why young animals are used is to describe the painter’s life that experienced the Great Japan Earthquake in her 30s, living in Tokyo, Japan. The young animals can be the childhood of the painter, her parents, her daughter, or whoever. Human lives go through infants, children, adults, the elderly, and the dead. Through this painting, time returns repeatedly to recursive time in a linear time. Through the crown and necklace of a young animal, the fear of an unfamiliar world as a child and the reality that it is difficult to get close to an adult after becoming an adult are expressed. 

The young animals are expressed using the “Squeezing technique” which is a method of squeezing paints by putting them in tubes. For the viscosity and transparency of the paint, about 100 kinds of paints are made by herself. Your feelings might be different depending on the light and shadow of space. 

The background is expressed as “diorama-style” which places reduced models on background as three-dimensional figures. Also, like “Hidden Picture Puzzles”, stories are hidden by disassembling shapes and expressing only the silhouette. In fact, the hidden stories are as follows: baby angels holding flowers, musicians and audiences in an opera house, and collection boxes of tiny toys and so on. In short, with subtle white glitters, you can see shadows caused by uneven surface from a distance while you can find the hidden stories if you come close.

name: Jae Seok Lee
bio: It was an accident during the military service when Jae Seok Lee's vision in art was born. Putting a screw between broken bones became an opportunity to be aware of the pain and heterogeneity his body could bear, which paradoxically had not been in the artist's mind. Through this, Lee came to perceive the human body as an aggregate of each organ that functions and moves, just like a firearm triggered by small iron parts operating at each location. This imagination expanded to other figures and objects, nature and city, life and death, to find harmony in heterogeneous matters. Each represents the invisible structure of the society portrayed in the composition of vertical, horizontal alignments.

name: Jaehyo Lee
bio: Working with wood and metal, Jaehyo Lee produces immaculately formed, intricate sculptures that reveal a mastery of his materials and a winking, sophisticated wit. Lee eschews traditional distinctions between the fine and applied arts and makes both functional and functionless works, presenting benches, stools, and tables alongside abstract, [biomorphic](/gene/biomorphic) forms. Burnt-black wood often serves as the sculptural ground into which Lee embeds discs of fresh wood or bent steel bolts and nails. His wood-on-wood combinations read as playful meditations on the multifaceted nature of wood itself, while the nails that often cover his wooden surfaces seem transformed into worms or spermatozoa—recalling a slithering, energetic galaxy of organisms.

name: Yuyun Hwang
bio:
Hwang Yuyun is a Korean based artist. She focuses on objects, particularly those with unexpected qualities. The objects that draw the artist’s attention include items discarded after losing their utility, the reverse sides of objects, cold and rigid objects imitating living things, and shadows cast behind illuminated objects. Hwang’s work highlights the hidden, often overlooked aspects of objects—the negative space. In their paintings, what is typically considered the “negative” comes to the forefront, transforming into the “positive.” As viewers examine the objects depicted on the canvas, they begin to perceive the presence and static stillness of forgotten or ignored items, recognizing them as another form of existence or “aliveness" and "being.”
Hwang Yuyun is currently pursuing a master's degree at Ewha Womans University and received BFA at the university. Her solo shows were held in Gblue Gallery, Gallery Ichon, and Seojin Art Space, and had participated in group shows in many others.

name: Yiseo
bio: Yiseo (b. 1990) is an artist who explores emotional life through three recurring characters—Netty, Todori, and Okayun-Gonyang—each with a distinct personality. Through their stories, Yiseo traces a process of accepting and affirming the feelings learned through living. The work is ultimately offered as a small comfort to viewers, inviting them to meet their own emotions with a gentler gaze.

name: Byungkoo Jeon
bio: Artist Jeon Byung-goo renders views of everyday scenes, inviting them as the subjects of his paintings. “Things that are ordinary and boring become a picture. The things that are close but also far, things that are repeated but with subtle differences, everytime we see such things there is a sense of ecstasy but also the creation of a world far beyond reality where reality cannot be measured; the world of pictures without words. I wanted to capture it.” The artist concentrates on the world of images, that which cannot be reduced to words. Expressed through a method that creates multiple waves of paint with a brush that cuts quickly and thinly.

name: KIMI JAAK
bio: KIMI JAAK works based in Hawaii. She carries out a variety of works covering graphics, illustrations and painting. KIMI JAAK is less about the objects she paints and more about achieving a balanced and pleasing composition, attaining this by flattening perspective, omitting non-essential details and focusing on tone, and their bold color that create sensitive, substantive forms.
