name: Alice Yaelin Yang
bio:
Alice Yaelin Yang is an artist based in New York and Seoul. After receiving her BFA from the School of Visual Arts, Yang continues her graduate studies at Hongik University, Seoul, Korea. 

Yang’s paintings are created in order to show a world of her own. This work is not to be defined into one single concept or derived into one solid visual piece, but instead into many different aspects that touch people differently in this diverse world we  all live in. Even though she is inspired by the relations between human and nature, reproducing these images that already exist in real life isn’t enough for Yang to capture the essence and complexity of the inner mind.

Yang’s work has been shown around the world, including The Other Art Fair, Brooklyn, NY (2021); Hong Ik Museum of Art, Space MM, and Atelier I, Seoul, Korea; and Galerie BDMC, Paris, France.

name: Jungyoun Kim
bio:
Seoul-based artist Jungyoun Kim works on a variety of works, from hand-painted watercolors and brush pens to digital drawing, manga, and GIF animation production. He was greatly influenced by the ‘Slam Dunks’ from his childhood, and in an honor of ‘Slam Dunks’ he was drawn to basketball and cartoons.

Graduating from the Department of Animation at Konkuk University, the artist has been working on multiple exhibitions and collaborations with various brands, and most recently did an international collaboration with Nike. Portraying the stories of current generations as the main subject, his work centers around fashion items, brands and sneaker culture. Through the characters with his detailed expressions on objects and fashion items, he brings the characters to reality, and connects the audience with his painting.

name: Mari Kim
bio: Mari Kim calls the recurring figure in her work “Eyedoll,” a cartoon-like, porcelain-skinned female distinguished by her large oval eyes. In Kim’s lustrous ink-on-canvas prints, Eyedoll stares directly out from the surface; she dons different outfits and guises while standing against different backgrounds. As Eyedoll shifts through identities, Kim makes subtle alterations to the figure’s iris patterns, matching changes in costume to changes in mood. The relentless seriality of her work attends to questions of how identity can be altered with props and fashion, and it also models a kind of fetishistic Asian female identity that is confrontational in its forwardness.

name: Son Bong Chae
bio: Son Bong Chae employs a layered painting process to create haunting landscapes characterized by a poetic sense of history. The artist paints ethereal oil works of silhouetted trees with expressive limbs, layering the images—often inside light boxes—so that each work contains five or six fields. Son Bong became interested in layering while traveling to his father’s hometown in South Korea. He was struck by how the natural beauty of the landscape eclipsed the country’s violent past in the Korean War. His work echoes this duality with its overlapping images of trees; one layer of history is superimposed atop the next.

name: Siyoung Yang
bio:
Born in 1999, Yang was diagnosed with autism at the age of five. Despite the developmental disabilities that followed, there was evidence to suggest that Yang was drawing and painting in top form well before learning to speak. Now in his early twenties, the artist has been honored with participation in numerous high-end exhibitions both in his own country as well as internationally. These include the Seoul Museum of Art, the Art Students League in New Yok City, and the BIAF international art fair where he was chosen as a delegate from South Korea. In the meantime, Yang has received considerable attention from the media as an artist who represents his generation’s neo-pop, pictorial playfulness in contrast to the qualitative standards of the abstract painters that preceded him.

A newcomer to the Korean art scene, Yang's work is full of humorous and essential [PEOPLE] and vividly beautiful images of animals and flowers, with a distinctive line and color that only he can show.
Having proven his commercial viability by becoming the biggest selling artist at several art fairs, Yang was not satisfied with this and moved to New York City to work alongside international artists at the ART STUDENT LEAGUE OF NEW YORK (ASLNYC), a 150-year-old school in Manhattan where Edward Hopper, Yayoi Kusama, Basquiat, Mark Rothko, and others have studied, where he received rave reviews for his creative work.
He participated in a group exhibition with international artists at ASLNYC in the shortest period of time ever. His work has been featured on ASLNYC's Instagram and website stories.
In New York, the home of contemporary art, ASLNYC is the center of the world's leading artists, and he is convinced of the possibility of his work to be recognized globally and is on the verge of entering the New York gallery scene.
Today, he continues to work tirelessly to become the “BTS of the art world” with his unique uniqueness and influence on the global cultural scene.

name: Bin Woo Hyuk
bio:
The main theme of the works by Bin Woo Hyuk is his attitude and time while reacting to the external stimulation such as memory and experience. He visited a forest in Berlin to empty out psychological agitation and complex inner thoughts from past memories, and he constantly delivered them onto canvases. The forests, lakes and parks are places he often visited and found great peace and meditation.

In recent works, without familiar typical figures of the forest, the giant plane of the work gives a glimpse of its original motif through only other adjacent figurative paintings. When he delivers the landscapes onto his canvas, he concentrates on them by removing narrative elements rather than conveying any implications and criticism. When Bin could not find the landscape of Berlin, he began to fill this sense of emptiness caused by the forest’s absence by concentrating on imaginary locales or scenery seen from airport runways and the inside of airplanes. In this process, he discovered the existence of ‘marble walls’. The obscure patterns of the walls offered Bin a reprieve as he wandered in the midst of a void trying to once again regain the forest. His artistic subject matter shifted completely.

Bin Woo Hyuk has been a member of the BBK Berlin-Professional Association of Visual Artists Berlin since 2021. His work is represented in the collections of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, Seoul Museum of Art, Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art in Korea and Maryland Institute College of Art in the USA.

name: Minyoung Choi
bio:
Minyoung Choi enhances the surreal atmosphere by dramatically framing the edited scenes in a multi-layered structure that transcends time and space with her unique expression of light and color. As in the Dépaysement technique, countless images drawn from the artist's experiences and psychological emotion are combined with a provocative imagination to break down the boundaries of reality. She creates her own fantasy in which the familiar and the strange overlap in a paradoxical way, arbitrarily borrowing from Eastern and Western myths, fables and common oral stories. Memories and imagination are intertwined with a sense of anxiety and chaos, leading to an ephemeral inner landscape, where space and place, human and animal, city and nature merge to form a new world.

Minyoung Choi's paintings are full of imaginative energy, creating a dream-like mood through the expression of unpredictable compositions that emphasise the uniqueness of color and light. She ingeniously introduces thought-provoking elements into her images, beckoning contemplation on the complex rapport between imagination and tangible truth. By depicting herself and her surroundings that had isolated in an unfulfilled relationship in her hazy moment of unconsciousness, as an everyday life in which mysterious creatures coexist, she builds up her own fictional narrative that experiences an escape from a peaceful yet tedious life. This unfamiliarity in her works symbolises an understanding and acceptance of relationships and a balance between the inner mind and the outer environment through the interplay of darkness and light, the contrast of complementary colours or the flat spatial composition that blurs the boundary between inside and outside.

name: Jiwon Choi
bio:
Jiwon Choi holds a BFA and MFA in Painting from Ewha Womans University. 

Choi explores the space between life and death—a void where the present and future converge—capturing the world within this gap. She creates chambers of vacuum where secretive energies intersect, using frames and doors as portals between the realms of life and death. Through various artificial and natural elements collected from everyday life, such as dolls, crafts, and taxidermied insects, Choi brings these worlds together. The objects in her works, including porcelain dolls, are often things that have ended their life yet continue to influence the artist's present. Thus, these objects serve as a symbolic effort to understand the lives of her contemporaries and the world she inhabits, rather than merely reflecting reality.

name: Jeongmo Ahn
bio:
Artist Jeongmo Ahn said that ever since she was young, she always believed that there was a door to another world in a dark, tree-filled corner of his home garden. The artist's work, which started from this imagination, fights against the absurdity of reality through characters such as Bigfoot, a rabbit, a cat, and a girl in a virtual world, or delivers a message of hope by cultivating a garden and making flowers bloom even in a barren environment. It is a dense work with a rich narrative, lovable characters, colorful and bright colors, and a three-dimensional effect.

The main theme of my paintings is to satirize a situation that is not very different from human society through characters from the world of animal spirits.


Artist's note:
The world of animal spirits is somehow very similar to the human world. Characters such as wild beasts that wield power and violence against weak animals and righteous animal characters, who is weak but becomes a superhero for his colleagues, appear.

 My paintings mainly tell the story of a girl and her cat, characters created by reflecting my childhood, in search of their mother, and various characters appear in the world of animal spirits, a huge virtual empire.

Bigfoot is a legendary monster known for its sightings of a half-human, half-animal monster with white fur and large feet in the cold snowy mountains. However, I drew Bigfoot as a lovely, innocent child rather than a scary monster. I wanted to show that their lives are no different from humans in their own way. Bigfoot, who loves flowers, and Bigfoot children, who are mischievous and unruly, are no different from human children.

name: Jinwoo Kim
bio:
Animation and toys, which have been the artist's interest since childhood, have naturally become subjects of paintings. The comical and radical slapstick expressions used in animations such as Disney, Betty Boop, and Tom and Jerry had strong attraction points, yet gave a discomfort as well. The metaphors of social phenomena seen in the 21st century, such as tragedy, splendor, and death, are expressed in Jinwoo Kim’s works.
In his practice, he recreates images with the characteristics of old animations-such as slapstick effects and breaking down the motions into several layers on the flat screen. The same visual direction shown in his flatwork is extended to various media, leading to installation works using animations and objects.
Using traditional oriental painting materials, black and white colors in his paintings are made by subtractive blending method by repeating CMYK color thinly and repeatedly. Beneath the imagery of adorable characters in colors, the artist throws a conversation on the paradox of splendor, death, and freedom.

name: Lee Jung Yong
bio:
Lee Jungyong is an artist who questions the unexamined belief that “seeing is believing,” reconsidering the way visual perception shapes our understanding of reality. He argues that the power to form an image of an object lies not in sight itself but in the subjective act of imagining and interpreting—within the self.
Using colored clay as his primary material, the artist begins by shaping a form derived from an internal, mental image. He then translates this form into painting, repeating this process as a mode of exploration. Since the clay has no predetermined shape or color, it becomes an abstract sculptural element shaped by the artist’s experiences, emotions, and aesthetic perspective. When this abstract form is rendered realistically on the canvas, it opens a new perceptual space that challenges the limitations of hyperrealistic painting. By bringing previously unseen, non-visual forms into the realm of painting, his work invites viewers to engage in imagination, association, and diverse interpretation.
Through this method, Lee embeds the notion of “shell and essence,” exploring the tension between external appearance and inner truth. The ongoing accumulation of works allows his inner states and emotions to naturally merge with the canvas, ultimately turning each piece into an outer shell that encapsulates the essence of the artist himself.
In contrast to the materialized and surface-driven nature of contemporary culture, Lee Jungyong regards art as a medium for seeking identity. He continues to focus on inner transformation and the emotional landscapes within, pursuing visual expressions that probe the essence of objects and the self.

name: Haneul Kim
bio:
At the core of Haneul Kim's art practice is an immense love for the people, the planet and their future.  Granted his roots in the most contemporary today Haneul prophetically vision a world where harmony can be achieved.  Nothing is wasted, on the contrary, waste is the starting point of Haneul's inspiration. Grasping the powerful energy of transformation and so to make art, Haneul re-invents what is discarded today into high-tech objects for our quotidian life. Old material breathes new life and we do with it.
@arteglobale all rights reserved

Haneul Kim is a Korean designer who mainly uses upcycled materials to create furniture and objects. He suggested ways to recycle plastic masks, inspiring many people during the COVID-19. He focuses on the effect of art on the world, regaining new functions of being abandoned.

He has been featured in many publications and participated in many prestigious projects like Frieze Seoul 2024 to mention a few, he is an award-winning artist AWARD 2022 10th Recycling Designpreis, Grand Prize Award 2021 9th Gwangju Design Biennale d-Revolution Award, General Director Award.

His collaborations span from NIKE to ROLLS-ROYCE.

name: Ryu In
bio:
Born as the youngest son of RYU Gyeong-chae (1920-1995), a pioneer in the field of Korean abstract sculpture, and a playwright mother (1921-2009), RYU In left an indelible mark on Korea’s contemporary sculpture history before his passing at the age of 43 (1956-1999). He launched his career as a sculpture from a strong desire to escape from the shadows of his father and an irrepressible desire to work with the materiality of soil. Introducing precise and powerful depicts of the human body to the Korean art world in the ‘80s, where abstract and installation were the dominant mode of expression, RYU In came into fame as a figurative sculpture artist, winning awards ranging from Korea Fine Arts Association top award, Chungang Arts Association first prize, and the “Today’s Young Artist Award” sponsored by the Ministry of Culture and Sports. Since then, he introduced new figurative sculptures by incorporating formal properties, along with the first combination of sculpture and installation. Adopting new modes of expression for traditional depictions of the human body, RYU In won a number of prestigious awards and became known as a great genius of his time. However, due to excessive drinking and a variety of physical ailments including tuberculosis, hepatocirrhosis, and arthritis, he passed away at the age of 43.

He featured reconstructions of the most dramatic scenes, fusing the extraordinary senses he inherited from his father who was a leading figure in abstract art, a talent in stage production his mother gifted him with, and a unique sense of imagination, based on realistic representation. His innovative spatial interpretation conveys fundamental anxiety, indignation, and complexity along with a powerful desire for life as an innate drive in humanity, expressed through distortions or transformations of realistically represented human bodies and theatrical props.

name: Byeongseok Hwang
bio:
This work presents a state of existence shaped like tools, reflecting life within systems of production and consumption.
These figures neither work nor speak; they appear only as packaged, playing, or resting forms.
Through these suspended moments, the artist asks what remains of a being once the standard of “usefulness” has been exhausted.
These sculptures are not tools that perform functions, but tools as a condition after function has been removed.

name: Gyuyoung Lee
bio: Gyuyoung Lee is a sculptor who works with a playful, intuition-led process grounded in sincerity. Rather than treating presentation as an afterthought, Lee considers the public life of a sculpture—how it is shown, shared, and discussed—as an essential part of the work. Taking on the title of “sculptor” is also a commitment to act with honesty, especially when the work moves beyond the studio and into wider circulation.

name: Doyim Kim
bio:
I am a calligrapher and installation artist recontextualizing the philosophy and aesthetics of traditional Korean calligraphy within a contemporary framework. Through the rhythm of the brush, the tonal nuances of ink, and the performative nature of repetitive strokes, I investigate fundamental questions regarding emotion, existence, love, and self-reflection.

Specifically, my practice involves the repetitive inscription of the word "Love," manifested across paintings, performances, and installations. This act transcends mere writing to become a meditative ritual and prayer. Ultimately, my work serves as an artistic conduit designed to evoke a deep emotional resonance and communion with the viewer.

name: Hong Ji Oh
bio: I believe that the essence of travel is seamlessly woven into the fabric of ordinary life. My work layers personal reflection onto photographs taken during these journeys, capturing not just the visual moment, but the intimate narrative felt within.

name: JOY
bio:
JOY develops a practice shaped by the movement of water, using its restless surface and underlying currents to think about direction, drift, and endurance. Rather than treating wandering as a detour, JOY approaches it as a threshold state—an in-between condition where fragments of memory, sensation, and perception begin to gather. The work considers eternity not as something given, but as something chosen: a moment held long enough to become lasting.

Across JOY’s practice, what remains after disappearance becomes a central concern. Faint afterimages, residual light, and traces that resist erasure recur as key motifs, suggesting that loss is never absolute. Moving between instability and persistence, JOY records the subtle sensations that stay behind after everything else seems to have passed, turning them into quiet studies of memory, time, and what endures.

name: Choi Yeol
bio:
Choi Yeol is a painter who explores how urban environments shape and shift human perception. His work begins with familiar places and everyday scenes, asking how the same object or space can be experienced differently depending on one’s position, time, and sensory awareness.

In his early practice, Choi observed moments when a single place or subject could take on multiple meanings. This interest has expanded into a broader examination of urban structures, industrial sites, and the changing landscapes of daily life. Through architectural light and shadow, factory forms, and repeated spatial patterns, he reveals the unfamiliar qualities hidden within ordinary environments.

For Choi, the city is not a fixed physical setting but a field of perception, continually reconstructed through experience. His paintings invite viewers to reconsider the scenes they usually take for granted and to question how they come to see and understand the world.

name: Boomoon
bio:
Born in Daegu, Boomoon lives and works in Seoul and Sokcho, South Korea. Having commenced his artistic studies as a painter, Boomoon began to explore photography in the early 1970's and enrolled in the Photography department at Chung-Ang University, Seoul. Throughout the 1970's Boomoon passionately recorded the rapid transformation taking place in Korean society, looking at deserted villages and the heightening contrast between rural and urban communities. Since the 1980's he has been engaging with the natural landscape in his work as a means of self-reflection, producing large format photographs of vast expanses of sea, sky and land. Devoid of human presence, the central emphasis of his work is the experience of the infinity of nature and the representation of its presence.

Boomoon has exhibited internationally, including in South Korea, Japan, Istanbul, New York, London and Paris and his work is in the collections of the Yokohama Museum of Art and the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Gwacheon. From October 2013 to January 2014, a retrospective exhibition of Boomoon's major landscape series was held at the Daegu Art Museum in South Korea. Entitled Constellation, the show gave a comprehensive overview of Boomoon's practice and confirmed his significance as a photographic artist.

name: Hyesung Nam
bio: Hyesung Nam is a multidisciplinary artist whose practice explores spatial experience at the intersection of art, architecture, and design. She received a B.F.A. in Fine Arts from Kookmin University, where her studies extended beyond studio practice to contemporary and classical philosophy and critical theory. This foundation informs work shaped by close attention to social structures, material environments, and the ways people move through space. After graduation, Nam worked across media art, pop merchandising, and fashion design, developing a practice that combines humanistic inquiry with practical knowledge of production and industry. She is particularly interested in architectural art installations and edition-based projects that bring sculptural form into dialogue with the public. Across her work, Nam emphasizes sustainability, formal clarity, and technical precision, while seeking to create works that support more thoughtful and inclusive ways of living together.

name: Hey June
bio: Hey June explores the emotional textures of everyday life through a visual language of lightness, subtle gesture, and quiet optimism. Moving away from excess and spectacle, the artist treats “lightness” not as superficial pleasure but as a way of stripping away emotional weight to reveal more distilled and honest feeling. In paintings and drawings, figures are defined by wavering lines, tilted postures, and slight shifts in expression, suggesting the fragile yet persistent fact of being present and feeling. Hey June often turns to the rhythms of love and separation, tracing how weather, places, music, and memory shape the emotional afterimage of relationships. Small misunderstandings, anticipation, hesitation, and heartbreak become part of a broader process of growth. Through intimate scenes of ordinary emotion, Hey June invites viewers to recognize the tenderness, vulnerability, and possibility embedded in daily life.

name: BK Lee
bio: BK Lee is an artist whose work reflects on the value of everyday life and the passage of time. Believing time to be the most essential resource given to us, Lee approaches art as a way of attending closely to the present. Memories appear in this practice as traces of time already lived, while the future remains a field of possibility not yet reached. Between the two, Lee focuses on the fleeting intensity of the current moment. The work becomes an attempt to record what is here now and to hold onto sensations just before they disappear. Rooted in lived experience and quiet reflection, Lee’s practice invites viewers to consider how time is felt, remembered, and anticipated, and how meaning can emerge from fully inhabiting the present.

name: Sang Ha Yoon
bio:
The artist might be one of those who, with infinite imagination, embarks on a journey exploring the border between reality and fantasy. His works are the result of countless thought bubbles of vanishing dreams, with each action and thought fleetingly appearing and disappearing. Through his distinctive, subjective style, unique colors, and the countless strokes of his brush, the products of imagination and contemplation come to life. Observing his works, we soon encounter moments where the boundaries between reality and imagination become ambiguous.

I'm looking for images between extremes, from the ridiculous to the bizarre, from happiness to loneliness. The goal is to find a new balance between these unstable images. The attempt to find a balance begins with the fictional desires and delusions that we dream of in real life, which are introspective and introspective, treading the line between the darkness and humor of reality, just as the characters in anime are destroyed and scattered.
Despair and hope, suffering and playfulness. These words, which seem to be at the extremes, are in fact closely related to each other. As I playfully cross the boundaries of the meanings assigned to words, my canvases become messy, messy tapestries of consciousness, playful spaces that skewer the fictions of fantasy and pleasure compressed into reality through play.     - Artist Note

name: Hee Sun Kim
bio:
Kim Hee-sun utilizes the fluid properties of alcohol ink and resin to explore the interior lives and silent resilience of women from Korea’s Joseon Dynasty. Inspired by the historical constraints placed on women of that era, Kim translates their unspoken dreams and sorrows into abstract "textures" (gyeol). Her practice draws on the physical metaphors of traditional Korean attire—specifically the hidden folds of a skirt and the layered ties of a collar—which served as repositories for concealed emotions.

Through a process of pouring, seeping, and layering, Kim builds rhythmic compositions where colors settle like the accumulation of time and memory. The resulting works function as a visual record of historical grief transformed into a gesture of quiet consolation. By bridging traditional narratives with contemporary materiality, Kim offers a meditative space to reflect on the endurance of the human spirit and the beauty found in life’s traces.

name: Eunmi Han
bio:
Eunmi Han is an artist who records narratives of destruction, creation, and growth through one of the most fragile and everyday materials: eggshells. For the artist, an egg represents a complete world, and the act of breaking its shell signifies not an end, but an inevitable beginning for new birth.

In pursuit of constructing a singular artistic world that cannot be replicated even in the age of artificial intelligence, Han has pioneered a distinctive practice known as eggshell painting. Her work is grounded in an intensive, almost ascetic labor process: eggs are broken, cleaned, dried, crushed once again, colored, and then meticulously reassembled piece by piece. This process transcends the act of painting itself, becoming a layered record of endurance and time accumulated through sustained effort.

Rather than concealing irregular gaps and cracks between fragments, the artist embraces them as core compositional elements. Through this approach, she generates a new sense of order and vitality emerging from imperfection. At close range, viewers encounter the material’s unique textures—the fissures, gaps, and cross-sections of the shells—revealing traces of an intense and painstaking process. From a distance, however, the fragments coalesce into an image reminiscent of watercolor painting, where colors intermingle and breathe together in an organic visual rhythm.

The act of reconstructing resilient trees from fragmented shells reflects the artist’s own inner transformation and growth. Just as broken pieces come together to form a solid forest, Han’s work offers a gentle message of consolation: the wounds and fractures of our lives, too, can become fertile ground for beautiful growth.

name: Junyoung Yu
bio: Junyoung Yu is a figurative painter who depicts the human body in states of suspension. His figures do not fully collapse; instead, they remain intact yet unable to move, suggesting moments when accumulated thought and emotion delay action and turn inward. Within these paused bodies, Yu traces emotional residue through skeletal forms, mechanical structures, and tangled lines that read as records of overthinking and stalled function. A recurring motif in his work is the flower-shaped eye. For Yu, the flower stands in for the gaze of others—something both feared and desired—and introduces a fragile form of tenderness into scenes of psychological tension. Color seeping through cracks, drifting marks, and forms that resist disappearance suggest that depression is not an end point, but a process through which the self may be reconfigured into another form.

name: Soyoon Choi
bio:
My work explores the emotional space between the familiar ground we walk on and the distant universe we long for.
In this series, penguins become gentle travelers—figures that mirror our inner journeys as they move across rainbows, blooming planets, and moon-jar worlds.
I imagine the cosmos not as a cold void, but as a warm, living garden where daisies bloom and quiet hopes take root.
By blending Korean aesthetics with fantastical imagery, I create a lyrical universe where small beings find their place within vastness.
Through these scenes, I hope to offer viewers a moment of rest and a reminder of the tender, personal cosmos each of us carries within.

name: TEO
bio: I am Teo, an artist exploring the boundary between abstraction and figuration.

name: DONGZADONGHWI
bio:
My work originates from an exploration of the stimuli arising between the everyday and the ideal, the internal and the external, and emotion and experience. The freedom I experienced in my youth, alongside the reality I encountered while pursuing that freedom, forms the foundation of my practice. I seek to express my emotions and contemplations as I navigate between these two worlds, unraveling the intricate interactions between emotion and existence.

My artistic vision is a continuous process of experimentation and evolution. Through diverse media—including painting, animation, and video—I reveal my inner world, depicting the pursuit of a personal utopia while acknowledging the constraints of reality. For me, art is a journey of exploring the fundamental questions of human existence, and through this process, I aim to externalize internal emotions.

My primary intention is to transform emotional shifts into energy and manifest them visually. I often narrate these emotions through a recurring figure named ‘Bird,’ expressing the energy gained during the creative process. This figure is a concrete embodiment of the emotional flows within me. ‘Bird’ plays a pivotal role in my work, serving as a medium for emotional resonance and comfort. Through this, I hope to provide viewers with an experience where they can confront their own emotions, empathize, and share a collective emotional journey.

The core message of my work is hope and healing. While the world undergoes complex and multifaceted emotional changes, my work is rooted in the belief that we can find a ray of light to comfort one another and grow together. I hope that through my art, viewers discover positive energy and feel the hope necessary to move toward a better world.

name: Tae kyun Lim
bio: Leaving a Trace.

name: Mi Young Um
bio:
I am an artist who visualizes invisible emotions and thoughts by combining natural materials with symbolic signs.
In particular, I work with sawdust from poplar trees, a distinctive natural medium, constructing my works through its textures and traces of time, and transforming them into symbolic forms.
My work does not aim for a single, closed interpretation.
The signs and suggestive symbols within each piece invite viewers
to project their own experiences and emotions, discovering meanings for themselves.
I believe that art is not something to be simply explained,
but something that asks questions and awakens thought.
Through the union of symbols and natural materials,
my work evokes philosophical depth and layered symbolism,
revealing questions about emotion, relationships, and human existence.
The moment a viewer encounters their own interpretation through my work,
I regard that moment as the true starting point of understanding art.

name: Kyunghwa Park
bio:
In the fleeting currents of ordinary days, I gather small glimmers of light. My work holds onto the fading glow of childhood innocence and captures the breath of nature as it dims with time.

Using luminous colors, I depict the persistence of life that shines even in the darkness, breathing precious narratives into the smallest existences, such as a vanishing bee. Blooming a quiet fantasy at the boundary of reality and imagination, I hope my canvas offers a gentle solace to the viewer’s heart.

I am Park Kyung-hwa, an artist painting for the restoration of the soul.

name: Shin Insoo
bio:
The artistic process of Shin Insoo begins only after a profound passage of time—the meticulous pressing and drying of mulberry pulp (Dakjuk) and the slow, deliberate corrosion of iron. Rust water seeps into the surface like morning dew, while the mulberry paper (Hanji) clings to the weathered iron, creating a composition that captures a "cosmic irony" born from the synchronization of material essence and temporal progression.

This sequence of creation reveals the "aesthetics of slow labor," a testament to the artist’s patience and the quiet strength found in enduring the flow of time.
Active since the early 2000s, Shin has garnered significant international acclaim through recent invitational solo exhibitions and global art fairs. In particular, his showcases in New York have been recognized as a pivotal and meaningful milestone, marking a major breakthrough in his career.

name: Kibong Rhee
bio: Water is the primary element that informs Kibong Rhee's ephemeral landscape paintings. The artist believes that water, in all its forms, embodies life's fleetingness, existing somewhere between the spiritual and physical worlds. Kibong incorporates these qualities into his work, emphasizing the mutability of forms and our perceptions of them. Layering clear Plexiglas atop canvas, he creates painted scenes from the natural world that are hazy and dreamlike, almost apparitions. In [*Thought, Action, or Dream*](/artwork/kibong-rhee-thought-action-or-dream) (2013), a hillside of trees is partially obscured by fog. The trees seem to be simultaneously taking shape and disappearing, caught in a perpetual state of flux.

name: Minseok Jang
bio:
Minseok Jang born in South Korea and Chicago-based artist who is not afraid to take on new challenges
This is evident in his work. He has challenged himself to try various types of art such as painting, new media
art, art technology, 3D modeling work, and VR art. He enjoys combining these different styles and genres.
Minseok Jang, building on a foundation in fine arts, has cultivated a distinctive sense of creativity and extensive
experience by combining various media and genres. His expertise extends beyond personal artistic creations
to include product design, brochure design, website design, art direction, and exhibition planning, demonstrat-ing his versatility across a wide range of fields.

Recently, he successfully completed an internship as an Art Director in Tokyo, further expanding his profes-
sional capabilities. His skills were recognized, leading to multiple recruitment offers from prominent companies.
While he began his journey as an artist, Minseok has not confined himself to a single discipline. Instead, he
continues to pursue new challenges with a diverse set of experiences, a multifaceted approach, and a creative
vision.

name: Junho JUNG
bio: I use the forest as a medium to bring my future imagination to life. In my ongoing series, A Dreamy Forest, I explore the natural contrast between the forest's warmth, its eeriness, and its dreamlike qualities. You can follow my journey and see my latest works on my social media.

name: SeungYeon Kim
bio:
The Odyssey of "Lucky": A Quest for the Universal Dream

My work chronicles the ongoing odyssey of "Lucky," a baby tiger embarking on a quest for his aspirations. In the Korean cultural consciousness, the tiger is a quintessentially mystical and revered presence. By reimagining this powerful archetype as "Lucky," I seek to transform this cultural symbol into a totem of fortune—a benevolent presence that bestows hope upon all who encounter it.

The yearning for dreams and good fortune is a universal human constant. My own longing is no less profound; it is the engine of my practice. I channel my creative faculties and disciplined labor into a constant forward momentum, navigating the path toward my own realized aspirations.

Within my compositions, the recurring motifs of fish and rabbits serve as allegorical representations of the collective. They symbolize the constellation of people who inhabit my world: my devoted parents, my partner, siblings, friends, fellow artists, and my students—as well as the audience who resonates with my vision. Their presence is the very foundation upon which I stand.

Though our individual trajectories toward fulfillment may diverge, the fundamental desire to lead a life enriched by the realization of one’s dreams remains a shared human endeavor. It is because of this shared journey that I continue to evolve as an artist. Today, as I have done before, I set out once more to pursue the horizon of that dream.

name: Eun Ee Yoon
bio:
My artistic practice is rooted in the contemporary reimagining of traditional Korean folk painting, or Minhwa. By distilling the symbolic lexicon of our ancestors and filtering it through a modern aesthetic lens, I explore the profound theme of harmonious coexistence.

Utilizing a diverse array of motifs—ranging from the delicate flight of butterflies to the vibrant vitality of birds and flora—I create a visual language of freedom. These subjects are not merely decorative; they serve as a conduit for universal values such as hope, love, and profound solace. My work seeks to transcend the boundaries between the past and the present, fostering a space where tradition breathes alongside modern sensibilities.

In an increasingly fragmented world, my paintings aim to function as a medium of connection and emotional healing. Ultimately, my creative journey is dedicated to the viewer’s well-being; I do not just capture images, but rather, I paint the very essence of your happiness.

name: Kyungwon Yoon
bio: Kyungwon Yoon (b. 1999, Seoul) is an interdisciplinary artist whose practice merges painting, relief, and sculpture. Grounded in a painterly approach, Yoon challenges the flatness of traditional painting by transforming surfaces into dimensional, hybrid forms. His work often begins with cutting plywood, uncovering irregular edges and fragments that he assembles into compositions evocative of organic or fantastical structures. Yoon incorporates materials such as wood, leather, suede, and canvas to explore the materiality of the picture plane, encouraging a dynamic, multi-angled engagement with the work. Influenced by the conceptual hybridity of the chimera, his practice blends abstract and figurative elements without relying on direct representation. Yoon holds a BFA in Oriental Painting from Seoul National University and is currently pursuing graduate studies at the same institution. He lives and works in Seoul.

name: Sungjae Lee
bio:
Born in Seoul in 1985, Lee Sungjae completed his undergraduate studies in Cartoon and Comics at Kongju National University before earning a Master of Fine Arts in Experimental Animation and Integrated Media from the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts), a premier institution for visual and performing arts in the United States. This rigorous scholarly and practical foundation in sequential art and moving-image media serves as the structural underpinnings of his contemporary practice, which manifests in highly innovative idioms of three-dimensional drawing and spatial installation.

Lee’s artistic trajectory is underscored by numerous solo exhibitions at prominent venues, including the SOMA Museum of Art, Youngeun Museum of Contemporary Art, the Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency, and Gallery 825. Furthermore, his work has gained extensive international visibility through participation in major institutional exhibitions and art fairs, such as Frieze House Seoul, the Fiber Art Biennale at the Tsinghua University Art Museum, the SOMA Museum of Art, Ars Electronica, the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art, and the LA Art Show. His critical acclaim within both domestic and global artistic discourses is well-evidenced by prestigious accolades, notably the Grand Prize at the 2024 Galleries Art Fair Zoom-in Edition 5, the ZHENHU Award at the 2021 Suzhou Craft Biennale, and the Moving Image Award at the 2018 Lumen Prize.

name: PARK HYUN WOONG
bio:
Park Hyun Woong's work is embodied on a unique structure in which wood is cut and then the pieces are put together, breaking away from the usual painting technique of drawing on a regular canvas. Wood is cut into pieces to be assembled according to the relevant image, and some of his works even have 8 layers of wood. Details with intricate outlines are made with a fretsaw. The emphasis is placed on 'making' rather than 'drawing'. After the birch wood is cut into pieces, the pieces are put together and then colored. It is also sculpted on top of it to give it a different texture. Through the process of pasting and piecing together the wood, the layers of the image are gradually thickened, and shadows that cannot be seen in paintings are cast on the surface depending on the lighting. Rather than expressing a three-dimensional object or attaching an object on a plane, the images are synthesized by overlapping the planes. The structure in which separate plates are stacked rather than connected in one plane like a painting is similar to the mechanism of memory in which fragments are connected to each other. 
 The artist devotes an average of 10 to 12 hours a day to the work, because it takes time and devotion to express the surface of the relief, which is completed by stacking layers one by one by hand. Since wood has physical properties that allow the artist to express warmth and softness, it is a material that fits well with the artist's delicate personality, and it is also an optimal material to reproduce his imagination and put warmheartedness into it.

name: Jae Hoon Lee (b. 1978)
bio:
The sculptural painting style of artist Lee Jae-hoon, which has been used since 2008, is a tactile painting that uses dry mural techniques and an experiment on the expandability of Oriental painting as a modern art.

First of all, the tactile aspect of this sculptural painting is the application of the material texture to the painting in the order of human five senses rather than the visual composition of the sculpture. It is used to create a link between the viewer-media-native in a way that stimulates the viewer's sense.

In other words, this is a visual art that attracts the viewer's attention to access social problems. And we're implementing these methods through mural techniques." – Artist's Note

name: Jahyun Seo
bio: Jahyun Seo (b.1968, lives and works in Seoul, Korea) pursued her studies in Textile and Fiber Arts in Paris at Ecole Superieure D'art Neufville Conte and later completed her PhD in Fiber Art at Hongik University in Seoul. Seo’s work has been shown at the LaMama Gallery, Cast Iron in New York, Kunst Stock Gallery in Germany, Seoul Museum of Art, Seoul Arts Center, Cheongju Arts Center, and Gana Art in South Korea.

name: STEPPER
bio:
STEPPER is a visual art duo based in Korea, composed of siblings who explore various forms of image-making through painting, silkscreen,and digital drawing. Each piece reflects a collaborative yet distinct artistic voice — where one’s free-spirited sense of form meets the other’s cinematic, painterly lens.

Our works are driven by ordinary emotions and fleeting thoughts. Rather than seeking grand narratives, we aim to highlight the poetic value hidden in the everyday — transforming simple fragments into meaningful visual stories. We believe art is not about discovering something new under the sun, but about seeing the familiar with new eyes and giving it renewed resonance.

By collecting, rearranging, and reconstructing moments, we create a visual frame where memories, emotions, and phenomena are intricately connected. Our works often embrace symbolic elements, abstraction, and a structured sense of form, aiming to tell our stories in the most genuine way — slowly, intentionally, and honestly.

In this process, we become both the creators and observers of our own visual frames.

name: Jieun Uhm
bio:
jieunuhm.com
instagram@uhm_g


Jieun Uhm graduated from the Department of Fine Arts at Korea National University of Arts and went on to specialize in Intermedia, earning her master’s degree from the same institution. Using ‘the body holding the camera’ as her medium, Uhm creates video, performance, and installation works that focus on moments when an individual’s subjective experience aligns with the world’s rhythm. She aims to uncover how human aspects—microscopic bodily sensations, inner beliefs, and cultural behaviors—are deeply interwoven with global physical conditions. To achieve this, Uhm gathers sensations she discovers through empirical research and reshapes them into non-linear narratives. She employs temporality-based media to explore how personal sensations can transition into collective experiences and the conditions necessary for coexistence.

In addition to her solo exhibitions, including Life Vest Under Your Seat (Sahng-up Gallery, Seoul, 2017) and Walking Medley (Onsu-gonggan, Seoul, 2021), and her solo  performance Navel Point (Theatre Sinchon, Seoul, 2023), Uhm has participated in numerous group exhibitions, screenings, and performance events. She has also been involved in collaborative projects such as Orbit Library (MMCA Cheongju, Cheongju, 2023) and Sliding Invitation (Theater QUAD, Seoul, 2022), and was a member of the art collectives The Good Neighbor and Practice of YSGY. She engaged in a one-year residency program at the Seoul Museum of Art Nanji Residency in 2023.

name: Eun Young Shin
bio:
My contemplation on the “residual presence of memory and emotion” has continued to expand in relation to the environment of contemporary society.
In an age where digital information explodes and non-face-to-face communication has become routine, we experience new forms of absence and loss as the boundary between reality and non-reality becomes increasingly blurred.

In this world, I feel that emotions no longer remain as simple experiences.
Like data, they are stored, transformed, and distorted, accumulating deep within the inner self.
Emotions that appear to disappear are never completely erased instead, they remain by changing form, quietly composing our present perceptions and emotional landscapes.

My current work focuses on visualizing these accumulated fragments of emotion and the structures of feelings stored within.
I trace the point at which emotions originate — the roots where loss and anxiety emerge — and record the flow of emotion across the canvas as if it were a wave.

The repetitive lines, overlapping layers of time, and subtly diffusing colors reflect the emotional vibrations of individuals unsettled by a digital environment.
Through this, I seek to reveal the invisible emotional noise and the traces that continue to persist within contemporary life.

Ultimately, my work does not remain as a simple record of the past, but confronts the emotional anxiety and confusion of the present, raising questions about modes of existence that are not about “disappearance,” but about transformation.
I hope that viewers will revisit the source of the emotions that linger within themselves, encounter the traces of feelings they have long overlooked, and deepen their own field of contemplation.

By revealing layers of emotion that exist clearly yet invisibly, and that remain not as disappearance but as transformed presence, I hope my paintings expand into a contemplative space where memory and emotion continue to reside.

name: Ewha
bio:
Ewha is a South Korean printmaker who explores the density and intervals of forms while translating botanical subjects onto the surface. Rather than mere reproduction, her subjects are selected and transformed through the artist's gaze, reconstructed into condensed scenes. The depth of her meticulous depiction, which captures the original essence of plants, expands the viewer's perspective and leads them to encounter the surrounding landscape in a fresh, unfamiliar light.

A defining characteristic of her work is the three-dimensional matiere that emerges through the physical resistance inherent in printmaking. This serves as a record of presence, created by compressing and fixing the vitality of plants. Particularly in the Light and Shadow series, the delicate embossing that extends beyond the boundaries of the black frame into the white void is noteworthy. This represents a tactile translation of the space where light once lingered, an extension of life that refuses to be confined by standardized frames, and the point where the artist's sensory perception expands into reality.

This texture stands as a powerful trace through which the artist's acute inner sensibilities encounter the external world to affirm her identity. Meanwhile, by departing from familiar proportions or distances, her work rearranges the sensory perception of forms we once believed we knew, offering a transformative experience that rediscovers the everyday.

name: Hug
bio: hug is an artist whose drawing-based practice examines life and death, hometown and community, and the fragile existence of endangered species. Working across experimental media, hug often incorporates recycled cardboard and plastic containers, treating the material life of discarded objects as part of the work itself and aligning the practice with ideas of sustainability and social responsibility. In the Hometown and Village series, developed during the uncertainty of the pandemic, simplified landscapes and natural forms evoke the warmth of memory, shelter, and shared life. Trees, infants, children climbing mountains, and dogs appear as symbols of care, continuity, and the cycles of existence. This reflection on life extends in Not Just Another Animal, a series focused on endangered and protected species, grounded in close research. Across these works, hug moves from personal reflection toward a broader meditation on coexistence and responsibility toward other living beings.

name: PARKHA
bio:
Barkha constructs pictorial “structures” in which emotions can temporarily reside through painting. In the early phase of her practice, she employed language and sentence forms to test personal definitions, using deliberately ungrammatical phrases, raw words, and the juxtaposition of text and line to reveal pre-linguistic emotional states. These early works focused less on explaining life than on recording instability and absence prior to interpretation.

Over time, her focus shifted from the surface of language to the conditions and rhythms through which emotion operates. This transition led to the emergence of the forest as a central motif. Rather than representing nature, her forests function as structures that embody accumulated emotional density and time. Through layered brushstrokes, restrained color, and the tension of negative space, she constructs a sense of life that persists even after collapse. The forest exists not as an image that erases wounds, but as a regenerative system that includes them.

Her experience as a lyricist informs a disciplined approach to emotion, preventing its excessive consumption. Text within the image is not decorative but serves as a minimal unit that resists fixed meaning. Image and language coexist in tension, allowing viewers to locate their own emotional positions within that gap.

From her early works to the ongoing forest series, Barkha has pursued a continuously renewed consistency rather than a fixed style—an approach that reflects an ongoing formal inquiry responsive to changing conditions of life. Her paintings do not demand answers; instead, they offer a place for emotion to rest and a direction from which to begin again.

name: Yejin Oh
bio:
Yehin Oh’s practice begins with long-standing metaphysical questions—what remains after death, whether the soul exists, and why the world is here at all. Drawn to territories that science cannot fully explain, the artist approaches art as a way of searching, testing, and living with these uncertainties.

Across paintings and imagery, figures and symbols from unseen realms—shamans, mountain spirits, mythic narratives, and cosmic space—form a personal iconography that moves freely between reality and unreality, matter and immateriality. These motifs reframe the relationship between humans and nature while opening a wider reflection on contemporary conditions, including environmental crisis and a pervasive sense of spiritual lack.

Positioned against a modern culture shaped by technological acceleration and material values, Oh focuses on what structures the world but cannot be seen: energies, interdependence, and networks of relation. The work invites viewers to consider meaning in an unstable era, and to encounter the artwork as a site for contemplation—one that mirrors each person’s inner landscape.

name: Jinhyun Nam
bio: Born in 1963 and raised in Seoul, Jinhyun Nam creates acrylic abstract paintings that use the human face as a recurring motif. His work is shaped by a life marked by political conviction, imprisonment, and later reinvention through art. After entering Seoul National University’s College of Engineering in 1981, Nam left his studies while participating in the student movement. He was imprisoned in 1990 and spent eight years in prison before his release under a special amnesty in 1998. Nam began studying art in earnest in 2008 and presented his first solo exhibition in 2012. Since then, he has continued to explore the complexity of human society and the tensions between reason, conscience, and desire. Characterized by intense colors and intersecting geometric lines, his paintings transform personal history into broader reflections on time, conflict, and human existence. His essay

name: Jennifer Hur
bio:
I always stand before my canvas with a focus on the layering of colors and techniques, and the coexistence of East and West.

While I apply countless layers of color, I strive to keep their weight infinitely light. Through repetitive brushstrokes—much like a meditative practice—I scrape away and rebuild time and again. In this process, it is not just the painting on the canvas that is refined, but my own inner self that is slowly purified.

Within the structure and depth of Western painting, I seek to instill the sensibilities and "empty space" (yeobaek) of the East. Though the colors accumulate, they leave behind a texture as thin and ethereal as the wind. Within these layered traces, I capture the moment where the boundaries between East and West dissolve.

My work is not a mere combination of forms or techniques. It is a journey where different cultures and emotions converse and reflect one another on a single surface, ultimately culminating in a harmonious resonance. Today, as always, I stand before the canvas—layering color, scraping it away, and gazing once more.

The quiet vibration that crystalizes at the end of this process is the very essence of the art I pursue.

name: Kyu bong Kim
bio:
My work begins with trust in uncertainty.
I paint without preliminary sketches, allowing water and pigment to move freely across the canvas. Rather than controlling the outcome, I respond to what emerges. This process mirrors how I navigate life — accepting flow, timing, and change.

The recurring presence of the ocean and whales in my work represents liberation from fixed roles and expectations. Beneath the surface, light fractures and shifts, creating moments where contrast and calm coexist. These spaces reflect emotional states that are difficult to define but deeply felt.

My recent works belong to the Liberation series, where abstraction and figurative elements intersect. What begins as a self-portrait gradually transforms into a personal seascape — a place where solitude is not loneliness, and freedom is found in simply being.

Through painting, I seek not resolution, but openness: a quiet release from the need to be understood or contained.

name: Heeju Moon
bio:
Heeju Moon’s work explores the emotions of solitude and isolation through a series of symbolic images. In a society becoming increasingly individualized, the artist reflects on social loneliness and personal seclusion, specifically observing those who end their lives in solitary silence.

The artist uses fish in a restaurant aquarium—creatures unable to utter a sound even in their final moments—as a metaphorical symbol for the voiceless emotions shaped by social issues. Moon highlights the emotional resonance felt by those whose existential value has been lost by overlapping human forms with the imagery of these captive fish.

By treating each canvas as a disconnected object, the artist intentionally stages a scene of detachment that amplifies the sense of solitude and isolation. Through this approach, the work seeks to evoke deep empathy for those who pass away in isolation, their lives having gone unnoticed and their stories left untold by the world.

name: SJ Park
bio: SJ Park is an artist who chronicles inner landscapes through the medium of painting. He perceives the flow of human emotion and consciousness as a singular world, capturing the moments of fissure, chaos, and harmony that arise within it onto his canvas. His work avoids imposing fixed forms or narratives, instead leaving deliberate space for the viewer’s own interpretation. While his pieces appear still, they possess a constant internal vibration, inviting viewers to reflect their own experiences and complete a personal narrative within the frame.

name: Noori Noh
bio: Noori Noh’s practice centers on the visibility of internal struggle and the transformative potential of light. Working primarily in painting, Noh refrains from concealing emotional "wounds," instead utilizing the canvas to recontextualize them through a deliberate and luminous application of color. A recurring motif in her work is the horse, which functions as both a resilient guardian and a vessel for healing. These figures serve as an allegorical extension of the self, embodying the tension between vulnerability and strength. Noh’s compositions are defined by a measured, rhythmic pace, mirroring a steady progression toward emotional restoration. By bridging personal introspection with symbolic figuration, her work offers a contemplative exploration of the journey toward wholeness and the quiet clarity found in the process of recovery.

name: Keunhyung Park
bio:
Keunhyung Park (b. 1993) rethinks persona not as a temporary “mask,” but as a paradoxical kind of armor—something that both conceals and reveals what lies within. In Park’s practice, this armor works as a defense mechanism that can block sincere communication, while also functioning as an ontological interface that makes relationships possible in a complex social world. Their work gives form to inner emotion through the figure of armor.

Park observes how people meet others without ever fully defining themselves, instinctively building protective networks as they move through life. What once appeared as a simple mask has evolved into a more rigid armor, shaped by the layered interactions contemporary society demands. Through this lens, Park examines the emotional landscapes and survival strategies of modern life.

Early on, Park inhabited the “good person” as a hardened suit—avoiding conflict, refusing enemies, and seeking social approval. Over time, that posture became a persistent question: is this protection an expression of the self, or a fiction assembled by expectation? In Park’s images, armor is not a display of toughness, but a total portrait—an accumulation of temperament, interests, habits, and the deep defenses and longings a person carries. By visualizing armor’s contradiction—hiding the self while enabling connection—Park invites viewers to consider their own: what kind of armor are you wearing right now?

name: Bokhyun Shin
bio:
My work originates from an exploration of the invisible world and the cyclical currents surrounding human existence. In Eastern philosophy, 'Samsara' (the cycle of rebirth) and 'Karma' are symbols of a grand order where life and death, cause and effect, are inextricably linked. I seek to translate these concepts into visual textures within the medium of painting.

In my process, rather than representing specific forms, I actively embrace the materiality and spontaneity of the medium. Layers of pigment, rough surfaces, and repetitive brushstrokes and scrapings remain as marks that elude conscious control, accumulating on the canvas like 'karmic traces.' Beyond mere visual effects, these elements reflect the layers of memory and the scars left by life.

To me, painting is akin to a ritual approaching the sacred. The collisions and cracks that occur on the surface—and the moments they eventually reach harmony—resemble the cyclical nature of human life: a constant process of enduring suffering and rising again. Therefore, rather than presenting a fixed image, I hope my paintings serve as an open field where viewers can discover their own inner narratives within the textures.

name: Hanok Kim
bio:
Hanok Kim is a multidisciplinary artist who dismantles boundaries between abstraction and figuration, painting and narrative, tradition and digital media, and the roles of artist and curator. Rooted in feminist inquiry, Kim investigates misogyny not as a surface-level phenomenon but as a set of deep structures that shape culture and everyday life. Across painting and expanded formats, the work seeks to expose these foundations and imagine their undoing—treating resistance as a starting point that opens toward compassion, solidarity, and care.

Kim’s paintings often begin as condensed stories, built through hybrid materials such as plaster, digital print, and oil paint to form cracked, tactile surfaces where rupture and endurance coexist. These images frequently extend into graphic novels, shifting from the private space of the canvas to the shared space of reading, and blurring the line between visual art and literature. Projects including The Daughters of Pandora and Hela’s Mjolnir reframe mythological women—Pandora, Hela, Medusa—not as passive symbols but as agents of resistance, carried forward through exhibitions, publications, and participatory models such as crowdfunding. For Kim, research, process, presentation, and expansion operate as connected stages of one practice—building platforms where art can mediate empathy, dialogue, and change.

name: Hong Soun
bio:
Hong Soun’s discipline in painting is described by a re-contextualization of images of people, objects, and situations based on photographic references, named in his past exhibitions as Sidescape works. His means of understanding how to address his concerns about the medium points towards an analysis of his observations on how photographs and paintings can be viewed, and this includes presenting a visual experience through extracting parts of images he has chosen from newsprint photographs. These are pictures of objects, people, current natural phenomena and socio-political happenings that are then dissected by the artist: he divides the imagery into segments and re-focuses the pictorial merit on the periphery of the scene by painting them individually. As an example, he references a war-related photograph by isolating areas such as the sky, ground, or a fragment from a wall or a person’s clothing. Using these sources, Hong overcomes the attributed functionalities of the objects and landscapes in the respective contexts of the moment they were captured on camera, thereby emphasizing the independence and transcendence of specific and/or implied situations.

Hong Soun was born in Seoul, Korea, in 1959. He graduated from the Busan National University in Korea and continued his studies at the École National Supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris, France. The artist has been awarded nationally and internationally for his work and has participated in numerous exhibitions worldwide. Hong has been invited for solo exhibitions by the following institutions: the Maraya Art Center (Sharjah, AE), the Mimesis Art Museum (Paju, KR), the National Museum of Contemporary Art (Gwacheon, KR) and the Savina Museum of Contemporary Art (Soul, KR). He was part of the Santa Fe International Biennial in 2008 and his works are included in numerous international institutional collections.

name: Hong Junghee
bio: HONG JUNGHEE (b. 1945) is a contemporary Korean painter. She graduated from the painting department of Seoul National University and was a Fulbright professor at the College of Fine Arts, University of Michigan. She held many solo and group exhibitions at institutions such as the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul National University Museum of Art, Seoul Arts Center, Hoam Art Museum, Seoul Museum of Art, Logos Gallery in London, U.N Gallery in New York and participated in many international fairs such as Swiss Basel. Her works are in the collections of the British Museum, the University of Michigan Museum of Art, MMCA, Seoul Museum of Art, Hoam Art Museum, and more. Artist’s journey first began in the mid-1970s with the ‘Myself-Korean’ series. She developed into the ‘Off Self’ series in the 1980s, the ‘Passion’ series in the 1990s and her artistic creations lead to the ‘Nano’ series that she has been working on since 2005. The ‘Nano’ series features a concise formality among her existing colour abstract works, adding depth to the image by simplifying and the overflowing intense colour condensation. Symbolised shapes acquire a sense of rhythm in a repeated arrangement and a thick material with the colourful pigments adds a mellow depth to the canvas. Known as the “Alchemist of Color,” the ‘Nano’ series in her solo exhibition

name: Ryeong Ah Kim
bio:
NEOILLUSION
" Illusion : Utopia : Hallucination : Fragment"

Like a part hidden deep inside and a fragment of memory.
The afterimages of emotions are superimposed and shaped into a single scene.

This scene is not just an image, but a door to another world,
It is a quiet resting place and a fairy tale-like space where you can spread your free imagination, and it becomes a space that embraces your wounded heart and leads to healing.

The scene created by overlapping is a newly reconstructed space where emotions and memories meet,
visually embodying the process of understanding and accepting inner pain,
It is defined as a utopia as a space that gives peace and freedom away from pain.

We invite you to "NEOUTOPIA".

name: Hee Seon Kim
bio:
My work is an expression of the emotions I feel and the rhythmic joy I find in life. I strive to live without fear of the new, embracing movement and pursuing my desires with bold determination.

I want my art to be a direct reflection of this philosophy. With every piece, I pour my heart into the canvas, growing through the excitement of the creative process. Through color and rhythm, I hope to share my perspective of the world and the small yet radiant joys of being alive.

name: Soohyun Cho
bio:
Soohyun Cho is a painter who explores how time, memory, and perception accumulate within everyday objects. Rather than depicting subjects as fixed forms, she reconstructs them as layered sites of experience, where emotions and memories remain embedded over time.

Working primarily with acrylic paint, Cho builds her surfaces through repeated acts of layering and removal. These traces create a sense of depth, not as simple texture, but as evidence of time that cannot be fully erased. Her use of multiple viewpoints further reflects the way perception shifts, allowing a single object to hold different moments and perspectives at once.

Books appear frequently in Cho’s work. More than symbols of knowledge, they function as vessels of memory and personal time. Through these recurring forms, Cho visualizes how experience is stored, altered, and reassembled on the painted surface.

name: Eunjung Park
bio: Eunjung Park (b. 1978) works with everyday motifs—plates and fruit—to bring attention to the quiet value embedded in moments we often pass without noticing. In the ongoing project

name: Dae Hyun Kim
bio:
South Korean visual artist Daehyun Kim translates internal psychological states into tangible visual forms. By integrating disparate materials—including ceramics, acrylic paint, and industrial architectural elements—Kim constructs "psychological landscapes" that capture the nuances of memory and emotion.

His practice focuses on the intersection of form and texture, emphasizing the underlying tension and fluid movement of the inner self rather than mere representation. For Kim, physical materials serve as a vital bridge, pulling internal reflections to the visual surface. The resulting works act as visual maps of the subconscious, documenting the subtle shifts and instabilities of the human psyche.

Kim aims to create a shared space where his work functions as a mirror for the viewer’s own experiences. By inviting the audience to recall their personal histories, he explores the point where the boundaries between the self and the other intersect, fostering a collective emotional resonance.

name: Choi Sangchul
bio:
Sangchul Choi was born in Korea in 1946 and graduated in 1969 from Seoul National University's College of Fine Arts. He won a number of significant awards including The Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan Award in 1970 at the 1st Grand National Exhibition.

Choi has participated in major institutions and museum exhibitions in Seoul National University Museum of art (Seoul), Moran Museum (Seoul), Gail Art Museum (Seoul), National Museum of Contemporary Art (Gyeonggi), Hanwon Mueum of Art (Seoul), Daejeon Museum of Art (Daejeon), Kumho Museum of Art (Seoul), Seoul Museum of Art (Seoul), Seoul Art Center (Seoul), Arts Council Korea (Seoul), Fukuoka Art Museum (Fukuoka), Kyoto Municipal Museum of Art (Kyoto), Museum of Contemporary Art (Tokyo), National Museum of Contemporary Art (Seoul) and last but not least at the Sao Paulo Biennale in 1981.
Choi’s works are in the permanent collections of Hangaram Art Museum, Seoul Arts Center, National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Gwacheon and Daejeon Museum of Art.

Sangchul Choi lives and works in Paju, South Korea

name: Darae Lee
bio:
Darae Lee creates images that transform small, happy memories from everyday life into the figure of a turtle. Her practice begins with a question shaped by the speed of contemporary life: amid constant pressure to achieve, where is happiness actually found? In Lee’s work, leaves, petals, wind, and childhood memories become quiet reminders that joy often exists in passing, easily overlooked moments.

The turtle serves as the central character in her work. Moving slowly but steadily, it reflects the emotional weight of carrying life’s burdens while continuing forward. It also draws on the turtle’s traditional associations with longevity and good fortune—not simply as symbols of a long life or luck, but of a healthy, stable, and fulfilled life. Through this figure, Lee suggests that happiness is not waiting at a distant finish line, but already present in the world around us.

name: Sanghee Jung
bio: Jungsang Hee explores inner landscapes and the texture of time through images of reflection and gentle instability. Her work centers on rippling surfaces, where past and present, reality and fantasy, come briefly into contact. Recurring motifs such as carousels, clocks, lamps, and chandeliers function as carriers of memory, holding emotional residue within familiar forms. Blurred and fractured reflections suggest the imperfect, shifting self and the process of coming to terms with it. Drawing on the experience of seeing oneself as both familiar and strange, Hee uses water, light, and the horizon as spaces where consciousness and imagination meet. Her compositions treat instability not as loss, but as a condition of growth, reconciliation, and self-recognition. Through these layered symbolic scenes, Hee invites viewers to face their own quiet unrest and to find, within it, a more grounded sense of peace.

name: AmonMazdah
bio: If a single day passes without working, it feels as though my spirit is withering away. This is why, every morning, I force my heavy eyelids open and head to the studio. I never pick up a brush with a preconceived plan; instead, I let it move as my heart dictates, following the impulses of the moment. Because my thoughts and life shift daily, I often layer over the same spot dozens of times. Yet, this very act of layering is the process of breathing life back into my soul.

name: SIEUN KIM
bio:
The moment deficiency vanished,

life collapsed into emptiness.

An endless darkness swept over me,

and as I fell past the rock bottom into the depths,

I was consumed by pain.

The darkness swallowed me whole,

until I eventually became the darkness itself.

It spread beyond me, bleeding into my surroundings

and devouring everything in its path.

It was there that I let everything go.

Yet paradoxically,

within that infinite shadow, I found clarity.

From the very place where I had completely crumbled,

I survived once more.

Life sometimes wanders endlessly

through an inexplicable void.

But even within that void, there was a distinct resonance.

That sensation became the starting point of my work.

The colors and lines upon the canvas

stand in for the traces of my inner self—

traces that language alone cannot fully capture.

Within them,

I face my past self,

test my present self,

and seek out my future self.

My paintings are not answers;

they are the lingering marks of a question that continues to this day.

name: 120do
bio:
120d_O is an artist name that began with the angle of lifting one’s head to look at the sky.
It originates from the wish that people, who often live with their gaze fixed on the ground, might pause for a moment, look upward, and face their own emotions.
Like the act of looking up at the sky, I focus on moments when relationships and emotions briefly come to a standstill.
Within this short pause, I believe emotions such as joy, sadness, desire, and longing quietly continue to operate inside.
My work moves between digital art and fine art, with a preference for a 1:1 aspect ratio.
To capture the unstable flow of emotions as they are, my lines remain uneven.
At the same time, I place these emotions within the stable structure of a square frame, seeking balance through form.
Rather than recording encounters themselves, my work documents emotional states that remain after a relationship has passed.
This is not a story about me, but a record of emotions that do not disappear.

name: Jaehee Jang
bio: Jaehee Jang (b. 1968) is a painter who explores inner light and beauty through the circular structure of the mandala. Working on hanji, she applies traditional Korean pigments in more than ten layers, allowing each to dry naturally in a slow, meditative process. Each painting takes at least a month to complete, resulting in surfaces of rich depth and subtle luminosity. Her mandalas give visual form to values such as love, gratitude, hope, and courage—qualities that are often carried within but easily forgotten in daily life. The works invite viewers to pause and reconnect with these inner qualities. Jang participated in an invited exhibition of Korean artists in Paris in 2012 and ran a studio and gallery in Seoul’s Anguk-dong for a decade. In 2022, she published

name: Hari Park
bio: Hari Park is an interdisciplinary artist and director whose practice expands from a foundation in East Asian painting. She graduated from Sookmyung Women’s University with a degree in Korean painting and has since developed projects across painting, video, 3D media, and architectural materials. Park often collaborates with creators from different fields, including dancers, musicians, and calisthenics athletes, building exhibitions and performances that emphasize live exchange with audiences. Movement is the central thread in her work, guiding her exploration of both internal states and physical motion. By moving between still and time-based media, she creates works that test how gesture, rhythm, and spatial experience can be translated visually. Park’s practice brings together image, body, and environment to open up new forms of communication across disciplines.

name: Jinhee Kim (b. 1990)
bio:
Jinhee Kim holds BFA in Hongik University and MFA in Visual Art for Painting(Meister schülerin von Prof. Burkhard Held) from Berlin Art University. 

Kim delves into the colorful spectrum of everyday life, capturing the essence of oneself, others, and our shared experiences. Kim utilizes ordinary acts and primordial states of characters as visual allegories that transcend divisions of race, culture, gender, and language. She also challenges existing perceptions that define one's identity by reflecting on the differences and feelings of alienation that arise from geographical, political, and social environments. The subtle movements of the figures, revealed under dramatic light, reflect our will and desire to affirm our fragile existence in each moment.

name: MOND
bio:
Within this vast universe,
I was born from a single breath.
With twenty thousand breaths a day and tens of millions through each passing season,
I move quietly through immeasurable time.

I gather those breaths—those tremors—
and place them into paint.
I lay the invisible rhythm of life onto the canvas,
each stroke carrying a pulse of air.

This is not merely a painting.
It is a record of being alive—
a trace of existence.
In every vanishing breath, I leave a small warmth of life.

As I breathe into the work,
I draw yet another life today—
a record of breath,
a memory of living.

name: Kim Sun Doo
bio:
Kim Sun Doo (b. 1958, Jeollanam-do) is a leading figure in contemporary Korean painting, recognized for transforming traditional materials—jangji (thick Korean paper), ink, and mineral pigments—into a distinctly modern formal language.
