He earned both his BFA and MFA in Korean Painting from Chung-Ang University, studying under Oh Tae-Hak and learning jangji-based techniques from Lee Jong-Sang. He first gained major recognition in 1984, winning the Grand Prize at the 7th JoongAng Fine Arts Competition, and served as a professor in the Department of Korean Painting at Chung-Ang University from 1994 to 2024, where he is now professor emeritus.
Rather than following the ink-centered discourse that dominated Korean painting after Liberation, Kim foregrounds color as a structural element, building pictorial depth through thirty to fifty translucent layers of pigment absorbed into paper—a process he describes not as "applying" color but "brewing" it. The depth he achieves is not material thickness but the accumulation of time itself. For Kim, painting is less the invention of something new than an act of faith: as he writes of his night-road paintings, "art is not the invention of a new road, but the power that allows an old one to be walked again."
A painter who also writes poetry, Kim draws on the literary tradition of his native Namdo region and his long collaboration with novelist Lee Cheong-jun. Across series including Namdo, Slow Landscape, On the Way in Midnight, Unwithering Flowers, and The Day Stars, his work moves from urban figure painting through landscape to a contemporary reinvention of flower-and-bird painting (hwajo). He served as the stand-in painter for the protagonist in Im Kwon-taek's acclaimed film Chihwaseon (2002), and his work is held in major public collections including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul Museum of Art, Seonggok Museum of Art, Ho-Am Art Museum, and Kumho Museum of Art.

name: Saewon Lee
bio:
Saewon Lee (b. 1991) pursues an ongoing inquiry into everyday life, mortality, and the weight of being. Like small fragments assembling into a larger landscape, Lee gathers scattered pieces of time to build an emotional order—linking fleeting sensations into a quiet, sustained terrain.

Moving through overlaps of life and death, presence and feeling, what disappears and what remains, Lee’s work holds onto the instant before it fades. Layers of afterimage and rhythm accumulate, forming a single scene in which the grain of emotion becomes visible rather than declared.

Material is central to this process. Paper pulp made from discarded sheets enters the work as a cycle of return—residue ground down, rebuilt, and pressed into new “pieces” of life and surfaces for feeling. Breathable hanji becomes a ground that absorbs light and texture, while repeated layers of varnish catch everyday instants and lift them onto a subtly shimmering skin.

These fragmentary records are meant to awaken the viewer’s own memories and emotions, casting light back onto the ordinary moments that once passed by in a blur.

name: Rakeum Rhee
bio:
Rakeum Rhee (b. 1964) is a Korean artist who expands traditional chaesaek (mineral pigment painting) through contemporary materials and processes, including ottchil (lacquer), gold leaf, and paraffin. Trained in craft and design at Inha Technical College, she worked as a designer before dedicating herself fully to painting. Her work has been recognized through awards at national minhwa (Korean folk painting) competitions, including a top prize at the Kim Satgat Cultural Festival Minhwa Competition (2018) and a special selection at the Daegal Cultural Festival (2019). 

Rhee has presented solo exhibitions in Korea and Germany, and has participated in group exhibitions in Seoul, New York, and Los Angeles. Moving from classic symbolic figures such as tigers and qilin, her imagery widens to leopards, foxes, and snakes—building a contemplative view of coexistence among nature, humanity, and other forms of life.

name: byeolhee Jeon
bio:
Byeolhee Jeon is drawn to beings that feel fragile and fleeting—clouds, young and gentle animals, and plants that recur throughout her paintings. She builds these presences into a safe, warm fantasy world of her own making.

Within this imagined realm, unicorn-like creatures and other horned beings appear, but their horns are not weapons and do not exist for self-defense. In a place where no one harms another, protection is unnecessary. Instead, horns become sites of care and growth: plants with auspicious meanings take root, heart-shaped clouds gather, and rainbows bloom. These magical forms spread outward, filling the world with softness.

What unites the elements in Jeon’s universe is their temperament—nothing sharp, toxic, or aggressive. Everything is gentle, harmless, and peaceful. While this may sit slightly apart from reality, she sees that distance as the source of fantasy’s beauty: a space that can offer a kind of purity and comfort that reality rarely provides.

Through these tender creatures and calm landscapes, Jeon aims to extend a message of solace and healing. Her paintings imagine a place to pause when life feels tiring or heavy—an inner refuge that helps viewers return to reality with renewed courage and steadiness.

name: Gong
bio:
Gong explores the quiet force of nature through abstract forms shaped by sensation, memory, and inner movement. Rather than depicting landscapes directly, the artist focuses on the emotional traces that arise from being in contact with the natural world. In Gong’s work, nature becomes both a source of perception and a stabilizing presence—something that plants calm strength within the self and holds the mind through moments of collapse or uncertainty.

Through layered shapes, organic rhythms, and intuitive compositions, Gong gives visual form to feelings that are difficult to describe in words. The works invite viewers to look closely at how nature is internalized, transformed, and reimagined as a personal language of resilience, stillness, and quiet renewal.

name: Nohvan 노반
bio:
My work explores the narrative of women who have journeyed through a “crack in time” to arrive in the present. Moving fluidly between past and present, I reinterpret the painting style of Shin Yun-bok—a renowned artist of the Joseon Dynasty—through a contemporary lens. Using traditional Korean mulberry paper (hanji) and mineral pigments, I delicately capture the emotions and everyday moments of women.
In the past, I focused on expressing the landscape of urban desire through acrylics—observing and interpreting the external world. Now, my gaze has turned inward. With a more intimate and sensory perspective, I portray the very essence of “woman” itself.
The women I paint are not passive subjects of representation. They are living, breathing presences that transcend time—engaging emotionally with the viewer while embodying humor, wit, sensuality, and human vulnerability. Sometimes provocative, sometimes playful, they always carry a story to share.
My work is not intended to resemble minhwa (Korean folk painting). The present-day stories layered onto hanji are not nostalgic reproductions of the past, but visual narratives of contemporary women, reconstructed in my own artistic language.
At the boundary where tradition meets modernity, where stillness meets vivid emotion, I seek to reawaken the presence of women as multidimensional and alive. Through this, I invite viewers not simply to look at an image of the past, but to encounter the face of a woman who continues to breathe and exist—here, now, and beyond time.

name: Kyungjoo Hyun
bio: Kyungjoo Hyun creates paintings that translate moments of healing, meditation, and inner balance into layered visual fields. Her practice centers on gyeolmyodo, a self-defined method of repetitive line-making through which sensation, time, and emotion accumulate on the surface. Working with brush, pen, and densely built layers of color, Hyun develops intricate patterns that recall dancheong, tiled rooflines, and ornamental forms found in Indian and Islamic visual culture. Vivid hues such as cobalt blue, emerald green, and pink bring a contemporary intensity to these meditative structures. Emerging from this process are imaginary flowers, or gyeolmyo simhwa: blossoms shaped by memory, comfort, and the unconscious. For Hyun, the flower becomes a symbolic form of individual existence, rooted in the belief that each person carries a distinct color, rhythm, and inner life.

name: Hyungsub Choi
bio: Hyungsub Choi (b. 1985) is a painter who explores the flow of emotion and existence through line. His practice is shaped by studies in fine art at the École des Beaux-Arts de Marseille and Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, as well as a background in Buddhist studies and Buddhist painting. These influences inform a visual language that brings together contemplation, movement, and restraint. Rather than treating line as a purely formal element, Choi uses it to trace shifting inner states and the subtle rhythms of being. His paintings suggest a space where perception, feeling, and spiritual reflection intersect. Rooted in both contemporary painting and philosophical inquiry, Choi’s work reflects an ongoing search for how invisible states of mind can be given form through disciplined, meditative gestures.

name: Stella Park
bio:
Stella Park is a painter who translates moments of connection with her three companion dogs into layered, tactile images. Her work begins with brief exchanges of gaze—small instances of recognition and quiet communication that do not rely on words. These encounters shape paintings that hold a sense of warmth and ease, where affection becomes an atmosphere rather than a narrative.

Working on rough canvas, Park builds surfaces through accumulated color and repeated touch. Each layer registers time and experience, allowing traces to remain visible rather than smoothed away. Through this material process, she reflects on everyday imperfection and the forms of beauty that emerge within it, inviting viewers to slow down and feel the presence of intimate, lived moments.

name: Yongjin Lim
bio: Yongjin Lim works across sculpture, painting, and digital media to explore endurance, time, and the quiet emotional weight carried through human life. The artist’s recurring figure, “Tabom,” symbolizes patience, fragility, and the gradual accumulation of experience. Often appearing imperfect yet steadfast, Tabom becomes a vessel for hope, resilience, and the possibility of growth. Lim’s practice draws parallels between life and the labor-intensive process of making sculpture, where repeated gestures, waiting, and careful refinement allow a form to slowly reveal its presence. In the works, Tabom may gaze toward the sky, hold a small flower, or carry signs of life, creating a gentle emotional connection with the viewer. More than a character, Tabom functions as a shared self-portrait of people enduring, surviving, and becoming stronger through time.

name: Gabby Chu
bio:
Hwapi World is an inner landscape shaped by moments where sensory intuition precedes conscious thought. In this space, the hand moves before the mind can intervene; the work is a record of tremors and raw emotion rather than a calculated explanation.

The forms and sceneries within this world do not follow a linear narrative but exist as "states of being." They linger on the canvas like the traces of fleeting emotions passing through a physical space. Ultimately, Hwapi World serves as a quiet sanctuary opened for self-understanding—an expansive realm that invites viewers to project their own internal landscapes onto the work.

name: Do Jun Na
bio: My work draws inspiration from the traditions of celadon.

name: Kim Dohee
bio:
www.kimdohee.com

Kim Dohee was born in Busan in 1979. She graduated from the Hongik University Department of Painting and went on to pursue an MFA at the same institution. Her work scopes out the relationship between the primal form of our material senses and the characteristics of human beings as organisms, drawing on the material characteristics of her subject to amplify our sense of existence beyond concept and conception and expand our sense of life itself. Through olfactory stimuli, vibrations, actions, labor, and the like, Kim prompts us to perceive material characteristics within their intimate connection to the body. The performative stance that emerges from time to time within this work is intended to underscore the extant significance of such processes. Kim engages in the relentless scrutiny of her own physicality, one of multiple ways in which she uses rigorous action to unearth from the body the fragments carved into a space far beyond experience and memory. She draws on a variety of media—including installation, video art, and performance—and deftly navigates between deeply personal solo work and social solidarity and collaboration.

name: Geon U Cha
bio:
Cha Geon u’s sculptural practice eschews direct emotional pronouncements in favor of staged ‘situations.’ Rather than delivering a didactic message, his work invites viewers into a meticulously constructed atmosphere where meaning emerges through the density of the scene and the resonance of silence. This approach distances itself from narrative excess, opting instead to generate significance within the poetic gaps of the emotional landscape.

The animal figures in Cha's work function as allegorical agents reflecting human attitudes and social dynamics. These figures do not mimic humanity; they mediate it—revealing psychological states through precarious balance and ambiguous gestures. By refusing to speak, they articulate the very conditions in which emotion resides. Beneath vibrant colors and fluid silhouettes lies a subtext of contemporary malaise: anxiety, helplessness, and the exhaustion born of hyper-connectivity.

Central to his practice is the concept of ‘relationship.’ Rather than focusing on isolated forms, Cha juxtaposes multiple elements—human-animal hybrids and rigid structures—to visualize the tension of entities that are acutely aware of one another yet remain fundamentally misunderstood.

The artist’s choice of materials—resin, metal, wood, and carbon fiber—further intensifies this sensory experience. The woven patterns of carbon fiber, shifting with the light, mirror the volatility of modern emotion—at once solid and precarious. Ultimately, Cha’s work prioritizes the ‘state of being’ over the ‘act of telling,’ providing a contemplative space for viewers to confront their own interiority within the sculptural field.

name: EunYoung Choi
bio:
Eunyoung Choi is a multidisciplinary visual artist whose practice spans installation, sculpture, painting, photography, and video. She earned her BFA as valedictorian and her MFA with honors (Distinction) from the École Supérieure d’Art et Design (ESAD) in Grenoble, France.

Choi’s work explores the boundaries of various media, creating a nuanced visual language that has gained recognition through numerous juried selections and institutional support. Her exhibition history includes notable presentations at the Museum of Contemporary Art (MoCA) Busan and the Daegu Art Factory. In 2023, her cinematic exploration was awarded first prize (Regional) in the short film category at the French National Student Creation Competition (Concours de création étudiante).

Currently, Choi maintains a dynamic presence in the contemporary art scene, actively participating in solo and group exhibitions as well as international art fairs. Her work continues to evolve through a rigorous investigation of materiality and the moving image.

name: Lee Eun
bio:
Lee Eun paints her own sea through the use of earth and brush. Her choice to depict the seascape using soil may seem unconventional, yet it evokes a longstanding symbolic connection between earth and water as primal substances associated with maternity and origin. In particular, the sea—unfixed, ever-shifting, and ceaseless in its cycles of emergence and dissolution—evokes the transience of life and the limits of human existence.

Her work captures the sea’s mobility between horizon and skyline, as well as the scattering of light across its surface, through layered blue brushstrokes and the tactile density of soil. This is not a literal representation of a specific landscape, but a subjective one—distilled from memory and sensation. For the artist, the sea of her hometown is both a point of departure and a sustaining spiritual anchor. The process itself mirrors the rhythm of waves—repetitive and meditative. Lee cuts and dries coarse, thick clay into warped, varied forms, then hand-paints each one in cobalt blue. This labor-intensive method demands focus and patience, and her brushwork—reminiscent of the way wind and light brush across the sea—imbues the clay with a quiet vitality.

name: Jeong In Weon
bio: Jeongin Won (b. 1994) is a Seoul-based artist whose practice centers on ceramics and extends into sculpture, artist books, and experiments with digital imagery and photography. Her work explores how memory connects to material forms, using natural shapes and industrial components to create objects that reflect on what is remembered, lost, or altered. Through clay, wood, and printed surfaces, she considers how physical matter can hold fragments of personal and collective experience. Won’s works often move between familiarity and ambiguity, inviting viewers to reflect on presence, absence, and the layered nature of meaning. She studied at the Korea National University of Arts and continues to develop a cross-disciplinary practice grounded in material sensitivity and spatial awareness.

name: Jaiyoung Cho
bio:
Jaiyoung Cho (b. 1979, South Korea)
Jaiyoung Cho is a Seoul-based artist whose practice spans sculpture, installation, and drawing. Working with materials such as cardboard, thread, and fabric, she constructs delicate, open forms that respond to surrounding space and architecture. Her works range from small-scale objects to large public installations.

Cho’s sculptures reinterpret everyday materials and structures, often questioning the boundaries between object and space. She builds flexible compositions that evolve through layering, cutting, and spatial arrangement, creating a physical dialogue with viewers and their environment.

She received her BFA and MFA in Sculpture from Ewha Womans University in Seoul, and an MA in Fine Art from the Utrecht School of the Arts in the Netherlands. Her work has been exhibited at Wooson Gallery (Seoul), Kumho Museum of Art (Seoul), Atelier Hermès (Seoul), and Carvalhopark (New York), among others.

name: Sojung Jun
bio:
https://junsojung.tumblr.com/

  Sojung Jun is an artist based in Seoul, South Korea. Working in diverse mediums including video, sound, sculpture, and publications, she is interested in creating a nonlinear space-time to awaken a new awareness of history and the present or in how the changes made in physical boundaries penetrate daily sensorial experiences. In particular, she has produced works that weave and crisscross with her personal experiences by paying attention to people standing on the boundaries amid the ruins of modernity and invisible voices. She has newly established what she has fragmented through interviews, historical materials, and narratives appropriated from classical texts, and carries out experiments that intersect personal, psychological and aesthetic factors with political ones in life. 
   She has held solo and group exhibitions at a number of institutions including the Leeum Museum of Art (Seoul, 2022), Sharjah Art Foundation (Sharjah, 2022), National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (Seoul, 2021), Kunstmuseum Bern (Bern, 2021), Nam June Paik Art Center (Gyeonggi-do, 2021), Atelier Hermès (Seoul, 202), Tai Kwun JC Contemporary (2020), Ottawa Art Gallery (Ottawa, 2020), Art Gallery of New South Wales (Sydney, 2019), ARKO Art Center (Seoul, 2018), Palais de Tokyo (Paris, 2017), SongEun art space (Seoul, 2017), Villa Vassilieff, (Paris, 2017), 11th Gwangju Biennale (Gwangju, 2016), Doosan Gallery (Seoul, 2015), Seoul Museum of Art (Seoul, 2015), The Cube Project Space (Taipei, 2014), The National Museum of Art, Osaka, (Osaka, 2013). She is the recipient of the Hermès Foundation Missulsang 2018, Villa Vassilieff Pernod Ricard Fellowship, Paris, France 2016 and Noon Art Prize, Gwangju Biennale 2016.

name: Um Hyo Yong
bio:
Based in Seoul, Um Hyo-yong explores the ontological essence of nature through a lens that bridges the singular and the collective.
In his celebrated Tree series, Um meticulously superimposes hundreds of individual roadside trees into a single frame,
distilling their multifaceted histories and temporal depth into a singular, profound visual experience.
Conversely, his Snow series marks a return to traditional "straight photography," utilizing strobe lighting to capture
the aleatory, vertical trajectories of snowflakes against the nocturnal void, evoking an infinite space-time beyond the frame.
At the heart of his practice lies a rejection of binary opposition; instead, he visualizes a state of dynamic harmony
where dualities—inside and out, light and shadow—coalesce into a cosmic "Oneness."
Through geometric abstraction and a minimalist intervention, Um’s work transcends mere documentation
to reveal the hidden synthesis and fundamental order of the universe.
An MFA graduate in Photography Design from Hongik University, Um has exhibited extensively on the international stage,
including the PhotoBrussels Festival and numerous solo exhibitions such as Auspicious Snow and Little Forest.
His mastery of the medium continues to redefine the boundaries of photographic record and artistic meditation,
securing his position as a significant voice in contemporary Korean photography.

name: Lee Bul
bio: Crafted from materials including metal, silicone, resin, chains, crystal beads, and organic matter, Lee Bul’s cyborgs, monsters, and glittering architectural structures may seem futuristic but are influenced by specters of the historical avant-garde, like 18th-century Italian artist [Piranesi](/artist/giovanni-battista-piranesi)’s labyrinths; the [Futurist](/gene/futurism) dreams of Italian architect Antonio Sant’Elia; and Weimar architect Bruno Taut’s fantastic crystalline cities suspended in mid-air. Though Lee was academically trained in sculpture, her early works were often interactive, inviting viewers to create private performances in sleek karaoke pods or to pump air into monumental balloons mimicking manga and anime heroines. Lee’s diverse body of recent work—including installations of sculptures, drawings, and maquettes—continues to cross genres and disciplines, exploring themes of beauty, corruption, and decay.

name: Nanan (b. 1979)
bio: Nanan (B.1979) is called a visual artist and window painter who has a strong career in the commercial art field. She studied Advertising at Seoul Institute of the Arts and started her career as a senior reporter and illustrator in street culture magazine “Lunchbox” and an editor of “Kai” magazine. She was at the center of Young Culture in the early 21st century when Korean pop culture was born. Afterwards, she expanded her range of activities to show her talent in public media. She collaborated on big commercial projects with KBS, MTV, Shinsegae, Samsung, and Adidas and actively worked as an art director in Hong Kong, New York and London. As an omnidirectional visual artist, her work reflects a Neo pop character from a macroscopic perspective yet her work is difficult to distinguish into one genre. It is because her works show her identity, the boundary between pure art and popular culture, melts deeply throughout the work and shows a new direction in itself. Her work closely communicates with the audience and is transformed at the interface, receiving public affection and leads to various brand collaborations. The key to understanding Nanan's artistic world is sharing, communication and communion. The series, which contains a warm anthropological gaze, has implications for the eternity of keeping the moments of gratitude and celebration approaching each individual's life in a flower that does not wither. As such, the art she sees exists as an active message to the viewer as a communication and is like a living being that gains new vitality in each life. In particular, the performance exhibition "Nanan's Flower Shop," held with 2GIL29 GALLERY in Art Busan in 2019, caused a great sensationby redefining the perspective of communication art. Nanan hopes to restore the viewer's life and provide positive redirection through work. She continues to deliver therapeutic, delightful and comforting messages in the Pandemic era.

name: Suk Chuljoo
bio:
Chuljoo Suk graduated from Chugye University of the Arts and completed his master at Graduate School of Education at Dongguk University. He has had 29 solo exhibitions(Gyeomjae Jeongseon Art MuseumKorea University Museum, Hakgojae, and etc.) as well as about 400 group exhibitions(National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul Museum of Art, Art Fair HongKong, and etc.). He was awarded the 2nd, 3rd, 4th Jungang Fine Arts Prize, the 9th Annual Journalist of Fine Arts Award in 1990, the 6th Korean Artist Award in 1997, and the Grand Prize from the 2nd Korean Art Critics Association Awards in 2010. 

石铁周毕业于秋溪艺术大学、美术大学、东洋画系和东国大学教育大学院。 1990年至2015年历任秋溪艺术大学美术学院东洋系教授，现为秋溪艺术大学东洋画系名誉教授。 包括29次个人展(谦斋美术馆、高丽大学博物馆、学古斋、金山画廊、东山坊等)，400余场国内外邀请展及团体展(国立现代美术馆、首尔市立美术馆、香港艺术博览会等), 他每年在中央美术大展上获得了3次特别奖，1990年获美术记者奖、1997年获韩国美术作家奖、2010年获韩国评论家协会创作部门大奖。 石铁周的作品收藏于国立现代美术馆、省谷美术馆、首尔市立美术馆、Leeum美术馆、湖岩美术馆、国会议事堂、青瓦台、迪拜大使馆、光州市立美术馆、南北出入事务所等。

name: Seo In Jung
bio:
My practice explores the profound intersection of destruction and creation through the transformative power of fire on Hanji (traditional Korean mulberry paper). By utilizing fire as a surrogate for the traditional brush and ink, I engage in a ritualistic process where burning and extinguishing paradoxically yield new forms. This method subverts the conventional act of filling a canvas; instead, I "burn" to counteract the void, accumulating charred layers to give tangible shape to emptiness.

To me, burning is a meditative ritual. As I layer paper and navigate the flame, I empty my own thoughts, allowing the visceral scent and textures to guide the work. Each layer of Hanji represents a mental topography, expanding the finite surface into a space of deep reflection. My work captures the perpetual flux of nature—a realm where life and death, and creation and destruction, are inextricably linked. While I approach the canvas with a structural plan, the flame possesses its own agency, leaving behind unintended patterns that create a tension between artistic control and material spontaneity.

From a distance, these compositions may evoke the serene atmosphere of traditional landscapes. However, a closer inspection reveals the raw, tactile reality of charred edges and paper collage. I intentionally arrest the burning process at a precarious midpoint—a state where "extinction" is rebranded as "birth."

Recently, my practice has evolved toward the spatial dimension, transforming these burnt forms into three-dimensional objects. By bridging the gap between the material and the observer, I invite the audience to occupy the interstitial space between memory and reality, contemplating the cyclical principles that govern our existence.

name: Jeongwoong Lee
bio: Lee Jeongwoong reconstructs one scene of history or memory with another point of view. He conveys his own thoughts and emotions to viewers. In particular, he intentionally rearranges the structure portrays it in a realistic way. After he graduated from ‘SungKyunkwan University’ which is a top priority university in Korea, he has been exhibited extensively in Seoul, Korea and abroad such as Artspace Hue in Seoul, Gallery Hyundai in Seoul, Pontone gallery in London, Shineartists Gallery in London and etc. Moreover, he has been participated in various group exhibitions such as KT&G Sangsangmadang in Seoul, Ilmin Museum of Art in Seoul, Space K in Seoul and etc.

name: Jimok Choi
bio: Jimok Choi suggests new interpretations and alternative perspectives contrasting to rigid formality and stereotypical view towards the traditional painting. Working with painting, installation, performance, he has developed unique artistic style. He selects ordinary objects containing cultural symbolism and signs as staple medium; then, by dissembling and recombining them to let their insides out, he reveals his personal attitudes towards social stereotypes. New painting series by Choi can be perceived as a rich pictorial archive of afterimages left on his retinae exposed to an overwhelming light. The documentations delivering his resistance against ever-changing optical stimuli are multifarious, although they are responses of a single organ—eyes; therefore, his practice encourages the audience to contemplate the arbitrary relation between experiences per se and how they visually manifest.

name: Youngjoo Kim
bio: Youngjoo Kim was primarily inspired by the forlorn cityscape juxtaposed to the spectacular fantasy of a city. In the process of visualizing the energy of a city into ‘an image’, she acknowledged the image a surplus of mixed forms that are repeatedly created and vanished. For Kim, such creation and deletion are not differentiated as a dichotomy, but rather as an obscure reciprocity. She parallels the progress of her work as an artist, to the search for ‘the ideal state’, constantly seeking for the finished work that is yet to be seen. As she believes that a finished work is a result of repeated process of elimination, she translates such series of processes into a visual work of art by twisting and overlapping the frame of canvas. Working in both two- and three-dimensions, she endorses the energy emitted by the negative and positive space of the individual volume of the elements. Her works may not be how she originally intended, but they still narrate how individual elements come together to form a unified story.

name: Tae-Jin Seong
bio: Tae-Jin Seong is a well-known figure in the Asian contemporary arts. He is known for his woodprints of vivid colors in acrylic and oil crayon and his motif, which is based on Korea’s famous animated film, Robot Taekwon V. Although Robot Taekwon V was once a hero to all, in Seong’s works, the robot is portrayed barefooted in jumpsuits, just like one’s common neighbor. Realistic, yet witty, Seong impersonates the robot to portray the mechanical life of our contemporary society, especially that of the forlorn, unemployed youth in Korea. Through a nexus of traditional printmaking technique, contemporary imageries, and a unique narrative, his works appeal to many, sympathizing and encouraging those worn out and lost.

name: Jung Yeondoo
bio:
Yeondoo Jung (b. 1969, Korea) is one of the most prominent Korean artists today, working with lens-based media, performances and photography. He received his BFA from Seoul National University and a MFA from Goldsmiths College. 
Jung is the recipient of the 2007 Artist of the Year Award, awarded annually by the National Museum of Contemporary Art in Seoul. He has had solo exhibitions in Asia, Europe as well as the United States, most prominently marked by the recent presentations at La Maison Salvan, France (2016), MAC/VAL, France (2015), Art Tower Mito, Japan (2014), and Plateau, Samsung Museum of Art, Korea (2014). Jung has also participated in international biennales on a number of occasions, including Taipei Biennial (2006), Gwangju Biennale (2004, 2006), Venice Biennale (2005), Liverpool Biennial (2004), and Istanbul Biennial (2003). His most recent endeavor unveiled at the Korean Pavilion presentation for the 15th International Architecture Exhibition at la Biennale di Venezia 2016. 
The artist’s work is represented in numerous collections worldwide, including the Museum of Modern Art, New York, ESSL Museum, Vienna, The Calder Foundation, New York, The RISD Museum, Providence, RI, MAC/VAL, Vitry-sur-Seine and Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art, Seoul, among others.

name: LEEJE
bio:
www.leeje.net

Leeje (b. 1979) graduated from the Department of Painting at Kookmin University in 2002 and completed her master's degree at the same university in 2004. Her first solo exhibition followed shortly in 2005. Initially, her artwork focused on the urban exteriors of the new millennium, but it has since evolved to encompass abstract landscapes that reveal the obscured facets of society and human psychology. Leeje utilizes a diverse array of painting techniques and styles to capture the era in flux, exploring themes such as local identity, gender, the idiosyncratic nature of Korean capitalism, and social calamities.

Her art, marked by heterogeneity of technique, the embrace of chance, and thematic ambivalence, embodies the indeterminate essence of life and the fluidity of time. Her ambiguous painting images also represent her intention to construct various independent spacetimes, a departure from the ever-expanding nature of the contemporary world. In addition to her artistic practice, Leeje has been running Hapjungjigu, a non-profit exhibition space, since 2015.

name: Myung Sun Ju
bio:
Peinture sur sel gemme (Rock Salt Painting)

JU Myung Sun is a Korean artist who has been active in France for over 20 years. She introduced a new concept called peinture sur sel gemme (rock salt painting) and has developed it into what she terms Self-evolving art. This practice goes beyond fixed forms, allowing images to emerge, move, and continuously transform on their own.

Rock salt, a material carrying the weight of millennia, serves as a medium of memory and life. Responsive to air, light, and humidity, it undergoes constant variations within her works, inscribing the passage of time, traces, and transformations naturally into the artwork.

Through this process, JU Myung Sun explores notions of impermanence, traces, and the quiet rhythm of the world. Her works transcend the boundaries between painting and sculpture, oscillating between presence and absence, offering viewers a poetic and meditative experience.

Her art is situated within the horizon of lebendige Kunst (living art). The works are not merely aesthetic objects but living entities imbued with memory and healing, carrying a presence that resonates beyond the visual.

name: Shin  Minjoo
bio: Shin Minjoo has consistently been exploring the essence of paintings based on ‘brushwork,’ which is a basic and essential practice in Art. Shin imprints different psychological experiences as images within her mind, then realizes them on canvases through powerful brushstrokes and her technique of pushing paint with a squeegee. The contrast between chromatic colors of the background and powerful brushstrokes expresses Shin’s understanding of the prevalent yet contradictory feelings, and contrasting yet co-existing conditions such as light and shadow. Shin earned a B.F.A. and M.F.A. in painting at Hongik University and has held numerous solo and group exhibitions at renowned Korean museums and galleries such as Ilmin Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), Kumho of Art (Seoul, Korea), Hanwon Museum of Art (Seoul, Korea), Kwanhoon Gallery (Seoul, Korea).

name: Chung Sang Gon
bio:
Printmaker Chung Sang Gon, who has gained global attention and numerous awards for his work, has also been working actively on oil painting. His works, both prints and paintings are collected by many museums and art centers including National Museum of Contemporary Art of Korea, Hungary, Tallinn and Great Britain. He began using digital media very early in his career, throughout which he has consistently expanded the expressive range of his prints, which look like water painting. To create the prints, he takes an unconventional approach, i.e., the expansion of the digital in the realm of the analog, allowing him to create a platform for a humanities-rooted exploration of our relationship with the existence of technology rather than its role. Chung’s works, in which reality is made alternately visible and invisible and phenomena are revealed through repeated drawing and erasing, pose to viewers the philosophical question of whether our reality is an illusion created through the repetition of human concepts and prejudices. Shapes; old palaces, trees, landscape and etc. are vague and overlapped to achieve that intention. The kind of space that is naturally formed through Chung’s creative process brings to mind the concept of “empty space”, which is crucial to traditional oriental painting, revealing his identity as a Korean artist despite of applying cutting-edge technology to his work. 

Chung’s oil paintings are honest depictions of strong, dramatic, and unrefined emotions. The artist’s entire body and all of his emotions “become” the brush, immediately funneling his energy onto the canvas and thereby materializing the fictitious landscapes that existed in his imagination. The location of Chung’s studio (at a secluded place next to the forest on the outskirts of Seoul) also inspire artist to convey the emotions with intense depth and energy. Chung’s artworks always generate a visceral resonance in everyone who views them.

name: Kim Byungkwan
bio:
Byungkwan Kim was born in Seoul, South Korea and graduated in Fine Arts from the University of Hansung. 
Described as a modern Expressionist and widely recognised as one of the finest painters in contemporary art today, Byungkwan paints from images of well-known figures – Hollywood starlets, political dictators – transforming their familiar faces into strange and disconcerting paintings. His expressive paintings stop us in our tracks and challenge us to step outside what he terms “visual habit.”  

Byungkwan draw famous person like a politician or an actor/actress. He try to extract unfamiliarity from the person who is familiar to everybody.  “You can feel the unfamiliarity not from alien which you have never seen before, but from the things which you know well. The unfamiliar image I draw affects to break the way we see the things usually. I think that one of the important functions of art is to show the new-vision to the world.” He said.

His work has been widely exhibition in South Korea where he has been nominated as one of the most talented emerging artists.

name: Vanessa Su
bio: Vanessa Su is an accomplished artist who began her formal education at the Seoul Arts High School, where she majored in Western painting. She further honed her artistic skills at Ewha Womans University, where she pursued a double major in Western Painting and Sculpture within the College of Fine Arts.

name: Saebyeok Jo
bio:
I paint portraits, yet these faces are not mere representations of individuals. I depict figures who have lost their way within a labyrinth of emotion—faces drifting through a forest of incomprehensible feelings. An invisible forest resides within their gaze, their expressions, and their subtle tremors.

Perhaps this is the universal human condition. We interpret the world and define emotions through our own subjective lenses, never fully understanding one another.

I am no exception. Having lived with a sense of deprivation since childhood, I view the world through a deeply personal gaze, unraveling these childhood voids onto the canvas. I wander through this forest, navigating a nameless melancholy. This forest represents the complex, indecipherable emotions we all harbor.

I am still wandering within this wood, and on this path, I paint yet another face.

name: Yumi Jang
bio:
Yumi Jang creates paintings that reflect on privacy, rest, and the quiet need for a space of one’s own. For the artist, space is more than a physical environment; it is a personal refuge shaped by desire, imagination, and the effort to protect the self within contemporary life.

Her works often center on intimate interiors and curtain-like barriers that softly divide the inner world from the outside. These elements function as emotional thresholds, at once concealing and revealing what lies beyond. Through them, Jang considers how individuals navigate uncertainty, preserve their beliefs, and search for moments of calm within a complex social world.

Rather than describing fixed realities, her paintings offer spaces of projection—places where longing, stillness, and hope can quietly gather. In sharing these scenes, Jang invites viewers to reflect on their own inner shelters and the fragile hopes they continue to hold.

name: Kim Guiline
bio:
Kim Guiline (b. 1936) graduated from Hankuk University of Foreign Studies with degree in French in 1960. After moving to France, Kim studied art history at Dijon University and graduated from Ecole Nationale des Beaus-Arts in Paris, where he lives and works to this day. Throughout his 30 year career as an artist, Kim has consistently pursued the idea of flatness. While he showed tendency to objectify pure black and white flat paintings in the 70s, Kim improved flat monochrome works which consist of small squares and egg-shaped dots as basic units within rectangular canvas in the 80s. Reaching 1990s, Kim used bright primary colors to present works that affirmed the dualistic relationship.

To work within physical phenomenon, Kim chose black and white and worked with them for more than ten years. Following the principle that colors change along with time, Kim considered black as a color and painted over it multiple times to reach a point where the black emits light and can’t absorb any more light. In opposition to black absorbing light and white emitting light, Kim painted over the surface until black emitted light and white absorbed light. Although black and white are normally disregarded as colors in Western paintings, Kim’s monochrome works show that black and white can function as colors.

The colors—white, gray and black—that form Kim’s work are commonly known as achromatic colors. However, for Kim, the achromatic colors are not confined to its physical conditions—difference in brightness but without color and purity—but contain equivocal meaning of appearance and disappearance as logical conclusion to all colors in that they come to fade and ultimately disappear as result of passing time. And rather than limited to achromatic colors, it should be seen as characteristic of the color itself.

name: Hyun Jin Oh
bio:
I capture moments that profoundly resonate within the mundane rhythms of daily life. Rather than seeking the extraordinary or the dramatic, I focus on the fleeting instances within landscapes where an emotional afterglow lingers—moments that might otherwise be easily overlooked. These scenes are quiet and lucid; they possess a softness, yet carry a commanding presence.

For me, a landscape is never merely a backdrop; it is a vessel for emotion. A path once walked, light caught in a brief pause, the sunset over a familiar street—these sites, permeated with the passage of shared time, manifest as "forms of memory." The solace, love, longing, and warmth felt in those moments remain more vivid than any spoken word or facial expression. Through my work, I summon these internal states back to the surface via the landscape.

While the pictorial space is rooted in representational detail, it is reconfigured according to the "affective temperature" of the emotion. Upon a foundation of structural composition and restrained negative space, I layer colors from my memory to build a texture of feeling. Though based on actual locations, these landscapes are transformed by the idealized way they persist in my mind, allowing me to articulate a certain density of emotion.

Ultimately, I do not paint mere scenes; I paint the affective world that sustained me in those specific moments. I hope that within my landscapes, viewers can encounter a space to recall and inhabit their own moments of solace.

name: Jason Ha
bio:
The artist’s practice is centered on the translation of visceral emotions into a formal language of color and line. Utilizing abstraction as a tool for self-discovery, the work functions as a visual record of the artist's internal dialogue. The compositions are characterized by a compelling duality, oscillating between moments of soft, fluid lyricism and intense, gestural energy. This technical contrast reflects the fluctuating nature of the human psyche, capturing both the tranquility and the turbulence of lived experience.

By prioritizing the expressive potential of mark-making, the artist moves beyond literal representation to evoke a raw, psychological resonance. The interplay of vibrant hues and dynamic strokes creates a meditative space where personal introspection becomes a shared universal experience. Ultimately, the work seeks to establish a profound emotional connection with the viewer, inviting them to encounter the lingering echoes of their own inner landscapes through the sensory power of the canvas.

name: Soosan Park
bio: Soosan Park explores the unseen inner space she calls the “abyss,” understood not as darkness alone but as a deep register where emotion, memory, and traces of existence gather. Beginning from a central point or source of light, her compositions unfold through organic movement, allowing form to emerge through a balance of intention and chance. This process gives visual shape to emotional motion and the shifting rhythms of the inner self. Across her work, the abyss appears in different states: as blooming fields of color and light, as moments of tension and stillness at the edge of perception, and as lingering traces that remain afterward. Park approaches the abyss as a space of reflection and healing rather than fear, inviting viewers to quietly encounter their own emotions and reconsider the depths within themselves.

name: ZZOZZI
bio:
“The Artist Chasing the Contours of Clouds”

Artist Jang Jjo-jji explores the fundamental oneness of subject and object, grounded in the premise that all existence is intertwined like a meshwork, forming a single continuous line. To manifest this, the artist harmonizes traditional East Asian painting techniques with the materiality of diverse modern mediums, capturing the "tenacity of life that persists even at the brink of breaking."

With 'clouds' as the primary medium, the work reflects on the finitude of time and the primordial meaning of existence. By shaping images along the free and fluid lines of clouds, the artist internalizes concepts of connection, circulation, and regeneration.

The unique forms birthed from the artist's gestures and internal rhythms explore new possibilities in contemporary painting. These works offer viewers a profound visual experience, filled with an organic energy that pulses with life even within repetitive patterns.

name: Sungmi Lee
bio: Sungmi Lee creates dreamlike images by working with the physicality of materials and a range of media. Embracing the organic, ever-shifting nature of their materials, they allow chance to generate unique shapes and rich colour combinations. This process uncovers quiet moments from everyday life and the emotions beneath them, offering a space to pause, breathe and hold on to a sense of rest and hope.

name: Sung Han
bio:
Sung Han explores everyday moments as powerful sites of perception, memory, and sensory experience. The artist’s practice grew from a period of exhaustion and disconnection, when repeated routines made daily life feel distant and empty. After stepping away from that cycle, Han began walking without a fixed purpose and became newly aware of the sky, wind, flowers, and other passing scenes that quietly shape the present.

In Han’s paintings, ordinary moments appear enlarged, distorted, and reassembled. These shifts are not meant to create fantasy, but to reveal how strongly a simple scene can register through personal perception. Rather than pursuing accuracy, Han focuses on feeling, using lines, spatial structures, and organic forms to evoke sensations that remain in the body after memory has faded.

Through this work, Han invites viewers to encounter familiar moments through another person’s sensory filter and to reconsider the density of everyday life.

name: Song Zungmin
bio:
Born with an interest in Japanese animation during the 1980-90s, artist Song Zungmin embarked on his journey into drawing and art. Majoring in Korean painting, Song explores a multitude of domains, ranging from traditional painting to comics, illustration, animation, and tattooing, engaging with audiences through his innovative visual expression.

The artist manifests his messages within his works through a worldview that intersects reality and the metaverse. The characters portrayed in his art, crafted through a fusion of analog and digital techniques, serve as a unique conduit that connects audiences to the artist's worldview. These characters capture the juxtaposition between reality and the ideal, offering a glimpse into the artist’s dreams and aspirations.

Employing a blend of comics and digital animation, the artist unravels the storyline within his creations, capturing pivotal moments of the narrative through his unique painting style. Through dynamic compositions, he brings dramatic narratives to life, utilizing a bold and daring color palette seldom seen in traditional painting, thereby infusing his works with an intense emotional energy and dramatic impact. Moreover, the fluid lines in his art eloquently convey the emotions and situations of characters, offering a glimpse into the psychological conflicts and inner struggles experienced by modern individuals.

Through the amalgamation of diverse techniques and materials in the realm of visual arts, Song Zungmin endeavors to demonstrate the potential for fields once classified as subcultures to claim significant positions in contemporary art, thereby broadening the scope and possibilities of the visual arts landscape.

name: 양지원 Yang Jiwon
bio:
Artist Yang, Jiwon b.1981
 
Graduated from the Department of Animation at Namseoul University.
 
From the 5th grade of elementary school, I started drawing while watching cartoons. In middle and high school, I showed my own cartoons to my friends and spent them working in circles, and the university went on to study animation and graduated. After that, I spent time studying religion and language in Italy, Switzerland, and Brazil. After drawing in Switzerland, where the emotions that began to be drawn without sketches were expressed, I realized that the act of drawing itself has the power of self-healing and continued to draw.

name: Jina Park (b. 1980)
bio:
Jina Park (b. 1980) is a Korean artist currently based in Berlin. She majored in Oriental Painting at Korea University in Seoul and relocated to Leipzig, Germany, to study at the Hochschule für Grafik und Buchkunst under the guidance of Neo Rauch and Heribert C. Ottersbach. 

In Park’s work, space is created for memory and illusion to come together. The elements of her paintings are surrounded by feelings of misplacement that lead the viewer to self-interrogation. Her subdued color palette combined with surreal objects and creatures instill a need for categorization of that which is foreign. Yet, there is also harmony in her paintings and all the elements she introduces are able to live together in the illusory setting in which she places them. Park’s dichotomy stems from her personal experiences of being a South Korean artist in Berlin. Her concerns of individuality versus identity arise from biases of viewers’ desires to categorize elements of her work as inherently “Korean” or “German”. 

Park’s recent solo exhibitions include Collector’s Room at UNC Gallery, Seoul in 2018, and Guardians of Cabinets at Projektraum Meinblau, Berlin in 2020, where the painting was combined with augmented reality technology.

name: m0No.
bio:
m0No. is a South Korea–based emerging artist whose practice moves across digital art, marker drawing, album art, and video collaboration. Working fluidly across mediums, m0No. explores the tension between the tactile discomfort of analog processes and the polished language of contemporary digital culture. Vintage sensibilities, stark contrasts, and pared-down compositions play a central role in this evolving visual language.

Recently expanding their practice to Tokyo, m0No. has also incorporated portrait photography into their work, using the viewfinder to capture fleeting narratives and rework them into image-based compositions. Familiar scenes are often transformed into something slightly unfamiliar, revealing a quiet sense of strangeness within everyday life. Through the essential qualities of black and white, alongside broader variations in contemporary visual culture, m0No. continues to build a distinct artistic world.

name: Yeesookyung
bio:
Yeesookyung (b. 1963) is an interdisciplinary artist living and working in Seoul, Korea. She received both her undergraduate degree and MFA in painting from the National University in Seoul. She has completed notable residency programs at Villa Arson, Apex Art, and the Bronx Museum. Internationally known for her acclaimed Translated Vase series, Yee combines histories: art historical, spiritual, and cultural into unique objects, imagery, and performances that reflect both her personal heritage and a global borderless moment. Many of her works mix distinct historical references, for example: combining the Japanese art of mending ceramics with gold (kintsugi) and traditional white and celadon porcelain traditions from Korea, or the meditative process-based Tibetan Buddhist silk scroll painting (thangka) with the flat graphic style of Goguryeo Dynasty era cave paintings. Yet the voluptuous forms of Yee’s signature ceramic sculptures and the iconography within her paintings and drawings produce a uniquely contemporary experience with her work.

Yee’s work has been shown internationally at the 6th Gwanju Biennale (2006), ARCO (2007), the 5th Liverpool Biennial (2008) the Vancouver Biennale (2009), the Buson Biennale (2010), and the 18th Biennale of Sydney (2012). She has been included in notable recent exhibitions including Women In-Between: Asian Women Artists 1984–2012 at the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, the 2012 Korea Art Prize exhibition at the National Museum of Contemporary Art in Seoul, Korean Eye 2012 at Saatchi Gallery in London, The Collectors Show: Weight of History at the Singapore Art Museum in 2012, and K.P.O.P.: Korean Contemporary Art at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Taipei.

name: Jungmook Jung 海晴 鄭正默 해청 정정묵
Celly
bio: Celly is a South Korea–based artist whose paintings reflect on light, imperfection, compassion, and the quiet dignity of ordinary beings. Rather than focusing on decorative technique or formal beauty, Celly turns attention to what is often overlooked: an imperfect face in the mirror, an unremarkable passerby, or a wildflower that takes root wherever it can grow. These subjects become vessels for exploring tenderness, vulnerability, and the hidden narratives beneath appearances. Celly’s work seeks to awaken senses dulled by familiarity and to recover the light that is easily missed in the pursuit of illusion. Through painting, the artist traces moments of love, fracture, and renewal, suggesting that even within a broken material world, each being carries the possibility of enduring grace.

name: IVAAIU City
bio: IVAAIU City is a collective based in Seoul and Tokyo. IVAAIU stands for Idea, Visual Audio, Architecture, Infrastructure and Urbanism. The collective works in multiple disciplines with artists from various genres, making continuous efforts to materialize the contemporary era.

name: John Pai
bio:
John Pai was born in Seoul, Korea in 1937 to Reverend father and mother who was raised in Russia. He and his family came to America in 1949 when he was 12 years old. His father and mother went back to Seoul since it was the time of radical political change. He lived in West Virginia alone with American family. He remembers drawing in countryside of Korea and being interested in art at a young age. Pai held a one-man show of 24 paintings at the Oglebay Institute at the age of 14. In 1958, Pai got a four-year scholarship to attend Pratt Institute.
 
Pai received a full-time fellowship for graduate study at Pratt and he concentrated on sculpture. At that time, he began teaching at both the Parsons School of Design and at Pratt. In 1965, he became chairman of the undergrad sculpture program at Pratt Institute. In 1974, he resigned as Director in order to give fuller time to his own work. Pai has been showing his work in Seoul, Paris, and New York.

name: Jong-Tae Choi
bio: Choi Jong-Tae, a renowned elder among Korean sculptors, has been recognized since the 1970s for his sculptures combining figurative and abstract forms. 1960s-70s Korea was an era when amorphous abstract form influenced by European Art Informel dominated the art scene, as seen in Dansaekhwa. In that atmosphere, Choi began building a unique world of work through sculptures appropriately combining the characteristics of abstract and figurative art, and he continues to use this method even today. His comment, “I have experienced long-lasting conflicts between the two poles of Giacometti and Brancusi, Chang Ucchin and Kim Jong-Young, Egyptian and Greek art, and East and West,” clearly reveals the work philosophy he has followed. That is, he has wanted to create works that narrowed the gaps between different historical styles of art and aesthetics of the East and the West, while remaining within the bounds of two-dimensional and three-dimensional art, painting and sculpture.

name: Shunita
bio: Shunita’s work begins by talking about human emotions and expressions, but also creating and imagining “beings” that deal with the emotions evoked in ourselves. These “beings” live in the artist’s unique world, and work to solve complicated emotions or thoughts caused by obscurity of human world. Human life necessarily loses balance or is amorphous because of the existence of emotions, and this can be a gift or a punishment at the same time. The artist works are expressions of those experiences.

name: KIM Woojin
bio:
www.woojin-kim.com

   KIM Woojin’s art projects begin with small questions that catch her attention while she observe or experience various societies. she try to identify specific elements, or "dispositifs," that operate within individuals' everyday lives in response to those questions. With the process, she aspire to rupture that which we hold steadfastly true, such as 'good/bad' or ‘true/false'. She held several solo shows such as 'The Freezing Point, The Evaporation Point', KIMCHONGYUNG Museum, Seoul, 2022, 'You will have to follow the directions you hear', Alternative Space Loop, Seoul, 2019, 'Brave New Exercise: Memorized Movements' Tokyo Art and Space Hongo, 2017. She participated in many group exhibitions such as 'Language the between', Kimhongdo Museum, Ansan, 2022, 'Songeun Art Award' , Songeun, Seoul, 2021, 'Surim Art Prize', Kimheesoo Art Center, 2021, 'The Future of Silence: When your tongue vanishes', Nam Jun Paik Art Center, Yongin, 2019, 'Kotodama', Para-Site, Hong Kong, 2018. She was selected to many grant programs such as art grant from Gyeonggi Cultural Foundation, 2022, art grant from Seoul Foundation of Art and Culture, 2019. As well as she participated in many residency programs internationally, such as Sema Nanji residency, 2023, Incheon Art Platform, Incheon, 2022, Bamboo Curtain Studio, Taipei, Taiwan, 2016 and MMCA Goyang residency, Goyang, 2014.

name: Shumu
bio:
Shumu (b. 1994, South Korea) graduated from the Central Academy of Fine Arts in Beijing in 2017, majoring in woodcut and copperplate printmaking.

Shumu’s work explores how life takes form, reflecting on rhythms shared by human and non-human beings alike. Rather than depicting specific species, she evokes inner human sensations and emotions through non-human presences.

Her woodcuts engage not only with visual form, but also with touch, durational time, and the relational processes that sustain life. In her works, the physical act of carving leaves traces of breath on the surface, while layers of ink absorbed into the wood accumulate over time. These gestures invite an attunement to what flows and what remains—between creation and decay, between what is seen and what is felt.

name: Lim Soosik
bio: Photographer Lim Soosik draws inspiration from the traditional form of Chaeckgado, a style in Korean painting, for his photographic portrait work. His Chaeckgado series, ongoing since 2007, is a representative series of the artist spanning 15 years. Chaeckgado, a style from the Joseon Dynasty, portrays various items such as bookshelves and books. Lim Soosik uniquely creates his Chaeckgado by stitching pieces of printed Hanji (traditional Korean paper) like a patchwork quilt. The visual aim is to convey that individual books, like pieces of a quilt, come together to form a bookshelf. When the personal life contained in the bookshelf is laid bare, the bookshelf becomes the owner's inner face. Lim Soosik's Chaeckgado, with its hand-stitched details and rustic charm, reflects the passage of time.

name: JeongMee Yoon
bio: JeongMee Yoon’s work has been widely exhibited in galleries and museums around the world, including the Busan Biennale and Gwangju Biennale in South Korea, Casa Asia in Barcelona, Spain, Paris Cinema in Paris, France, The 12th Annual International Exhibition in New York City, the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, USA and the National Museum of Contemporary Art, South Korea.  Her work has won numerous awards, including the prestigious 2006 Daum Prize, presented by the Geonhi Art Foundation, Seoul, South Korea and The Sovereign Asian Art Prize, Hong Kong, in 2011.  Images from The Pink and Blue Project are held in the permanent collections of The Museum of Fine Art, Houston, USA, Philadelphia Museum of Art, USA, Library of Congress, Washington, DC, USA and Seoul Museum of Art, Seoul, South Korea among numerous other museums and public corporate collections.  The work has been published and reviewed in publications including The New York Times, LIFE magazine, Art in Culture, Art News, American Photo, Esquire and many others.  The artist’s book, “The Pink & Blue Project” was published by Geonhi in Seoul, South Korean during 2007.  The artist earned both a B.F.A from Seoul National University and a M.F.A from Hong-Ik University in South Korea and in 2006 received her M.F.A. from the School of Visual Arts in New York City.  JeongMee Yoon was born in Seoul, South Korea in 1969 and currently resides in that city.

name: Moka Lee
bio:
Moka Lee is a figurative artist who paints portraits, still lifes, and landscapes that explore relational dynamics between subject matter, viewer, and the artist. Drawing inspiration from social media, analog photography, film, and modern master paintings, her works convey unsettling emotions of conflict that are pervasive yet often remain unsurfaced. Lee’s painterly techniques call attention to the process of painting, which is similar to that of a digital printer. Often inspired by social media, her subject matter resists straightforward interpretation, incorporating innuendos and double entendres. Lee has had solo presentations of her works in Hong Kong and Seoul with [Jason Haam](https://www.artsy.net/partner/jason-haam). She has participated in group exhibitions at the Seoul Museum of Art and Museum of Contemporary Art Busan, among others.

_Submitted by [Jason Haam](https://www.artsy.net/partner/jason-haam)_

name: Lee
bio: Lee explores the emotional states that shape human experience, focusing less on moments of ease than on feelings of exhaustion, hardship, anxiety, and despair. Rather than treating these emotions as purely negative, Lee sees them as formative forces through which people endure, change, and grow. The work reflects the inner struggle to avoid pain, while also recognizing that these restless efforts become part of one’s lived experience. Alongside unease and vulnerability, Lee’s practice also holds space for the human desire for happiness and emotional renewal. By bringing these conflicting states into view, Lee creates work that considers how wounds, resilience, and longing coexist within everyday life, and how emotional difficulty can leave lasting traces that shape who we become.

name: AMBER PARK
bio:
The attitude toward life and emotions, and the resulting shifts in the state of mind, are central themes that permeate Amber Park’s work. For the artist, the canvas serves as a sincere channel to reveal her innermost thoughts, where layers and textures act as a visual text connecting fragments of invisible emotions.

Amber Park candidly captures the sense of loss, the uncertainty of identity, and relentless introspective inquiries. These explorations manifest as both abstractions and figures reminiscent of childhood emotions, weaving a narrative where reality and imagination, memory and fantasy, intersect.

The artist describes her approach as “a meeting of encounters.” Within a single work, personal memories, traces of others, and the spirit of the times accumulate to form a dense forest of emotions. Bold yet gentle colors, repetitive brushstrokes, and delicate lines serve as tools for documenting emotional moments, inviting viewers into a space of deep empathy and reflection.

In the midst of life’s weariness, Park’s work navigates the question, “Is this really reality?” by embracing the inquiry—reflecting, recalling, and attempting to recover. These themes resonate with the complexity of the modern psyche, offering a warm sense of solace and connection.

Between illusion and reality, fragile yet striving for resilience, her work mirrors the human heart in its many contradictions. Through her paintings, Amber Park hopes viewers can engage with her sincere narratives and share a moment of collective healing.

name: Koh San Keum
bio: The korean artist Koh San Keum recreates newspapers and books. Every letter or sign is substituted by an artifical pearl to create not the context but the structure of the written. Through this shapes, design and the rythm of the written language are focused and presented in a new perspective.

name: Song Burnsoo
bio: Song Burnsoo is a leading figure of Korean modernism and avant-garde featuring his own practice by encompassing a wide range of art. He has been dedicating himself over a half century to figure the unique identity of Korean contemporary art. His practice has expanded to the religious reflection on human existence through lifelong investigation, and shows outstanding achievements not only in the contemporary art but also in the realm of religious art.

name: Jongju Yoon
bio:
Jongju Yoon was born in Daegu in 1971 and earned a master’s degree in Western Painting at Keimyung University. She is currently based in Daegu and maintains an active presence in the art scenes of Seoul and Daegu.
  Yoon’s Cherish The Time series began in 2012, evolving through sub-themes such as She & Her, Breath, Be You, Composition, Space, Line, and Voyage. 
  The artist has been fascinated by the materiality of the fluid matte medium, as it is warm and translucent and also enables three-dimensional surfaces. She mixes it with acrylics and sieves the mixture; the resulting refined, consistent liquid is poured onto a canvas, which is then slanted to allow it to flow. To create depth of color, space, light, and lines on canvas, she repeats the process of pouring, drying, and sanding several dozens of times.
  Each work by Yoon consists of multiple canvases, the sizes of which are determined by a regular sequence of multiples such as 1, 1.5, 2, etc. This method of sizing allows the canvases to be neatly grouped together, and because of the modular structure of the pieces, her work has the potential for limitless expansion.
  The artist’s work method and structure is simultaneously maximal and minimal and holds infinite potential. Yoon aspires to continue her work, which is like a long journey in search of the profound and mysterious nameless colors that result from the accumulation of countless layers of color.

name: Doki Kim
bio:
Doki Kim takes a profound interest in the various layers of the world, including space and nature, society and culture, matter and energy, and time and space. Using immaterial media such as light, heat, gravity, and language, she creates works that explore the 'phenomena' that occur in the interaction of matter. Continually questioning 'what' we are and 'how' we exist, Kim's work is scientific, philosophical, sometimes poetic, and shamanic. Through her multi-media installations that operate in various ways, the artist invites viewers to open their senses and engage as a passionate interpreter of her work. 

Doki Kim lives and works in Busan. She has participated in group exhibitions at Ha Jungwoong Museum of Art(2023), Busan Museum of Art(2023), MoCA(2021), and Boan1942(2020). Her work is represented in the collections of MoCA Korea, Tokyo University of the Arts Museum.

name: Ik Soo Kaay
bio: Ik Soo Kaay constructs virtual 3D imagery based on fictional narratives to create imaginary artifacts, presenting them within his work as surrogates for himself. Since 2020, he has collaborated with novelist Choi Chu-young as a "Jangso Translator" exploring the sensory remnants of vanished locations. Additionally, he serves as the art director for the electronic music label GUCHUK, where he translates musical impressions into visual media and imagery.

name: Minji Ku
bio:
Minji Ku is a contemporary painter who revitalizes the narratives of mythological entities from Eastern folklore to explore the complexities of the human condition. Drawn to the dual nature of these stories—at once serene and tempestuous—the artist identifies these legendary beings as vessels for fundamental human experiences: desire, fear, and loss.

In her practice, Minji Ku examines the inherent imperfections of existence, using the enduring vitality of folkloric figures to address personal and collective deficiencies. Her work functions as a site of transformation, where the sense of "lack" is channeled into the potent, creative energy of desire. By bridging ancestral mythology with contemporary psychological inquiry, she reframes ancient tales as mirrors for the modern self. Through a refined application of Korean painting techniques, Minji Ku invites viewers to confront their vulnerabilities and find resonance in the persistent voices of the past.

name: Xiu Kwon
bio: Xiu Kwon is a South Korea–based visual artist whose paintings explore emotional afterimages, the distance between relationships, and the fragile sensations of disappearing moments. Working primarily with acrylic and oil, Kwon develops layered images that reconstruct personal memories and everyday scenes through a quiet, psychologically charged visual language. His practice focuses on themes such as disappearance, residue, and the invisibility of emotion, translating subtle shifts in human relationships into open-ended compositions. Rather than presenting fixed narratives, his paintings leave space for viewers to project their own experiences and emotions onto the work. Through ongoing exhibitions, interviews, and online presentations, Kwon continues to expand his presence as a contemporary painter while deepening his exploration of how images can hold traces of feeling, memory, and time.

name: Lee Yoon Seo
bio: Yoonseo Lee is an artist who uses internet sources to select subjects for her paintings, focusing on depicting the shortcomings of image representation. Her quick brushstrokes create smudged images that reflect the challenges faced by painting as a medium in keeping up with the overwhelming quantity and speed of information available online. She was born in Seoul in 1983, graduated with a Bachelor's degree in Fine Arts in 2006, and completed her Master's degree in the same field in 2017. One of her notable series is "Image Defragment" (from 2020 onward), where she collects images from various online sources, sketches impressions onto canvas, and allows the images to overlap, resulting in glitch-like and fragmented compositions. Yoonseo Lee has also been recognized through selections in programs such as RE: SEARCH (Seoul Foundation for Arts and Culture, Seoul, 2022), Artist Incubating Program (Open Space Bae, Busan, 2017), and Daum Kakao Story Funding Project (Seoul Foundation for Arts and Culture, 2016).

name: Yomahon
bio:
Yomahon is an artist who explores difficult emotions—such as anxiety, fear, and anger—through the recurring figure of a “monster child.” Rather than treating horror as something purely threatening, Yomahon uses its visual language to give form to feelings that are often hidden or left unspoken. The work appears eerie at first, yet it also carries a sense of playfulness and familiarity that invites viewers in.

In Yomahon’s practice, the monster is not simply a fictional character but a reflection of inner discomfort, vulnerability, and emotional tension. Small traces of hope, love, and humor remain present within these dark atmospheres, opening space for empathy and release. By reshaping fear into something approachable, Yomahon encourages viewers to confront avoided emotions from a different perspective—and to find comfort, recognition, and even laughter within them.

name: Byeol Muffin
bio: Byeol Muffin is a painter whose work centers on the image of the beluga whale as a symbol of life, family, protection, and recovery. Through soft forms, repeated patterns, and symbolic color, she creates gentle narratives in which small beings support one another and continue to live with quiet resilience. Her paintings often suggest a shared world where vulnerability is not hidden, but held with care. The beluga becomes both a guardian and a companion, carrying emotions of tenderness, healing, and connection. By emphasizing rhythm, repetition, and intimate relationships between forms, Byeol Muffin explores how life is sustained through mutual dependence. Her work invites viewers to reflect on the fragile yet enduring bonds that allow living beings to survive, recover, and move forward together.

name: Yeju Kwon
bio:
The artist explores the profound interconnectedness of life through the motif of ancient trees, viewing them as sentient repositories of memory. In this practice, nature is repositioned from a passive object to an active subject that archives the passage of time—encompassing ancient organisms, the shifting of seasons, and the collective history of the Earth. By weaving together narratives of humans, animals, and celestial elements, the work creates a dreamlike space where reality and the subconscious converge.

Working with a mixed-media approach of acrylic and oil, the artist employs a palette dominated by varying shades of blue. While often associated with coldness or solitude, blue is utilized here as a warm, multifaceted medium to mirror the spectrum of human emotion. The technique is characterized by a dynamic tension between raw, spontaneous brushstrokes and intricate detailing. Ultimately, these works evoke a "sense of connection," reminding viewers that individual existence is part of a larger, enduring organic whole.

name: Juwon Ju
bio:
Juwon Ju’s painting explores the distance between the life one imagines and the life reality requires. Working through narrative scenes, Ju follows antlered figures who embody displacement—marked for the forest yet unable to live within it. A recurring deer appears as an omen and guardian, guiding a search for a “personal forest,” a place of belonging shaped on one’s own terms.

Ju builds each work by collecting visual references and recomposing them into hybrid interiors and landscapes. Space and color function as psychological devices: fractured architecture, thresholds, and shifting hues externalize hesitation, longing, and resolve. Rather than offering a fixed ending, the series stays with the act of moving forward—through solitude, difficulty, and unexpected warmth—suggesting that desire can be recovered and pursued again.

name: 한해숙 Hae Suk Han
