name: Ryu  Ayoung
bio:
Ryu Ayoung @art.studio.ray (b. 1982) is a contemporary artist based in Korea. Her works are characterized by a refined visual language that evokes nostalgia and invites introspection. With a fairy-tale-like atmosphere and delicate use of color, her compositions serve as poetic metaphors for the passage of time.

The backgrounds in her paintings reflect the cyclical rhythm of the seasons, functioning as a narrative structure. The sunlight of summer fills the canvas with warmth and brightness, symbolizing growth and vitality, while the ice and snow of winter evoke stillness, introspection, and inner reflection. These seasonal transitions act as visual mediators that express the rhythms of personal and emotional growth.

Through symbols and allegorical imagery, Ryu explores the intricate layers of memory. She intertwines the coexistence of remembrance and oblivion with personal identity and narrative, thereby constructing a universal emotional story. Her works unfold slowly, like scenes painted on a scroll, revealing depth of sentiment and multilayered narratives.

Her art invites viewers to contemplate the boundaries between memory and imagination, reality and reverie, evoking the subtle and ambiguous emotional structures of the human psyche.

name: Kim Se-han (김세한, b.1981)
bio:
Kim Se-han (b. 1981) creates artworks centered on nightscapes, capturing the distinctive beauty of city lights. Since night views are defined by the interplay of light and shadow outlining objects, the depiction of light is the core focus of his work. To achieve this, Kim meticulously applies primary-colored acrylic paint in a range of dot sizes, from tiny specks to larger points, using a fine brush.

Reimagining familiar nighttime scenes, his art transforms them into reflective spaces shaped by a contemporary lens. Through the vivid glow of city lights spilling from storefronts, Kim symbolically delves into the inner desires of urban dwellers seeking spiritual escape. His works, infused with warm and radiant light, mirror the complexities of modern life while offering a hopeful message of healing and comfort for those navigating the challenges of city living.

name: Kang Minsoo
bio: Kang Min-Soo (b. 1972 in Seoul, Korea) received his B.F.A. and M.F.A. in Ceramics from Dankook University. He currently lives and works in Gwangju, Korea. For over 20 years, Kang has adhered to the traditional white porcelain production techniques of the Joseon Dynasty. His Moon Jar is crafted using these time-honored methods. To preserve the unique rustic beauty of Joseon white porcelain, he uses peeled pine trees to fuel a wood-fired kiln. The pine ash burning inside the kiln was left behind, touching the surface of the body. Kang uses white clay sourced from the Yanggu region, which is the traditional raw material for Joseon white porcelain, to achieve a soft, milky white color. His works embody the essence of 18th-century Joseon Dynasty white porcelain, with the Moon Jar serving as a striking representation of this artistic heritage.

name: Sunrise no9
bio: Artist specializing in leather carving. I craft and showcase fine art, handmade shoes, and custom designs.

name: Daeuk Kim
bio: Dae Uk Kim is born in Busan, South Korea. He studied industrial design in Seoul National University of Science & Technology, Seoul, Korea and got a MA in Design Academy Eindhoven, Netherlands as Contextual Design. He works in Eindhoven, Netherlands and Seoul, South Korea. As a man growing up in Korea, Dae always felt as if he was a mutant, an aberration from the heterosexual norm. He decided to turn shame into pride, by making mutants that proudly display his hitherto secret desires. The refined detailing, the finishes, the skin and the colour palette – they all show the hand of a skilled maker and talented artist who is able to translate his personal imagination into a project that communicates excellently to a wider audience.

name: Chu Mirim
bio: Chu Mirim has explored across the border of design and fine arts by using the pixels, computer graphics, and etc. to relate the gap between art and our lives around the world. She has been actively collaborated with GAP, UNIQLO, Converse and other brands to bring her relevant ideas to our lives much easily. Moreover, as she recently awarded one of the renowned award, 'the Grand Prix Winner of UNKNOWN ASIA 2019' in Japan, she has been highly received a great attention from abroad.

name: Zong Hyuk Kim
bio: Moon Jars are made by fusing two bowls of equal diameter. In life, when we find a partner or someone with whom we share a deep connection, we describe it as being 'in harmony' or 'perfectly aligned.' In my work, the Moon Jar symbolizes the profound encounter of meeting a person who shares the 'same diameter' as myself.

name: Daha Kim
bio: Daha Kim works across media art and writing, utilizing digital media including generative video and the web. With an interest in the concept of time, her practice revolves around the transition from the immaterial and intangible to the material and tangible, as well as the inverse process. She reinterpret cultural memory in contemporary contexts.

name: HwaYeon Lee
bio:
ㅡ I collect stillness.
I create abstract gardens using hanji (traditional Korean paper).
My work is not merely a painting—it is a meditative process of organizing emotion and restoring inner order.
Inspired by the dry landscape gardens of Kyoto, I pursue jeongon (靜穩)—a state of quiet stability—through repetition, minimal forms, structured lines, and silence.
Hanji is a delicate material, but through the process of tearing, layering, drying, and building, it becomes firm and resilient.
This transformation mirrors my own practice.
Using rulers and compasses, I draw precise lines and carefully apply torn paper fragments, one by one, gradually forming layers of emotion.

Rather than depicting form, I sculpt an architecture of the inner self.
Each surface accumulates time—and within that time, stillness condenses.
That stillness became the force that grounded me when I needed it most. Now, I hope the quiet within these works may gently reach others as well.

name: Jiwoo Hong
bio: Jiwoo Hong is a visual artist whose practice explores how inner life can be mapped through the forms and structures of nature. Beginning with plants as a key motif, Hong’s early work used organic growth and cycles of transformation to reflect the accumulation of emotion and lived experience. This inquiry has since expanded into a broader investigation of memory, perception, and the psychological architecture of the mind. In Hong’s paintings, landscape functions less as representation than as a visual framework for thought: mountain ridges, forests, and branching formations evoke neural pathways, layered memory, and shifting states of awareness. Drawing on psychology and philosophical reflection, Hong moves between the natural world and interior experience, treating both as interconnected systems. The work ultimately considers the mind itself as a kind of landscape—formed through relation, shaped over time, and continually in flux.

name: Jae-Eun Choi
bio:
Known for her intense visual imagery based in architectural-scale grandeur and meticulous aesthetic sensibility, Jae-Eun Choi’s oeuvre spans diverse disciplines including sculpture, installation, architecture and film. Choi’s work springs from an innovative interpretation of space and the relationship between life and nature and has since expanded its parameters through an experimental approach that combines art and science. She continues to utilize an array of techniques to explore issues of time and existence. In 2016, Choi participated in the 56th Venice Architecture Biennale with her recent project “Dreaming of Earth,” which aims for the eternal and sustainable peace in the De-militarized Zone in Korea and the reunification of the Korean Peninsula. Jae-Eun Choi’s work is widely collected by the world’s prestigious museums, including Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art, Seoul and National Gallery in Prague, Czech Republic.

Born in Seoul, Korea in 1953, Choi immigrated to Japan in the mid-1970s and has lived there since. In Tokyo, she enrolled in the Sogetsu School, where she studied Ikebana (the traditional Japanese art of flower arrangement). Her training there in the spatial relationship of organic forms became the foundation for her visual arts practice. Choi was exposed to a variety of media and styles and it was these early encounters with both Japanese and international artists that eventually led her to look beyond the traditional techniques and practices in which she was trained.

name: Kijin Park
bio:
People perceive a situation as they see it. The facts are so different from one another, like fingerprints. The amount of common sense in our society is equivalent to its members. There are things you cannot see because they are too far away. There are things you cannot see because they are too close. And there are things I cannot see because of myself. And sometimes there are things you cannot see because of yourself. Once in a while, we face a situation in which we have mixed emotions. In my case, I first had that feeling the day I saw the DMZ. I have tried to explain this feeling to many people, but emotions are so different from person to person, from moment to moment, and from situation to situation, that it is not easy to share it. Today, I miss the moment when I felt that rush of complex emotions all the more. -Artist Statement

Kijin Park's work begins with his experience of 'boundary' in a special strip of land called the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone). The DMZ is a borderline that we cannot cross, but in legal terms it is an outcome of a measure taken by international law that declared demilitarization of a particular area. From a political and military standpoint, the DMZ is recognized as a means of cease-fire and peacekeeping by suspending combat and securing temporary peace. It is a zone that is spaced apart from each other to prevent a direct military conflictsuch a zone exists another 'boundary' within the boundaries of South Korea. -WonSun Seoung (Art critic)

name: Pablo Daniel
bio:
As an interdisciplinary artist, my practice fluidly navigates the intersections of painting, poetry, and tattoo art, weaving a cohesive narrative across diverse mediums. My work seeks to bridge the gap between commercial aesthetics and environmental consciousness, leading to high-profile collaborations with global brands such as MCM and CASETiFY.

Beyond the canvas, my commitment to social and ecological discourse is reflected in my partnership with Greenpeace, where I utilize my visual language to amplify urgent environmental messages. By integrating the rhythmic precision of poetry with the indelible intimacy of tattoo art and the expressive freedom of painting, I explore the evolving relationship between the human experience and the world we inhabit.

name: Junho Park
bio:
Confronting reality is, at times, a process of acknowledging that abstraction can grasp the essence of existence more closely than figurative reality. Junho Park’s work does not merely stop at reproducing the external appearance of a subject; rather, it presents the fundamental form that lies beyond it. It is a refocusing on reality—an attempt to break away from transient phenomena that shift with time and environment, and instead capture an unchanging essence.

This process entails a sober awareness of the imperfection of the empirical world we inhabit, combined with the tragic condition of humanity encountered within that very lack. It is a deepening of consciousness, as well as a harmonious collaboration of chaos, control, and chance. Moving fluidly between reality and fantasy, disrupting perceptions with unfamiliar viewpoints, Park’s visual language condenses the discovery of existence and the accumulation of experience onto a single, unified plane, inviting us into a new realm of perception.

name: Green Lee
bio:
Green Lee  is a Korean artist who began drawing during the COVID-19 lockdowns, when extended time at home opened space for a sustained studio practice. After completing more than 80 works, Lee held a first solo exhibition in 2022. In 2024, an exhibition centered on “quietness” articulated a core artistic perspective: gratitude discovered within a silent world. That body of work explored beauty found in stillness and proposed new ways of communicating beyond sound.

Rooted in lived experience as a deaf artist, Lee’s practice focuses on “speaking with the hands” and translating stories that are often overlooked into visual form. Through the act of drawing and painting, Lee addresses social isolation and imagines expanded possibilities for connection—creating moments that can be shared meaningfully, regardless of hearing. Lee’s work traces an ongoing journey toward communication that moves past disability as a boundary and toward art as a common language.

name: Haru Lee
bio:
Haru Lee (b. 1997) is a painter who approaches “a day” not as a unit of time, but as a journey toward personal freedom. Working from the pace of everyday life, Lee invites viewers to pause—if only briefly—and return to a sense of self that can feel easily lost in the rush of the present.

Lee’s practice centers on holding the immediacy of the moment at the tip of a brush, translating fleeting feelings into images that read like small acts of release. Rather than offering spectacle, the work proposes a gentle reset: an invitation to meet one’s own freedom inside ordinary time.

At its core, Lee’s work carries a quiet wish—that each viewer’s day might feel “like a painting,” and that something bright and sustaining might still be waiting ahead.

name: Eunjoo Rho
bio: Rho Eunjoo has captured the incomplete ambiguous state which could be seen as the time of amorphism on the canvas. She reaches the medium of painting through stages of drawing, modeling, and photography, and focuses on the transmission of senses that may occur as the properties of media and materials change in the process.

name: Yuzu Kim
bio: Yuzu Kim creates work that is at once rough and delicate, reflecting a sensibility shaped by both resilience and vulnerability. Her practice centers on misalignment, imperfection, and emotional wounds, treating them not as flaws to conceal but as elements to reveal and emphasize. Through this approach, Kim explores how beauty can emerge from fracture, tension, and exposure. For the artist, making work is also a deeply personal act of immersion and contemplation—a space apart from daily life where focused attention becomes a form of meditation. Within this intimate realm, she continues to expand the meaning of her practice and develop a visual language of her own through material experimentation and sustained reflection.

name: Jungwan Chae
bio: My work focuses on visualizing the dissatisfaction individuals experience within the framework of society through the medium of painting. Rather than referencing specific people or events, my practice features a recurring motif: an anonymized figure, bald and dressed in a suit. This figure serves as a conceptual device to reveal the universality of structural issues shared across our society, transcending personal grievances. Through these figures, I aim to articulate the oppression and irrationality individuals encounter, as well as the resulting emotional conflicts. My goal is to explore the potential for this dissatisfaction to move beyond isolated emotion and evolve into empathy, dialogue, and broader social discourse. While my paintings are rooted in a critical perspective, they simultaneously maintain a subtle thread of hope for the possibility of change.

name: Haesun Choe
bio:
My practice primarily centers on paintings of the human eye. I view the eye as a unique site—one that reveals emotions most directly while simultaneously possessing the power to deliberately conceal them. Rather than constructing a specific narrative or setting, my work focuses on the tension and sense of distance created by the act of gazing itself.

The figures on the canvas do not offer clear explanations of their emotions. I consider the moments of discomfort or estrangement felt by the viewer to be an integral part of the work. However, I hope these feelings are perceived not as exaggerated horror or dramatic spectacle, but as sensations that gradually unfold through sustained observation.

My creative process does not follow a linear pace. It involves a repetitive cycle of intense focus and pauses, adjusting the surface of the canvas over time. I feel this inherent rhythm is reflected in the final output. Ultimately, my work is not intended to provide a definitive interpretation; rather, I hope it serves as an opportunity for viewers to confront and examine their own emotional states.

name: PANMOOK KIM
bio:
We view the world through a specific framework and interpret it through our values and concepts, as it is impossible to see the world without any prejudice during our limited time in this world.
My art explores the duality between different worlds, such as the inner and outer self, diverse individuals, reality and virtuality, and truth and lies. I focus on the collision of opposing worlds, where social norms and individual desires meet. My artistic interests have led me to explore the concept of compromise through the use of masks or personas.
Masks represent a division between our social and true identity. The more masks we wear, the more fragmented our true identity becomes, risking the loss of our genuine selves. These ironic phenomena are not only applicable to me, but are also typical symptoms of identity confusion and loss that modern individuals are experiencing. Despite the signs and symptoms of these issues, we are hesitant to give up our masks. The fear of exposing our hidden desires and reality holds us back. As a result, we continue to change our masks according to the situation and hide behind them, feeling protected from the world. We constantly play a role and pretend to be someone we are not.
However, this does not necessarily mean that I criticize this phenomenon.
As an artist, I focus on exploring societal deformities and projecting our current era, reflecting on alternative solutions through artistic language and symbols. In this era, we are all standing between extreme polarization, and the gap facing the boundary is rapidly narrowing. Therefore, I continue my artistic pursuits by adapting to the rapidly changing flow of the times, changing masks as needed.

name: Hae lyn Hwang
bio:
The wounds born from the unstable truthfulness of human beings possess a subtle beauty.
The more transparent and honest a heart is, the more easily it wears away, leaving scars in its wake.
These scars are both marks of pain and beautiful marks that prove our authentic existence.

name: Jeongsoon Kim
bio:
Jeongsoon Kim is an artist whose practice reconsiders inherited imagery through the lens of the present moment. Rather than reproducing the past, Kim breaks familiar motifs apart and rebuilds them into new visual structures shaped by contemporary sensation. Through this process of deconstruction and reconfiguration, recognizable forms become openings for poetic imagination and a renewed sense of lyricism.

In recent work, Kim turns toward memory and place, grounding images in the emotional landscape of their hometown. Nature appears not as scenery, but as a felt atmosphere—something held, recalled, and translated into form. Kim’s work invites viewers to linger with what feels familiar, then encounter it again as something newly tender, offering a quiet space for reflection and restoration.

name: Yuyeol Byeon
bio: Yuyeol Byeon is a media artist and composer whose practice explores the shifting boundary between sound, image, technology, and thought. Working across digital art and interactive installation, he uses artificial intelligence, computer vision, 3D graphics, game engines, and custom-built software to create works that unfold as events rather than fixed objects. His practice is rooted in the idea that meaning does not remain stable, but emerges through relationships, context, and continuous transformation. Moving between music and visual art, Byeon treats this in-between position not as a limitation, but as the driving force of his work. Through algorithmic processes such as interpolation and generative transformation, he visualizes a world shaped by collision, resonance, and becoming. His works examine how perception, internal intensity, and external conditions continuously reshape one another.

name: siren eun young jung
bio:
sirenjung.com

  Born in 1974 in Incheon, South Korea, siren eun young jung currently lives and works in Seoul. She studied the visual arts and feminist theory at Ewha Womans University in South Korea and the University of Leeds in UK. She is interested in how the seething desires of anonymous individuals encounter events in the world and become resistance, history, and politics. She believes that, by ceaselessly reexamining feminist-queer methodology, artistic praxis that is simultaneously aesthetic and political is possible. 
  Her representative works include the “Dongducheon Project” (2007-2009) and the “Yeoseong Gukgeuk Project” (2008-present), and she works across genres including visual art, film, and theatre. She has grown mainly through major exhibitions in Asia such as “Tradition (Un)Realized” (2014), “Ghosts, Spies, Grandmothers: SeMA Biennale Mediacity Seoul” (2014), “Discordant Harmony” (2015, 2016), Asia Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art (2015-16), Gwangju Biennale (2016), Taipei Biennial (2017), Shanghai Biennale (2018), Tokyo Performing Arts Meeting in Yokohama (TPAM 2014, 2018), and Serendipity Art Festival (2018). She has received the 2013 Hermes Foundation Art Award, 2015 Sindoh Art Prize, and 2018 Korea Artist Prize and participates in the exhibition in the Korean Pavilion at the 2019 Venice Biennale.

name: MyungSeop Hong
bio: Hong Myung-Seop, born in 1948 in Pyeongyang, studied sculpture at Seoul National University. He drew attention of the art world at home and abroad when he was invited to the 44th Venice Biennale in 1990. He has been invited to prestigious exhibitions such as ASIANA, special project of the Venice Biennale (1995), Fellbach Triennial of Small-scale Sculpture (Triennale Klienplastik Fellbach, 1995, Stuttgart, Germany), National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (1995, Korea), Kunstforum International (1997, Dresden, Germany), Special Exhibition at the Gwangju Biennale (1997), Media City-Seoul (2000), Pusan International Contemporary Art Festival (2000), the Biennale of Ceramics in Contemporary Art (2003, Savona, Italy), Art Canal International (2006, Biel, Switzerland), the Busan Biennale (2008), Incheon International Digital Art Festival (2009), “FLOW” Kunstbad (2012, Graz, Austria), Exhibition at Cultural Center of Novi Sad (2012, Serbia), and the Busan Biennale (2016). name: Huisu Hyeon
bio:
Huisu Hyeon (b. 2001) is a digital artist and visual director who builds richly colored worlds using AI and 3D technologies. With hyperreal attention to light, surface, and texture, she recreates the feel of the real—and then pushes it further, expanding everyday objects and cultural symbols into surreal, dreamlike scenes. Moving fluidly across fashion, interiors, food, and brand imagery, Hyeon connects these fields into a single immersive visual experience, shaping future-facing aesthetics from concept development through final image production.

Her practice is driven by a desire to “repaint reality”: to sculpt light and materiality into sensory environments that can feel more vivid than life itself. At once sweet and uncanny, her images open onto landscapes that seem to belong to a world not yet here—inviting viewers into a polished, speculative vision of what reality might become.

name: Beaver
bio:
Beaver focuses on capturing the pure and serendipitous moments of unfamiliar places through the eyes of an outsider, letting my footsteps guide me to scenes that unfold naturally. Before embedding stories into the photographs, I prioritize the atmosphere, colors, and the actions of the subjects as felt in the moment, drawing the viewer's attention first and foremost.

Photographs that emphasize a sense of presence serve to enhance the narrative. It’s not the story that comes first, but the vivid sense of the scene that breathes life into the story. A single photograph captured in this way can inspire countless imagined stories, offering the joy of interpretation and discovery.

name: Heya
bio: I am Heya, an artist who explores the intersection where fantasy meets reality.

name: Nahwoe Park
bio:
Nahwoe Park utilizes traditional materials—including ink, oyster shell powder (gofun), animal hide glue, and quartz powder—on linen to explore the boundaries between life, death, presence, and absence. Her practice is rooted in the language of still life and the Vanitas tradition, using symbolic iconography to investigate how we confront loss and the lingering traces of memory.

For Nahwoe Park, death is not a terminal point but a mirror that reflects the vitality of life. Her process of painting serves as a ritual for transforming the void of absence into a "poetic presence." By layering textures and historical symbols, she creates a contemplative space where silence, desire, and the cycles of nature converge. Her work invites viewers to navigate the delicate emotional textures found within the flux of existence, offering a meditative reflection on the transience and resilience of the human spirit.

name: Jinhyeok Lee
bio:
Lee Jin hyeok is an artist who visualizes the flow of the mind and the grain of time through paintings rooted in traditional Korean ink wash painting (Sumuk). Rather than defining distinct forms, his works reveal intangible states—emotions, memories, and seasons—through ink diffusion, negative space, and condensed brushstrokes. Upon the surface, black ink exists not as a static image, but as a ceaselessly shifting and dynamic flow.

Having long explored the structures of calligraphy, Eastern painting, and traditional brushwork, the artist expands his visual language by deconstructing and reconstructing the forms and meanings of Chinese characters. In his work, text remains a structure to be felt rather than read; each stroke embodies the rhythm and breath of nature, as well as the inner resonance of the human spirit.

Lee’s paintings possess both vigorous brush power and profound stillness. While the traces left on the surface may appear spontaneous, they are the culmination of long-term discipline and a restrained aesthetic sense. The balance between ink tones, diffusion, void, and substance alludes to the harmony between nature and humanity, emotion and reason.

In his representative series, Heart Flow, Lee translates the process of the mind flowing, lingering, and moving forward into abstract imagery, offering a painterly interpretation of emotional undulations and the potential for healing. Furthermore, works that combine the sensory experience of seasons and nature with calligraphic imagery demonstrate the intersection where Eastern philosophy meets contemporary abstraction.

Lee Jinhyeok’s art is grounded in the spirit of traditional ink wash painting but transcends mere reproduction of the past. Using the ancient tools of ink and brush to chronicle the emotions and existential states of the present, he continuously explores the new possibilities of Sumuk as a form of contemporary painting.

name: Seunghyun Na
bio:
Seunghyun Na explores the shifting space between inner emotion and outward composure. Her work begins with a process of tracing feelings back to their source, observing the quiet yet intense waves that emerge between the self one experiences internally and the self presented to the world.

Using strawberries as symbols of emotion and bluebirds as symbols of reason, Na builds compositions where contrasting colors, textures, and forms reflect the conflicts that continually exist within us. Rather than presenting emotion as a fixed state, her paintings capture fleeting moments of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure as they transform across the surface. Through expressive color, tactile layering, and fluid distortion of form, Na gives visual shape to the fragile balance between feeling and thought, inviting viewers to confront the emotional tensions that shape everyday life.

name: purume hong
bio: Hong Purume’s painting has a unique atmosphere for incorporating elements of traditional Korean painting through use of ink on paper and abstract composition. Unlike the realistic landscapes of most oriental paintings, Hong gives modern twist by painting in abstract style. The chunks of dark shades seem to be depicting land or mountain and whites implying light, snow or water. The smooth transition of ink into blank space makes the painting seem light and airy. The dream-like atmosphere reflects the artist’s hope to help audience find their peace and overcome their anxiety.

name: Jieun Jang
bio: Korean artist Jieun Jang (b. 1984) is concerned with calling attention to the commonplace and ennobling the invisible and neglected objects that populate our world. Working in drawing, sculptural installation, and video, Jang’s practice emphasizes subtle movement and the hidden life in inanimate objects. Laboriously folding tracing paper with powdered graphite on her hands, her pieces retain a deliberate delicacy and carefulness, requiring the viewer to approach her works with an increased care and sensitivity–qualities Jang believes are necessary to see and experience them. Her simple pieces can be seen as metaphors for finding inner strength, which requires time, effort and mindfulness, but are treasures once found. Jang earned her B.F.A in painting from Hongik University in Korea, and received her M.F.A from School of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

name: Keunwoo Lee
bio: The artistic expression refers to the possibility of a work of art created by artistic means to affect its observer. It is a possibility of communication and it is often a portrayal of the artist’s inside. The diversity as an expression is what stings in the eye first of the work of the artist Keun Woo Lee. Born in 1970 in Incheon (South Korea) she graduated in 1993 as a Bachelor of Fine Arts in the painting department. Shortly after that, she moved to Europe, studying fine arts and painting with Max Uhlig at the Hochschule für Bildende Künste. In 2002, she achieved the graduation of a diploma there. Following, she completed a Master’s degree with the ceramist Marit Tingleff at the art school in Oslo as well as a Master’s degree with Kerstin Abraham in Kiel.

name: Hyeshin Yun
bio:
Hyeshin Yun is a Korean artist whose work examines the power of appearance in contemporary society. Combining the symbolism of luxury goods and animals, she explores the tension between inner emotion, outward image, and social identity. In Yun’s practice, luxury objects are not treated simply as signs of vanity or consumption. Instead, they function as a form of social armor, concealing vulnerability and helping individuals face the pressures of public life.

Animals in her work represent symbolic selves, each carrying psychological traits associated with instinct, strength, desire, or authority. The tiger, for example, appears as an image of power, wealth, and inner force. By bringing luxury items and animals together, Yun visualizes the gap between what is displayed and what is hidden, revealing how people construct protective identities within society.

name: Jiyoung Moon
bio: Moon Jiyoung raises questions surrounding the power of the gaze toward people who have been excluded from society or forced into its margins. Through images of her mother’s long devotion to the progression of her disabled siblings and of herself caring for her now elderly mother, she explores human existence and raises endless questions about the meaning of “ordinary.” Recently, she has broadened the scope of her work into images related to blind faith, focusing on situations in which disadvantaged members of society see nowhere else to turn except the religion in the hope of wellness and fortune. In addition to various solo exhibitions such as Melting Pile of Candies—For What the Woman Prays (Space Dot, Busan,2019) and A Condition of Ordinary (Pusan National University Arts Center, 2015), she has taken part in group exhibitions including So-called Normal Family (Suwon Museum of Art, Suwon, 2023), Caring Society (Gyeongnam Art Museum,Changwon, 2021) and Stranger in a Strange Land (Busan Museum ofArt, Busan, 2020).

name: Woolim Lee
bio: Woolim Lee who was born in 1972 in Kyoungnam Province in South Korea is a Korean Asian Modern & Contemporary painter. He received both his BFA and MFA from Youngnam University. The figures that appear in the mysterious landscape/portrait paintings of Woolim Lee project the artist’s utopian desire for protection and insulation from the consequences of a rapidly expanding and fiercely competitive modern world. People look for beauty in nature, heal their wound through nature, and seek repose and meditation within nature. We dream and have a vision of another world through nature. His work is an evocation of the spirituality of modern people derived from their secret, mystic contact with nature. His work is steeped in a longing for mystic power and incantational imagery.

name: Choi Jae-Hyug
bio:
Choi Jae-hyuk graduated with a bachelor's and master's degree in painting from the College of Fine Arts at Hongik University. 

He has received the Excellence Award at the 1st Korea Young Artists Art Competition and a Special Prize at the 13th Danwon Art Festival. 
Additionally, he was selected as a resident artist through the 4th Gana Atelier Residency Programme. 

Choi specialises in contemporary still-life paintings, drawing inspiration from antiques and traditional Oriental painting styles. 

His works often incorporate compositions such as gimyeongjeolji-do, chaekgado, and chaekgeori, through which he captures and conveys the value of everyday life.

name: lillodoodle
bio:
Working at the intersection of Pop Art and imaginative illustration, my practice begins with the sensory experience of a "pause"—the moments of stillness, leisure, and respite found within the relentless pace of daily life.

My work constructs an utopia that mirrors reality yet remains distinct. In this realm, small beings drift across oceans and wander through forests, inhabiting a time where there is no need to hurry. These scenes are an attempt to capture moments that are intrinsically valuable—not because they achieve a specific purpose, but simply because they exist.

I repeatedly explore the themes of life, freedom, and circulation. Overlapping lines, intricate patterns, and rhythmic color flows symbolize the continuous movement of a life in flux, expressing the natural cycle of emotions that emerge and dissipate. Within this process, I focus on a specific kind of happiness: one that is invisible, indefinable, yet undeniably present.

To me, happiness is not a grand event. It reveals itself quietly in the time taken to catch one’s breath, in the moments when the mind spontaneously relaxes, and in the mindless contemplation of color and form. By translating these intangible sensations into a visual language, I invite viewers to naturally overlay their own memories and emotions onto the canvas.

Ultimately, I hope my work serves as a small sanctuary—a space where one can set down complex thoughts and encounter a sense of warmth and profound ease.

name: Kim In Kyum
bio:
Kim In Kyum represented Korea in the 1995 Venice Biennale and Korea's first artist invited to the Centre Pompidou, Paris Atelier Resident and had a solo exhibition at the Atelier Pompidou in Paris in 1996.  His transparent drawings bear bright space in its constructed plane and his so-called ‘Drawing Sculpture’ represents ‘Space-less’, the state of being free from given space transforming across two and three dimensional space. By inverting traditional modes of volume and proportion, flat stainless steel sculptures interplay with the three-dimensionality of his highly detailed drawings, creating an unexpected complement in colour, form and space. 
 
His work has been shown in numerous exhibitions worldwide.

name: Kyojun Lee
bio: Kyojun Lee (b. 1955), known as a geometric abstract painting artist, focuses on the perceptual aspect of art, and creates artworks composed of geometric lines and surfaces. Lee’s photographic works from the 1970s and 1980s record experimental installation art and conceptual performance art. The two overriding themes of his art are ‘flat surface’ and ‘division.’ He began producing flat surface works in the early 1990s, whereby attempts have been made to divide the screen using materials such as lithographs, charcoal, acrylic, watercolor and paper. From the late 1990s, he experimented with geometric division of surfaces on media such as canvas, aluminum, lead plate, and plexiglass. Since the 2000s, Lee has focused on canvas itself, highlighting both the stability of the surface induced by homogeneous proportions, and the tension between different formative elements. He continues to create his own unique geometric abstract art, engaging with only the basic elements of form: dots, lines, and sides.

name: Sojin Park
bio:
Sojin Park is an artist and a fashion designer. Her works include drawing, painting and textile art. She often uses a mixture of embroidery, collage and painting to express her dynamic dreamlike stories and feelings of life. “The beauty of synthesis “and “sprit of Bibim” (“Bibim means in Korea a mix of different things). These expressions seem to tell the ancient memory of a contemporary person.

She has created a one- designer brand Assembled Half, design and produce all by herself. 

"I have always been attracted to mysterious and paranormal phenomenon between nature and humans. I often find myself observing people who look either similar to or different from me. Showing shameful moments or hidden scenes, I focus on the feelings and ambiguity emerging between them. I think about the status where many different notions and absurd images are entwined into a mess. Meaninglessness, oneness and incompetence all repeat, revive and disappear. 
I visualise the phenomenon and nature that are constantly circulating. They seem like a consistent and monotonous addition, but they change subtly collapsing and being distorted between relations. 
A thread freely penetrates through fabric. Thin and thick lines cross, making patterns. The flexibility of the fabric and threads and the time for my fingers to remember the threads are important elements in the process of weaving. 
A “thread” is a material that penetrates the subtle gaps and tears the fabric which feels like the second skin. Such an action looks like weaving a net and setting a trap. The process itself is a work, and as the action repeats, I get something more than my expectations. Before starting a project, I collect and analyse information of many phenomenon. This information is reproduced through my work. Part of the information becomes new images, and the meaning of it gets intensified and flows to many different directions. It is re-born into an independence format in the process. "           -- Sojin Park

name: Min KyoungKap
bio:
Min Kyoung Kap (1933–2018)

Min Kyoung Kap, also known by his pen name Usan, was a seminal figure in modern Korean painting, renowned for reinterpreting the traditional identity of Korean art through a modern visual language. A graduate of Seoul National University, Min spearheaded the experimental art group "Mukrimhoe" (Ink Forest Society) in the 1960s, challenging the conventions of traditional ink painting and pioneering the movement toward abstraction and non-figurative experimentation.

His oeuvre is best defined by his Nature and Mountain series, which explore a spiritual communion with the natural world. Transcending traditional ink materials, Min incorporated bold primary colors, decisive plane divisions, and geometric elements, thereby expanding the contemporary possibilities of Korean painting. Grounded in his philosophy of "painting the providence of nature rather than its outward appearance," Min sublimated Korean spirituality into a modern aesthetic. His works are held in major collections, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA), Korea.

name: Youkyeong Oh
bio:
Oh Yukyoung (b. 1979, Korea) is a contemporary South Korean installation and sculpture artist whose practice investigates the intricate interactions and cyclical systems binding nature, humanity, and objects. Operating under the philosophy that "nothing stands completely alone," Oh reconfigures ephemeral, mundane, or discarded materials into immersive environments that explore relationality, coexistence, and material transformation.

Oh studied Environmental Sculpture at the University of Seoul before graduating from the prestigious École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts (ENSBA) in Paris. This dual background infuses her work with both a rigorous understanding of public space and the conceptual depth of the avant-garde. Utilizing everyday items and elemental matter—such as paper cups, salt, and crystals—she aggregates fragile components into expansive formations to visualize the dialectical processes of proliferation, growth, and obsolescence.

Her distinguished career features acclaimed solo exhibitions at Space K, Art Sohyang, and Chapter II, alongside major institutional group showcases including the Gangwon International Triennale and the Amorepacific Museum of Art (APMA).

Extending her environmental commitment into design, Oh also leads the upcycling brand STUDIO OHYUKYOUNG. A notable cross-disciplinary milestone includes her high-profile collaboration with Amorepacific, where she spearheaded a sustainable initiative transforming discarded corporate uniforms into functional, aesthetically refined cushions. Through this holistic integration of art, design, and activism, Oh seamlessly bridges the gap between artistic contemplation and ecological daily living.

name: Ji Yong Ho
bio:

2005    B.F.A. in Sculpture, Hongik University, Seoul

name: Kim Sang Gyun
bio:
Kim Sang Gyun (b. 1967) lives and works in Seoul, South Korea. He studied sculpture at Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea and at the State University of New York, USA.
Kim creates an exceptional commentary on the city and the boundaries between interior and exterior space through the use of two visual components: the reproduction of building façades and heavy blocks of repetitive, yet unique architectural frontages. The form of the buildings’ exteriors comes from careful observation and study. Kim meticulously measures each façade and transforms them into three-dimensional miniatures. Each individual element is laid on top of one another in a brick-like pattern to create a larger surface or wall: a city made of millions of concrete facades is transferred to a flat, linear depiction, almost like a puzzle. 
Kim has held exhibitions at museums and galleries worldwide including Gallery Baton the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul, Korea; the Seoul Museum of Art, Seoul, Korea; and the Samuel Dorsky Museum of Art, New York, USA. He is also the recipient of the Vermont Studio Center Freeman Fellowship and the Korean SongEun Art Grand-Prix. His works are held in numerous collections.

name: mannan
bio:
Mannan explores the theme of human connection through a lens of optimism and reconciliation. In response to the growing isolation and social fragmentation of the modern era, the work investigates the "joy of encounter" as a catalyst for unity. The artist utilizes a recurring cast of animal and plant characters to evoke a sense of childlike wonder, aiming to dissolve the rigid perspectives and emotional callouses of adulthood.

These figures inhabit narrative scenes that emphasize empathy and shared existence, reflecting a belief in the transformative power of unconditional love. By blending approachable imagery with profound themes of relational harmony, Mannan’s practice functions as a visual bridge, inviting viewers to move beyond individualism. The work seeks to restore communal bonds and encourage an openness toward others, ultimately envisioning a path toward a more harmonious and evolved collective identity.

name: Kwon Oon
bio: Kwon Oon (b. 1991) uses the image of the cloud as a metaphor for the self. Defined by formlessness, changeability, and potential, clouds become a way for the artist to reflect on the shifting nature of identity and the challenges that shape a life. Kwon’s work centers on the belief that each person carries an inner light—an enduring source of hope, resilience, and self-compassion. Rather than treating hope as an abstract ideal, the artist understands it as the ability to care for oneself, especially in moments of exhaustion and uncertainty. Through this perspective, Kwon Oon’s practice highlights the quiet strength found within the self, suggesting that the light needed to endure hardship is already present. The artist invites viewers to consider tenderness toward oneself not as weakness, but as a vital force for moving through life.

name: VanIst.
bio: VanIst. is a visual artist and storyteller whose practice brings together e-sports, contemporary visual culture, and the emotional vocabulary of Korean folk tradition. Working across illustration, exhibitions, publishing, and digital formats such as Instagram comics, she reinterprets themes like han (a deeply rooted feeling of sorrow and resilience), fate, and collective identity through a distinctly narrative lens. Her major series—including Dandelion Seeds, The Child Wearing a Ggalkkal Cone Hat, Stories on Five Roads, Before the Rabbit Grows Horns, and Even If by Chance, I Hope It Becomes Fate—translate sadness, growth, and transformation into symbolic characters and fantastical journeys. Drawing on the warmth of rural life and the atmosphere of Korean folktales, VanIst. creates contemporary fairy-tale worlds that connect memory, emotion, and imagination. More recently, she has expanded this storytelling practice through AR and metaverse-based projects that turn exhibition spaces into immersive narrative environments.

name: Yunju Park
bio:
To exist by one’s own rhythm, unshaken by the currents of the world.
I focus on an aesthetic that knows how to linger in emptiness—an attitude of accepting the flow without haste and living in harmony with nature.
Such a perspective has long permeated daily life, shaping a uniquely Korean sensibility.
The subjects in my work are reflections of our own lives and the emotions we encounter; they serve as mediums that embody our attitude toward life.

name: MO KIM
bio: Mo Kim was born in Seoul in 1980. He graduated from the Department of Sculpture at the College of Fine Arts, Seoul National University, Korea, in 2009, before earning his master's degree at Glasgow School of Art in the U.K. in 2016. Kim's works are primarily installation-based and aim to deliver an aesthetic experience by engaging audience participation. The artist delves into how the institutional mechanisms of the art scene operate, as well as the underlying value judgments inherent within such systems. He reimagines these institutional mechanisms into conditions or situations that are presented to the spectator, bringing his works of art to completion through audience interaction. These aspects of Kim's work render them as critical tools, offering diverse perspectives on the habitual functioning of the art institution. They simultaneously serve as attempts to experience the significant distance between art and everyday life.

name: Lee Eun Kyong
bio:
Lee Eun Kyong is a visual artist based in Seoul, specializing in paintings and prints. Having grown up in Senegal and begun her artistic journey in Russia, Lee has developed a keen interest in the subtle insecurities that lurk within social structures and human relationships, striving to render these underlying tensions visible in her work.
Her collection of self-portraits, executed in a variety of styles and techniques, brings to life the complex emotions she has encountered. These emotions, which elude verbal expression, range from the stark realities of life and the unspoken sensation of being marginalized to the anxiety and fear associated with coercion. Employing dramatic composition and the intricate juxtaposition of mundane subjects, her art vividly captures these experiences. Similarly, the mountains, objects, animals, and plants that populate her more recent works are not only remnants of her personal experiences of feeling excluded but also act as vessels reflecting her inner emotional landscape.

name: Unhappy Circuit
bio:
www.unhappycircuit.com 
 Unhappy Circuit is a multidisciplinary artist in Korea. His work is based on a fusion of art, science, technology and multidisciplinary perspective that encompasses linguistics, anthropology, ecology, futurology, and cosmology. The pursuit of his art is the connection between human beings and the universe. He wants to expand human perception and consciousness into the universe through his art and connect the vast universe with the meaning of our lives, minds, and existence, which are essentially finite and lonely.  He has participated in various exhibitions hosted by art institutions such as Hyundai Motor Group's ZER01NE, Asia Culture Center, Arts Council Korea, C-LAB (Taiwan), BeFantastic (India), ARCOLABS (Indonesia).

name: Jiwoo Oh
bio: Jiwoo Oh is a Korean artist born in 1995 who lives and works in Seoul, South Korea. He fully devotes his artistic career to depict sea life, especially dolphins. He participates to many art fairs in Korea. His artworks belong to many private collections in the Korean Peninsula, China and others Asian countries.

name: Dan Kim
bio: My works from 2021 to 2025 represent a Neo-Pop exploration of fine art expressed through commercial aesthetics. Drawing from the 'popular culture' of our time—specifically the Japanese manga and anime that dominated the 80s and 90s, as well as the Korean MMORPGs of the 2000s—I have transformed these commercial mediums into a 'Dungeon' teeming with monsters.

name: 이숙자 Sook-Ja Lee
bio:
Korean painter Lee Sook-ja has dedicated her life to advancing the art of traditional Korean color painting. She is known for her 'Barley Field' series, which began in the late 1970s. In these paintings, Lee encapsulates the sorrow and sentiment of the Korean people within the endlessly unfolding barley fields, a symbol of robust vitality. To complete a single painting, she has spent decades meticulously painting each barley grain and awn, often until her palms bruised, a testament to her commitment and endurance.

Her finely detailed and elegantly colored depictions of vast barley fields have consistently overwhelmed viewers with their beauty and intricacy. In the late 1980s, Lee introduced a groundbreaking concept in her 'Eve's Barley Field' series, where she portrayed Eve amidst the barley, symbolizing nature's origin and the source of life. Entering the 2000s, Lee completed monumental works showcasing Korean spirit, including themes like military horses and Mount Baekdu.

Throughout her career, Lee Suk-ja has strictly adhered to using traditional mineral pigments, a challenging medium, and refined coloring techniques to continue the legacy of Korean color painting. Her work has firmly established her as an artist who upholds the identity of Korean painting, rooted in its traditional values and authenticity.

name: Ido Park
bio:
On the boundary between reality and fiction, Park Ido surveys the universal human life patterns or circumstances around them and investigates the function of painting corresponding to them. By experimenting with a variety of painting techniques on canvas, particularly the three-dimensional and tactile texture of wax, layered and infused over oil and mixed media, he expresses complex emotions of anxiety and expectation in an autobiographical story amidst unpredictable changes of time. The actual thickness of the surface arouses a new inspiration by simulating tactile sensation and gives the fresh effect of perspective over the possibly monotonous plane. The artist metaphorises the role of the painter in the face of today's radically advanced digital technology by emphasising his physical process of artwork creation and the experiential process of viewer appreciation. 

What painters depict includes the objects per se and immaterial elements outside human visual perception, such as light, temperature, seasons, emotions and time. Thus, to transcend a thing into a theme, they tend to come up with ‘a probable phenomenal world’, where these invisible features construct themselves on a two-dimensional surface. Not only increasing a sense of abstraction, but Park Ido also embraces invisible factors, such as air density, humidity, and the intensity of radiation, in his practice to create a dreamlike ambience and depth by efficiently employing the layers caused by materialistic properties the dominant medium of this exhibition, wax. 

Park Ido (b.1983) completed a BFA in Fine Art at Ecole Nationale Supérieure d'Art et de Design de Dijon and an MFA in Fine Art at Haute école des arts du Rhin.  He had participated expositions at Chapter II (2022), Incheon Art Platform (2020), Moran Museum of Art (2018), Chang Ucchin Museum of Art (2017) and more.

name: Kang Tae Hun
bio:
www.kangtaehun.com

 Kang Tae hun is a Busan-based artist who was born in Busan, South Korea. He earned a bachelor's degree from Dongeui University, Department of Fine Art, in 2002 and received a master's degree in sculpture major in 2004. For the past two decades, Kang Tae hun has been working conceptually to reveal secret but powerful social ideologies and systems that control individual thinking and behavior. Whether it is a regional event, government system, territorial issues, or the world's economic system, he has warned of invisible power that suppresses our lives with various formative languages, such as impressive installations with symbolic objects and texts, film, and new media. Kang has been invited to many solo exhibitions where he spread his theory based on personal experiences, including (Space Bandee, 2006) that talks about totalitarianism and the system base on personal experiences,

name: KIM  JEESOO
bio: Kim Jeesoo gives expression to ‘olfactory art’ in the form of ‘synesthetic art’ that her audience can both see and sense. She showcases work that explores the origins of life, drawing on the use of smell to commune with fauna and flora alike. Kim collects the scents of diverse spaces and subjects—from old cathedrals to her father’s garden to the body odors of her acquaintances—in a sustained effort to draw on our olfactory imaginations and thereby bridge space and time and the world as perceived through the artist’s senses. Her father’s ‘study’ and ‘garden’ in particular constitute the steadiest source of Kim’s inspiration, as well as the birthplace of her olfactory practice. Kim maintains an active rapport with scientists, architects, dancers, and musicians as she communicates the scent associations of certain situations through paintings, installations, video art, and text. Kim’s published papers on her work include “A Study on the Synesthetic Expression of Smell” (Journal of Korea Society of Basic Design & Art, 2020) and “A Study on Smell, Memory, and Temporality” (Journal of Korea Society of Basic Design & Art, 2020). In 2021, the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (MMCA) selected Kim as one of the country’s representative figures in the area of ecological art, the details of which have been made available in the exhibition publication entitled The Evolution and Status of Korean Ecological Art(2021).

name: Jamsan
bio: C.V SOLO Exhibition 2026 《It’ OK》, Collast Gallery, Seoul 2025

name: Kang Soolsaeng
bio: Kang Soolsaeng, an eco-artist born in Jeju, Korea in 1970, is deeply interested in the existence of living organisms, the natural processes of nature, and the transition of artificial elements into natural ones. Recently, she has immersed herself in farming to illustrate, through her art, the intricate interconnections among a myriad of life forms. Her paintings, photography, video, and installation works depict the process of planting native seeds and harvesting the fruits in accordance with the cycles of the sun and moon. This exploration began with her eco-art project, A Child in the Island and the Ladybug (2004) and took deeper root with The Ladybug Becomes Flowers (2005). Amid the endlessly deferred end to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, she presented The Seed’s Hope, in which she counted the number of hopes contained in the seed.

name: Daum Kim
bio:
https://vimeo.com/kimdaum

  Daum Kim (b. 1983. Seoul) graduated from Kookmin University with BFA in Sculpture, and he is currently based in Seoul. Kim is interested in exploring different residues and sensations derived from places and people he encounters in his context. The artist’s practice ranges from film, sound, installation, and various other mediums. Recently, as the main caregiver of his two children, he’s been focusing on his current status and is in process of developing it into a subject matter of his practice. 
  The artist held multiple solo exhibitions including dazzled & muddled, Primary Practice, Seoul, 2023; Blind Road, Factory2, Seoul, 2019; By the Bamboo Forest, Space Willing and Dealing, Seoul, 2014; and RSVP, Art Sonje Center, Seoul, 2014. Kim took part in various group shows such as Songeun Art Award Exhibition, SongEun, Seoul, 2022; Gwangju Biennale, Imagined Borders_the Art of Survival: Assembly, Sustainability, Shift_Momentum Temporary, Asia Culture Center, Gwangju, 2018; Common Front, Affectively, Nam Jun Paik Art Center, Gyeonggi-do, 2018; Urban Ritornello, The Archive on Community, Ilmin Museum of Art, Seoul, 2017; Activating the City: Urban Gastronomy, Modern Museum of Contemporary Art, Seoul, 2016; Sound of Community, Arko Art Center, Seoul, 2015.

name: Hong  Bomi
bio: Artist Hong Bomi engages her body as a conduit for thought. It was almost predestined that she would gravitate towards drawing, which for her entails walking, as she existentially values physical movement and sensory perception. The artist navigates a complex interplay between her subjective senses and the objective world, questioning and affirming her perceptions. Hong assesses the world that she would reach through the lens of bodily sensations, memories, and pertinent information. Consequently, drawing, for the artist, is not only a record of her sensory experiences but also an encapsulation of her reflective practice concerning these sensations. In her previous works, Hong's focus on the quantitative aspects of presented images and her spatially reconstructive installation methods encourages viewers to contemplate what we ought to perceive and ponder amidst the wider spectacle of images. She has conveyed this emphasis through intensely physical performances, ceaselessly walking and physically engaging with objects. Hong continually investigates the existence and role of art in her immediate real-life surroundings, exploring physical distance, time, and emotional relationships. Hong’s art embodies the inherent destiny of drawing: a medium destined to continuously evolve from bodily-learned memories, overlaid by imagination, to an unfinished conclusion — a trait that likens drawing to a living entity. At present, the artist has ventured into media experiments, creating drawings that are incorporated into installations both inside and outside gallery spaces, as well as videos.

name: Dukhoon Gim
bio: Dukhoon Gim only uses graphite for his drawings. Gray of graphite, being the color of the mixture of all colors, represents a certain sensibility that he has on this world. In his drawings, the use of graphite can be considered an idea, material, and energy at the same time. He wants to show a "liquified" state of the world in which we live, that often feels too rigid and sharply divided due to conventional and banal ideas. His world, often feels like existing behind a veil, or a veil itself, is in flux, organically connected in one, and a constant flow of energy.

name: Louise Yang
bio:
I exist in a perpetual cycle of leaving and returning. Born on Jeju Island and now residing in Seoul, my life feels less like a settlement than a pause between movements. With my family scattered across different locations, the airport has become more than a transit hub for me; it is a poignant space of temporary reunion and inevitable separation. Here, profound sadness often precedes excitement, for to leave is always to leave something behind.

Amidst crowds of returning travelers, I often stand on the side of waiting or saying goodbye, observing an unnameable solitude. The humid wind, the horizon-bound runway, and the blue island seen from a window seat linger in my memory. Jeju remains a place of eternal return and departure, its atmosphere permeating my canvas.

My Passenger series captures these ordinary yet difficult-to-articulate moments of parting. These paintings are not about destinations, but about the transient intersections of relationships and the deferred emotions of meeting and separation. I depict the scenery of the "in-between"—a state of never fully arriving and never completely leaving.

name: Hee Bae
bio:
Hee Bae (born South Korea) is a painter whose work combines drawing and painting to explore personal narratives shaped by movement between Korea, the United States, and India. Working in abstract compositions, Bae transforms forms inspired by flora, fauna, and landscape into fields of vibrant color and rhythmic shapes. Her practice reflects shifting perceptions of place and memory, translating lived experiences across different cultural and geographic contexts. Experiences in India have been particularly influential, inspiring atmospheric imagery that evokes clouds, wind, rain, and changing light.

Bae received an MFA in Painting from the San Francisco Art Institute and a BFA from Korea University. Her work has been presented in solo exhibitions in Seoul and Incheon, and in group exhibitions across Korea, India, Europe, and the United States. Her works are held in collections including the Art Bank of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea.

name: Eunjoo Choi
bio: Eunjoo Choi paints landscapes that move between memory, perception, and imagination. Her practice began with Serendipity and Cloud, a series inspired by a moment during travel when a familiar view became strangely unfamiliar as a large cloud passed overhead. Since then, she has layered elements such as clouds, stars, the moon, and wind onto observed scenery, creating spaces where reality and unreality quietly intersect. This approach extends into her more recent series, Traces of Bloom, which records fleeting changes in flowers and the lingering emotions they leave behind. In her recent works, Choi simplifies form and intensifies color to emphasize emotional resonance over description. Ambiguous floral shapes and vivid, sometimes unreal hues allow her landscapes to hold traces of passing moments while inviting viewers to re-experience them through their own memories and sensibilities.

name: Taeseok Ju 주태석
bio:
Taeseok Ju does not seek to depict trees merely as representations of trees, but rather strives to express their essence. This approach makes his work more object-like than purely painterly. His highly realistic technique supports this perspective, revealing the subject with direct and unfiltered clarity. This method extends from his earlier Rail Series, where bold cropping and tense angles closely align with the close-up perspectives in his Tree Series.
Ju is an artist shaped by the era of hyperrealism, trained in a visually rigorous, emotionally detached methodology. His artistic stance—portraying trees purely as trees—originates from this disciplined framework. However, his recent work introduces a dual structure that transcends cold logic, moving toward a contemplative realm of silence and meditation. Rather than mechanical detachment, his trees open a quiet, introspective space, enveloping the viewer in a world of reflection.
The question, “Why trees?” finds its answer in this meditative context. Trees evoke the primal essence of nature—perhaps more than any other subject. In a landscape dominated by concrete, trees remain as the last link to raw, unfiltered nature. The choice of trees is not arbitrary; rather, it is a deeply necessary response.
Taeseok Ju’s works are both philosophical and primal. While rooted in fundamental artistic inquiries about the relationship between image and reality, his approach—seeing and shaping the world through trees—embodies a natural, organic sensibility. His trees serve as gateways to contemplation.

This passage is an excerpt from the preface written by art critic Kwang-soo Oh

name: Youyoung Oh
bio: Youyoung Oh (b. 1986) paints to share the images she holds in her mind. She hopes that every living being in this world can move freely—able to choose for themselves and experience life on their own terms. At its core, her practice is a quiet wish for freedom: that everyone, and everything, can be free.

name: Son Hyunseon
bio: Son Hyunseon (b. 1987) lives and works in Seoul, and studied a BFA and MFA of Fine Arts at the School of Visual Arts, Korea National University of Arts. Exploring the (im)possibility of representation through the act of painting, Son’s practice engages not only with the cognitive experience but also the corporal relationship with the environment within which her subjects are surrounded by. She rigorously studies color and shape and ultimately liberates these elements into a mental space where the concrete information is missing while the pictorial experience is immersing. In search of the afterimage beyond the superficial imagery, her artistic investigation continues to interrelate the different awareness of bodies, perceptual capabilities, and our mental and physical constraints.

name: Jungin Kim
bio:
www.kimjungin.com

Jungin Kim, born in 1991, completed his undergraduate studies at Mokwon University’s Department of Painting, then proceeded to earn both his master’s and doctoral degrees from Hongik University’s Department of Painting. Kim focuses on rapidly changing paradigms and the power structures that govern them and provides a critical viewpoint towards the system’s unilateral compulsion for acceptance imposed through marginalization in cultural and social domains. The perspective gradually deepened and triggered the artist to seek painting practices as a countermeasure against the progressive power. In pursuit of this goal, Kim constructs certain solidarity on his canvas using temporality of slow painting, neglected objects and forsaken places, or image aspects of distant memories. He then disrupts straightforward comprehension by fragmenting the viewer's visual perception. Through this, he presents a critical perspective and sociological attitude to the audience.

name: PARK  KWANG-SUN
bio:
Park Kwang-sun is a graduate of the Department of Painting at the Chugye University for the Arts. He has held solo exhibitions at Artertain and Artnoid178 and participated in numerous group exhibitions at the Yeongdeungpo Cultural Foundation, Sejong Center, Gallery Gwak, Artertain, Artnoid178, and Studio126. He has been an artist in residence at the Hue+ Network Art Studio since 2019.
  Park paints portraits—or rather, he blots them out. His portraits on plywood permeate the distinctive roughness and desiccation of their surfaces as soon as they are drawn. The artist&s gaze lingers on plywood (abandoned plywood, at that), canvas as of yet striking him as an overly sleek form of material. Virtually the only backdrop that Park has chosen to use since his early years, plywood is here taken as an entity of devotion and self-sacrifice, employed and cast aside at the whims of some sort of utility and yet reluctant to put itself forward and instead keeping itself hidden. Park tears away the edges of the plywood to give it a human outline and proceeds to paint on it portraits of himself, his closest acquaintances, and his family members. These individuals surface after having churned their way through through the artist&s memories before they once again submerge, wordlessly obscuring their bodies and slowly dissipating from view. By enshrouding or blotting out the persons whom he portrays, the artist himself thus undoes the traces of the loss and desolation which derive from the rift between reality and recollection.

name: Uni Hyomin
bio: Uni Hyomin creates paintings centered on “Uni,” a furry monster that serves as both a character and an alter ego for the artist’s emotions and narratives. Through Uni, the artist gives visual form to imagination, play, and layered messages that are often difficult to express directly in everyday life. The motif of fur suggests a being that is easily shaped and affected by its surroundings. At the same time, Uni’s soft and approachable exterior conceals an interior that remains uncertain and unreadable. This tension between what is visible and hidden reflects the social masks people wear. Drawing on the fear of others, as well as the awareness that the self can also become a source of fear, Uni Hyomin presents the monster as a figure where vulnerability and threat coexist.

name: Heyo Lee
bio:
Heyo (b. 1983, Jeju, South Korea) is a painter based on the island of Jeju, where he paints every day. Working in acrylic on linen, his practice moves fluidly between portrait, landscape, and still life — treating every element on the canvas as an object, arranged like props on a quietly theatrical stage.

Since 2024 he has been exploring still life with fresh curiosity, experimenting with ways to bring figures and landscape elements together as if they were objects — creating scenes that feel at once composed and alive. His ambition is to blur the traditional boundaries of painting, collapsing its biggest genres into a single frame.

name: E.SUN
bio:
My work navigates the ambiguous boundaries between dream and reality, consciousness and the unconscious, utilizing the elephant as a primary alter ego. Rather than depicting the human figure directly, I project deep-seated emotions onto the elephant—a creature symbolizing memory, resilience, and the silent bearing of weight.

In my paintings, the elephant is not merely an animal but a vessel for grief, longing, and the will to move forward. Specifically, the "Pink Elephant" serves as a visceral manifestation of my inner self. The intense, searing pink I employ is not a color of softness, but a conduit for confronting unbearable emotions and trauma. It represents an energy of resilience that pushes against sorrow.

I define my artistic realm as an "Eternal Dream"—not a fleeting image during sleep, but a continuous, essential layer of existence that intertwines with reality. Through a theatrical mise-en-scène and high-saturation colors, I construct a psychological landscape. Here, traditional symbols of longevity (reinterpreted from Shipjangsaengdo) appear: the Baobab represents memory, the Black Leopard symbolizes anxiety, and the Blue Bird signifies liberation.

Recently, my practice has evolved into "Now, Dream," where I blur and fade forms to defamiliarize these subjects. By rendering the elephant faint and ephemeral, I invite the viewer into a forest of the unconscious—a surreal space where past wounds and future hopes coexist. Ultimately, my work is a journey of reconciling with the present, offering a visual meditation on the resilience of life.

name: Hyunjee Kim
bio: Hyunjee Kim (b. 1983) is a contemporary abstract painter who captures the flow of life and the vibration of light through a distinct pictorial rhythm. Working with repeated pulses of color and form, Kim visualizes the energy of nature and living systems—translating movement, breath, and radiance into layered, resonant compositions.

name: Kim Yeonok
bio:
Artist Yeonok Kim(1960~) is a well establish artist who is active in the Korean art market. Her works are in the archives of Korean Modern Arts Museum and Inchon Cultural Foundation. 
She started painting the moon jar which not only looks like a full moon, it  is symbolic of bringing and holding good luck and fortune for the family. Being a 2nd generation artist, her father was a ceramist so the art and moon jar has always been part of her life. 

Moon jars are also known as baekja in Korean. They are characterized by the beauty of modest forms, and minimal use of color, which conveyed the ideals of Korean Confucian state, that was preeminent at the time. The inimitably unique beauty of Korean culture came to be mirrored in baekja and gradually diversification in color and design became shared by both the court and the common people.

Bringing peace and serenity to the mind & the soul, her paintings will withstand the test of time during these busy modern days.

name: Fi Jae Lee
bio:
Fi Jae Lee (b. 1981) graduated from a BFA and a MFA in Art and Technology Studies at School of the Art Institute of Chicago. She has been living and working in Korea and abroad. Starting with the first solo exhibition early in 1997, the artist has participated in fifteen solo exhibitions so far recently including "Phanerozoic Eon, Cenozoic Era, Leeficene (Lotte Avenuel Art Hall 2019)"; "Enshrine our Woman Ancestors' Tablets (Zaha Museum of Art, 2018)"; "Finimism, Fnosticism (Artplace, 2018)" as well as a number of group exhibitions. She was granted with Arko Young Art Frontier Grant by Art Council Korea in 2009 and selected for Goyang Art Residency, MMCA in 2011, Nanji Residency, Seoul Art Museum of Art in 2014 and BilbaoArte Residency,Fundación Bilbaoarte Fundazioa in 2017.

Contemplating on the question 'who am I', Fi Jae Lee works with varied mediums including painting, sculpture, performance, and installation. Her works are based on her daily journal and drawings and focus on her own daily experience as well as relationships between the self-the other, material-society-artwork, and so on. The works are embodiments of the artist's life stories experienced with the feminine identity and cross between her daily life and imagined world. In her delicate painting, which remind of lines and colors of Buddhist paintings from the Goryeo Dynasty, a female figure and its surroundings are placed upon altar, retaining the sense of feminine holiness.

name: Juhee Lee
bio: The artist paints a fleeting moment that feels unfamiliar and special in the gaps between objects and spaces that pass by in common daily life. The artist's tree paintings, which have continued to work with trees as the foundation, started with healing their own inner problems. She receives a lot of comfort from seeing a tree that heals itself even after being scratched and keeps its place silently. You can feel the lyrical atmosphere through the branches and leaves expressed by layering colored pigments between the paper cut out in the shape of leaves. Furthermore, the artist carries out paper-cutting work that cuts out the landscape with a sharp blade, keeping in mind the landscape and atmosphere of the day. It is a useful tool for reinvention.

name: Hyeonji Do
bio: My work begins with the question of how invisible experiences—memory and emotion—can be revealed through painting. Although the flow of emotion cannot be seen, it is summoned and structured on the surface through repeated layers of lines, colors, and light. This process is an act of recalling memory within the sensations of the present and reinterpreting it anew. For me, subjects such as waves, light, and ripples exist as independent forms that intertwine to create a single world. Within them, I discover an organic connection between relationships, emotions, and memories.

name: Kyu-Hak Lee
bio:
Over a period of a decade, South Korean artist Kyu-Hak Lee has immersed himself in recreating paintings by Van Gogh in a distinctive method of mixed-media mosaic, which involves using Polystyrene foam, or Styrofoam strips as building blocks of his paintings. These constituents are wrapped in magazine and newspaper, which are then covered by a layer of hanji, traditional handmade Korean paper. The components adhere to one another on the canvas creating a mosaic-like assemblage that very much resembles the visible brushstrokes of Van Gogh. 

Lee’s unconventional artistic approach is a social commentary on consumerism of modern civilization, and questions the intrinsic values of the millennial era. Using everyday materials as a gesture of upcycling, Lee uses Styrofoam as the base of his material as it best represents the vanity of contemporary culture. Styrofoam, whose fragility and flammability are subject to transience, is simultaneously non-biodegradable like plastic. The translucency of hanji wrapped over the layer of magazine and newspaper represents a reflection on human involvement in the world through the eyes of tradition, and the torn publications show letters and writing have lost their purpose as the fundamental tool for shaping tradition and modern society.
